task: Each item is the BACKGROUND section of a public EEOC appellate decision (never its analysis or order). Flag the decisions whose agency decision was not affirmed. Outcomes are given for the development split; tools must be fixed before scoring the test split.

development.background: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Transportation Security Officer (TSO), 1802, G Band, at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SeaTac) in SeaTac, Washington. Complainant is a Caucasian male, and he was born in 1949. He identified his religion as Christian. In early to mid-January of 2017, Complainant was talking to a TSO (C1) in the Control Room. C1 is an African-American male, he stated that he was 51 years old in 2017, and he identified his religion as Muslim. A Lead TSO (C2) stated that he overheard part of the conversation between Complainant and C1. C2 is a Caucasian male, he stated that he was 59 years old in 2017, and he identified his religion as “no denomination.” Report of Investigation (ROI) at 85. In his investigative affidavit C1 stated that, in January 2017, Complainant called President Obama a Muslim and that he responded by asking what was wrong with Muslim and whether Complainant planned to “lock [him] up” because he was Muslim. ROI at 80. According to C1, Complainant said that he would not lock C1 up but that he “would put [C1’s] wife’s ass in jail.” Id. C1 averred that he told Complainant that his wife was an American citizen but that Complainant responded, “I do not care. They are all Muslim so they should be locked up.” ROI at 81. C1 stated that Complainant cited the internment of Japanese Americans after the bombing of Pearl Harbor as precedent for “locking up” Muslims in the United States. Id. C1 denied referring to Complainant as a bigot or as a racist, and he stated that he did not report this conversation with Complainant to management. On January 21, 2017, Complainant provided a written statement to a Supervisory TSO (S1; 40- year-old Caucasian female, not religious) about his discussion with C1. 2 In his written statement, Complainant stated that C1 asked him if he was “a bigot and a racist like Donald Trump” and whether Complainant was going to “lock [C1] up” because he was Muslim. ROI at 63. According to Complainant, he said he would not lock C1 up because he was “a federal employee, a law abiding citizen and a contributing member of society.” Id. Complainant averred that C1 asked him whether he would lock up his wife, who was also Muslim, and that he responded by asking C1 whether his wife was born in the United States. Complainant alleged that C1 did not answer, so he said, “Well, in that case, your wife is a Muslim and we do not know where she came from. Lock her up.” Id. Complainant stated that C1 told him that he was a bigot and a racist and that he responded to C1, “Lock them all up. There is a precedent for this in America’s history. During WWII we inter[n]ed Japanese-Americans after the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor.” Id. Complainant concluded by stating that wanting to lock up Muslims “whose origins are unknown” does not make him a bigot or a racist and that, if C1 did not “want to hear the response,” he should not have asked Complainant that question. Id. On January 24, 2017, Complainant submitted another written statement to S1. He stated that he had known C1 for almost 13 years and that they were friendly with each other to the point that they exchanged gifts, and he described an interaction with C1 in 2016. According to Complainant, sometime in 2016 he asked C1 if he was sensitive and C1 responded that he was not sensitive and that Complainant was a bigot and racist. Complainant accused C1 of calling him a bigot and a racist behind his back for approximately a year. Complainant denied that he was a racist or a bigot, and he alleged that C1’s accusation was based on these factors: “that I am white, that I am male, that I am old, and that I am a Republican.” ROI at 64. The EEO Investigator requested that Complainant answer questions in a sworn affidavit, but Complainant did not answer the majority of the questions and attached written statements instead. Complainant stated that C1 accusing him of being racist and a bigot was insulting, bullying, intimidating, and threatening. In his rebuttal affidavit, Complainant characterized his January 24, 2017, statement as a “complaint of harassment” that was ignored by management. ROI at 74. In his investigative affidavit, C2 stated that he overheard part of a conversation between Complainant and C1 in January 2017. According to C2, “[Complainant] mentioned shooting Muslims if they are coming to the U.S. to shoot Americans. [Complainant] said all Muslims should be locked up, including [C1]’s wife.” ROI at 85. C2 averred that C1 called Complainant “an angry old man,” but he denied hearing C1 refer to Complainant as racist or a bigot. Id. A Transportation Security Manager (S2; 58-year-old Caucasian male, did not identify religion) stated that he heard through the grapevine that Complainant had been discussing religion and stated that C1’s wife should be “locked up” if the government could not identify where she was from because she was Muslim. ROI at 98-99. S2 averred that he investigated the matter and determined that Complainant had been making inappropriate comments about religion. According to S2, he decided to issue Complainant a non-disciplinary Letter of Counseling (LOC) because he had no disciplinary history and because there were no aggravating factors under the Agency’s table of penalties. On March 6, 2017, S2 issued Complainant a LOC for Failure to Follow Regulation. S2 stated that Complainant’s January 2017 conversation with another TSO about confining Muslims in the United States if the government could not confirm their origins, including the wife of the TSO he was talking to, violated the Agency’s Employee Code of Conduct. S2 referenced Complainant’s written statement, “your wife is a Muslim and we do not know where she came from. Lock her up.” S2 averred that this was an inappropriate comment and that Complainant should refrain from making offensive comments about religion and other protected categories in the workplace. S2 noted that, although the LOC was not disciplinary and would not be placed in his Official Personnel File (OPF), future misconduct could result in disciplinary action. The record contains a March 17, 2017, email from Complainant to S1 with the subject line “EEO Complaint.” Complainant wrote: Because management has refused to address my EEO complaint, others have become emboldened to taunt and bully. Instead management decided to retaliate against me for speaking up. Evidently, if you are male, white or a senior you are expected to suffer a hostile work environment in silence. However, working under these conditions has begun to affect my health. I am unable to sleep at night, my work performance has suffered because of an inability to focus or concentrate while performing work assignments and I have serious concerns about my personal safety at work and away. ROI at 68. S1 stated that she forwarded Complainant’s email up the chain of command. Complainant stated that because management was not supporting him, “it became necessary for me to take personal action to protect myself,” so in March 2017 he contacted Agency Headquarters in Virginia and requested that his retirement be expedited so he could “get out of SEATAC as soon as” possible. ROI at 73. According to the record, March 18, 2017, was the effective date of Complainant’s retirement. ROI at 149-50. The record contains an April 2, 2017, letter from Complainant to the Commission, alleging that he was retaliated against for providing statements about his conversation with C1. According to Complainant, when S2 gave him the LOC he said that “two others would be receiving disciplinary action also.” ROI at 69. Complainant stated that he “was the only one disciplined. Id. Complainant averred that the Agency was more interested in political correctness than “determining the truth.” Id. Complainant alleged that he was “forced into retirement against [his] wishes” because he had to “physically remove” himself from the Agency and the SeaTac Airport for his “personal safety and well-being.” Id. On June 10, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (Caucasian), sex (male), religion (Christian), age (68 years old), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (opposition to alleged discrimination) when: 1. In January 2017, C1 accused Complainant of being a bigot and a racist; 2. On March 6, 2017, Complainant received a LOC; and 3. In March 2017, Complainant was forced to retire early, which allegedly constituted a constructive discharge. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Mail Handler at the Agency’s Kansas City Processing and Distribution Center (P&DC) in Kansas City, Missouri. In a formal complaint (complaint number 1E-641-0015-15) filed on June 22, 2015, and subsequently amended, Complainant alleged that the Agency discriminated against her and subjected her to a hostile work environment. The Agency defined the accepted allegations as follows: (1) whether the Agency subjected Complainant to a hostile work environment on the bases of race (African American), sex (female), age (47), and reprisal for protected EEO activity when on February 20, 2015, she was sexually harassed by a co-worker against whom she had filed sexual-harassment charges in the past and, when she reported the matter to management, they failed to take her seriously; (2) whether the Agency discriminated against Complainant in reprisal for protected EEO activity when, on June 20, 2015,2 and thereafter, she was harassed by a co- worker; and (3) whether the Agency discriminated against Complainant in reprisal for protected EEO activity when, on June 23, 2015, and ongoing, her supervisor harassed and disrespected her. On June 14, 2012, Complainant filed a prior EEO complaint alleging, among other things, that a co-worker (CW1) sexually harassed her. She and the Agency settled the complaint on December 5, 2013. By memorandum dated October 4, 2014, the Agency’s Operations Support Specialist notified Complainant that the Agency would abolish her job effective October 18, 2014, because the Agency was relocating an “APPS machine” to a different facility. The Specialist stated that the Agency would reassign Complainant to an unassigned regular position and encouraged her to bid on vacant duty assignments. Complainant subsequently bid for and received a job on Tour 3. In her affidavit, Complainant stated that, on February 20, 2015, she and a co-worker (CW2) were at a vending machine in the break room. She alleged, “We were at the vending machine when I felt someone come up on me very close and stand extremely close to me from the side. So close he was breathing on my neck. When I turned around he walked away [and] it was” CW1. She started to cry and “immediately left the break room and went to the union office.” In a handwritten, signed statement that Complainant submitted with her affidavit, CW2 stated that CW1 “walked on the side of [Complainant,] which caught her off guard,” that Complainant “became very nervous,” and that CW2 “left right afterwards.” Complainant asserted that she tried to report the incident to the Labor Relations Manager (LRM), but he “brushed her off” and told her to tell her supervisor. She also asserted that she tried to report it to a Labor Relations Specialist who was serving as her supervisor (LRS), but he told her to tell her supervisor and to “put it in writing.” Complainant stated in her affidavit that the incident occurred on June 10, 2015. She stated that she reported the incident to the Acting Manager of Operations (AMO1) the next day. According to Complainant, AMO1 subsequently told her that CW1’s supervisor would inform CW1 of the Agency’s zero-tolerance policy and would direct CW1 to stay away from Complainant. She stated that she submitted a written statement regarding the alleged harassment on February 24, 2015. Complainant contended that management did not take immediate action after she reported the alleged harassment. According to Complainant, the Acting Lead Manager of Distribution Operations (MDO) informed her on April 9, 2015, that he had told CW1 to stay away from her. She also contended that, although the harassment does not occur every day and does not involve sexual harassment, CW1 “intimidates” and “antagonizes” her by going to her work area “as often as he can.” In addition, she alleged that management subjected her to a hostile work environment because she reported the harassment. Complainant asserted, “Management did not listen to me and then started harassing me more.” She alleged that the Agency discriminated against her because she is “an older African American woman,” that management did not take her seriously because she is African American, that management is “male dominated,” and that “all of the managers” were aware of her prior EEO activity. Complainant stated that, after management abolished her Tour 2 “bid job,” she bid for a job on Tour 3, which was the tour that CW1 worked. Complainant argued that management should have permitted her to remain on Tour 2. She asserted that the Agency treated four named employees more favorably than it treated her by granting their requests for schedule changes. She contended that the Agency separated other employees because of altercations, argued that the Agency should have separated her from CW1, and alleged that the Agency would have done so if she had been a white woman. Complainant asserted that, on June 10, 2015, CW1 drove power equipment in her work area, stared at her, and made faces. She stated that she informed LRS, but “nothing was done.” Complainant also asserted that CW1 again drove power equipment in her work area on June 30, 2015. She stated that she reported the matter to an Acting Supervisor (AS), who told her that CW1 had claimed that he could go into her work area if he was being watched. According to Complainant, AS later told her that CW1 had been told not to go to the area and had lied to AS. Further, according to Complainant, a union representative told her that CW1’s supervisor (S1) had told CW1 not to go to Complainant’s work area, that S1 and an Acting Manager of Operations (AMO2) spoke to CW1, and that CW1 left work. Complainant stated that she attached a copy of her written statement to her affidavit. The record contains approximately 75 pages of documents attached to Complainant’s affidavit. None of them is dated February 24, 2015. According to the EEO Investigator, the Investigator “was notified by management that the IMIP [Initial Management Inquiry Process] inquiry had not been completed by the time this investigation was conducted. Therefore, any documentation submitted by the Complainant regarding this inquiry will not be included in this report.” Complainant stated that two named individuals conducted an “inquiry of incidents” on June 16, 2015, and that she told them that she opposed discrimination. She asserted, “I have been working the day shift since May 2014 with only two incidents from [CW1] and things had been good until he saw me on the first floor in the break room on February 20, 2015.” Complainant alleged that CW1 continues to harass and intimidate her “whenever he gets a chance.” Complainant further alleged that, on June 23, 2015, LRS yelled at her on the workroom floor, “timed [her] out,” and required her to use sick leave. She stated that she asked to change her break and lunch times, which were scheduled for three and six hours after her 5:00 p.m. arrival at work, to 7:00 p.m. and 9:00 p.m. According to Complainant, LRS became upset, asked if she was requesting preferential treatment, refused her request, and told her that everyone took breaks at the same time. Complainant asserted that LRS became angry, talked loudly, yelled and waved his hands around, told her to get to work, called her “Ma’am,” and refused her request to call her by her name. She also asserted that he spoke so loudly that other employees stopped working and looked at them. She stated that she told LRS that her arms hurt and that he told her to have a doctor fill out a light-duty request, placed her off work, and charged her 7. hours of sick leave. In his affidavit, the MDO stated that he learned of the February 20, 2015, incident approximately one week after it occurred and that he interviewed CW1. According to the MDO, CW1 stated that he stood in line behind Complainant at the vending machine and that, when Complainant noticed him behind her, “she changed the look on her face,” as if he had startled her. CW1 denied breathing on Complainant’s neck and accused her of harassing him. The MDO stated that he “put [CW1] on notice and told him to stay away from” Complainant. He did not “call in a sexual harassment team for further investigation of the matter” because he determined that the incident did not involve sexual harassment. The MDO, who acknowledged that he did not inform Complainant of the results of his investigation “immediately,” stated that he met with Complainant in April 2015. He asserted that there were “no other issues until Complainant chose a job on the 1st floor” in May or June 2015. He stated that Complainant could not remain on Tour 2 because she was not the senior bidder. He believed that he became aware of Complainant’s prior EEO activity when he learned of the February 2015 incident. LRS stated that he was aware of a complaint that Complainant made against another employee. He did not witness CW1 driving equipment near Complainant and staring or making faces at her. He asserted that, when Complainant told him that CW1 was driving in her work area, he told S1 that CW1 should not be driving in the area. According to LRS, S1 “was not aware of the situation between the complainant and [CW1] and agreed to address it with him.” In his initial affidavit, LRS asserted that not all employees under his supervision took breaks at the same time and that he did “not recall exactly what occurred” when Complainant asked him about her break and lunch schedule. In his supplemental affidavit, he asserted that he had “a matter-of-fact conversation, devoid of any emotion or passion, about the break schedule with complainant” and that employees who begin their tours at the same time have the same break schedules. He further asserted that, on June 23, 2015, he “timed out [Complainant] upon her request.” LRS confirmed that he called Complainant “Ma’am.” He denied that he was loud or unreasonable when speaking with Complainant on June 23, 2015. On September 14, 2015, at the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. On December 8, 2015, Complainant filed a second EEO complaint (complaint number 1E-641- 0033-15). She alleged that CW1 continued to harass her and that two investigators who interviewed her in August 2015 told her that she was harassing her co-worker. She also alleged that she met with the Labor Relations Manager and the Senior Plant Manager on August 26, 2015, and they offered her a transfer that would result in a loss of seniority. The Agency defined the complaint as alleging that the Agency subjected Complainant to a hostile work environment based on race, color, sex, age, and reprisal for protected EEO activity when: (4) after February 20, 2015, she was sexually harassed by a co-worker and management failed to investigate properly or take steps to stop the harassment. In a December 28, 2015, Motion to Consolidate Claims, the Agency asked the EEOC AJ to consolidate the pending complaint (number 1E-641-0015-15) with the December 2015 complaint (number 1E-641-0033-15). The Agency noted that, in the new complaint, Complainant alleged that two investigators who interviewed her in August 2015 told her that she was harassing her co- worker. The Agency also noted that Complainant alleged that she met with the Labor Relations Manager and the Senior Plant Manager on August 26, 2015, and they offered her a transfer that would result in a loss of seniority. The Agency argued that the two complaints “are sufficiently similar to warrant consolidation” and that consolidation of the complaints would conserve resources. In addition, noting that discovery had begun in the first complaint, the Agency contended that the issues in the second complaint “could be developed sufficiently without the need for an independent Report of Investigation.” On January 12, 2016, the Agency issued a final decision dismissing complaint number 1E-641- 0033-15 (claim (4)) pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(1) on the ground that it stated the same claim as complaint number 1E-641-0015-15. The Agency stated, “The fact that you provide different communications that have occurred since then does not raise a new complaint, but rather are facts which are inexorably intertwined with the issues in your June 22, 2015, complaint.” Noting that Complainant’s prior complaint was pending a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge, the Agency concluded that Complainant’s “allegations that management failed to properly investigate or did not take appropriate actions to abate [her] concerns are inexorably intertwined with this prior complaint, and now, only the judge assigned to said complaint can rule on those matters.” By order dated March 19, 2018, the AJ granted the Motion to Consolidate the complaints. On April 12, 2018, Complainant withdrew her hearing request. By order dated April 16, 2018, the AJ dismissed Complainant’s hearing request and remanded the case to the Agency for the issuance of a final decision. Final Agency Decision The Agency issued a “Final Agency Decision -- Consolidated Case” on June 7, 2018. The Agency found that it properly dismissed claim (4), and it “endorsed and incorporated by reference” its January 12, 2016, decision. Further, the Agency concluded that Complainant established prima facie cases of reprisal with respect to claims (1), (2), and (3). The Agency also concluded, however, that Complainant did not establish her hostile-work-environment claim. In that regard, the Agency found that Complainant did not establish that the incidents at issue were based on her protected status. The Agency determined that there was no evidence that management officials singled out Complainant or treated her unfairly due to her protected classes. Instead, according to the Agency, “the record is clear that various management officials listened to her complaint, told her to write down her contentions, spoke with [CW1], followed up with his manager to ensure that he was informed that his actions were not appropriate, and warned him to stay away from her.” With respect to claim (1), the Agency found that the employees who Complainant alleged received more favorable treatment were not similarly situated to her or were not treated better under similar circumstances. With respect to claims (2) and (3), the Agency found no basis from which to infer that discriminatory or retaliatory animus motivated management’s actions. The Agency further found that the incidents at issue were not sufficiently severe or pervasive to create an abusive or hostile environment. It stated that “Complainant largely complains of isolated incidents, such as one incident when [CW1] stood next to her, one time when he came into her work area, and one day when she was allegedly sent home early and charged with sick leave.” In addition, the Agency found that there was no basis for imputing liability to the Agency. Finally, the Agency found that Complainant did not establish her claim of sexual harassment with respect to claim (1). The Agency concluded that Complainant did not show that CW1’s actions on February 20, 2015, were of a sexual nature or were based on her sex. The Agency further concluded that Complainant did not demonstrate that CW1’s actions on that date were sufficiently severe or pervasive to constitute harassment. Noting that the parties settled Complainant’s 2012 EEO complaint, the Agency stated that there was no evidence in the current record that the alleged prior harassment actually occurred or that CW1’s conduct on February 20, 2015, “was similar to a prior act of a sexual nature, such that an inference of an unwelcome sexual advance is warranted.” The Agency ruled that there was no basis for imputing liability to the Agency and that Complainant did not prove that the Agency had discriminated against her as alleged.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Reader Assistant, GS-5 at the Agency’s Region V facility in Columbus, Ohio. On August 15, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of age (48) and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when her two- year limited appointment as a Reader Assistant was terminated on May 17, 2017. Complainant was responsible for, inter alia, reading and assisting C1, an Agency employee who was blind. Complainant was hired on a time-limited appointment (2 years) with a service compensation date of March 30, 2003. The Agency extended the appointment six (6) times between 2003 and 2016; the last extension was on April 18, 2016. Complainant worked as a Reader Assistant for C1 for 14 years prior to her termination. Complainant’s first level supervisor was the Assistant Manager (RMO1). The District Manager (RMO2) served as Complainant’s second level supervisor. Complainant stated that management was aware of her age due to its accessibility to her personnel documents. She also recalled that RMO2, and she had discussions regarding her adult children, and RMO2 was present when she received a birthday card from all the staff. Complainant stated that, on May 3, 2017, she was notified that her employment with the Agency would be terminated, effective May 17, 2017. She stated that RMO2 was responsible for her termination. She further stated that RMO1 informed her that she was being terminated for telling a non-governmental employee that the Agency “had bed bugs,” and because C1 was not getting along with her and no longer wanted her as his Reader. Complainant stated that she received a notice informing her that the termination was based on her failure to follow Agency policy regarding treating other employees with courtesy and respect. The notice also indicated that management had had several prior discussions with Complainant on the “expectation of professional and courteous behavior towards co-workers.” Complainant further stated that RMO1 informed the EEO counselor that there were also problems with her work. Complainant asserted that she discussed the bed bug problem with a friend, but, according to Complainant, this was not a ground for dismissal. Complainant contended that she was a good employee who would do additional work. She stated that she received good performance evaluations, and a rating of “Successful Contribution” in all categories of her 2016 evaluation regarding interpersonal skills; specifically, participation in “demonstrating job knowledge and maintaining generally positive and productive working relationships within the office.” Complainant stated that her age was a factor in her termination because during the fourteen (14) years, she worked with the Agency, she was not allowed to apply for any internal jobs unless they were also open to the public. She stated that RMO2 treated younger employees more favorably than the older employees. She also stated that several employees were very disrespectful towards employees with disabilities, yet management took no action. RMO1 stated that Complainant’s two-year appointment with the Agency was terminated because she failed to communicate with C1 in a professional manner and that her services were no longer meeting RMO1’s needs. RMO1 further stated that she had received “numerous” complaints regarding Complainant’s conduct, work performance and work ethic. RMO1 stated that she had discussed these concerns with Complainant during the midterm evaluation. RMO1 specifically discussed with Complainant the “negative impact of communicating about assigned work through emails only, as opposed to reading the paperwork to C1.” She also discussed the need for Complainant to pay attention to her spelling and grammar in order to improve her writing skills. RMO1 denied that age was a factor in the decision to terminate Complainant. RMO1 noted that Complainant’s contract provided that she could be terminated if her services were not acceptable to C1 or the assigned component. RMO2 stated that C1 met with her and described his frustration with Complainant. He and Complainant had four to six outbursts between June 2015 through May 2017. An example included the statements concerning Complainant’s discussion of the bed bugs. Management spoke with both C1 and Complainant regarding a lack of professionalism in their communications. RMO2 testified that she decided that termination was appropriate since Complainant’s services were no longer acceptable to C1. RMO2 denied that age was a factor in her decision. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge. When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Program Analyst, GS-13, at the Agency’s Office of Language Services in Washington, D.C. motion in Complainant’s neck, right arm, and hand. Complainant stated that she also has a lumbar disc condition, which causes pain and difficulty with weightbearing on her lower extremity. In her formal complaint, Complainant stated that she requested ergonomic office equipment in 2014, which was not approved until July 2016. Complainant asserted that during the wait for reasonable accommodation, a car accident aggravated her condition in 2015. Complainant contended that the two-year delay in providing an accommodation caused her condition to deteriorate and worsened her mobility. Complainant averred that during this period, her job responsibilities eroded. Complainant stated that on October 5, 2017, she experienced a medical emergency at work and required assistance from two nurses from the medical unit until she was taken to the hospital via ambulance. Complainant asserted that she was diagnosed with non-small cell adenoid carcinoma of the right lung at the hospital. Complainant noted that when she returned to work, she informed management officials of her diagnosis; that she fatigued easily; and that she had difficulty breathing in specific environments. Complainant stated that on October 17, 2017, the fire alarm sounded, and employees were directed to exit the building. Complainant asserted that she did not evacuate the building because she did not believe she could descend 14 flights of stairs with dozens of employees evacuating at the same time. Complainant stated that a colleague informed her that another employee with a medical condition was notified when a drill was to be conducted to avoid stress over whether there was a need to evacuate. EEO Complaint On March 20, 2017 (and later amended), Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of disability (physical), age (DOB: 1950), and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity arising under Title VII when: 1. Between 2014 and August 2016, her requests for reasonable accommodation were denied; 2. In 2015, her duties were reduced; 3. She was subjected to a hostile work environment characterized by, but not limited to, dismissive comments, isolation, management not acknowledging her accomplishments, and the removal of personal items from her office; 2 and 4. She was denied reasonable accommodation on October 17, 2017. In her affidavit, Complainant maintained that dismissive comments, isolation, management not acknowledging her accomplishments, and the removal of personal items from her office did not constitute the basis of her claims. Report of Investigation, at 81-82. On April 17, 2017, the Agency dismissed claims (1) and (2) for untimely EEO Counselor contact. The Agency found that Complainant did not contact an EEO Counselor until December 15, 2016, which was beyond the 45-day contact period. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation (ROI) and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. In the decision, the Agency noted that Complainant failed to aptly respond to questions presented during the investigation. The Agency stated that Complainant declined to provide specific responses to the Investigator’s questions with respect to her claims that she experienced a hostile work environment when she was subjected to dismissive comments, isolation, the removal of personal items from her office, and when management failed to acknowledge her accomplishments. The Agency noted that although the claims related to work assignments and reasonable accommodation requests between 2014 and 2016 were not accepted because they were untimely, most of the evidence Complainant produced during the investigation pertained to those claims. Moreover, Complainant did not respond to the Investigator’s request for an affidavit regarding her claim of denial of her reasonable accommodation request in October 2017. As for Complainant’s failure to accommodate claim, the Agency deemed Complainant an individual with a disability and noted that the record established that she was a qualified individual with a disability. However, the Agency found that Complainant did not establish that management failed to provide her reasonable accommodation. In doing so, the Agency noted that on June 30, 2017, Complainant informed her first-level supervisor that she believed she would need assistance in the event of an emergency evacuation. Complainant stated that she would be unable to go down 14 flights of stairs if needed, and Complainant was informed that a portable evacuation chair was available for her situation. The Agency determined that there was no evidence in the record indicating that Complainant objected to the plan and noted that Complainant seemed to have generally been aware of the procedures relative to the use of an evacuation chair since she had previously signed up to assist others in an emergency. Complainant did not inform management officials that the evacuation chair was not a viable option until the October 17, 2017 fire drill. On that date, Complainant completed paperwork to have the Office of Emergency Management’s Facility Emergency Action Planning staff develop an emergency plan. On the following day, Complainant was advised that she would be able to use an elevator for drills and that in an actual emergency, emergency personnel could also accommodate her egress via elevator. Complainant’s second-line supervisor suggested a Buddy Monitor be designated for Complainant as well. Regarding pretext, the Agency found that a review of the record did not reveal any information indicating that Complainant’s age, disability, or participation in prior protected activity were factors in management’s actions or decisions. Moving to Complainant’s hostile work environment claims, the Agency noted that Complainant did not allege that any of her interactions involved physically aggressive or intimidating behavior, nor did Complainant describe disagreeable or objectionable verbal interactions. The Agency stated that Complainant’s primary complaint was that due to technology issues, she was hindered from performing some of the functions of her job, however, based on the evidence in the record, technology issues were widespread and applied to others. Moreover, the incidents were the type of routine challenges that occur in the workplace and Complainant did not experience any corresponding adverse action during the technology glitch. The Agency further noted that Complainant did not allege that management used hostile or insulting language, or that they engaged in an any conduct that was designed to humiliate, embarrass, or disparage Complainant.

Complaint (1) (2017-0055-R05) On March 26, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), national origin (Haitian), sex (female), age (49), and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity arising under Title VII when: 1. On January 23, 2017, she learned that S1 failed to add her name as the technical contact on reports that are submitted by the Ohio EPA, and put her name as the technical contact on nearly every quarterly report, in order to derail and discredit Complainant’s career and work; 4. On February 1, 2017, S1 denied her the opportunity to accumulate credit hours when she arrived earlier than her usual work schedule for training, while others were allowed such latitude; 5. From October 6, 2014 to January 30, 2017, management subjected her to arduous and unnecessary official time request procedures, while others, including S1, were not; 6. From 2015 to January 30, 2017, management denied her requests to transfer out of her Division and within the Division with the Regional Capital Officer and the Land and Chemical Division; and 7. On April 17, 2017, S1 approved her leave request, but deleted the record after Complainant took leave. Compliant (2) (2017-0073-R05) On May 20, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), sex (female), national origin (Haitian descent), age (over 40), and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity arising under Title VII when: 1. On March 20, 2017, the Acting Land and Chemicals Division Director issued her a proposed 30-calendar day suspension without pay; and 2. On March 21, 2017, S1 notified Complainant of her decision to withdraw approval for Complainant’s participation in the Flexiplace program. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation (ROI) and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing for both complaints, but subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a consolidated final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. In the final Agency decision (FAD), the Agency determined that Complainant failed to state a claim with respect to Complaint (1), allegation (2). Specifically, Complainant failed to show that management denied her the opportunity to attend the training. Management officials maintained that Complainant had been notified of the same opportunities to train and gain experience on Subpart AA/BB/CC detection equipment as other members of CS1 and CS2, however, Complainant failed to respond to the email about the training opportunity by the deadline. The Agency found that Complainant failed to establish disparate treatment for either of her complaints. Regarding MLLDP, Complainant failed to show that she was qualified for the position because she did not demonstrate leadership in the prior three years or obtain management support. The Agency determined that Complainant failed to show that she was treated less favorably than a similarly situated employee outside of her protected class with respect to credit hours. Employees who were not on an approved Maxiplace were not permitted to accrue credit hours or overtime. Complainant also failed to identify employees who were allowed to transfer or treated more favorably, and S1 stated that there were no other employees who requested a transfer out of the Division or within the Division in the prior two years. Management officials testified that no other employee received a suspension in the prior two years and no other employee engaged in similar behavior. As for the Flexiplace program, S1 stated that she had not removed any other employees in her section in the prior two years. Regarding reprisal, the Agency determined that Complainant failed to show a causal nexus between her prior protected activity and the adverse treatment in the complaints. The Agency noted that aside from the close proximity of time between Complainant’s prior EEO activity and the alleged adverse treatment, Complainant did not present any additional evidence that would support the inference of retaliatory animus in allegations (1), (2), (4), and (6) of Complaint 1 or Complaint 2. The FAD further noted that assuming, arguendo, that Complainant established a prima facie case of disparate treatment and retaliation, management set forth legitimate, nondiscriminatory explanations for the challenged conduct. Regarding claim (1), Complainant failed to demonstrate the requisite leadership experience and had received multiple disciplinary actions during that time. As for claim (2), Complainant had been notified of opportunities to train. Complainant was not given credit hours because she did not follow the process and did not submit any credit hour requests. With respect to the transfer requests, management indicted that there was a desire to retain the resources in RCRA, however, an email went out notifying other Divisions and Offices to contact Complainant directly if vacancies were available. As for the suspension, management officials stated that the discipline was based on Complainant’s past disciplinary record, which included two suspensions and a reprimand; Complainant’s past inability to work effectively and cooperatively with her colleagues; and Complainant’s inability to work through conflicts. Finally, Complainant was removed from the Flexiplace program due to documented conduct deficiencies and the fact that she had been issued a proposed 30-day suspension for failure to follow instructions, conduct unbecoming, and failure to follow leave procedures. Participation in the program requires no documented performance or conduct deficiencies within the preceding 12 months. The FAD concluded that Complainant failed to establish that management’s legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons were pretext. Regarding Complainant’s claims of a hostile work environment, the Agency determined that Complainant failed to establish that the alleged actions were taken based on her race, sex, or prior EEO Activity. It found that the actions, taken cumulatively, do not rise to the level of severe and pervasive. The Agency noted that training, non-selection, personality conflicts, and day-to-day managerial activities do not constitute severe or pervasive harassment.

In September 2011, Complainant was hired as an Airway Transportation Systems Specialist (ATSS) for the Agency’s Cleveland System Support Center in Oberlin, Ohio. Complainant’s job duties included installing and maintaining electronic equipment and lighting aids associated with facilities and services required for aviation navigation. The position involved working with radar, communications, computers and navigational aids. It was considered a Safety Sensitive Position, subjected to an Alcohol and Drug Testing Program. Complainant’s work hours were 7:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., Monday through Thursday. late in reporting to work. On November 17, 2011, Complainant informed his supervisor that he was a disabled veteran and suffered from depression, anger issues, and anxiety. Further, Complainant explained that since he had run out of his medications 2 he was having difficulty awakening in the morning. Because of these circumstances, Complainant asked his supervisor if he could either: (1) change his shift to 1:00 p.m. to 11:00 p.m. or (2) start an hour later, at 8:00 a.m. The supervisor denied both requests. The supervisor stated that, as a new hire, Complainant needed to work administrative hours until he obtained equipment certifications and could stand watch. As to the later start time, the supervisor reasoned it would not be fair to the other employees. Alternatively, the supervisor suggested that Complainant work eight-hour days, instead of his current ten-hour days. This proposed modification, however, would not alter his 7:00 a.m. start time. Complainant was also offered an 8:00 a.m. start, but he would have to use an hour of leave. Complainant rejected the offers. From November 17, 2011 to December 20, 2011, Complainant was not late. On December 19, 2011, Complainant was sent a letter written by an Agency Human Resources Specialist, referencing his November 17, 2011 meeting with his supervisor, and asking whether Complainant was seeking a reasonable accommodation. If so, Complainant needed to provide medical documentation and a list of his current medications. The next day Complainant submitted a letter from his physician, stating that Complainant was being treated for depression and identified which medications he was taking. On the same day, December 20, 2011, Complainant also met with his supervisor and explained that because he was now taking his medications, he was no longer having difficulties getting to work on time. He was no longer requesting any accommodations. However, on December 21, 2011, Complainant was late to work. Complainant did not call his supervisor until 8:30 a.m., and then asked for the rest of the day off. A week later, Complainant was terminated due to excessive tardiness. On April 15, 2012, believing that he was subjected to discrimination based on his disability (depression, sleep apnea), Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint. The Agency framed the claims as follows: 1. Since his date of hire on September 19, 2011, Complainant was denied a reasonable accommodation. 2. On or about December 28, 2011, he was terminated from his position of ATSS, FV-2101-F, during his probationary period. According to the Report of Investigation, Complainant had previously obtained therapy and medication from the Columbus VAMC. When he relocated to Cleveland for this position, the Cleveland VAMC required a reassessment before allowing him to receive his medication. After an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Following a one-day hearing on June 26, 2013, by video conferencing, the AJ issued a decision on October 1, 2014. The AJ concluded that Complainant did not establish he was denied a reasonable accommodation or was discriminatorily terminated. On October 9, 2014, the Agency issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s finding of no discrimination. Complainant appealed the decision to the Commission. The Commission found that Complainant’s termination was not discriminatory. However, the Commission disagreed with the AJ’s conclusion that the Agency had met its reasonable accommodation obligation when it offered Complainant an 8:00 a.m. start time with the use of one hour of his leave. See Complainant v. Dep’t of Transportation (FAA), EEOC [number removed] (August 17, 2017); EEOC [number removed] (Feb. 28, 2018) (req. for reconsid. denied). Citing previous Commission cases, the Commission specifically noted that, “forcing an employer to take leave when another accommodation would permit an employee to continue working is not an effective accommodation.” See id. To have enabled Complainant to continue working a full day, with the 8:00 a.m. start, would not have created an undue hardship. See id. Further, the supervisor’s concern that allowing such a schedule change for Complainant “would not be fair to the other employees” also fails to establish an undue hardship. See id. The Agency was found to have denied Complainant a reasonable accommodation from November 17, 2011 through December 20, 2011. Accordingly, the matter was remanded to the Agency for a supplemental investigation regarding Complainant’s entitlement to compensatory damages. Complainant’s attorney was advised to submit a verified statement of fees to the Agency for processing. See id. In compliance with the Commission’s orders, on July 18, 2018, the Agency issued a decision addressing compensatory damages and attorney’s fees. According to the Agency, in response to its request for the fees sought, Complainant’s attorney stated: “From November 17, 2011 to December 19, 2011, which is the period of violation against [Complainant], my client did not suffer and (sic) damages.” The Agency stated that nothing more was provided by Complainant or his attorney regarding compensatory damages. Therefore, the Agency did not award compensatory damages. As for attorney’s fees, Complainant’s counsel requested $368,550, for 819 hours at a rate of $450 per hour. Finding that Complainant’s attorney failed to provide support for his hourly rate, the Agency reduced the base hourly rate to $300. As for the number of hours expended, the Agency made several deductions reasoning that the statement of hours lacked necessary detail, the entries were inflated, excessive and sometimes duplicative. Finally, the Agency applied an overall reduction of 50% based on the limited success of the complaint. The Agency awarded $29,175 in attorney’s fees (194. hrs. x $300/hr). Complainant filed the instant appeal.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Postal Support Employee (PSE) Mail Processing Clerk at the Agency’s Hikes Point Station in Louisville, Kentucky. At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Mail Handler Assistant (MHA) at the Agency’s Processing and Distribution Center (P&DC) in Charleston, West Virginia. Report of Investigation (ROI), at 6. Complainant was hired on May 19, 2018, and was subject to a 90-day probationary period. ROI, at 52. The Supervisor of Distribution Operations (Caucasian) was assigned as Complainant’s first-level supervisor (S1). On June 6, 2018, S1 issued Complainant with his 30-day Employee Evaluation and/or Probationary Report. Id. at 75. Therein, S1 rated Complainant as unacceptable in the areas of work quality, work quantity, dependability, and personal conduct. S1 rated Complainant satisfactory in the areas of dependability and work relations. Id. Thereafter, on July 18, 2018, S1 presented Complainant with his 60-day Employee Evaluation and/or Probationary Report. Id. 76. S1 rated Complainant unacceptable in each and every work area, including dependability and work relations. Id. However, in both evaluation reports, S1 did not specifically explain why he considered Complainant’s work performance to be at an unacceptable level. A short time later, Complainant was issued with a Letter of Separation on July 24, 2018, before the end of his 90-day probationary period. Id. at 79. In the Letter of Separation, S1 noted that Complainant’s performance had been unsatisfactory, but S1 again did not specifically identify why he considered Complainant’s to be unsatisfactory. Id. On October 18, 2018, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (African-American) and color (black/brown) when on July 25, 2018, he was issued a letter of separation. Following the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The Agency initially found that Complainant did not establish a prima facie case of discrimination based on race and color. The Agency specifically found that Complainant did not show that he was treated differently than similarly situated individuals outside his protected classes. In so finding, the Agency noted that two other employees (Caucasian) were also both later fired for unsatisfactory work performance, like Complainant. The Agency further assumed, without finding, that Complainant established a prima facie of discrimination, and determined that it articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for Complainant’s firing. Namely, that in Complainant’s 60-day Employee Evaluation and/or Probationary Report, he received unacceptable ratings in work quantity, work quality, dependability, work relations, work methods, and personal conduct. The Agency also found that Complainant did not establish that its reasons for his firing were pretext for discrimination. The Agency observed that S1 averred that he was unaware of Complainant’s race and there was no evidence of discriminatory animus.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Mail Handler in Palatine, Illinois. Complainant alleged discriminatory harassment based on sex (male) and disability when: 1. on March 21, 2017, Complainant’s supervisor (“S1”) sexually assaulted him and management did nothing; 2. on March 22, 2017, S1 took his fork lift away and continuously paged him on the loud speaker; 3. Complainant was taken out of his bid assignment; 4. management said Complainant had a mental illness; 5. on or around April 11, 2017, Complainant was accused of being Absent Without Leave (AWOL); and 6. on or around April 20, 2017, Complainant was sent home and instructed to provide medical documentation to return to work. After an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ).
