On January 21, 2017, Complainant was allegedly denied a request for a tour change to start work at 7:00 a.m. instead of 8:00 a.m.; 7. In or about February/March 2017, management again informed Complainant that he could not use power tools without supervision by a higher graded employee; 8. On March 16, 2017, the Maintenance Supervisor “reprimanded” Complainant for using power tools without supervision by a higher graded employee; 9. On or around September 28, 2017, the Maintenance Supervisor “reprimanded” Complainant for not removing a pen from his uniform before sending it to laundry and sent him a daily calendar invite reminding him to check his pockets; 10. Between May 29, 2018, and August 24, 2018, Complainant’s coworkers allegedly expressed unwillingness to communicate with Complainant; 11. On July 18, 2018, Complainant became aware that he had allegedly been excluded from forklift training; 12. On August 24, 2018, an unidentified employee informed the Housekeeping Aid Supervisor that Complainant was bothering them during their lunch break; 13. On unidentified dates, Complainant was excluded from daily “huddle” meetings during which coworkers were briefed on the daily agenda and action items; 14. On an unidentified date, a coworker allegedly called Complainant “rain man”; and 15. On an unidentified date, a coworker allegedly stated: “if we want something screwed up, we ask [Complainant] to work on it” or “hire the disabled.” At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). 2 The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Complainant’s mother, who is his non-attorney representative on appeal, contends that Complainant did not receive the Agency’s notice of his right to request a hearing before an AJ after she checked his “email account on record.” However, the record shows that the notice was delivered to Complainant’s Agency email address and contains a read-receipt. In addition, we note that Complainant does not expressly request a hearing on appeal. In its final decision, the Agency first addressed claim 1 regarding Complainant’s request for a reasonable accommodation. The Agency found that Complainant was a qualified individual with a disability and that management was aware of his disability. In his affidavit, Complainant said he had made a written reasonable accommodation request on June 17, 2019, which was then given to the Local Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator (LRAC). Complainant requested that he be provided an English Sign Language (ESL) interpreter of his choosing during weekly meetings with his supervisor, morning “huddle” meetings, job training sessions, and other work events as needed. He also requested hearing assistive technology, such as Communication Access Realtime Translation captioning services, text-based communication devices, and/or Video Remote Interpreting. Before making his written request for accommodation in June 2019, Complainant indicated that he had requested an interpreter “for anything major” during 2018 and 2019. Complainant’s supervisor referenced invoices for interpreting services for Complainant dating back to November 2016, and averred that he held supervisory meetings with Complainant every two weeks beginning in July 2018, which were eventually reduced to meetings as needed at Complainant’s request. Complainant’s supervisor stated that an interpreter was provided for all of those meetings. 3 The Agency found that, in his affidavit, Complainant repeatedly stated that his request for a reasonable accommodation “was not denied.” The Agency also concluded that management had provided Complainant a “video relay machine” where an interpreter would voice for Complainant based on his signs to the interpreter. The Agency also provided interpreters for as- needed supervisory meetings between Complainant and his supervisor and whenever Complainant requested them. The LRAC averred that Complainant’s requests for accommodation, including his requests for an interpreter from prior years, were granted. The Agency ultimately determined that Complainant received an interpreter, either via video or in person, whenever he requested one, and was given “translation apps” that he used with his supervisor during meetings. In sum, Complainant averred that the Agency did not deny his reasonable accommodation request, and we find that he did not identify any specific occasion where the Agency denied him an ESL interpreter or any other requested accommodation. 4 The Agency therefore found it had satisfied its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act. Although claim 1 identifies the relevant time period as beginning in February 2016, Complainant’s affidavit did not refer to any reasonable accommodation requests he made during that year. Complainant stated that he had been “afraid to ask” his then-supervisor for an interpreter, and when he and his mother eventually approached that supervisor in October 2017, about needing an interpreter, he “scoffed and laughed.” However, the record shows that Complainant was provided with an interpreter at least as early as November 2016, and he states elsewhere in his affidavit that his requests for accommodation were not denied. The LRAC stated that Complainant’s mother, who also works for the Agency, expressed to management that she wanted an interpreter for Complainant more often than Complainant requested it for himself and that Complainant “did not want what his mother wanted for him.” As to his remaining claims, the Agency found that Complainant failed to show that the complained-of incidents were based on his disability or that the conduct was sufficiently severe or pervasive to establish a hostile work environment. Regarding claims 2, 12, 14, and 15, which involved alleged comments or conduct by Complainant’s coworkers, Complainant did not provide any statements in his affidavit about the incidents but instead referred to statements by his parents. The comment as stated in claim 2 was heard by Complainant’s father, who told Complainant’s mother about it after the fact. Complainant’s mother said she was told by the spouse of one of her son’s coworkers that the coworker had confronted another employee who had referred to Complainant as “rain man.” As to the comments as alleged in claim 15, Complainant’s mother stated she had heard those comments made. The Agency found that Complainant did not appear to be present for any of the alleged statements or that Complainant ever reported them to management. Complainant did not provide any statements in his affidavit about coworkers not communicating with him, as stated in claim 12, again referring the investigator to a statement by his mother. Regarding claims 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, and 11, Complainant requested permission to use the riding lawn mower, use power tools unsupervised, and operate a forklift, and he claimed that he was “being held back” by management’s refusal to allow him to do so. The Agency stated that its reason for refusing Complainant permission to use power tools and other equipment unsupervised was because he had injured himself with an electric drill in January 2017, and had damaged Agency equipment in the past. Management also noted that Complainant’s position description does not require the use of power tools except trimmers, blowers, or clippers used to maintain lawn and grounds. The position description also explicitly states that Complainant’s work should be done “in conjunction with a higher graded/skilled employee who provides immediate supervision,” which the Agency found was consistent with the instructions given to Complainant not to use power tools unsupervised. As to Complainant’s claim that his supervisor reprimanded him in front of other employees about the use of power tools in an embarrassing manner, the supervisor denied doing so. When Complainant asked his supervisors for additional work, management expanded his duties within the parameters of his position description, such as pulling water samples, replacing ceiling tiles and light bulbs, maintaining sprinkler heads, and assisting “journeymen” (Agency’s term for higher-skilled workers). However, because Complainant’s position does not require the use of a forklift, Complainant did not receive forklift training, as it was only journeymen who received such training, though the record indicated he took some online courses related to forklifts. While Complainant claimed that other employees were allowed to use power tools, cut the grass using the riding mower, and receive forklift training, the Agency found that those employees had different positions than Complainant and therefore did not share the same job duties. The Agency found that Complainant had not been singled out for “menial tasks” or had otherwise been denied opportunity for advancement. Regarding claim 6, Complainant requested to change his tour of duty by one hour in 2017, and that the request was denied. He averred, however, that the request to change his tour of duty was eventually granted about a year later. One of Complainant’s supervisors stated that prior to January 21, 2017, all maintenance staff were required to have tours of duty from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., but that once the supervisor became Maintenance Chief, he agreed to change Complainant’s start time to 7:00 a.m. The record indicates that in August 2020, Complainant stated he was no longer happy with the 7:00 a.m. start time and requested to return to the 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. tour of duty, which his supervisor granted. Regarding claim 9, a laundry department attendant emailed Complainant and copied two of his supervisors, stating, “I found a pen in your uniform pocket again this morning . . . I am done pulling pens from your pockets. . . . You could [have] ruined 65 pounds of uniforms. It’s not my job to check pockets. Thanks.” Complainant claimed the email was “nasty” and that as a response his supervisor sent him berating emails about it, though the record indicates that it was actually Complainant’s mother who sent him the daily reminders to check his pockets as stated in the claim. Regarding claim 10, which involved the complaint about Complainant bothering employees during their lunch break, Complainant averred that he had been in the housekeeping department lunchroom speaking with a friend about something he had read in the newspaper. Afterward, an unidentified employee complained about him to the Housekeeping Aid Supervisor. As a result, he was asked not to go into that lunchroom. Regarding claim 13, two of Complainant’s supervisors indicated that Complainant was never excluded from “huddle” meetings and that Complainant never raised the issue with them. While Complainant alleged that, “[n]obody lets [him] know when these meetings take place or what was discussed,” the Agency found that there was no evidence Complainant was excluded from any meetings or that he missed any meetings that were necessary for the performance of his job duties. The Agency concluded that, even accepting all of Complainant’s allegations as true, he had not shown by a preponderance of the evidence that the Agency’s actions were based on his disability. As to the alleged comments made by coworkers, the Agency found that the only information provided about those comments came from Complainant’s mother, who claimed to have heard about them from third parties, and that Complainant had not informed management about such comments. The Agency further determined that even if the alleged conduct had been based on Complainant’s disability, the events were not sufficiently severe or pervasive to constitute unlawful harassment and for the most part involved “ordinary workplace experiences and the routine exercise of supervisory responsibilities.”

On November 13, 2018, Complainant began a temporary appointment as Area Manager, GG- 0301-13-00/01, with the Agency’s Chicago Regional Office. An Area Manager is responsible for assisting the Assistant Regional Census Manager (ARCM) in the management of all field, office, and evaluation operations for the Decennial Census over an assigned geographic area. On April 4, 2019, Complainant was assigned to oversee the Kansas City Area Census Office (ACO). During the relevant time, the ARCM was Complainant’s first line supervisor. The Deputy Regional Director (DRD) was Complainant’s second level supervisor. Person A, working as the Lead Census Field Manager, was a subordinate to Complainant. On December 12, 2019, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of sex (male) and in reprisal for protected EEO activity (opposition to discrimination) when: On September 6, 2019, Complainant was terminated for what he states were false allegations surrounding a romantic relationship between himself and another employee, as well as false allegations of unacceptable performance. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. The Agency filed a motion for summary judgment. Complainant filed a response to the Agency’s motion. The Agency filed a reply to Complainant’s response. Over Complainant’s objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on August 3, 2021. In his decision, the AJ found Complainant had not established a prima facie case of reprisal. The AJ noted Complainant claimed opposition to unlawful discrimination as his protected EEO activity. Complainant claimed that he opposed unlawful discrimination when he approached the DRD on multiple occasions to voice his concerns of sex-based discrimination from the ARCM. The AJ noted the DRD’s affidavit stated Complainant raised “concerns, but didn’t go into specifics. He didn’t say he was being harassed based on his sex or reprisal. He expressed some concern about [the ARCM’s] management style.” The AJ noted Person A’s affidavit provided evidence of statements the ARCM made; however, it did not offer information regarding anything Complainant related to the ARCM or the DRD. The AJ noted in Complainant’s affidavit, in response to the question to identify the EEO activity he engaged in, he stated, “On numerous occasions, I approached [the DRD] about the inappropriate activities by [the ARCM].” The AJ noted in the next question, Complainant also discusses additional personal notes about the ARCM’s behavior, but that this did not reflect the content of the communications Complainant made to the DRD. The AJ concluded that even taking Complainant’s evidence at face value, he did not provide sufficient evidence for a reasonable factfinder to conclude that he engaged in protected activity in the course of communication with the DRD. The AJ found Complainant established a prima facie case of disparate treatment on the basis of sex. The AJ noted that Complainant alleged, which was supported by affidavit testimony, that the ARCM referred to him as “that man” in a variety of demeaning statements. The AJ found Complainant’s allegation was sufficient to provide some evidentiary link between his membership in the protected class and the adverse employment action. The AJ noted as a result the burden moved to the Agency to articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for its actions. The Agency stated on August 14, 2019, during a visit to the Kansas City Office, it was discovered that field workers were showing up to training locations with no trainers present, classes were held with no appointment packets, badges were missing, and in some cases, laptops were not sent to the trainer. Also, it was noted the Record of Training was not being shipped to the ACO in a timely manner, there were delays in receiving orientation packets, and the new hires were therefore delayed. Further, problems with the Production Lister Classes in Little Rock, Arkansas were noted, to include the short length of the class, the absence of laptops in one class which resulted in field workers being sent home without training, and two classes which had laptops but in which the field workers could not log in and were sent home without full training. It was also noted that the Quality Control program was not managed properly. The AJ found the Agency met its burden. The AJ found Complainant failed to present grounds for finding the Agency’s actions were a pretext for discrimination. The AJ noted Complainant’s affidavit response provided meager grounds to question the accuracy of the allegations surrounding Complainant’s performance. Complainant stated he was unaware of some of the problems, some were nationwide problems unrelated to him, and one he had addressed concerning time and attendance training. The AJ found this statement did not refute the allegations. Specifically, Complainant did not state which problems he was unaware of or why he would not be responsible for them despite being the Area Manager. Similarly, he did not state which problems were nationwide or why he would not have responsibility for them even if they were widely occurring. Further, time and attendance training did not appear as a significant problem in the deficiencies identified. The AJ found “in light of the existing non-discriminatory reason, which is unquestioned on the basis of its accuracy and for which there are no comparators, references to ‘that man’ would not show pretext.” Finally, the AJ noted Complainant claimed he was subjected to harassment on the basis of sex stating the ARCM treated him in an unprofessional and disrespectful manner, countermanded his instructions, purposefully excluded detailed information from him, spoke to him in a derogatory manner, and removed him on frivolous charges of poor performance. The AJ noted that as the termination was not due to discrimination, it could not contribute to a hostile work environment. The AJ noted the derogatory treatment consisted of comments about not wanting to hear from “that man” and words to that effect. When the ARCM countermanded Complainant, she held a higher supervisory position to Complainant. Complainant did not articulate what information was excluded from him. The AJ found Complainant attempted to convert Title VII into a code of civility and found that while unpleasant, the interactions, did not rise to the level of severity or pervasiveness as to constitute a hostile work environment. The Agency subsequently issued a final order on September 9, 2021. The Agency’s final order fully implemented the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. Thereafter, Complainant filed the instant appeal.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a City Carrier Technician, A-02/Q, at the Agency’s Village Station in New York, New York. 1. Since June 26, 2016, and continuing, management has assigned Complainant work outside of her medical restrictions and failed to pay her properly and/or on time; 2. On October 4, 2016, and other unspecified dates, her clock rings were deleted; and 3. On unspecified dates, Complainant’s request to be detailed as a 204-B has not been granted. 2 Complainant was employed as a City Carrier Technician, assigned to the Village Station. Report of Investigation, Affidavit A at 190, Exhibit 1. The duties of a Carrier Technician were to case and deliver mail for several carrier routes. The duties include pushing, lifting, simple grasping daily for eight hours a day. ROI, Affidavit C2. Complainant attributes her medical conditions to a recurrence of an on-the-job injury. She was first diagnosed on May 10, 2014, which is noted in the record by her physician as the date of the injury. ROI at 64-65. She averred that her medical conditions are a back sprain, displacement of lumbar intervertebral disc without myelopathy, and a hernia, which she had repaired after the on- the-job injury. ROI, Complainant’s Affidavit, at 191. Complainant’s medical restrictions include sitting three hours, walking limited to 30 minutes, standing 10 minutes, avoiding reaching above the shoulder, twisting, bending, stooping, pushing, pulling, lifting, squatting, kneeling, and climbing. She also required 15-minute breaks every hour. ROI at 191. She had been out on leave for an extended period. When she returned, she was assigned to the Lenox Hill Station. On June 22, 2016, an offer was made to Complainant for a limited duty modified assignment to work at the Lenox Hill South Station from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The position was not a vacant, funded position. The position involved shuttling carriers by van to and from their routes and delivering express mail under five pounds for up to four hours a day and up to 30 minutes respectively. On paper, this met Complainant’s restrictions. Complainant signed the modified job offer on July 1, 2016, and she began the assignment on or about July 18, 2016. ROI at 196, 233. Although Complainant felt the modified job assignment would be too much for her, she told her Manager that she would try it, and let him know if she was unable to handle it, and he agreed. ROI at 196. The Manager testified that he became aware of the Complainant’s medical condition through the job offer. He denied receiving, or having, any medical documentation for Complainant. The Agency dismissed an additional claim for failure to state a claim. Complainant raised no challenges regarding this matter and the Commission can find no basis to disturb the Agency’s dismissal decision. The record shows that Complainant had been offered another light duty job, to serve as a lobby attendant. Complainant declined the lobby attendant position. Complainant believed it would be beyond what she could do, given her restrictions. The undisputed record shows that the Manager gave her instructions to make an express delivery, which he believed conformed to her medical restrictions. ROI at 196. Complainant claimed that, on August 29, 2016, she walked an hour (with breaks), even though she was not supposed to walk more than 30 minutes. She was not permitted the use of the van. Using the van, as indicated in the modified job offer, would require her to stoop and twist to get in the vehicle. Even picking up an envelope that dropped on the ground would be a violation of her restrictions to avoid stooping. ROI at 196. The record shows that Complainant was out on leave for significant periods of time in July and August 2016. Some of Complainant’s clock rings had been deleted for the dates July 18, 2016, through July 28, 2016, and her time was coded as full workers’ compensation. Complainant had just started working at the Lenox Hill Station and the receiving station should have entered her time. ROI, Affidavit A. The Manager averred that Complainant had an incorrect leave code in the system. ROI, Affidavit B. She did not return to work until October 4, 2016, to fill out workers’ compensation paperwork and again on November 14, 2016, to fill out additional paperwork. As further background, Complainant had recently come back from being on full time workers’ compensation. Because Complainant switched from one facility to another – from Village Station to Lenox Hill, there is insufficient evidence that the supervisor at the receiving facility realized she had returned to work from being out on workers’ compensation. Complainant asserted that her Manager’s poor organization was another reason for the errors that were made. ROI at 197-198 (209-210). The deletion of the clock rings was discovered before her EEO filing that is the subject of this appeal. Meanwhile, on September 14, 2016, she filed a grievance regarding the payment failures and the deleted clock rings. The Agency maintained that the payment failures were due to plain error. 3 In addition, Complainant averred that she requested to serve as an acting supervisor (204B) over the carriers. On or about November 14, 2016, the Manager did not offer her a 204B detail as a reasonable accommodation. The Manager averred he did not need any acting supervisors for his operations. In addition, he averred that he believed that supervisors must be punctual and reliable, which were attributes that he did not observe in Complainant. ROI, Affidavit B. In addition, the record shows that manual timecards had been submitted and lost. Complainant cited the errors that had been made and believed they may have been caused by the Agency not having a disk which would have allowed Complainant to log her hours automatically, rather than manually. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ assigned to the case issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency finding that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination or reprisal as alleged. In the decision, the AJ found that Complainant was not denied reasonable accommodation as alleged in claim (1). The AJ determined that Complainant was provided a modified limited duty assignment of shuttling carriers in a van and delivering express mail which was within her documented medical restrictions. Complainant believed that the job was too much for her. The Agency offered Complainant another modified assignment of lobby attendant, but she declined the position. The AJ noted that Complainant claimed another modified assignment that was offered and rescinded would have met her needs, but that position contained similar tasks as the lobby attendant position that she declined. The AJ determined that there was no evidence that Complainant was forced to work outside of her medical restrictions. Thus, Complainant appeared to have been unable to perform her job with or without a reasonable accommodation as her medical restrictions were so severe. Therefore, the AJ found that Complainant was not denied reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. With respect to the remaining issues, the AJ determined that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. More specifically, with respect to her claims that she was not paid properly and her clock rings were deleted, Agency officials explained that errors occurred for a number or reasons. For example, Complainant returned to full-time duty from workers’ compensation so supervisors at the other facility may not have realized she had returned to work. In addition, Complainant switched from one facility to another. Another reason was because manual timecards were submitted and lost instead of digital submission which would have prevented the issue. Finally, Complainant herself noted that the Manager had poor organizational skills which contributed to the errors. As to her claim that her request to be detailed as a 204-B acting supervisor was not granted, Complainant claimed that the Manager and another manager “brushed her off” and that she mentioned the detail as a way for her to be accommodated. The Manager offered her the two above-discussed positions as accommodations. Complainant stated that instead of training her for a 204-B position, she was told she could apply for a city-wide position that would take time to obtain. The AJ determined that Complainant wanted a manager to promote her on the spot rather than actually applying for the detail assignment. The AJ found that Complainant failed to show that the denial of the detail was a result of discriminatory or retaliatory animus. The AJ concluded that Complainant failed to show that the Agency’s reasons for its actions were pretextual. As a result, the AJ found that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination or reprisal as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully adopting the AJ’s decision. This appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant was employed by the Agency as an Air Condition Operator, WG-11, at the Edward Hines Jr. VA Hospital in Hines, Illinois. On September 21, 2020, Complainant filed a Formal EEO Complaint alleging discrimination by the Agency on the bases of race (Black/African American), disability (70% disabled veteran, PTSD) and reprisal for engaging in protected EEO activity (opposition). a. Complainant was subjected to a hostile work environment/harassment when, since 2018, he has been required to train new supervisors in their position(s) for which he previously applied but was not selected. b. He was subjected to the following independently actionable claims: 1. On an unspecified date in 2018, Complainant was not selected for the position of Supervisor, and, 2. On May 12, 2020, he was not selected for the position of Air Condition Operator Supervisor, WS-5415-10, advertised under Vacancy Announcement No. HN-10796266-20-AM. Prior to investigating Complainant’s complaint, the Agency dismissed Claim b(1) as untimely raised pursuant to 29 C.F.R § 1614.107(a)(2). The Agency then conducted an investigation into the remaining claims which showed that in April 2020, Complainant applied for the position of Air Condition Operator Supervisor, WS- 5415-10, (“AC Supervisor”) through Human Resources (“HR”). Complainant’s application indicated that he was a disabled veteran and schedule A (disability hiring) status. HR deemed Complainant qualified and forwarded his name for an interview. He was the only candidate to interview for the position. On May 8, 2020, Complainant was interviewed by a 3-person outside panel. The Chief of Maintenance and Operations, WS-15, (“Maintenance Chief”) (white) was Complainant’s second level supervisor and the selecting official for the AC Supervisor position. At the recommendation of the panel, Maintenance Chief opted not to select Complainant and instead the AC Supervisor position was re-posted. On May 13, 2020, Complainant emailed Maintenance Chief, the Engineering Chief, and the Assistant Engineering Chief seeking feedback on why he was not selected for the AC Position. The Assistant Chief offered to meet with Complainant to discuss the matter. It appears that Maintenance Chief met with Complainant and suggested he improve his interview responses and revise his resume. The Engineering Chief provided a statement for the ROI, asserting that Complainant “was provided feedback by both the Assistant Chief of Engineering and [Maintenance Chief] within the bounds of what could be provided as part of an ongoing recruitment.” Complainant states that he “didn’t agree at all,” with Maintenance Chief’s advice regarding his resume and interview and disputes receiving any meaningful feedback. On June 15, 2020, Complainant emailed Maintenance Chief requesting a department-wide meeting to address diversity issues. 2 Complainant indicated that he and unspecified coworkers believed his nonselection for the AC Supervisor position was related to the fact that there were no non-white supervisors or managers in their department. Complainant concluded that if diversity were not the issue, he believed that Maintenance Chief’s decision not to select him as AC Supervisor was “personal.” Maintenance Chief responded the same day, denying that Complainant’s nonselection was related to lack of diversity or personal reasons and suggesting that Complainant raise the matter with the Agency’s EEO office, noting the 45-day time limit to report allegations of discrimination. Maintenance Chief also asked if Complainant re-applied to the AC Supervisor or other positions, and if Complainant rewrote his resume or brushed up on his interview skills. It does not appear that Maintenance Chief responded to Complainant’s follow up request for resources to improve his interview skills and resume. Complainant decided not to apply to the re-posted AC Supervisor position. Complainant recounts that he ended up training the selectee, an electrician with no background in AC Operations, on the technical aspects of his position. At the conclusion of its investigation of the remaining claims, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation (“ROI”) and notice of his right to request either a FAD or a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (“AJ”). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a FAD pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The FAD concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Mail Processing Clerk at the Agency’s Cleveland Annex facility in Cleveland, Ohio. 1. Complainant was not paid for hours worked. 2. She was denied Higher Level pay. 3. On October 8, 2020, a co-worker yanked a piece of equipment out of her hands. 4. A co-worker intentionally provoked her to try to get a reaction out of her. 5. On October 11, 2020, she was sent home from work. 6. On or about November 7, 2020, a supervisor threatened her job. 7. On or about December 2, 2020, she was issued a letter of separation. 8. On or about February 22, 2021, she was issued a letter of separation. The Agency accepted the claims for investigation and an investigator was assigned to investigate the complaint, sending Complainant an affidavit to complete by letter dated May 6, 2021. When Complainant did not return her affidavit, the Agency dismissed the complaint pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(7) for failure to cooperate. Complainant appealed. In Helen G. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC [number removed] (Nov. 8, 2021), we reversed the Agency’s dismissal finding Complainant’s failure to respond did not inhibit the Agency’s ability to otherwise investigate the complaint in order to adjudicate the complaint. The complaint was remanded to the Agency for further processing. While the remanded case was before the Agency, Complainant mistakenly filed the instant appeal. However, the Agency continued processing the complaint on remand and, thereafter, provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Prior to a hearing, the AJ directed Complainant to complete the affidavit she had not submitted during the investigation. Complainant failed to do so. The AJ issued an order to show cause, to which Complainant also did not respond. On July 13, 2021, the AJ issued an order finding judgment in favor of the Agency as a sanction for Complainant’s failure to respond to both of the AJ’s orders. In the alternative, in reviewing the record, the AJ found that there was no evidence in the record to support any of Complainant’s claims. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding. On August 13, 2022, Complainant filed another appeal of the Agency’s final order, which was administratively closed as a duplicate of the instant appeal by letter dated September 22, 2022. See EEOC [number removed] (September 27, 2022). Complainant’s only statement on appeal appears to be a letter reiterating the claims made in her formal complaint. 2 The Agency did not file a brief in response. To the extent Complainant’s statement on appeal appears to raise issues concerning her claim for workers’ compensation, we note that the Commission does not have jurisdiction over the workers’ compensation process and any issues related to the adjudication of her workers’ compensation claim may not be raised during the EEO process. See Lashaunda G. v. Dep’t of Veterans Affs., EEOC [number removed] (Jan. 25, 2018).

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as an Office Support Assistant at the Agency’s Integrated Disability Evaluation System, Patient Administration Department at Fort Hood in Texas. According to Complainant’s position description, her position provides clerical administrative processing of forms, reports, and other material to support health care treatment services provided to service members undergoing the Physical Disability Evaluation processing. The assignment primarily involves assurance that the service member is eligible for treatment in accordance with the Agency’s regulations and guidelines. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 75. On June 3, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of her race (African American), sex (female), and disability (Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS)). By letter dated June 14, 2021, the Agency accepted Complainant’s complaint for investigation and determined that it was comprised of the following claims: 1. On April 14, 2021, [Complainant’s supervisor] denied [her] reasonable accommodation request to telework; 2. [A co-worker] ordered her bed/dog training pads as an alternative to [her] reasonable accommodation request. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). Under a disparate treatment analysis, the Agency found that assuming Complainant established a prima facie case of discrimination, the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscrimination reasons for its actions which Complainant failed to establish was pretext for discrimination. Final Agency Decision (FAD) at 5-6, 12. The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. Under a reasonable accommodation analysis, the Agency found that Complainant was a qualified individual with a disability. FAD at 10. The Agency further found that Complainant’s supervisor and other Agency officials engaged in the interactive process with Complainant and provided her with alternative accommodations such as a sit-stand desk, a private office closer to restroom, toilet seat covers, an alternate work schedule and telework on Tuesday and Thursday. Final Agency Decision (FAD) at 10. Thus, the Agency found that it made a good faith effort to accommodate Complainant and that she was unable to show that the provided accommodations were not effective. Id. Regarding claim (2), the Agency also found no discrimination. The Agency reasoned: Complainant agreed to seat covers when she signed the alternative accommodation decision. The evidence in the record shows miscommunication as to what type of seat covers were requested. Complainant’s accommodation request states she had leakage of bodily fluids on her clothing and chair. No evidence in the record indicates the confusion over pad type was purposeful on the part of [named] Agency officials or counter to the medical information Complainant provided. No evidence indicates the pads were intended for animus or ordered to embarrass her. Additionally, no evidence or testimony in the record shows that [a co-worker] was made aware Complaint required the pads because of a medical need or that she had a disability requiring such pads. FAD at 11. The instant appeal followed. Complainant, through her attorney, asserts that the Agency failed to provide Complainant with an effective reasonable accommodation and requests that we reverse the Agency’s final decision regarding this matter. Complainant’s attorney notes that the Agency did not dispute that Complainant is an individual with a disability. In addition, Complainant’s attorney sets forth that Complainant’s HS substantially limited her ability to walk, sleep, sit, and concentrate. Complainant’s attorney sets forth that Complainant is also a “qualified” individual with a disability. Complainant’s attorney notes that the Agency does not dispute that Complainant can perform the essential functions of her position with or without accommodation. In addition, Complainant asserts that she successfully performed her duties while teleworking on a full-time basis during the COVID-19 pandemic. Complainant’s attorney asserts that Complainant provided medical documentation of her medical condition, limitations and recommendation for telework due to her condition. Complainant, on appeal, asserts “[t]he Agency did not contend that providing [her] episodic telework when her HS symptoms flared would cause it undue hardship or that it would require the removal of any of her essential functions.” Complainant further sets forth that the Agency’s alternative accommodations were ineffective. Specifically, Complainant’s attorney states “[n]one of the alternative accommodations the Agency provided [Complainant] alleviated her need to abstain from sitting, walking, and wearing clothing that aggravated her painful lesions during unpredictable flare-ups of her condition. The only accommodation the Agency provided that even remotely addressed her needs – the fixed telework days – was also ineffective because [Complainant’s] condition did not only flare on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Significantly and critically, neither [Complainant] nor her doctor can predict those days when her condition may flare.” Complainant’s Brief at 12 (internal citations omitted). Complainant asserts that the Agency never contended that providing her situational telework during her flare-ups would cause undue hardship. Complainant’s attorney notes that the Agency failed to consider effective accommodations until after she filed an EEO complaint, and did not take her condition seriously; thus, the Agency failed to make a good faith effort to accommodate her. Specifically, Complainant states that “the Agency refused to provide any telework at all until July 15, 2021, nearly four months after [Complainant] requested episodic telework, and over one month after she filed a formal EEO complaint about the Agency’s failure to accommodate her.” FAD at 16. In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision finding no discrimination. The Agency found that it articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions which Complainant failed to establish was pretext. Regarding a reasonable accommodation analysis, the Agency acknowledged that Complainant was a qualified individual with a disability and set forth that after the interactive process, Complainant agreed to an alternate reasonable accommodation. Agency Brief 11-12.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Supervisory Transportation Security Officer, SV-1802-G Band, at the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Atlanta, Georgia. On February 2, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him and subjected him to a hostile work environment on the bases of sex (male) and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when: 1. on November 24, 2020, a co-worker (CW1) claimed to do Voodoo and placed a flower on Complainant’s body; 2. 3. sometime after November 24, 2020, management failed to address Complainant’s concerns regarding the November 24, 2020, incident with CW1 and prevented Complainant from attending management meetings and scheduling operational meetings; and 4. on December 30, 2020, a manager (Manager) paced back and forth, stood over Complainant, and blocked the door when Complainant tried to leave. 2 In support of his allegations regarding Claims (1) and (2), Complainant alleged that he asked CW1 to step back and stay away from him, but CW1 would not, and that CW1 backed him into a corner. Complainant noted that he complained to Agency management on November 24 and 28, 2020, and that no action was taken. The record indicates that, in a December 21, 2020 memorandum, the Interim Federal Security Director (Interim Director) appointed Manager to investigate Complainant’s claims. Subsequently, and as alleged in Claim (4), Complainant stated that Manager approached him, demanding that Complainant answer questions about his allegations against CW1, but refused to show Complainant his authorization to investigate the claims. Complainant alleged that Manager offered to show the memorandum to Complainant on his computer, but every time Complainant went to look, Manager “would click off the screen to prevent [Complainant’s] view of it. Complainant added that Manager would not allow Complainant to leave without answering questions. Manager denied each of Complainant’s allegations against him, including Complainant’s claim that he was excluded from meetings. On December 31, 2020, Complainant emailed Manager and objected to Manager’s role in investigating Complainant’s claims because Manager was part of Complainant’s management chain. The record contains subsequent emails from Complainant to the Interim Director to similar effect. The Interim Director forwarded Complainant’s concerns to the Federal Security Director (Director). Subsequently, on January 5, 2021, Director appointed another individual, a Transportation Security Inspector (Inspector), to continue the investigation into Complainant’s allegations. Complainant agreed to be interviewed by the Inspector. On January 22, 2021, Inspector issued a fact-finding report in which he could not substantiate Complainant’s claims. Inspector interviewed Complainant, CW1, and several other employees who worked in the same area with both Complainant and CW1. The Inspector acknowledged that Complainant and CW1 had a “contentious conversation” but that the details were in dispute. Complainant alleged that CW1 asked to speak with him privately and backed her into a corner. CW1 responded that Complainant initiated the conversation and questioned CW1 about her relationship with another employee, which upset her. Coworkers confirmed that a conversation took place but could not confirm the substance of the conversation. The Agency initially dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, but in Norman S. v. Dep’t of Homeland Sec., EEOC [number removed] (July 22, 2021), the Commission reversed the Agency’s decision and remanded the matter for further processing. In failing to substantiate Complainant’s allegations, the Inspector noted that most of the evidence he discovered was “conjecture.” Complainant testified that he believed the entire sequence of events revealed a discriminatory pattern because CW1 and other women, are not subjected to discipline whereas men are treated more harshly. According to Complainant, “[a] fact finding inquiry was conducted, but this did not address [his] concerns, and did not prevent or lessen the acts of discrimination and retaliation, including subjecting [him] to a hostile work environment.” Complainant criticized the investigation as biased and artificial and suggested that security footage would have corroborated his claims. CW1 provided an affidavit in which she denied Complainant’s version of the events and provided testimony consistent with the statement she provided to the Inspector. The record contains statements from Complainant’s coworkers who states as they did in the investigation. Specifically, they claimed that Complainant and CW1 had a contentious conversation but they could not hear what was said or see what was done. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). In the decision, the Agency found that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination or reprisal as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as an Administrative Technician, GS-0303-05, at the Agency’s Chicago Regional Office in Oak Brook, Illinois. On August 24, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him based on disability (diabetes and liver fibrosis) and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (requesting a reasonable accommodation) when he was terminated, effective July 28, 2021. Complainant does not challenge the framing of the complaint. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge. In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. In its final decision, the Agency found that Complainant was an individual with a disability and that he was qualified within the meaning of the Rehabilitation Act. Assuming Complainant established a prima facie case of discrimination and retaliation, the Agency concluded that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons that Complainant failed to rebut as pretextual. Complainant began his employment with the Agency on January 17, 2021, with a Competitive- Career Conditional Appointment, which required him to be a probationary employee for one year. He had previously worked for the Agency as an Administrative Manager (Excepted Service Appointment) during the decennial census. In a progress review dated June 15, 2021, the person listed as Complainant’s first-level supervisor stated that Complainant was not performing at the fully successful level 3 or above and listed areas for improvement, including becoming familiarized with the onboarding and payroll processes and timely completion of assignments. In three emails from June 2021, S3 (third level supervisor, Program Coordinator) emailed Complainant regarding some performance issues, including partial or missing pay for two employees in Complainant’s service area, the payroll processing for pay period 11 of that year, and the status of several new hires. S3 also issued Complainant a memorandum on June 17, 2021, titled “Failure to Follow Up on Payroll Issues,” outlining his performance deficiencies. Another of Complainant’s first-level supervisors (S1), Administrative Officer, stated in her affidavit that Complainant had errors and issues with his work that caused several people not to receive their pay on time, which resulted in new hires resigning. S1, who became Complainant’s supervisor in early July 2021, retrained the staff upon learning of these errors. S1 stated that even after retraining, Complainant “continued to have unresolved pay issues for the new hires he was responsible for.” S3 issued Complainant a termination letter on July 28, 2021, citing his unacceptable performance during his probationary period. The letter stated that he had failed to ensure timely onboarding of new hires and tracking them through the hiring process. In addition, the letter stated he failed to successfully process payroll in a timely matter. Another supervisor, Administrative Specialist (AS), said she supervised Complainant until his termination, though her affidavit indicated that she supervised and assigned Complainant tasks related to the Census Investigative Service Missing Documents Project as opposed to payroll/timekeeping. AS claims that she did not observe any unacceptable job performance issues concerning Complainant and that no such issues were brought to her attention regarding his involvement in the Missing Documents Project. AS averred that she believed Complainant was terminated based on his disabilities and for requesting a reasonable accommodation based on her observation of “tension between the Complainant and [S3] regarding his work schedule.” The Agency found that management’s legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for terminating Complainant during his probationary period were based on his performance issues in processing payroll and new hire onboarding, which he often failed to complete without errors or on time. In addressing the question of whether Complainant established pretext, the Agency noted AS’s affidavit, where she stated she did not observe any performance problems by Complainant while under her supervision. The Agency determined that AS only supervised one aspect of Complainant’s work, the Missing Documents Project, not timekeeping and processing of new hires. Because three of Complainant’s supervisors confirmed his deficiencies in those areas, the Agency found that AS’s statements did not cast doubt on the Agency’s explanation. The Agency also reasoned that there was no evidence that S3 voiced opposition to Complainant’s reasonable accommodation or his telework schedule, especially given that all of the Administrative Technicians she supervised teleworked two days per week for at least a portion of the period at issue. The Agency therefore concluded Complainant could not show management’s reasons were pretext for discrimination or reprisal, beyond Complainant’s subjective belief.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Clerk at the Agency’s Fort Bend County Area Census Office, Dallas Regional Census Center in Katy, Texas. Operations Office Supervisor (OOS) 1 was her direct supervisor. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 116, 147. OOS 2 was Complainant’s superior but was not within her direct supervisory chain. ROI at 154. Administrative Manager was her second-level supervisor. ROI at 134. Area Census Office Manager (Manager) was her third-level supervisor. ROI at 144. 1. based on race (African-American), color (Black), sex (Female), age (year of birth (YOB): 1944), and retaliation for prior EEO activity (opposition) in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, she was subjected to harassment: a. On August 3, 2020, Complainant was accused of sleeping on the job by OOS 2, who then told OOS 1, Administrative Manager, and others that Complainant was old, tired, and was not use to the hours; b. On August 6, 2020, Complainant was accused of removing a headset from another workspace and was verbally counseled by OOS 1, despite having prior approval; c. On August 6, 2020, Complainant was stalked and threatened with a reprimand for allegedly sleeping on the job by OOS 1; d. On August 8, 2020, Complainant’s desk was surrounded by OOS 2, Census Field Manager (CFM) 1 and CFM 2, Agency Officials, who accused Complainant of sleeping on the job and told Complainant to leave in front of others; and e. Between August 2, 2020, and August 8, 2020, Complainant was subjected to sarcastic remarks by OOS 1; 2. based on race and retaliation, on August 10, 2020, she was terminated by Manager and Administrative Manager. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant makes several arguments as to the appropriateness of the Agency’s decision. She asserts that the Agency’s decision was “hostile, racial, inappropriate and inaccurate.” She argues that the documents relied upon by the Agency were “malicious, racial, retaliatory, coached and concocted lies.” Finally, she alleges that the EEO Investigator was unfair because the Investigator said they were unable to require people no longer with the Agency to participate in an EEO investigation. The Agency did not submit arguments in opposition to Complainant’s appeal.

During the relevant time, Complainant worked as an Aircraft Mechanic at the Agency’s Aircraft Maintenance Squadron facility in Robins Air Force Base, Georgia. At the time of the event in this claim, Aircraft Overhaul Supervisor (Supervisor) was his first-level supervisor. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 161-62. Production Team Lead (Team Lead) was his second-level supervisor. ROI at 169. On May 25, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency subjected him to a hostile work environment on the bases of race (African-American), color (Black), and age (52) when, on December 11, 2020, Supervisor refused to render first aide to Complainant for a bleeding head wound and verbally assaulted Complainant when he screamed to Complainant, "Get your ass back on the plane, you do not do shit every day, I want you off my fucking team immediately, and I am tired of your shit.” At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. On January 21, 2022, the AJ issued a Notice of Proposed Summary Judgment (Notice) and provided each of the parties an opportunity to respond. In the Notice, the AJ outlined the relevant facts of the case. The AJ indicated that Complainant had an accident that caused him to bleed from his head. While looking for the band-aid, Supervisor observed Complainant away from his work area and began to yell at Complainant, including the statement outlined above. The AJ noted that Complainant conceded that he did not believe that this was based on age or race. However, Complainant added that Supervisor treated him differently due to his protected classes due to past unspecified incidents, but Complainant did not approach Supervisor about the past incidents. Supervisor did not deny yelling at Complainant but said that he had numerous performance concerns with Complainant. After the incident, Complainant contacted Team Lead and another Agency official about the incident. Supervisor was suspended without pay for 10 days, reassigned to day shift, and precluded from supervising anyone for 90 days. Supervisor’s role as Complainant’s supervisor ended immediately after the incident. ROI at 162. The AJ found that Supervisor’s behavior was unprofessional and unacceptable but did not rise to the level of harassment. The AJ noted that this was a single incident where Supervisor lost his temper using facially neutral language. Even when considering the background allegations, the AJ found that the totality of the circumstances did not reveal a work environment permeated with hostility nor does the cursing demonstrate sufficient severity. Therefore, the AJ indicated the intent to issue a decision without a hearing finding in favor of the Agency. Both parties were offered the opportunity to respond to the Notice. Complainant provided his stipulations of fact which included, for the first time, additional allegations in support of his claim. Complainant stated without providing supporting evidence that Supervisor has a history of hatred towards him and of mistreatment of other African-Americans at work. Complainant asserted for the first time that Supervisor made comments about President Obama and displayed images of the confederate flag in the hangar. The Agency did not provide a response by the deadline to the Notice but did produce the suspension paperwork of Supervisor to the AJ. Over Complainant's objections, the AJ issued a decision without a hearing on February 25, 2022. The AJ incorporated the Notice. The AJ also noted that Complainant initially reported that he believed that the incident was not due to his race or his age. In addition, the AJ indicated that the background allegations were never included in the EEO Counselor Report, the formal complaint, or Complainant’s affidavit. Given the totality of the circumstances, the AJ found that Complainant did not prove he was discriminated against as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Complainant contends that he was “humiliated, intimidated, bullied and exposed to racist comments and treatment by [Supervisor].” He alleges that he provided the investigators a list of incidents that were racially motivated and he provided a list of witnesses to these events. He says that allegations of racial, age or color discrimination were made several times prior to summary judgment. Finally, Complainant claims that the Agency has withheld “vital information” about Supervisor and summary judgment denied him the opportunity to obtain this information which, Complainant asserts, “will prove a history of racial discrimination [of Supervisor] towards African Americans.” In response, the Agency argues that the AJ’s summary judgment was proper and should stand.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as an Information Technology Specialist at the Agency’s Office of the Chief Information Officer, Division of Customer Service Operations and Engineering in Columbia, South Carolina. 1. on September 26, 2016, Complainant was excluded from weekly meetings; 2. on September 17, and October 14, 2016, 2 management attempted to cancel Complainant’s maxi-flex schedule; 3. from 2015 to 2017, Complainant was not provided with quarterly performance reviews; 4. on or about August 1, 2016, the department timekeeper said that she would stop completing Complainant’s time and attendance; 5. in or around June 2016, management threatened to charge Complainant with absence without leave (AWOL); 6. on May 25, 2016, management made an unannounced visit to South Carolina; 7. on May 22, 2016, Complainant was forced to travel to Washington, D.C.; 8. on May 16, 2016, management attempted to make Complainant travel to Washington, D.C.; 9. on February 26, 2016, management insisted that Complainant work a full day; 10. on January 25, 2016, management attempted to make Complainant travel on the day before and the day of her Sabbath; 11. on January 12, 2016, management attempted to make Complainant travel on the Martin Luther King, Jr. holiday; 12. on August 15, 2016, Complainant was reassigned to Washington, D.C.; 3 13. since May 2016, Complainant was not assigned any new projects; 14. on May 25, 2016, management did not discuss Complainant’s fiscal year 2015 appraisal with her and accused her of refusing to sign; 15. on or around May 2016, Complainant submitted requests to attend training and all her requests were denied; 16. on February 8-12, 2016, Complainant was charged AWOL; 17. on February 11, 2016, Complainant had to edit four Standard Operating Procedure manuals while out sick; 18. in or around September 2015, Complainant was transferred to another division; 19. on January 19, 2016, Complainant’s pay was not deposited into her checking account; 20. on February 19, 2016, and May 19, 2016, Complainant was denied sick leave; 21. on February 4, 2016, Complainant’s leave was canceled; and 22. on February 4, 2016, Complainant was forced to travel to Washington, D.C. from February 8-12, 2016. On appeal, Complainant notes that this occurred in 2015, not 2016. Complainant also alleged that the Agency breached a 2007 settlement agreement when it reassigned her to Washington, D.C. The Commission found that the Agency did not breach the settlement agreement. Susie K. v. Small Business Admin., EEOC [number removed] (Mar. 9, 2017); request for recon. denied, EEOC [number removed] (Jun. 22, 2017). The Agency issued a partial acceptance and only accepted claim 1 for investigation. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 53, 110-17. Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ), who dismissed Complainant’s hearing request because she failed to provide an affidavit to the EEO Investigator. The Agency subsequently issued a final decision and concluded that Complainant failed to prove discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed the Agency’s final decision. The appellate decision found that the dismissal of the listed claims comprising Complainant’s hostile work environment claim was improper because the Agency fragmented the claims. While many of the incidents were untimely as discrete claims, they may be used as background evidence for the hostile work environment claim. As such, the appellate decision vacated the Agency’s final decision and remanded the complaint back to the Agency for processing. Tracey M. v. Small Business Admin., EEOC [number removed] (Sept. 16, 2020). At the conclusion of the supplemental investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the Supplemental ROI and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC AJ. Complainant initially requested a hearing but withdrew her request. The AJ remanded the complaint to the Agency to issue a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency noted that only claims 1, 3, and 12 were timely discrete claims, and that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for these actions. The Agency then found that Complainant failed to demonstrate that the Agency’s reasons were pretexts for discrimination. For Complainant’s overall harassment claim, the Agency determined that Complainant provided no evidence that any of the actions were due to her race, color, age, or prior EEO activity. Further, they were not intimidating, hostile, or offensive to rise the level of a hostile work environment. The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that she was subjected to discrimination as alleged. Complainant filed the instant appeal and submitted a brief in support of her appeal. The Agency opposed Complainant’s appeal. Complainant filed a response to the Agency’s brief on September 24, 2022, and the Agency moved to strike Complainant’s response.

At the time of events giving rise to the complaints, Complainants worked as Emergency Management Specialists (Regional and National Tribal Government Liaisons) at the Agency’s First Responder Network Authority, working remotely from Pauma Valley, California and Thousand Palms, California. Complainants began their employment with the Agency in October 2015 at the Pay Band IV level. Starting on June 13, 2019, Complainants each filed formal EEO complaints alleging that the Agency subjected them to discrimination and harassment on the bases of race (Native American), national origin (Native American), and sex, 3 and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity, when: 1. Since Complainants were hired by the Agency, they have been subjected to discrimination in pay when: a. Complainant 1 engaged in salary negotiations with the Agency prior to being hired and was told that it was only obligated to offer him 70% of his previous wages, and he could “take it or leave it”; and he alleged that non-Natives were not subjected to the same treatment during the hiring process. Complainant 2 claimed that the Agency failed to account for changes in her prior salary or teaching wages and only offered a salary that was commensurate with her current tribal salary. b. Complainants performed the same work as peers who were hired at the Pay Band V level, but they were hired at the Pay Band IV and paid at the lowest level. c. In or around April 2018, the Executive Director, Public Safety Advocacy Directorate (“Executive Director”) directed Complainants’ supervisor (“Supervisor 1”) to conduct a review to address wage and pay band disparities, but the Executive Director and a Senior Director took no action after the review was completed and failed to acknowledge that it occurred. d. In a May 31, 2018 telephone conversation, the Senior Director claimed that he was unaware of the above-referenced review, but Complainants later learned from Supervisor 1 that the Senior Director was “very well aware” of it. e. On June 15, 2018, Complainants inquired with the Deputy Chief Administrative Officer about hiring and direct hiring authorities but were told that the Agency “does not have personnel policies and practices.” The Deputy Complainants withdrew their claims of sex discrimination during the hearing process. 3 [number removed], [number removed] Chief Administrative Officer also failed to apprise Complainants of their right to pursue the EEO process to address their allegations of discriminatory pay. f. In or around July 2018, Complainants’ new supervisor (“Supervisor 2”) inquired with the Executive Director and Senior Director about the April 2018 review, but they denied any knowledge of committing to the review. g. In January 2019, the Executive Director acknowledged to Supervisor 2 that he had received the review but asserted that he felt no obligation to act on it. The Executive Director then instructed Supervisor 2 to “tamper any escalation of [human resources (HR)] issues for the tribal team,” but then backpaddled in a subsequent email and claimed that Supervisor 2 misunderstood his instructions. 4 2. Complainants were precluded from applying to senior leadership positions due to the discriminatory setting of their pay at the Pay Band IV level when the Agency made senior leadership positions available only to Pay Band V employees. 3. In June 2018, Complainants were “buried deeper” in the organization through a reorganization process, in an effort to provoke Complainants to quit their jobs and as a means to “limit any HR escalations from [the] tribal team”. 4. On an ongoing basis since at least June 2018, Complainants were tasked with creating separate strategic plans, while none of their non-Tribal team peers were required to do the same. 5. On multiple occasions between June 2018 and February 2019, Complainants and other Agency officials repeatedly apprised senior leadership that they (Tribal team members) were being subjected to hostile and discriminatory treatment by officials of an Agency contractor. However, senior leadership condoned the contractors’ treatment and continued to place the team in hostile situations with contracting officials. 6. On an ongoing basis, Complainants have been denied equal access to resources to perform their duties in the same manner as their peers when: a. Complainants were forced to coordinate all their activities through a separate, discriminatory process to access resources and their non-federal shareholders. We note that the Agency accepted claim 1 with subparts (a) though (g), as outlined above. However, one of the AJs did not include the subparts in the Case Management Order. Instead, the AJ noted a consolidation of the subparts and that claim 1 included the allegation that management officials took no remedial action after reviewing wage and pay band disparities. As such, we find that subparts 1(c) though 1(g) fall under that allegation. 4 [number removed], [number removed] b. Complainants have been forced to engage with the contracting staff and Tribal shareholders through a “gatekeeper.” c. The Agency limited the types of meetings Complainants were allowed to participate in. d. An Agency Contracting Officer’s Representative was required to participate in daily engagements between contractors and Complainants. 7. On May 5, 2019, the Agency failed to acknowledge Complainants and other Tribal team members’ accomplishments when issuing a tweet which thanked local, state, and federal workers for their dedication and service, but did not reference the Tribal team. At the conclusion of the investigations, Complainants were provided copies of the investigative files, and they requested hearings before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). The two complaints were assigned to different AJs in the Commission’s Washington Field Office. Complainants’ shared attorney filed motions to consolidate the complaints for joint processing before each AJ. The Agency opposed the motions. One AJ denied the motion and the other AJ did not address the motion. The AJs issued separate summary judgment decisions finding no discrimination or unlawful retaliation was established. The Agency’s final actions implemented the AJs’ decisions. The instant appeals from both Complainants followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Registered Nurse in the 4 East Medical-Surgical Unit at the Veterans Affairs Medical Center (VAMC) in West Los Angeles, California. During the relevant time, Complainant’s first level supervisor was the Nurse Manager for the 4 East Medical-Surgical Unit (S1). 1. Complainant’s first line supervisor, the Nurse Manager 4 East (S1), demanded that Complainant work twelve-hour shifts, which Complainant refused. 2 2. In May 2018, S1 stated in front of coworkers that because the Agency canceled her surgery, she should go to another hospital for services, thereby disclosing her confidential medical information in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. 3 3. During January 2019, Complainant was required to work with coworkers who had improperly accessed her confidential medical records without authorization. 4. During January 2019, management failed to resolve Complainant’s sick leave issues in a timely manner. 5. On March 5, 2019, Complainant’s coworker referred to her as “a 50-year-old mental patient.” 6. On May 1, 2019, S1 told Complainant’s coworker, who was allegedly bullying and harassing Complainant, not to worry and that she “had her back.” 7. On May 1, 2019, Complainant was accused of being intimidating and aggressive and was accused of engaging in harassing behavior by a coworker who was bullying Complainant. 8. On May 3, 2019, Complainant was accused of sending an email from another employee’s email account. 9. On May 3, 2019, S1 requested that Complainant sign a misconduct form. 10. On May 28, 2019, S1 paced in front of Complainant’s work area. 11. On May 28, 2019, S1 accused her of misconduct. 12. On June 6, 2019, an unnamed employee interfered with Complainant’s privacy violation investigation. 13. On August 20, 2019, Complainant discovered an article posted on the report table about nurses with mental disabilities, which she thought was directed at her. Originally this claim was listed as “management refused to change Complainant’s schedule to 12-hour shifts.” However, the Agency noted Complainant stated that she did not request to work 12-hour shifts, and S1 “demanded that she switch from 8 to 12 hours.” In a supplemental affidavit, Complainant stated this event did not happen in May 2018, but that it occurred in November or December 2017. 14. On unspecified dates, S1 “split the staff against each other” and did not properly resolve issues that occurred on the floor. The Agency’s Office of Resolution Management (ORM) issued a Notice of Partial Acceptance dismissing a portion of claim 7 in which Complainant claimed that she was accused of engaging in harassing behavior by a coworker, for failure to state a claim. The Agency accepted the remaining claims. The Agency noted that claim 1 constituted a timely raised independently actionable claim and was also part of the harassment claim. Further, the Agency stated claims 2, 3, and 12 were accepted for investigation as discrete events under the confidentiality provisions of the Rehabilitation Act, not as a violation of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act or the Privacy Act. The Agency accepted the remaining claims for investigation. Complainant noted that she was scheduled to have surgery at the VAMC and that it had been canceled several times. Complainant noted that each time her surgery was canceled, she had to redo her request for leave under the Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA) and have S1 sign the new form. Complainant stated that after the fourth time her surgery was canceled, in November or December 2017, she presented a new form for S1 to sign which she stated she presented to S1 in S1’s private office. Thereafter, Complainant stated that as S1 walked down the hallway between the reception station and the nurses’ station, S1 was talking loudly and said, “And you, you need to go somewhere else to have your surgery. If the VA is not taking care of you, you need to go to UCLA.” Complainant identified two witnesses to this event: Witness 1, who she stated heard S1 talking about her surgery and asked if she was okay; and Witness 13, who she stated was at the reception station and asked why S1 was telling everyone about her surgery. Further, Complainant stated that she overheard Witness 12 tell another coworker it was unfair for them to go through Complainant’s medical records and spread information throughout the ward. Complainant suspected employee(s) had improperly accessed her VAMC medical records. In April 2019, Complainant contacted the Privacy Office to request a printout of everyone who accessed her records for the past three years. She noted that she received a report in the mail. Upon review of the report, Complainant believed that several of the coworkers on the list accessed her medical records improperly and asked the Privacy Officer to investigate. She stated the Privacy Officer asked her to review the list and highlight the coworkers who accessed her record without being involved in her care while she was a patient. Complainant provided a printout of a list with four columns. The first column lists employees’ names; the second column lists dates and times; the third column lists notes such as “CPRSChart version 1, Appointment Management, Case No. Exam Edit, Register Patient, Clinical Scheduling;” and a fourth column lists “No” or “Yes.” Next to the first column is an arrow next to six names: Coworker 1, Coworker 2, Coworker 3, Coworker 4, Coworker 5, and Coworker 6. Next to the last column are handwritten notes indicating where the six employees with the arrow next to their names worked. The record contains a July 1, 2019 letter addressed to Complainant which was signed by the Privacy Officer on behalf of the Acting Director. The letter noted that on June 18, 2019, an email was received from Complainant stating that three coworkers: Coworker 2 (Nurse), Coworker 3 (Nurse), and Coworker 4 (Nurse) inappropriately accessed her medical record based upon the Sensitive Patient Access Report (SPAR) provided by their office on April 12, 2019. The letter stated during the fact-finding process, they discovered that “Ms. [Coworker 4], Ms. [blank] inappropriately accessed your medical record outside of her duties and responsibilities and had no valid reason to access your medical records.” The letter stated the other employees Complainant identified on the SPAR report as having inappropriately accessed her medical records, “did so within their job responsibilities.” The letter stated the employee’s supervisory staff were notified and it was “recommended the employee’s immediately retake the mandatory privacy and security training.” S1 stated that in response to Complainant’s April 9, 2019 email alleging that a coworker had possibly accessed her medical records, S1 immediately initiated an inquiry with the Privacy Officer to verify if a coworker had violated Complainant’s right to privacy by looking at her medical record.
