S1 stated that it was discovered that coworkers had violated Complainant’s privacy. S1 stated that two coworkers that were working with Complainant received disciplinary action. S1 provided documentation regarding discipline for two employees. Specifically, the record contains a letter from the Acting Director to an unidentified addressee dated September 4, 2019. The letter has a handwritten notation of “Employee 1” and indicates that a decision has been made to uphold the proposed suspension of seven calendar days for a Privacy Act Violation. The record also contains a letter from the Acting Director to an unidentified addressee dated September 5, 2019. The letter has a handwritten notation of “Employee 2” and notes a decision has been made to mitigate the proposed suspension of seven days to a one-day suspension for a Privacy Act Violation. The record contains a Privacy Investigation Report noting that on April 8, 2019, Complainant requested a SPAR and identified six employees that either currently work with her or on inpatient ward 4EAB or that worked with her on 4EAB in the past, that she believed inappropriately accessed her CPRS medical records outside of their job responsibilities. The report noted that Complainant also alleged that “her supervisor mentioned her surgery during the presence of other staff during a shift change and in meetings.” It was noted that Complainant had surgery on June 26, 2018. The report found that out of the six employees identified by Complainant, two currently working on 4E were determined to have inappropriately accessed Complainant’s medical record outside their duties and responsibilities. It was noted that Coworker 4 accessed Complainant’s medical records on June 15, 2018. The report noted that Coworker 4 said that “everyone was talking about [Complainant’s] surgery, including she and another employee that she witnessed accessing [Complainant’s] medical record under her [Coworker 4’s] access.” The report noted Coworker 4 did not have a valid reason for accessing Complainant’s medical record and that her actions were intentional. The report also stated that Coworker 3 currently worked on ward 4EAD had accessed Complainant’s medical records six times throughout 2018 and 2019. According to the report, Coworker 3 stated she wanted to check the schedule because Complainant had written her up on several occasions and she did not want to work on the same shift as Complainant. The report noted that Coworker 3 did not have a valid reason for accessing Complainant’s medical records and that “scheduling information is not located in CPRS therefore accessing this information is not for scheduling purposes and was intentional.” Further, it was noted that “[Coworker 4] and other employees stated that [Complainant] mentioned to them that ‘she was having surgery.’” The report stated that no evidence was found to confirm that Complainant’s supervisor disclosed any information regarding her surgery in any meeting. At the conclusion of the EEO investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). In its final decision, the Agency adopted the ORM’s decision to dismiss Complainant’s claim that on May 1, 2019, a coworker asserted that Complainant had subjected the coworker to harassment by being intimidating and aggressive. The Agency noted that the claim was accepted for consideration in Complainant’s overall harassment claim. The Agency addressed claims 1, 2, 3, and 12 under a disparate treatment theory. Regarding claim 1, the Agency noted the undisputed evidence showed Complainant remained on her eight- hour tour of duty at all times. The Agency found this claim was not supported by the record. Further, the Agency stated even accepting her claim as true, there was no indication of discriminatory motive. Regarding claim 2, Complainant claimed that S1 made a statement about her seeking surgery at another facility in an area where others could overhear S1’s statement, thereby disclosing her confidential medical information in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. The Agency noted that S1 stated she only discussed Complainant’s surgery with Complainant privately to offer her emotional support and argued there was no evidence beyond Complainant’s subjective testimony that anyone overheard the statement. The Agency noted the six coworkers who were interviewed as part of Complainant’s privacy investigation all confirmed that S1 did not disclose any information about Complainant’s surgery or any other confidential medical information to them. Instead, the Agency stated, they learned of Complainant’s surgery from Complainant sharing the information directly. The Agency noted Complainant admitted in her testimony that she told at least one coworker that she was going to have surgery, but it had been canceled. The Agency concluded that Complainant did not show that S1 improperly disclosed her confidential medical information. The Agency stated even if it credited Complainant’s version of the incident and assumed that others overheard the statement, of which it stated there was no evidence, the vague reference allegedly made by S1 did not disclose confidential medical information. Regarding claim 3, the Agency noted the Commission has held that allegations that the Privacy Act has been violated were not within the purview of the EEOC Regulations, without a further allegation that the Privacy Act violation resulted from prohibited discrimination. The Agency stated that Complainant did not provide evidence of discriminatory animus due to her disability, and the privacy investigation determined that the two coworkers who accessed her records did so to find out when she would be out for surgery, and because one of them did not want to work when Complainant was working. The Agency found no indication and no evidence was provided by Complainant of any discriminatory motivation or wrongdoing beyond the Privacy Act violation. Regarding claim 12, the Agency stated there was no indication of any alleged “resistance” from Complainant’s coworkers during the Privacy Investigation, or that even if accepted as true, any such resistance was based on discriminatory animus. The Agency noted S1 promptly reported Complainant’s concern that her privacy had been violated to the Privacy Office, a privacy investigation was conducted, and all the employees Complainant identified as potentially accessing her medical records were interviewed, and two employees were identified as having improperly accessed her records. The Agency noted those employees were subsequently disciplined and ordered to retake privacy training. The Agency stated there was no evidence that the failure to take other disciplinary measures was due to discriminatory animus. Regarding the hostile work environment claim, the Agency stated even accepting Complainant’s allegations as true, she has presented no evidence she was singled out for treatment based on her disability. The Agency noted Witness 1, who has not worked for the Agency since 2018, provided only a vague statement that S1 allegedly told him Complainant was having “mental issues,” which was contradicted by S1’s testimony. The Agency stated S1 was unaware Complainant had a disability, and although she noted Complainant had taken bereavement leave after the death of a parent, to S1’s knowledge, it was not related to any mental or other disability. The Agency noted Witness 2’s statement gave no indication of S1 having discriminatory animus against Complainant based on her disability. The Agency noted that both witnesses expressed personal complaints about S1, rendering their statements less credible. The Agency found Complainant failed to show that she was subjected to unlawful harassment based on her disability.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Supervisory Public Health Veterinarian in Seguin, Texas. On December 21, 2017, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her based on her race (Caucasian), color (White), sex (female), disability, age (62), and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity. 1. On February 6, 2018, management issued her a Letter of Instruction for Canceling Second Shift. 2. On December 12, 2017, she learned a management official discussed her medical condition and EEO complaint with other Managers, which led to other employees sharing information related to Complainant’s medical condition and EEO complaint. 3. On November 3, 2017, management issued her a Letter of Counseling entitled Untimely Completion of Performance Management Duties. 4. On September 21, 201, management subjected her to an investigation regarding her supervision of two employees. 5. On an unspecified date, management denied her request for a reasonable accommodation to work duty hours as prescribed by her doctor. 6. On an unspecified date, management denied her request to return to work and charged her with eight hours of sick leave. 7. Since September 2017, her supervisor has subjected her to various acts of harassment, including but not limited to the following matters: a. On an unspecified date, her first level supervisor stated being a woman, she (Complainant) had a different supervisory style than her male colleague; b. On an unspecified date, her first level supervisor instructed her to write up an employee for an event for which Complainant did not have firsthand knowledge; and c. On unspecified dates, management failed to keep her informed, in order for her to perform her duties. Following an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination. The Agency stated that it had articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its action. Regarding claim (1), the Agency stated that Complainant cancelled second shift when she did not have the authority to do so. Regarding claim (2), a management official discussing Complainant’s EEO complaint and medical information, the Agency asserted that Complainant’s second-level supervisor acknowledged that he shared Complainant’s reasonable accommodation with W1 because W1 is responsible for ensuring that the shift is sufficiently staffed. Regarding claim (3), the Agency asserts that Complainant failed to issue a performance appraisal in a timely manner. Regarding claim (4), being subjected to an investigation, the Agency stated that Complainant was subjected to an investigation due to complaints made by employees that Complainant was harassing them. Regarding claims (5) and (6), the Agency asserts that Complainant was eventually approved to work two to four hours a day and that a management official needed to discuss with Complainant what duties she would be able to perform. Regarding claim (7), the Agency found that the alleged incidents were not sufficiently severe or pervasive to constitute harassment. The Agency further found that Complainant failed to establish that the Agency’s articulated reasons for its actions were pretext for discrimination and/or retaliation. The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant reiterates that the Agency subjected her to discriminatory harassment.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Supervisory IT Cybersecurity Specialist within the Agency’s Financial Management Directorate (FMD) in Herndon, Virginia. On August 27, 2020, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of disability (vertigo) and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity. On November 9, 2020, the Agency accepted the formal complaint for investigation. and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. On September 15, 2021, the AJ issued a Post Conference Order. Therein, the AJ found that the parties agreed to the following framing of the issues: 1. Whether the Agency discriminated against Complainant based on her disability when it did not grant a reasonable accommodation request on or about February 19, 2020. 2. Whether the Agency discriminated against Complainant based on her EEO activity, including subjecting her to reprisal-based harassment, from March 2019 to February 2021 (as manifested by the numerous events averments to the Agency’s EEO Office in the ROI, Tab 3, and in the Complainant’s preliminary conference report to the [AJ]). The AJ also ordered, in pertinent part, that one sentence be redacted from the ROI at 173, an affidavit from an Agency official, no later than October 15, 2021. On November 15, 2021, Complainant withdrew her request for a hearing and requested a final agency decision. The AJ issued an Order of Dismissal and Remand for Final Agency Decision on November 15, 2021. On January 4, 2022, the Agency issued a final decision finding no discrimination. Regarding claim (1), the denial of a reasonable accommodation, the Agency found that it provided Complainant with her requested accommodation – a full-time telework. Final Agency Decision (FAD) at 36. Specifically, the Agency set forth, “[s]he requested full-time telework, and the Agency granted that accommodation. She has not alleged that the Agency has asked her to come back to the office since she was granted her requested accommodation of full-time telework in March 2020. While Complainant has disagreed with the Agency’s terminology related to her requested accommodation, the Agency nonetheless provided her with the requested accommodation.” Id. Regarding claim (2), a reprisal-based harassment claim, the Agency found that Complainant failed to establish that the numerous alleged incidents at issue were motivated by her protected activity. FAD at 35. The Agency reasoned, “[a]lthough some of the management officials knew of her previous EEO activity, there is no evidence that the conduct she alleged is related to her prior EEO activity…The record reveals that multiple employees who did not have a technical background completed the [Information Systems Security Officer, ISSO duties]. While Complainant characterizes the reassignment of these tasks as based on her protected EEO activity, there is no evidence that this is the case. To the contrary, the ISSO tasks seemed to be assigned to multiple individuals without a technical background. Id. The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant, through her attorney, requests that we reverse the Agency’s FAD. Complainant’s attorney sets forth that the FAD “relies on unauthorized confidential settlement disclosures made by a [named Agency official] in his declaration as a basis for reaching its conclusions – after the [AJ] initially assigned to the case ordered the Agency to have those portions of the affidavit redacted and the Agency failed to follow that order. The AJ instructed the Agency to redact the references to confidential settlement communications found in [a named Agency official’s] affidavit…The Agency did not follow the AJ’s instructions…” FAD at 1. Based on the foregoing, Complainant’s attorney asserts that the Agency should be sanctioned for failing to follow the AJ’s Order and for using what should have been redacted to form a conclusion that is adverse to Complainant. Complainant’s Brief at 1 n.1. Regarding claim (1), the denial of a reasonable accommodation, Complainant asserts that she was granted telework as a “temporary job modification” and not a reasonable accommodation. Thus, Complainant asserts that she never received notification that her reasonable accommodation was approved. Regarding claim (2), a reprisal-based harassment claim, Complainant asserts that the Agency assigned her ISSO duties based on her prior protected EEO activity in an effort to overload her with work. Complainant’s Brief at 23. Specifically, Complainant, through her attorney, asserts that “[m]anagement’s explanation that [she] was best qualified for the ISSO work defies logic, as she had never performed the tasks previously, nor had they ever provided her with any training before assigning her duties that required immediate action and no ongoing support.” Id. In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision. The Agency asserts it did comply with the AJ’s Order by submitting a redacted ROI on October 15, 2021 and a corrected supplemental ROI on October 29, 2021. The Agency set forth that “[w]hile the FAD does cite to and references [a named Agency official’s] affidavit in general, the information…which the AJ required redaction is never specifically referred to…in the FAD.” Agency’s Brief at 3. At the time of events giving rise to the complaints, Complainants worked as Emergency Management Specialists (Regional and National Tribal Government Liaisons) at the Agency’s First Responder Network Authority, working remotely from Pauma Valley, California and Thousand Palms, California. Complainants began their employment with the Agency in October 2015 at the Pay Band IV level. Starting on June 13, 2019, Complainants each filed formal EEO complaints alleging that the Agency subjected them to discrimination and harassment on the bases of race (Native American), national origin (Native American), and sex, 3 and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity, when: 1. Since Complainants were hired by the Agency, they have been subjected to discrimination in pay when: a. Complainant 1 engaged in salary negotiations with the Agency prior to being hired and was told that it was only obligated to offer him 70% of his previous wages, and he could “take it or leave it”; and he alleged that non-Natives were not subjected to the same treatment during the hiring process. Complainant 2 claimed that the Agency failed to account for changes in her prior salary or teaching wages and only offered a salary that was commensurate with her current tribal salary. b. Complainants performed the same work as peers who were hired at the Pay Band V level, but they were hired at the Pay Band IV and paid at the lowest level. c. In or around April 2018, the Executive Director, Public Safety Advocacy Directorate (“Executive Director”) directed Complainants’ supervisor (“Supervisor 1”) to conduct a review to address wage and pay band disparities, but the Executive Director and a Senior Director took no action after the review was completed and failed to acknowledge that it occurred. d. In a May 31, 2018 telephone conversation, the Senior Director claimed that he was unaware of the above-referenced review, but Complainants later learned from Supervisor 1 that the Senior Director was “very well aware” of it. e. On June 15, 2018, Complainants inquired with the Deputy Chief Administrative Officer about hiring and direct hiring authorities but were told that the Agency “does not have personnel policies and practices.” The Deputy Complainants withdrew their claims of sex discrimination during the hearing process. 3 [number removed], [number removed] Chief Administrative Officer also failed to apprise Complainants of their right to pursue the EEO process to address their allegations of discriminatory pay. f. In or around July 2018, Complainants’ new supervisor (“Supervisor 2”) inquired with the Executive Director and Senior Director about the April 2018 review, but they denied any knowledge of committing to the review. g. In January 2019, the Executive Director acknowledged to Supervisor 2 that he had received the review but asserted that he felt no obligation to act on it. The Executive Director then instructed Supervisor 2 to “tamper any escalation of [human resources (HR)] issues for the tribal team,” but then backpaddled in a subsequent email and claimed that Supervisor 2 misunderstood his instructions. 4 2. Complainants were precluded from applying to senior leadership positions due to the discriminatory setting of their pay at the Pay Band IV level when the Agency made senior leadership positions available only to Pay Band V employees. 3. In June 2018, Complainants were “buried deeper” in the organization through a reorganization process, in an effort to provoke Complainants to quit their jobs and as a means to “limit any HR escalations from [the] tribal team”. 4. On an ongoing basis since at least June 2018, Complainants were tasked with creating separate strategic plans, while none of their non-Tribal team peers were required to do the same. 5. On multiple occasions between June 2018 and February 2019, Complainants and other Agency officials repeatedly apprised senior leadership that they (Tribal team members) were being subjected to hostile and discriminatory treatment by officials of an Agency contractor. However, senior leadership condoned the contractors’ treatment and continued to place the team in hostile situations with contracting officials. 6. On an ongoing basis, Complainants have been denied equal access to resources to perform their duties in the same manner as their peers when: a. Complainants were forced to coordinate all their activities through a separate, discriminatory process to access resources and their non-federal shareholders. We note that the Agency accepted claim 1 with subparts (a) though (g), as outlined above. However, one of the AJs did not include the subparts in the Case Management Order. Instead, the AJ noted a consolidation of the subparts and that claim 1 included the allegation that management officials took no remedial action after reviewing wage and pay band disparities. As such, we find that subparts 1(c) though 1(g) fall under that allegation. 4 [number removed], [number removed] b. Complainants have been forced to engage with the contracting staff and Tribal shareholders through a “gatekeeper.” c. The Agency limited the types of meetings Complainants were allowed to participate in. d. An Agency Contracting Officer’s Representative was required to participate in daily engagements between contractors and Complainants. 7. On May 5, 2019, the Agency failed to acknowledge Complainants and other Tribal team members’ accomplishments when issuing a tweet which thanked local, state, and federal workers for their dedication and service, but did not reference the Tribal team. At the conclusion of the investigations, Complainants were provided copies of the investigative files, and they requested hearings before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). The two complaints were assigned to different AJs in the Commission’s Washington Field Office. Complainants’ shared attorney filed motions to consolidate the complaints for joint processing before each AJ. The Agency opposed the motions. One AJ denied the motion and the other AJ did not address the motion. The AJs issued separate summary judgment decisions finding no discrimination or unlawful retaliation was established. The Agency’s final actions implemented the AJs’ decisions. The instant appeals from both Complainants followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Census Field Supervisor, AD-0303-00, at the Agency’s Area Census Office (ACO) in Traverse City, Michigan. Complainant is a white Caucasian. The identified responsible management officials (RMOs) were aware of Complainant’s race and color from observation. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 101. Management terminated Complainant’s employment on September 18, 2020. On October 9, 2020, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him and subjected him to a hostile work environment on the bases of race (Caucasian), color (White), and age (unspecified). Complainant’s allegations are stated as follows. 1. Whether management subjected Complainant to harassment and a hostile work environment when: a. On September 19, 2020, Area Manager (RMO 1) accused Complainant of having violated Census policy by using his personal funds to reimburse an employee who traveled 130 miles to attend a training that she was not permitted to attend; b. On September 19, 2020, RMO 1 sent Complainant an email stating he was only permitted at the ACO when the workload called for it and at this time he was not needed at the ACO. If there were items he needed from the ACO, his Chief Financial Manager (CFM) could coordinate a way to get them to him; c. On an unspecified date, an employee from the Information Technology (IT [RMO 2]) office chased Complainant around the office harassingly telling him to "run" after RMO 1 threatened over the speakerphone to call U.S. Marshals on Complainant; d. On September 24, 2020, Administrative Manager (RMO 3) sent Complainant an email stating the U.S. Census was separating him due to his no call, no shows; since September 18, 2020, which it considered job abandonment; and e. Whether management discriminated against Complainant when on September 18, 2020, Complainant was terminated. The Agency conducted an investigation into the complaint. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. On October 18, 2021, the Agency submitted a Motion for a Decision Without a Hearing (Motion). Complainant responded to the Motion. On January 31, 2022, the AJ issued his decision. The AJ determined that the investigative record was adequately developed. After making all reasonable inferences in favor of Complainant, he determined that there were no material facts in dispute. Regarding the merits of Complainant’s claim, the AJ determined that the Agency had set forth non-discriminatory reasons for the above detailed actions and that Complainant failed to demonstrate that such reasons were pretext for discrimination. The AJ also determined that Complainant failed to demonstrate that the Agency’s conduct met the severe and pervasive elements needed to sustain a proper unlawful hostile work environment claim. The AJ found that Complainant’s complaint could essentially be characterized by her utter dissatisfaction and personal grievances against her coworkers and management. Ultimately, the AJ granted the Agency’s Motion. When the Agency failed to issue a final action, the AJ’s decision became the Agency's final action by operation of law. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as an Information Technology Specialist at the Agency’s Office of the Chief Information Officer, Division of Customer Service Operations and Engineering in Columbia, South Carolina. 1. on September 26, 2016, Complainant was excluded from weekly meetings; 2. on September 17, and October 14, 2016, 2 management attempted to cancel Complainant’s maxi-flex schedule; 3. from 2015 to 2017, Complainant was not provided with quarterly performance reviews; 4. on or about August 1, 2016, the department timekeeper said that she would stop completing Complainant’s time and attendance; 5. in or around June 2016, management threatened to charge Complainant with absence without leave (AWOL); 6. on May 25, 2016, management made an unannounced visit to South Carolina; 7. on May 22, 2016, Complainant was forced to travel to Washington, D.C.; 8. on May 16, 2016, management attempted to make Complainant travel to Washington, D.C.; 9. on February 26, 2016, management insisted that Complainant work a full day; 10. on January 25, 2016, management attempted to make Complainant travel on the day before and the day of her Sabbath; 11. on January 12, 2016, management attempted to make Complainant travel on the Martin Luther King, Jr. holiday; 12. on August 15, 2016, Complainant was reassigned to Washington, D.C.; 3 13. since May 2016, Complainant was not assigned any new projects; 14. on May 25, 2016, management did not discuss Complainant’s fiscal year 2015 appraisal with her and accused her of refusing to sign; 15. on or around May 2016, Complainant submitted requests to attend training and all her requests were denied; 16. on February 8-12, 2016, Complainant was charged AWOL; 17. on February 11, 2016, Complainant had to edit four Standard Operating Procedure manuals while out sick; 18. in or around September 2015, Complainant was transferred to another division; 19. on January 19, 2016, Complainant’s pay was not deposited into her checking account; 20. on February 19, 2016, and May 19, 2016, Complainant was denied sick leave; 21. on February 4, 2016, Complainant’s leave was canceled; and 22. on February 4, 2016, Complainant was forced to travel to Washington, D.C. from February 8-12, 2016. On appeal, Complainant notes that this occurred in 2015, not 2016. Complainant also alleged that the Agency breached a 2007 settlement agreement when it reassigned her to Washington, D.C. The Commission found that the Agency did not breach the settlement agreement. Susie K. v. Small Business Admin., EEOC [number removed] (Mar. 9, 2017); request for recon. denied, EEOC [number removed] (Jun. 22, 2017). The Agency issued a partial acceptance and only accepted claim 1 for investigation. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 53, 110-17. Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ), who dismissed Complainant’s hearing request because she failed to provide an affidavit to the EEO Investigator. The Agency subsequently issued a final decision and concluded that Complainant failed to prove discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed the Agency’s final decision. The appellate decision found that the dismissal of the listed claims comprising Complainant’s hostile work environment claim was improper because the Agency fragmented the claims. While many of the incidents were untimely as discrete claims, they may be used as background evidence for the hostile work environment claim. As such, the appellate decision vacated the Agency’s final decision and remanded the complaint back to the Agency for processing. Tracey M. v. Small Business Admin., EEOC [number removed] (Sept. 16, 2020). At the conclusion of the supplemental investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the Supplemental ROI and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC AJ. Complainant initially requested a hearing but withdrew her request. The AJ remanded the complaint to the Agency to issue a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency noted that only claims 1, 3, and 12 were timely discrete claims, and that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for these actions. The Agency then found that Complainant failed to demonstrate that the Agency’s reasons were pretexts for discrimination. For Complainant’s overall harassment claim, the Agency determined that Complainant provided no evidence that any of the actions were due to her race, color, age, or prior EEO activity. Further, they were not intimidating, hostile, or offensive to rise the level of a hostile work environment. The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that she was subjected to discrimination as alleged. Complainant filed the instant appeal and submitted a brief in support of her appeal. The Agency opposed Complainant’s appeal. Complainant filed a response to the Agency’s brief on September 24, 2022, and the Agency moved to strike Complainant’s response.

See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 3-4; 135. Complainant’s predecessor stated that it was “laughable” to think that external shareholder information was personal information of the sort to raise such privacy concerns. See ROI at 1520-21; 2277. However, Complainant’s subordinates further stated that even prior to Complainant’s arrival, they had experienced issues with the Deputy’s behavior when she assumed a temporary detail position as the acting Assistant Director of OFIBL after Complainant’s predecessor left and prior to Complainant beginning her position. One of Complainant’s subordinates stated that the Deputy had generally tried to create a hostile work environment for OFIBL but that her conduct became worse after Complainant was hired because the Deputy felt she should have been made the permanent Assistant Director and was upset when Complainant was hired for the position rather than her. See ROI at 2129-2134. Another of Complainant’s subordinates confirmed that he believed the Deputy felt entitled to the position of Assistant Director and was upset when Complainant was hired and stated that he believed part of the Deputy’s conduct was motivated by political differences because the Deputy knew that Complainant had previously worked for the Obama White House. See ROI at 2165-67; 2184. The Letter of Reprimand was issued to Complainant for unprofessional behavior, including refusing to follow the Supervisor’s repeated instruction to engage in one-on-one communication with staff and not informing the Supervisor that Employee and Labor Relations had advised Complainant against proceeding with a personnel action. See ROI at 3713. The Letter found that Complainant’s actions demonstrated an unwillingness to work cooperatively with Employee and Labor Relations in addressing the conduct and performance issues on her team. See ROI at 3714. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing, but the AJ denied the hearing request on the grounds that the hearing request was untimely. The AJ noted that Complainant did not deny that she received a copy of the report of investigation on October 25, 2021, which clearly informed Complainant of the 30-day time limit to request a hearing, but that Complainant did not request a hearing until November 29, 2021. The AJ therefore dismissed the hearing request and remanded the complaint to the Agency. Thereafter, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision thoroughly recounted the relevant facts and found that management witnesses articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for issuing the Letter of Reprimand and Complainant’s disagreement with the Supervisor’s decision to discipline her was not sufficient to establish pretext. The decision further went on to acknowledge that the record clearly demonstrated that the Deputy and the Outreach Analyst had behaved in “inappropriate, disrespectful, unprofessional, and potentially insubordinate behavior” but found that, ultimately, the preponderance of the record did not establish that either the Deputy’s or the Outreach Analyst’s behavior was motivated by any of Complainant’s protected classes rather than disgruntlement over the Deputy not being hired to perform Complainant’s job. The decision therefore concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination or unlawful retaliation as alleged. The instant appeal from Complainant followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Postal Police Officer at the Agency’s Career Development Unit facility in Potomac, MD. 1. On or about March 3, 2021 to March 23, 2021, he was denied mental health treatment through the Agency’s Self-Referred Counseling Program (SRCP); 2. On or about March 23, 2021, management failed to respond to his additional request to receive treatment through the Self-Referred Counseling Program; 3. On or about April 26, 2021, he sought treatment through another Agency program, Employee Assistance Program (EAP) and was denied treatment. 2 At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as an Industrial Engineering Technician in Albany, Georgia. On October 25, 2017 and January 4, 2018, Complainant filed two EEO formal complaints. 1. On April 28, 2017, the Director, Workload Manager did not select him for the position of Program Analyst, GS-0343-12, under job announcement number WJ- 17-BBu30763SO at the Maintenance Management Center (MMC) Division. 2. White employees with the same grade and series were not required to perform the same work measurement studies as he was required to perform. 2 The two formal complaints were consolidated for investigation. After an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing, but the AJ denied the hearing request on the grounds that it was untimely filed and dismissed the hearing request. On June 30, 2020, the AJ ordered the Agency to issue a final order within 40 days of receiving the AJ’s decision. On October 10, 2020, the Agency issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s decision. The final order did not address the merits of Complainant’s claims. Complainant filed an appeal. In EEOC Appeal [number removed] (Jan. 24, 2022), OFO vacated the Agency’s final order and remanded the matter to the Agency for it to issue a final decision on the merits of Complainant’s complaints. On February 23, 2022, the Agency issued a final decision finding no discrimination was established. The Agency found that it articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions which Complainant failed to establish was pretext for discrimination. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a City Letter Carrier, Grade 2, at the Agency’s Post Office facility in Clinton, Maryland. On February 13, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the basis of reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under an EEO statute that was unspecified in the record when: 1. On October 24, 2020, Complainant was not paid for overtime worked on his nonscheduled day; 2. 3. On January 8, 2021, management accused Complainant of falsifying a form; 4. On January 13, 2021, management spoke to Complainant and approached him in a loud and aggressive manner; 5. On January 24, 2021, management stared at Complainant and intimidated him while he worked; and 6. On January 29, 2021, Complainant became aware that the Postmaster did not provide him an opportunity to select his choice vacation. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. The AJ found that neither the Formal complaint nor Complainant’s affidavit indicated that Complainant has personally engaged in protected EEO activity prior to his complaint. The AJ directed Complainant to supplement the record with an affidavit showing that he had engaged in protected EEO activity. Complainant filed a timely response, but the AJ found that it was unrelated to the AJ’s order and was not “in the form of a declaration subject to the penalty of perjury as I had ordered . . . [and was] entirely nonresponsive to my order. . . . As best I can tell, Complainant simply ignored my directions to describe his protected activity.” The AJ found that Complainant failed to show that he had engaged in protected EEO activity and issued a decision dismissing the complaint for failure to state a claim. The Agency issued a final action implementing the AJ’s decision.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a City Carrier at the Agency’s Austin-South Congress Station in Austin, Texas. During the relevant time, Complainant was in receipt of workers’ compensation benefits from the Department of Labor’s Office of Workers’ Compensation Programs (OWCP). Report of Investigation (ROI) at 126, 130. 1. In January 2022, management refused [to] provide [him] an extension of time to review [its] job offer; and 2. In January 2022, management did not allow [him] to have another medical evaluation for his on-the-job injury. On March 25, 2022, the Agency dismissed Complainant’s complaint for failure to state a claim, as the Agency found that the claims were a collateral attack on the OWCP process. Complainant subsequently appealed the decision to the Commission. On August 16, 2022, the Commission issued an appellate decision, which found that the Agency had improperly framed Complainant’s allegations. See Elias M. v. U.S. Postal Service, EEOC [number removed] (Aug. 16, 2022). The appellate decision found that Complainant’s allegations were more properly framed as a denial of a reasonable accommodation for his on-the- job injury in 2018. As the appellate decision found that the issue of Complainant’s reasonable accommodation, beginning June 28, 2018, was decided in a prior final decision, dated May 15, 2019, with a finding of no discrimination, 2 the appellate decision limited the consideration period from May 16, 2019 to the present. The appellate decision remanded this issue to the Agency to be investigated. Neither party sought reconsideration of the appellate decision. Pursuant to the Commission’s remand order, the Agency investigated the reframed claim. The EEO Investigator attempted to obtain an affidavit from Complainant. ROI at 61-72. The letter from the Investigator specified that Complainant’s affidavit was due within 15 calendar days. ROI at 70. The letter, along with the affidavit, were delivered to an individual at Complainant’s home address on September 2, 2022. ROI at 73, 95. Complainant, however, did not return the requested affidavit. ROI at 61-69. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the ROI and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Over Complainant's objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s February 16, 2023, motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on March 9, 2023. The AJ adopted the Agency’s motion for summary judgment in whole. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. Complainant then filed the instant appeal. Complainant appealed the Agency’s May 15, 2019, final decision to the Commission. However, in EEOC [number removed] (Jan. 11, 2021), the Commission dismissed the appeal for untimeliness. On appeal, Complainant argues, in relevant part, that the Commission, in EEOC [number removed] (Aug. 16, 2022), improperly framed his complaint, and that the matter should be reinvestigated as originally framed. As Complainant did not seek reconsideration of the Commission’s prior decision, we decline to revisit it here.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Supervisor of Distribution Operations (SDO) at the Agency’s North Metro Processing & Distribution Center in Duluth, Georgia. She was directly supervised by Manager, Distribution Operations (MDO). On April 18, 2022, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of color (black) and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when: 1. on dates to be specified Complainant was constantly moved to different tours and operations; 2. 3. on dates to be specified, Complainant was not properly trained in the operations she was scheduled to be in charge of; 4. on dates to be specified, Complainant was not properly staffed in the operations she was scheduled to be in charge of; 5. on November 25, 2021, Complainant was scheduled to come in early to supervise employees, but they did not come in early; 6. on a date to be specified in November 2021, Complainant requested Sick Leave and did not receive a response; and 7. on dates to be specified beginning in December 2021, Complainant was charged Leave Without Pay (LWOP). While Complainant did not provide an affidavit in support of her complaint during the EEO investigation, the record reveals that all of the responsible management officials denied discriminating against Complainant. With regard to claims 1 and 2, MDO explained that due to her retirement, she no longer had access to Complainant’s personnel file. Complaint File at 54-60. 2 However, from what she could recall, she moved Complainant to different tours and operations and accused Complainant of poor performance because Complainant had deficiencies in her performance. Lead Senior Manager confirmed MDO’s explanation and added that the office had a goal of moving 5,500 pieces of mail per hour. However, Complainant and her employees failed to meet that goal, and Complainant ultimately moved to different tours and operations due to her failure to meet performance standards. ROI at 64 and 220-226. Lead Senior Manager also emphasized that Complainant’s performance deficiencies also including failure to hold employees accountable for their behaviors. Id. As for Complainant’s allegations regarding training (claim 3), Acting Manager maintained that Complainant received the requisite training in the necessary areas along with several other supervisors. ROI at 66, and 292-294. Operations Specialist confirmed Acting Manager’s statements and emphasized that Complainant shadowed other supervisors while on tour. ROI at 169. For claim 4, Acting Manager stated that she did not recall a time when Complainant was not provided with appropriate staffing, or had staffing issues and emphasized that staffing issues would have been addressed as they occurred. ROI at 68 and 296. As for claim 5, the record reveals that the responsible management officials denied awareness of Complainant’s allegation. ROI at 69- 70. For claim 6, the record reveals that Complainant did not receive a response to her sick leave request because she was not scheduled to work on November 29, 2021. ROI at 377. While MDO did not provide an affidavit during the EEO investigation, she subsequently submitted an affidavit, which the Agency included in the “Post Investigation” section of the complaint file. As for Complainant’s contention that beginning in December 2021 (claim 7), she was marked as AWOL, the record reveals that management sent Complainant various letters regarding her absences, including notices for investigative interviews, noting that Complainant had not kept her supervisor up to date on her attendance. ROI at 381-385. Complainant responded with medical documentation excusing some, but not all dates. ROI at 386-393. Complainant was later marked as taking sick leave for a portion of the time. ROI at 304. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), which concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. Complainant then filed the instant appeal.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as an Administrative Manager, AD-0301-00, for the Department of Commerce, Decennial Census, in the Hartford Connecticut Area Census Office (ACO). In July 2019, Complainant accepted a one-year appointment with the Agency. The Agency terminated his employment in November 2019. 1. Complainant’s Area Census Office Manager (ACOM) physically stepped in Complainant’s face while the ACOM was conducting new hire orientation. 2. Complainant was yelled at by the ACOM. The ACOM was in Complainant’s face yelling “pause, pause.” 3. Complainant was initially greeted by the ACOM, and the ACOM stated “I didn’t hire you, so I can’t fire you.” The ACOM made the comments before Complainant introduced himself. 4. Complainant was threatened by the ACOM when the ACOM told Complainant that he should not receive disabled veterans leave and questioned Complainant about his disabilities and religion. 5. Complainant made the ACOM aware of the fact he was homeless. In response to Complainant being homeless the ACOM told Complainant, “I don’t care, go to the Salvation Army.” The ACOM told Complainant to wear collared shirts. 6. Complainant was accused by the Assistant Regional Census Manager (ARCM) of inappropriate text messaging on another employee’s personal phone. 7. Complainant was the only employee to be booked in a separate hotel, in a different town, during an overnight stay. Complainant also alleged he was subject to disparate treatment based on race when: 8. On November 1, 2019, Complainant was terminated. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ assigned to the case determined sua sponte that the complaint did not warrant a hearing and over Complainant's objections, issued a decision without a hearing on June 28, 2022. The AJ noted that even viewing the facts in the light most favorable to Complainant, the evidence does not support a finding that the comments or actions were made because of his race. The first three incidents concerned new hire orientation training. The AJ noted even assuming the incidents occurred as described by Complainant, they constituted, at most, rude, unprofessional conduct. However, none of the facts presented indicated the treatment was based on race or any other protected class. In his affidavit, Complainant stated he was not sure whether the events were related to his race and that there was nothing to indicate race was a factor. Regarding claim 4, the AJ noted assuming these incidents occurred, at most, the comments constituted unprofessional commentary but there was no indication the treatment was based on race. The AJ noted Complainant stated in his affidavit that the comments were not based on race. Further, the leave Complainant requested was ultimately granted. Regarding claim 5, Complainant stated that he made the ACOM aware that he was homeless with regards to the dress code which required wearing collared shirts. The AJ found assuming the ACOM made the statement that he did not care and told Complainant to go to the Salvation Army, the comments may be considered unprofessional, but nothing about the comments demonstrated discriminatory animus. Further, Complainant stated in his affidavit those comments were about the dress code and not based on race. Regarding claim 6, a female coworker reported to her manager that Complainant sent her a text asking her “how does she taste.” In his affidavit, he acknowledged the text he sent was “possibly inappropriate.” The ARCM contacted Complainant regarding the message and instructed him not to contact the coworker as the message was inappropriate. The AJ found Complainant proffered no evidence that the ARCM’s reaction to the incident correlated with Complainant’s race. Regarding claim 7, Complainant complained about being booked in a separate hotel during an overnight stay for a work event. Complainant alleged he was the only employee booked at a separate hotel. The ARCM stated that Complainant was placed at a different hotel due to a miscommunication regarding how far away from the event he lived, and his relatively late communication to point out the mistake and request a room. Only employees living further than 50 miles away from the event were booked in hotel rooms, and because the Agency mistakenly believed Complainant lived within the 50-mile radius, he was not originally booked for a hotel. The record shows that another employee was originally booked in the hotel at which Complainant was booked but when an opening became available at the other hotel, the employee was granted the available room at the hotel which was closer to the event since that employee used a walker and was scheduled for a double hip replacement surgery. Thus, the AJ found Complainant did not show that he was subjected to harassment as alleged. Regarding the comments and actions in incidents 1 - 7, the AJ found the evidence did not support that the comments were made because of his race or that there was any discriminatory animus at all. Regarding claim 8, the AJ noted the Agency proffered legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. Specifically, the Agency received incoherent emails from Complainant, he engaged in unprofessional communications, he did not complete directives, he did not respond to requests, and he used unprofessional and abusive language when communicating with a coworker. Complainant alleged his status as the only African-American male manager was evidence of racial animus. However, the AJ found his response did not proffer sufficient evidence to suggest the Agency’s articulated reasons were pretextual. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged.
