At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Surface Transportation Center Coordinator, EAS-17, at the Agency’s Surface Transfer Center (STC) facility in Plainfield, Indiana. For most of 2021, Complainant served as the STC Acting Manager, EAS-21. On July 20, 2022, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when, since January 2021 and continuing, she has not been paid appropriately for overtime and higher-level pay on multiple paychecks. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. The AJ determined sua sponte that the complaint did not warrant a hearing and, over Complainant’s objections, issued a decision without a hearing in favor of the Agency. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. The AJ first found that Complainant presented no evidence to show that she had engaged in prior protected EEO activity under any of the antidiscrimination statutes. Reviewing the record, the AJ found that Complainant alleged management retaliated against her because she had corrected management officials, including a coworker, Networks Specialist (NS), in the performance of their duties. Complainant’s affidavit did not reference any specific EEO activity or the dates of such activity, but instead referred to unspecified attachments she submitted with her affidavit, none of which appeared to relate to EEO activity. The attachments included forms related to Complainant’s requests under the Family and Medical Leave Act and two complaints Complainant filed with the Agency’s Office of Inspector General (OIG). The OIG complaints appeared to have been made in 2022, after the alleged retaliatory acts took place. Complainant’s affidavit also mentioned, in relation to her retaliation claim, that a management official, Director of STC Operations, refused to interview Complainant for a position in Atlanta because Complainant had socialized with contract employees. The AJ reasoned that none of these events constituted prior protected EEO activity. The AJ also determined that, even assuming Complainant could establish a prima facie case of retaliation, the Agency had articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. NS was responsible for inputting employees’ hours into the timekeeping system. NS averred that Complainant would email her hours to NS for input into the timekeeping system, which NS never questioned or denied. However, NS stated that Complainant would almost always fail to timely submit her work hours, which resulted in problems with her pay being processed. For instance, when Complainant would email her hours to NS after the timekeeping system had closed for the week, NS averred that she would put Complainant’s reported overtime hours on her next pay period. During Complainant’s stint as Acting Manager of STC, NS input the higher-level pay into the system for Complainant, but NS later noticed that the timekeeping system failed to process or recognize the higher-level pay. NS averred that if there was any error on her part, it was unintentional. After Complainant filed the instant complaint and the parties participated in a “redress meeting,” NS requested that Complainant provide her with documentation to support the hours Complainant felt were missing from her paychecks, which Complainant eventually provided. NS reviewed the documentation and submitted the pay adjustments for the work hours, overtime, and higher-level pay that Complainant had requested. Subsequently, Complainant was informed that her payroll checks reflecting the pay adjustments were ready to be picked up. The AJ determined that Complainant failed to rebut the Agency’s explanations as pretextual. The AJ also found that Complainant failed to identify similarly situated employees outside of her protected basis who were treated more favorably.

During the relevant time, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Mail Processing Clerk in Birmingham, Alabama. 1. On or around September 19, 2022, management refused to schedule orientation around her physical therapy appointments. 2. Since her return to work on or around September 19, 2022 and continuing, Complainant has not been accommodated with a 5-pound lifting restriction and day shift work. 3. In September 2022, her paycheck was 40 hours less than what she should have been paid. In its June 26, 2023 final decision, the Agency dismissed the instant formal complaint, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(7), for failure to cooperate, asserting Complainant did not respond to a request for an investigative affidavit concerning the matters in her complaint. This appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant, through her attorney, argues that she never received the request for the investigative affidavit or notice that failure to provide an affidavit could result in dismissal of her complaint.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Manager, Customer Service, at the Agency’s Reynolds Corner Post Office in Toledo, Ohio. On November 24, 2020, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint. Complainant claimed that the Agency subjected him to disparate treatment and discriminatory harassment based on his race (African American), sex (male), sexual orientation (gay), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (instant EEO case) when: 1. On a date not specified in February 2020, a manager called [him] a schoolgirl. 2 2. On or around July 10, 2020, management discussed Complainant’s medical information with others. 3. On or around August 10, 2020, a manager made a derogatory comment to Complainant that [he] took as a threat. 4. On or around August 20, and September 3, 2020, Complainant was worked outside his restrictions. 5. On or around August 20, 2020, Complainant was accused of stealing time. 6. On September 1, 2020, Complainant was issued a Proposed Letter of Warning in lieu of 14-Day Suspension, and subsequently, on December 1, 2020, the Letter of Decision was issued. 7. Since October 27, 2020, and continuing, [two named Agency officials] have spoken to Complainant in a discourteous and unprofessional manner. 8. On November 16, 2020, Complainant was told to report downtown, sit in the computer room and complete training assigned to him, and then wait for additional instructions. 9. On November 17, 2020, Complainant was placed on Administrative Leave; and 10. On December 14, 2020, 3 Complainant was given a Pre-Disciplinary Interview. The record reflects that the Agency initially dismissed claim (1) on procedural grounds. Subsequently, the AJ reinstated this claim as part of Complainant’s overall harassment claim. The record reflects that the PDI actually occurred on November 24, 2020 and December 22, 2020. ROI at 270. After an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. On August 27, 2021, the Agency filed a Motion for a Decision Without a Hearing (Agency’s Motion). Complainant filed a response. Under a disparate treatment analysis, the Agency asserted that management officials articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the actions at issue and Complainant failed to establish that the articulated reasons were pretext for discrimination and/or retaliation. The Agency further asserted that Complainant did not establish a prima facie case of harassment because the alleged incidents were not sufficiently severe or pervasive, and Complainant did not establish that the alleged incidents were based on his protected classes. On September 22, 2021, the assigned AJ granted the Agency’s Motion without additional analysis. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding of no discrimination.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Taxpayer Advocate in Laguna Niguel, California. On November 4, 2021, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her based on race (Hispanic) and national origin (Mexican). By letter dated November 16, 2021, the Agency accepted the formal complaint for investigation and framed the claims in the following fashion: Whether a co-worker who was an On-the-Job Instructor (OJI), as well as a Lead, subjected Complainant to harassment based on her race/national origin (Hispanic/Mexican) on multiple occasions beginning in June 2020 and continuing through July 2021 when, among other matters, the OJI/Lead: 1. Made fun of Complainant’s accent and said she disliked speaking to Complainant. 2. Tried to sabotage Complainant’s work by creating a list of inventory late actions and expired casework, and purposely gave Complainant misinformation regarding how to process cases. 3. Filled Complainant’s calendar with unrealistic appointments that not even experienced employees could complete. 4. Advised Complainant’s manager to have Complainant process a fraudulent tax return. After an investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of the right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge. When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination. Specifically, the Agency determined that “assuming [Complainant’s initial supervisor, S1] made these and other similar comments [as set forth in incident (1)], the statements would be unwelcome verbal conduct based on Complainant’s protected categories of race/national origin/ethnicity.” Final Agency Decision (FAD) at 12. However, the Agency, in its final decision, further set forth that: Complainant has produced no persuasive evidence that management’s actions described in [alleged incidents] 2, 3, and 4 were harassment based on her statutorily protected classes. Complainant’s uncorroborated statements that management was motivated by race/ethnicity and/or national origin to take the actions complained of are not sufficient to sustain her burden of showing harassment…Finally, we note that Complainant’s allegations of harassment were addressed through an internal anti-harassment inquiry, which did not substantiate Complainant’s claims.” FAD at 13. The instant appeal followed. Complainant asserts that the Agency’s final decision did not properly set forth that the alleged harasser was initially her former manager (prior to serving as her Lead and OJI). Complainant reiterates that S1 made derogatory comments regarding her accent since her first day of employment. Complainant asserts that she provided notice to S2 regarding S1’s behavior and requested a change of supervisor, but that S2 ignored the harassment and allowed the behavior to continue. In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision finding no discrimination. The Agency reiterates that Complainant failed to establish that she was subjected to harassment. Regarding the alleged comments made by S1 to Complainant regarding her accent, the Agency sets forth that “[a]ssuming the truth of Complainant’s allegations, nothing in S1’s comments indicate she mocked Complainant’s accent or that the comments were based on her being of Mexican descent. At best, [S1] indicated she expressed difficulty in communicating with Complainant. At worst, S1’s comments were the type of insensitive, hurtful comments that the Commission has declined to find as discriminatory.” Agency Response Brief at 11. The Agency asserts that Complainant’s claims fall short of the severity and pervasiveness required for a hostile work environment. Furthermore, the Agency states that management promptly separated Complainant and S1. Specifically, the Agency states that after Complainant raised the issue of harassment by S1 in late July 2021, S4 separated Complainant and S1 and that Complainant set forth that she had no further contact with S1 after this separation. The Agency further sets forth regarding Complainant raising the matter of alleged harassment by S1 with S2, it “appears” that Complainant only expressed a “lack of support.” Agency Response Brief at 17- 18.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Manager, Customer Service, in Chesapeake, Virginia. 2 On May 4, 2021, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that she was subjected to discrimination based on age (64 years old at the time of the alleged incident). By letter dated December 12, 2019, the Agency determined that Complainant’s complaint was comprised of the following claims: 1. On or about December 18, 2020, management failed to address [her] safety concerns regarding an employee that showed aggressive behaviors toward [her]. 3 2. On an unspecified date, [her] job injury was not reported timely and [her] hours were not processed correctly for [her] injury claim. The Agency accepted claim (1) for investigation. However, the Agency dismissed claim (2) for failure to state a claim, reasoning that this matter was a collateral attack on the Department of Labor’s workers’ compensation process. 4 After the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. On December 15, 2021, the EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) issued a Notice of Intent to Issue Sanctions and Order to Show Cause. Therein, the AJ set forth that Complainant failed to appear for an Initial Conference on December 15, 2021, and ordered Complainant to respond with a reason that the hearing request should not be dismissed. On June 30, 2022, the AJ issued an Order of Withdrawal. Therein, the AJ dismissed Complainant’s hearing request and remanded the matter to the Agency for a final decision. In reaching this determination, the AJ set forth that Complainant responded to the Notice to Show Cause stating: In a document submitted to an EEOC Administrative Judge, Complainant stated that she retired effective September 30, 2021. Complainant asserted the female employee at issue called her a “bitch” multiple times and that the employee would have assaulted her if a shop steward had not grabbed her by the waist and escorted her out of the building. ROI at 87. Complainant does not expressly contest, on appeal, the Agency’s dismissal of claim (2), Therefore, we decline to address this claim further herein. that ‘[i]t was never [her] intention to take this matter to hearing’ and concluding with the statement that she ‘would like to put this ordeal in the rearview mirror.’ Additionally, Complainant attached to her [response to the Order to Show Cause] a letter from her psychologist indicating that Complainant is ‘emotionally unable to represent herself in a hearing…as her emotional condition is likely to worsen if [she is] forced to relive her traumatic experiences.’…Given Complainant’s statements…it appears to the undersigned that Complainant does not wish to proceed with the hearing process…However, Complainant does not indicate a desire to withdraw her formal complaint in its entirety. On remand, on August 12, 2022, the Agency issued a final decision finding no discrimination regarding claim (1). Therein, the Agency found that assuming arguendo that Complainant established a prima facie case of age discrimination, management officials articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the disputed actions. Management witnesses testified they did not find it necessary to keep the employee at issue on Emergency Placement after reviewing the Postal Inspector’s report and statements from employees. Rather, they addressed the matter through the disciplinary process by issuing the employee a letter of suspension. Final Agency Decision (FAD) at 10. The Agency further found that Complainant failed to establish that the Agency’s articulated reasons for its actions were pretext for discrimination. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a non-career City Carrier Assistant, Q-01, at the Uptown Station in New Orleans, Louisiana. The record reveals that on August 9, 2022, Complainant filed her complaint alleging discrimination based on race (Black/African American) and sex (female) when on May 18, 2022, she was terminated during her probationary period. The record indicates that on April 9, 2022, Complainant started her position subject to a 90-day probationary period. On May 13, 2022, Complainant was issued a Letter of Separation during her probationary period, in part, due to her unsafe work performance/accident on May 10, 2022. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at Exhibit 11. Complainant’s supervisor (S1), Supervisory Customer Services, EAS-17, indicated that Complainant was terminated during her probationary period because on May 10, 2022, she had an at fault Postal vehicle accident. Complainant’s manager (M1), Manager Customer Services, EAS-21, stated that on May 10, 2022, Complainant was assigned to three hours delivery on route 1547, but before she could complete her delivery, she side swiped a FedEx truck and totaled a Postal vehicle. Complainant claimed that she was treated differently than two other employees (E1 - African American, male, and E2 – White, female) who also had a car accident during their probationary period but were not terminated. M1 indicated that E1 tapped the side mirror of her vehicle, it had to be mounted back on, and there was no damage to a Postal vehicle. See ROI at Affidavit C, Page 5. M1 also indicated that there was no accident record of E2 at the Uptown Station. S1 indicated that she was not aware of E2’s accident. See ROI at Affidavit B, Page 65. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge or a final Agency decision. When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination. Further, the Agency articulated a nondiscriminatory reason for its action of which Complainant failed to show was pretext for discrimination. Complainant appeals from the Agency’s final decision.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Mail Processing Clerk at the Agency’s Atlanta Processing and Distribution Center in Atlanta, Georgia. Complainant stated that she had previously filed an EEO complaint in September 2018, which remained pending before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) at the time of her affidavit for the instant EEO complaint. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 97. She explained that she suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression as a result of an incident where she was sexually harassed by a co-worker (the subject of her prior complaint), and that she also suffers from back, foot, and knee issues so she is unable to stand or walk for extended periods of time, cannot climb or descend stairs, and has restrictions on bending, stooping, and lifting. See ROI at 97-98. She also stated that due to the PTSD she suffers as a result of the co-worker’s sexual assault, her doctor stated that she can no longer work in the same facility as the co-worker who assaulted her. See ROI at 98-99. Complainant explained that the sexual harassment/assault occurred in September 2019 after which she went on Family & Medical Leave Act (FMLA) leave. See ROI at 100. She stated that she was released to return to work at a different facility from her harasser in April 2020, but when she arrived at work, her harasser was still there. See ROI at 100. She further alleged that in June 2020, she suffered a knee injury in the workplace, and she submitted documents to the Agency pertaining to her knee injury in July 2020, but received no response. See ROI at 100. She stated that the Agency’s Reasonable Accommodation Committee requested additional documentation which she had already provided and that they ignored her limitation resulting from her PTSD that required she be moved to a different facility from her harasser, instead focusing only on her physical restrictions due to her knee injury. See ROI at 100. She stated that in July 2021, she was finally given a modified assignment to a different location that accommodated her physical restrictions. 2 See ROI at 100. She went out on COVID leave on August 16, 2021, and then was later hospitalized for sepsis so she was ultimately not cleared to return to work until September 21, 2021. However, Complainant stated that she has not been returned to work because the Agency has refused to accommodate her restrictions, and she has only been told by management that there was no work available for her based on her restrictions. 3 See ROI at 100-105. There is no explanation or documentation in the record of Complainant’s new position or why it took the Agency a full year to move Complainant to a different work facility than her harasser. We emphasize that there is no statement from any Agency official confirming that any effort was made to accommodate Complainant’s restrictions from September 2021 onwards or that such an effort was unsuccessful. Complainant further alleged that she should not have been placed on leave without pay (LWOP) since November 21, 2021, because she was not able to work due to the Agency’s failure to accommodate her restrictions. In January 2022, she was denied a bid position, and the position was instead given to someone who had less seniority, while Complainant was marked “ineligible” with no explanation. 4 See ROI at 105; 108-9. EEO Complaint On May 13, 2022, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American/Native American/Cuban), sex (female), color (Brown), disability (physical and mental), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 when: 1. Since November 10, 2021, she was not accommodated per her medical restrictions. 2. Since November 10, 2021, to present, she was charged LWOP. 3. On January 24, 2022, she was denied a bid position. 5 The Supervisor of Distribution Operations stated in her affidavit that Complainant’s bid was denied because she did not receive any updated medical documentation stating Complainant could fully perform her duties within 6 months. See ROI at 152. There is no evidence in the record indicating that Complainant was actually requested to provide such documentation or told she needed to do so as Complainant stated she was given no explanation for the denial. In addition, we note that the Collective Bargaining Agreement specifically states that in such a situation “management may, at the time of the submission of the bid or at any time thereafter, request that the employee provide medical certification indicating that the employee will be able to fully perform the duties of the bid for position within six months of the bid.” See ROI at 337. Complainant’s complaint also included three additional claims, specifically that between April 2020 and November 9, 2021, she was not accommodated per her medical restrictions; that on unspecified dates, her leave was not properly coded as workers’ compensation (OWCP) leave; and on unspecified dates, she was denied insurance benefits. Complainant had filed a motion to amend a pre-existing complaint to include her denial of reasonable accommodation claim for the period from April 2020 onwards but the AJ assigned to her other case denied the motion, finding that the denial of accommodation claim was not sufficiently like or related to her existing claim and noted that the time limits on EEO counseling be tolled from November 11, 2021, the date she filed the motion to amend. See ROI at 17-20. The Agency dismissed the denial of reasonable accommodation claim for the dates prior to November 10, 2021, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(1) because of untimely counselor contact. See ROI at 62-63. The Agency also dismissed the claims regarding her leave not being properly coded and the denial of insurance benefits as collateral attacks on the workers’ compensation adjudicatory process. See ROI at 63-65. We find that the Agency’s affirmance of the claims regarding Complainant’s leave not being properly coded as OWCP leave and the denial of insurance benefits were On December 6, 2022, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency found that Complainant did not submit required medical documentation to support her request for a reasonable accommodation or to show that she could perform the positions of her bid position within six months. The Agency also determined that Complainant did not demonstrate pretext for discrimination. The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Senior Counternarcotics Advisor at the Agency’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Labor Relations (INL), United States Embassy in Kabul, Afghanistan. Complainant began his position in May 2020, as a Personal Service Contractor. Kabul Embassy, leading to a displacement of personnel. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 79, 167, 85, 174. On January 11, 2022, Complainant was verbally informed that there was no position available for his skillset and that his contract would be terminated. On or about March 1, 2022, Complainant received the official notice of the termination of his Personal Services Contract for convenience, effective March 28, 2022. ROI at 80, 194. On March 14, 2022, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him based on age (64) when: 1. on March 1, 2022, he was notified that his Personal Services Contract was terminated, effective March 28, 2022; and 2. on February 23, 2022, Complainant was informed that he was not selected for the Personal Services Contract position at the U.S. Embassy Dushanbe. 2 At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the ROI and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge. In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency found that Complainant did not establish a prima facie case of age discrimination, but even if he had, management provided a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for its action. Specifically, the Agency tried to reassign as many employees and contractors as possible, but it was not always successful and terminated contracts for convenience. While Complainant alleged that younger comparators were treated more favorably, the record showed that they were not similarly situated since they worked in different areas and were matched into new positions under the same statutory authority. Complainant’s contract was terminated because there was no longer a need for his services, and not due to his age. The Agency then found that Complainant did not show that the reasons were pretexts for discrimination. Complainant disagreed with aspects of management’s testimony, but he did not bring forth new or persuasive evidence to establish pretext. The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that he was subjected to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Complainant withdrew this claim during the EEO investigation because he was reemployed with INL. Report of Investigation at 88.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a General Expeditor at the Agency’s Processing and Distribution Center in Duncansville, Pennsylvania. On January 13, 2022, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint, claiming that the Agency discriminated against her based on sex (female), age (48 years old at the time of the alleged incidents), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (grievances alleging a hostile work environment and the instant complaint). By letter dated February 3, 2022, the Agency accepted Complainant’s complaint for investigation and determined that it was comprised of the following claims: 1. On September 30, 2021, [Complainant was] placed on Emergency Placement; and 2. On or around October 14, 2021, [she was] issued a Seven-Day Suspension. After an investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of the right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. On January 31, 2023, the EEOC AJ issued an Order of Dismissal. Therein, the AJ dismissed the hearing based on Complainant’s request and remanded the matter to the Agency for a final decision. The Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination or unlawful retaliation. The Agency found that assuming arguendo that Complainant established a prima facie case of discrimination and/or retaliation, the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. Regarding Complainant being placed on Emergency Placement, the Agency found that management asserted that Complainant became argumentative and yelled after being given a work instruction. Final Agency Decision (FAD) at 18. Regarding Complainant being issued a suspension, the Agency found that management asserted that Complainant initially refused to leave the building after being placed on Emergency Placement and the police were called. FAD at 19, The Agency further found that Complainant failed to establish that the Agency’s articulated reasons for its actions were pretext for discrimination and/or retaliation. FAD at 22-23. The instant appeal from Complainant followed. In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a PSE Sales and Services Distribution Associate, Grade Level 06 P, at the Agency’s Cape Central Post Office in Cape Coral, Florida. On April 4, 2022, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint claiming she was subjected to ongoing harassment based on her race (“White”) 2 when, in and around February 2022, her first- line supervisor (Supervisor) (African American) made racial slurs and threatened to physically assault her and when she informed management officials, they did nothing. 3 The Agency accepted the complaint and conducted an investigation into its claims. During the investigation, Complainant stated that in late January/early February 2022, she was told by Supervisor not to clock out for lunch due to overtime. She avers when she asked Supervisor if he would input her hours into the computer, he responded, "I'll slap the shit out of you." She stated later, when she asked if she could take her break, Supervisor responded, "people shouldn't be allowed breaks, Black people used to be slaves." On February 3, 2022, Complainant claimed that when she asked Supervisor for clarification of instructions he had given her, he responded, "I'll slap the shit out of you if you don't catch on." On February 5, 2022, she said that when she told Supervisor that a package that was too heavy to lift, he responded she was, "full of shit. You can't lift that?" On February 8, 2022, after she was instructed to bring the wagons around, she claims Supervisor said, "You need to do it because you're White...". On February 24, 2022, Complainant said she said "huh?" when she did not hear what Supervisor had said and he responded, 'What do you mean huh? I’ll slap the shit out of you." Finally, on March 3, 2022, when she was walking out of the housekeeping closet after getting disposable gloves, she said Supervisor yelled, "White people don't steal, they buy their own shit." Complainant said she reported Supervisor’s racial slurs and threats to the Manager, Customer Service (Manager) (Caucasian) and the union, but nothing was done. Report of Investigation (ROI), Affidavit A. Supervisor unequivocally denied making any of the statements alleged by Complainant. He said he believed they basically had a good working relationship until this complaint was filed. ROI, Affidavit B. Manager affirmatively stated that Complainant never reported to her any of the comments allegedly made by Supervisor. ROI, Affidavit C. Another supervisor (Supervisor 2) (Caucasian) stated that Complainant once told him that Supervisor told her he would "slap her upside the head." He said he told her to report the matter to Manager. He denied Complainant told him about any racial comments from Supervisor. He asserted that Complainant told him she did not want to report the matter to Manager. ROI, Affidavit D. Complainant originally also alleged unlawful retaliation but withdrew this claim during the investigation into her complaint, leaving only the racial harassment claim. Agency management has since apparently reassigned Complainant to a different supervisor. Complainant did not raise her reassignment as a claim. After the EEO investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. However, Complainant did not respond to the AJ’s October 24, 2022 order to submit preliminary case information and did not appear, as the AJ had ordered, at the initial conference scheduled for November 24, 2022. On January 19, 2023, the AJ dismissed Complainant’s hearing request and remanded the formal EEO complaint to the Agency for a final decision. 4 Thereafter, the Agency issued a final decision, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination or unlawful retaliation was established as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

During the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Rural Carrier at the Agency’s Gahanna Carrier Annex in Columbus, Ohio. On December 24, 2021, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (Black) and sex (female) when on or around September 17, 2021, Complainant was issued a Notice of Removal. In filing her formal complaint, Complainant identified two Black females who were treated more favorably than her, as management allegedly did not remove them even though they too had absences like Complainant. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 78. During the investigation, the investigator asked Complainant to complete an affidavit regarding her claim of discrimination. Though Complainant acknowledged receipt of the affidavit, she ultimately did not return a completed affidavit to the investigator. 2 ROI at 80-88. Complainant’s first-level supervisor (Supervisor) explained that Complainant did not show up for work for approximately six months preceding the proposed removal. ROI at 91, 101, 122-24. Supervisor therefore initiated the disciplinary process in July 2021 by sending Complainant return to work letters, which did not result in Complainant returning to work. ROI at 92. By the time Supervisor sent the first return to work letter, Complainant stopped using the call off work line and made no attempt to contact the management staff as to her absence from work. ROI at 92. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ determined sua sponte that the complaint did not warrant a hearing and issued the parties a Notice of Intent to Issue a Decision Without a Hearing in Favor of the Agency (Notice of Intent), as the probative record showed that the Agency removed Complainant because she failed to report for work for six months. Though the AJ afforded the parties to respond, only the Agency did so. The AJ ultimately concluded that Complainant failed to prove her claim of discrimination. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. Complainant filed the instant appeal. Due to Complainant’s failure to provide a completed affidavit, the Agency dismissed the complaint on March 18, 2022, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(7) for failure to cooperate. After Complainant appealed this decision to the Commission, the Agency rescinded the final decision and resumed its investigation into the complaint.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Physician Assistant at the Agency’s Medical Center in Temple, Texas. Complainant initiated contact with an EEO Counselor at the Agency’s Office of Resolution Management, Diversity & Inclusion (ORMDI) on August 3, 2022. When the matter was not resolved, a Notice of Right to File a Discrimination Complaint (Notice) was issued to Complainant and Complainant’s attorneys (Counsel and Co-Counsel) on August 26, 2022. Co- Counsel acknowledged receiving the Notice on August 26, 2022, and Complainant received the Notice on August 27, 2022. Subsequently, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency subjected him to hostile workplace discrimination on the bases of sex (male), disability, age, and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when: 1. On or about June 2, 2021, he was not selected for a BHIP position in Colorado Springs, Colorado. 2. On or about May 13, 2022, he was investigated regarding his “inappropriate conduct” on a Microsoft TEAMS meeting. 3. On or about May 25, 2022, he was accused of having “slurred speech” during a Microsoft TEAMS meeting. 4. On or about May 25, 2022, his telework agreement was terminated, and he was forced to return to working at the agency facilities in person. 5. On or about August 8, 2022, a second frivolous complaint was filed against him. 6. On August 11, 2022, his reasonable accommodation for full-time telework was denied. On March 23, 2023, Counsel contacted ORMDI stating that the formal complaint was filed over six months ago (on September 12, 2022) and asking for an update. In response, ORMDI stated that they had not received any further documentation since Complainant and his attorney acknowledged receipt of the Notice. On March 24, 2023, ORMDI issued a Notice of Receipt of the Discrimination Complaint (Notice of Receipt) acknowledging Complainant’s complaint was filed on March 23, 2023. After obtaining the Notice of Receipt, Counsel emailed ORMDI stating the firm had filed a formal complaint on Complainant’s behalf on September 12, 2022. Counsel informed that since it had been more than 180 days since the formal complaint had been filed, a request for a hearing had been submitted to the EEOC. In response, ORMDI replied that their records indicated the filing date for Complainant’s formal complaint was March 23, 2023. They requested documentation that the complaint was submitted prior to March 23, 2023, such as copies of emails and read receipts, and copy of all other mailings. Counsel replied that he was still speaking with Co-Counsel about tracking down the email sending the formal complaint but that they were forwarding a copy of the complaint sent via U.S. mail. Counsel provided a copy of the complaint allegedly sent on September 12, 2022, including a Certificate of Service signed by Co-Counsel certifying the complaint was sent via U.S. mail and email to the Agency’s ORMDI, and a copy of an envelope in which the complaint was purportedly mailed. The record contains a copy of the envelope. The top right of the envelope showed “First-Class,” “US Postage,” contained a zip code, and listed the amount of “$001.68.” There was no postmark date. The envelope contained a label from the law firm addressed to the Agency’s ORMDI address. ORMDI asked Counsel to provide a copy of the mailing payment receipt since the copy of the envelope did not have a clear date stamp documenting when it was mailed. In response, Counsel stated their office already provided evidence indicating the formal complaint was mailed and emailed on September 12, 2022, and for that reason they would not be producing any other documents related to the matter. ORMDI replied that they did not receive the formal complaint until March 23, 2023. They stated that in order to decide if the complaint was timely filed, they needed additional information to determine whether tolling or waiving the filing deadline would be appropriate. They noted it appeared counsel was refusing to provide the necessary information. They gave Counsel until close of business on April 11, 2023, to provide the requested information documenting the complaint was filed on September 12, 2022. Counsel responded on April 11, 2023, stating the documents provided previously, to include the envelope the complaint was sent in and the certificate of service, were adequate to show the formal complaint was mailed to the Agency on September 12, 2022. Counsel noted a hearing had already been requested with the EEOC. The record reveals Complainant filed a request for a hearing on his complaint with the EEOC’s Dallas District Office on April 6, 2023. He claimed that 180 had passed since the filing of his formal complaint and the Agency had not investigated the Complainant. Complainant requested his case be assigned to an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) for a hearing. On April 26, 2023, Complainant filed a Motion for Sanctions and to Invalidate Notice of Dismissal with the EEOC’s Dallas District Office. Complainant claimed the Agency failed to produce the Report of Investigation in connection with his allegation of being subjected to a hostile work environment. In response, the Agency argued that Complainant failed to timely file his formal complaint, which led to its issuance of a Notice of Dismissal to Complainant on April 24, 2023. 3 The Agency sought to have Complainant’s complaint dismissed by the assigned AJ because of Complainant’s failure to timely submit his formal complaint. On November 2, 2023, the AJ dismissed Complainant’s hearing request on the above complaint because Complainant failed to exhaust the procedural requirements for seeking a hearing before the Commission. Specifically, the AJ noted that under 29 C.F.R. §1614.604(b), a complaint is deemed timely filed if it is “received or postmarked” before the filing period ends or “in the absence of a legible postmark if it is received by mail within five days” of the filing period. The AJ found Complainant failed to produce evidence that he met the requirements of 29 C.F.R. § 1614.604(b). The AJ denied Complainant’s motion for sanctions because Complainant failed to show that the Agency received a timely complaint that triggered its duty to investigate the complaint. The AJ returned Complainant’s complaint to the Agency for issuance of a final decision. On November 28, 2023, the Agency issued a final decision on Complainant’s complaint. The Agency found Complainant failed to provide proof that his formal Complainant was filed via mail or email as alleged. The Agency noted regarding the envelope Complainant provided, aside from the postage amount, there were no visible dates to validate the claims from Co-Counsel that she filed the formal complaint on September 12, 2022. Thus, the Agency concluded the evidence did not show the complaint was mailed by the deadline for filing. The Agency also noted no proof was provided that the formal complaint was submitted by email. The Agency noted that had the formal complaint been submitted by email, an automated response acknowledging receipt would have been generated. The Agency determined no documentation was provided to establish the formal complaint was submitted electronically on the date alleged. Therefore, the Agency found that Complainant’s complaint was properly dismissed for failing to comply with the regulatory time requirements. On April 24, 2023, the Agency issued a Notice of Dismissal/Final Agency Decision dismissing Complainant’s complaint on the grounds the formal complaint was untimely filed. Complainant appealed the Agency’s decision to the Commission. In EEOC [number removed] (November 29, 2023), we initially upheld the Agency’s dismissal. However, in EEOC [number removed] (April 25, 2024), we vacated our initial appellate decision because the underlying matter was being addressed in the instant decision.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Security Specialist at the Agency’s Robins Air Force Base in Georgia. On December 5, 2022, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the basis of disability (knee condition and Post Traumatic Stress Disorder - PTSD) when, on September 21, 2022, Complainant received a letter of termination during his probationary period. 2 After the investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. In an August 21, 2023, the AJ issued an Order Requiring Parties to Supplement Record. This Order required, inter alia, that Complainant’s first-level supervisor (S1) provide a supplemental affidavit addressing whether Complainant ever provided him copies of the July 15, and July 22, 2022 medical notes appearing in the ROI at pages 47 and 319. 3 In his supplemental affidavit, S1 set forth that he was not aware of the July 15, and July 22, 2022 medical notes until he was asked to prepare his supplemental affidavit. S1 indicated that he contacted a named medical facility regarding the medical documentation “to inquire about the log numbers being the same and the font of the dates being different in the medical notes at issue.” S1 asserted that the named medical facility “informed me that [Complainant] was not seen by them on [July 15, or 22, 2022. Additionally, [the named medical facility] did confirm that he was seen on [July 26, 2022].” 4 On October 4, 2023, the AJ issued an Order Scheduling Status Conference, Notice of Additional Issue, and Opportunity to Supplement Pre-Hearing Report. Therein, the AJ, in pertinent part, identified the following additional claim based on S1’s supplemental affidavit: 2. Whether the Agency violated 29 C.F.R. § 1630. when on or about August 29, 2023, [S1] contacted Complainant’s [named medical facility]. The effective date of Complainant’s termination is September 24, 2022. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 138. The dates of July 15 and July 22, 2022, were referenced in Complainant’s termination letter. The termination letter set forth that on July 15 and July 22, 2022, Complainant was absent without authorization and was charged Absent Without Leave (AWOL). ROI at 138-139. S1 acknowledged that Complainant provided him a copy of the medical note dated July 26, 2022. The July 26, 2022 medical note sets forth a “Patient ID” number. The AJ held a hearing on October 12, 2023. During the hearing, S1 testified that he contacted, on two occasions (in August and September 2023), the medical facility at which Complainant alleged he received treatment on July 15, and 22, 2022 and set forth that he did not think the medical notes submitted by Complainant (dated July 15, and 22, 2022) looked legitimate. S1 further testified that he started to question whether Complainant had given him the medical notes in question. Hr’g Tr. at 123, 148. S1 stated that during the call with the medical facility, he gave the patient ID number set forth on a document that Complainant had submitted to S1 dated July 26, 2022, in order for the facility to provide him information on when Complainant was seen. Hr’g Tr. at 125-126, 160. Complainant, at the hearing, testified that he did not give the Agency or S1 permission to contact his medical provider or the medical facility. Hr’g Tr. at 74-75. On October 31, 2023, the AJ issued a bench decision. 5 Therein, the AJ found no discrimination regarding claim (1), Complainant’s termination. AJ Decision at 35. The AJ, however, found that the Agency subjected Complainant to an unlawful medical inquiry in violation of 29 C.F.R. § 1630.14(c) when, on two occasions in August and September 2023, S1 contacted a medical facility without Complainant’s permission. AJ Decision at 35. The AJ found that while Complainant was no longer an employee at the time of S1’s calls to the medical facility, Complainant had standing to pursue a claim of improper medical inquiry. AJ Decision at 36. The AJ set forth that “the Commission has repeatedly held that a former employee may have standing to pursue an EEO complaint…against a former employer even after the employment relationship concludes.” Id. at 37. The AJ found that S1’s calls to the medical facility constituted a disability-related inquiry. AJ Decision at 39. Specifically, the AJ set forth that: [S1] provided Complainant’s unique identifier, his patient ID, during both phone calls, and he inquired as to whether Complainant was seen by staff [at the named medical facility] on July 15, and July 22. These inquiries were likely to elicit medical information protected by the Rehabilitation Act, including not only whether Complainant received care, but also how long Complainant was there on those dates, what care Complainant may have received…and for what conditions. AJ Decision at 39. The AJ further found that these inquiries were not job-related and consistent with business necessity. Specifically, the AJ set forth that: [S1] did not have a reasonable belief that he needed to determine whether Complainant was able to perform the essential functions of his previous position as of August and September 2023, and he also did not testify that he had any basis On November 29, 2023, the AJ issued the Order Entering Judgment in the instant matter. to reasonably believe, nor did the Agency allege, that Complainant posed a direct threat to himself or to anyone in the Agency. Complainant also testified he did not give permission for [S1] to contact [the medical facility] on his behalf. AJ Decision at 41 (internal citations omitted). The AJ set forth that S1’s sole purpose for contacting the medical facility was to determine the authenticity of Complainant’s medical records for the purpose of the instant litigation. AJ Decision at 40. As such, the AJ concluded the inquiry violated the Rehabilitation Act. The AJ awarded $3,300 in non-pecuniary compensatory damages. AJ Decision at 47. The AJ also ordered the Agency to provide two hours of EEO training to S1 and S2. The AJ set forth that “[s]uch training should focus on an employer’s obligation under the Rehabilitation Act, including medical inquiries and medical examinations. Id. at 47-48. The AJ also ordered the Agency to post a notice regarding the finding of discrimination. Id. at 48. The Agency subsequently issued a final order rejecting the AJ’s finding that Agency committed a violation of the Rehabilitation Act regarding claim (2) and rejected the remedies awarded by the AJ. The Agency filed an appeal with the Commission regarding these matters.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Level 1 City Carrier at the Agency’s Meadow Mesa Station facility in North Las Vegas, Nevada. On February 25, 2023, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him and subjected him to harassment on the basis of age (born 1973) when: 1. On August 30, 2022, Complainant was put on Emergency Placement. 2. On September 14, 2022, Complainant was suspended. 3. On September 20, 2022, one of Complainant’s supervisors followed him to the bathroom, yelled at him to get back to work, and threatened him with discipline. 4. On September 24, 2022, one of Complainant’s supervisors accused him of not fastening his seatbelt before starting the engine. 5. On November 1, 2022, Complainant was escorted out of the facility. The Agency accepted these claims and conducted an investigation which produced the following evidence. Claim 1 In his investigative affidavit, Complainant stated that on August 30, 2022, he asked one of his supervisors, S1, to sign or initial his copy of a request for Union time. Complainant stated that S1 said she would do so later, and he then asked her why she could not just sign or initial the request at that time. Complainant stated that S1 repeated she would do so later and that he needed to get back to work. At this point, Complainant stated that Postmaster (PM) asked him what was going on, and after explaining the situation, PM asked him whether S1 gave him instructions to get back to work. Complainant stated that he said yes, and then PM asked him whether he was refusing to do so. Complainant stated that he said he was not refusing to get back to work but wanted to understand why he was being held to policy and not S1. After leaving the office area, and while he was in the locker room, Complainant stated that PM walked in and asked him why he had not left yet. PM further questioned what Complainant was doing for the last hour, and when Complainant tried to explain, Complainant stated that PM interrupted him, yelled at him, and leaned over him in an attempt to intimidate him. After this exchange, and while Complainant was still in the locker room, Complainant stated that PM walked in again and told him he needed to deliver to the apartments that day. Complainant stated that he asked PM whether he needed to finish the apartments that day because it would put him over eight hours. Complainant stated PM then accused him of failing to follow instructions, refused his request for a union steward, demanded his badge, yelled at him to clean out his locker, and threatened to call the authorities to have him removed from the premises. In his affidavit, PM stated that he observed Complainant engaging in several time-wasting practices and was given instructions which he failed to follow. PM further stated that in alignment with Agency policy, Complainant was placed on Emergency Placement (EP) in an off- duty status without pay for failure to follow instructions. With respect to Complainant’s intimidation claim, PM stated that the claim was ridiculous, and since having COVID, he does not get close to any employee. PM also stated that a union steward was not available, and Complainant was told he could speak with his union steward, but he had to leave the facility immediately. In her affidavit, S1 confirmed that she asked Complainant around three times to deliver his route, but he did not listen to her. S1 stated that Complainant then became argumentative with PM. With respect to Complainant’s intimidation claim, S1 stated that she did not have any knowledge of what might have occurred in the men’s locker room. S1 further stated that no employee placed on EP was allowed to have a conversation with the union before leaving the premises. Complainant stated that his age was a factor when he was placed on EP because he was tasked with trying to complete an overburdened route within eight hours and was compared constantly to younger carriers. Complainant did not have any specific examples of similarly situated employees outside his protected class who were treated more favorably under similar circumstances. Claim 2 In his affidavit, Complainant stated that on September 14, 2022, after completing vehicle inspection and as he was loading his mail truck, S1 and his other supervisor, herein identified as S2, approached him and S2 demanded his badge. Complainant stated that S2 explained he was being walked out because he did not fasten his seatbelt before starting the vehicle and that he got out of the driver’s seat while the engine was running. Complainant stated that he then asked for a union steward but S2 denied his request. Complainant further stated that it was his understanding that Section 812. of Handbook M-41 specified that seatbelts were to be worn at all times the vehicle was in motion. The record reflects that Complainant was again placed on EP in an off-duty status without pay. While Complainant received a Notice of 14-Day Suspension Letter on September 22, 2022, the letter cites to incident(s) of failing to follow instructions on August 30, 2022, as the reason for Complainant’s suspension. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 00192-00193. In his affidavit, S2 stated that Complainant was observed exiting the mail truck and walking in front of it while the engine was running. S2 stated that this was a safety violation, and it was Agency policy for seatbelts to be worn at all times while operating a vehicle. S2 further stated that since Complainant was immediately placed on EP, he had to contact the union off postal property. In her affidavit, S1 stated that she had no knowledge of this incident since she was not present when it occurred. Complainant stated that he did not think his age factored into this incident and did not have any specific examples of similarly situated employees outside his protected class who were treated more favorably under similar circumstances. Claim 3 In his affidavit, Complainant stated that on September 20, 2022, S2 followed him into the bathroom two separate times and yelled at him. Complainant further stated that S2 threatened to discipline him. S2 denied raising his voice to Complainant, and stated that if he followed him, it was because of Complainant’s performance. S2 further stated that rather than washing up in the bathroom, Complainant was spending a long time in the locker room and doing something in his locker. Complainant stated that he believed his age was a factor when he was purportedly yelled at and threatened with discipline because now that he is older, he has to use the bathroom more often than he did when he was younger. Complainant did not have any specific examples of similarly situated employees outside his protected class who were treated more favorably under similar circumstances. Claim 4 In his affidavit, Complainant stated that on September 24, 2022, he started the engine of his mail truck and was fastening his seatbelt when S2 walked up to the passenger-side window and yelled at him for not fastening his seatbelt before he started the engine. Citing to Section 812. of Handbook M-41, Complainant stated that S2 improperly demanded that seatbelts are to be fastened before the engine is started as opposed to before the vehicle is shifted into gear and put into motion. Complainant further stated that S1 walked over to them and S2 asked her whether she saw anything wrong. Complainant stated that S1 said no and while S1 and S2 were talking to each other and making calls, he called the National Association of Letter Carriers (NALC) office. Complainant stated that someone from NALC confirmed his understanding of the Agency’s seatbelt policy, and when he asked the NALC officer to repeat what he said to S1 and S2, S1 told him it was not necessary, and he could go and deliver his route. Complainant stated that S1 also told him he had to follow all supervisor instructions and starting right then, he needed to fasten his seatbelt before he started the engine. S2 stated that he thought seatbelts needed to be fastened before starting a vehicle. S2 stated that he called safety and was told that it was not a written Agency policy. S2 further stated that he informed Complainant of this conversation and Complainant was then allowed to continue to his route. S1 confirmed that S2 called her over and asked whether she observed Complainant doing anything wrong. S1 stated that she did not, and ultimately told Complainant to follow the instructions of his supervisor. When asked if the requirement to fasten seatbelts before starting a vehicle applied to all employees going forward, S1 stated that she was not sure whether the request was sent to all carriers or if other carriers already fastened their seatbelts before starting their vehicles. S1 further stated that the relevant conversation was between S2 and Complainant. Complainant stated that he did not think his age factored into this incident and did not have any specific examples of similarly situated employees outside his protected class who were treated more favorably under similar circumstances. Claim 5 In his affidavit, Complainant stated that on November 1, 2022, he gave S1 a doctor’s note for 30 days of no overtime due to repetitive motion pain in his right shoulder. Complainant stated that S1 told him she did not need to honor his doctor’s note. Later that evening, Complainant returned with undelivered mail and clocked out. Complainant stated that S1 told him he needed to continue delivering the mail until he finished his route. Complainant stated that he reminded S1 of his doctor’s note and that he was unable to work overtime. Complainant stated that S1 asked him whether he was refusing to follow instructions. Complainant further stated that he told S1 he did not have to follow unsafe supervisor instructions, and ignoring his doctor’s note and demanding he work overtime did not seem safe to him. 2 Complainant stated that S1 then demanded his badge, and he was escorted off the premises. The record reflects that Complainant was again placed on EP in an off-duty status without pay, effective November 2, 2022. S1 stated that Complainant told her, based on union advice, that he could bring his mail back and he did not have to listen to management. S1 stated that she asked Complainant three times to finish his route, but Complainant kept reiterating what the union told him. S1 stated that, while the union could provide guidance, she told Complainant that he had to follow supervisor instruction. S1 further explained that she sent Complainant’s medical documentation to Occupational Health Management (OHM) for guidance, and OHM advised her that Complainant could finish his route that day. S1 stated that OHM advised her that they were looking into the matter and to wait for an update as to whether the doctor’s note needed to be honored as a limited duty job offer, or if it needed to be a light duty request that required submission to the PM for approval. Complainant stated that he believed his age was a factor when he was escorted off the premises because he was expected to finish an overburdened route, and now that he is older, he has noticed that he does not recover from pain and injuries as quickly as he did when he was younger. Complainant did not have any specific examples of similarly situated employees outside his protected class who were treated more favorably under similar circumstances. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Disability was not a basis raised in Complainant’s complaint. Complainant timely requested a hearing. When Complainant did not object, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s December 14, 2023, motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on January 4, 2024. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination and harassment as alleged. The AJ found that the Agency's unrebutted facts served to establish nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. The AJ noted, for example, that Complainant argued with his supervisors, wasted time on his phone in the locker room, neglected to fasten his seatbelt, and failed to turn his vehicle off when exiting. The AJ found that these predicates, which Complainant did not dispute, provided sufficient nondiscriminatory justification for the discipline and other actions management meted out. The AJ found that Complainant did not offer evidence that management made biased comments about his age or that they treated younger workers more favorably. As a result, the AJ found that no reasonable factfinder, even viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to Complainant, could conclude the Agency's actions were tainted by considerations of Complainant's age. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s decision. The instant appeal from Complainant followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Mail Processing Clerk at the Agency’s Michigan Metroplex P&DC facility in Pontiac Michigan. On April 30, 2023, she was placed on Emergency Placement; 2. On dates to be specified, a manager constantly made inappropriate sexual remarks to her; 3. On dates to be specified, she was harassed when she requested a Change of Schedule to get away from a harassing manager; and 4. On August 4, 2023, she was issued a Notice of Removal. The Agency accepted the matter for investigation. On October 23, 2023, the EEO Investigator sent Complainant, via her personal email address, a request to complete an attached affidavit to obtain relevant information about her claims. When Complainant did not respond, the EEO Investigator sent a follow up request via email on November 6, 2023. The EEO Investigator notified Complainant that failure to respond to the affidavit request within 15 days of receipt could result in the dismissal of her complaint. Complainant did not respond to either email. The Agency dismissed Complainant’s complaint for failure to provide relevant information in accordance with 29 C.F.R. 1614.107(a)(7).
