At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Full-time Mail Handler Equipment Operator at the Agency’s Morgan Processing and Distribution Center facility in New York, New York. On November 18, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of sex (female), disability (physical), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII and the Rehabilitation Act when: 1. On June 25, 2021, and ongoing, she was denied overtime work within her limitations; 2. On July 19, 2021, she was verbally abused by a coworker and no action was taken; 2 3. Beginning on August 1, 2021, and ongoing, she was micromanaged and assigned to either the rewrap section or city manual section and/or confronted about her job duties; and 4. On August 31, 2021, her request for a temporary change of schedule was denied. After its investigation into the complaint, the Agency indicated that, on April 5, 2022, it transmitted to Complainant and her non-attorney representative a copy of the report of investigation (ROI) and notice of her right to request a hearing (Notice) before an EEOC AJ. On April 5, 2022, the Agency emailed Complainant and her representative, stating that a copy of the final ROI was available for download for a period of 30 days and requesting that the parties send an email confirming receipt. CF at 98-103. The record contains an April 5, 2022, message reflecting that the message was relayed to Complainant and her representative but that the destination server did not send a delivery notification. CF at 97. The Agency initially accepted the following for investigation: “On July 20, 2021, you were verbally abused by a supervisor and no action was taken.” CF at 60. Complainant clarified during the investigation that this incident occurred on July 19, 2021, that it was a coworker who verbally abused her, and that, when she reported it to supervisors, nothing was done about it. CF at 205-08. Also on April 5, 2022, the Agency provided Complainant and her representative 3 with a copy of documents that were submitted after the completion of the investigative file, asking that they be added to Complainant’s copy of the recently submitted file. CF at 85-96. The documents consist of an Acting Supervisor’s investigative affidavit, completed on March 28, 2022, and the Acting Supervisor’s Litigation Hold Notice, which was signed on March 31, 2022. CF at 86-95. In the affidavit, the Acting Supervisor stated that he had no organizational relationship to Complainant during the relevant time and that he was not at the facility on July 20, 2021. CF at 86-93. On May 17, 2022, the Agency again emailed Complainant and her non- attorney representative, notifying them that an electronic copy of the ROI would be available for download for a period of 30 days. CF at 82-83. The record contains a May 17, 2022, message reflecting that the message was relayed to Complainant and her representative but that the destination server did not send a delivery notification. CF at 84. On May 31, 2022, Complainant mailed a hearing request to the Agency and to the Commission’s New York District Office. CF at 40-42. The Agency stamped the mailing envelope and the hearing request form as received on June 6, 2022. CF at 40, 42. Complainant included a May 28, 2022, letter with her hearing request, in which she stated that, after receiving the Acting Supervisor’s affidavit in April 2022, she wanted to refute his response that he was not present on the date of the incident and requested a copy of his Employee Everything Report from the Agency. CF at 41. According to Complainant, on May 18, 2022, she called an EEO Services Analyst to refute the Acting Supervisor’s statement, and the EEO Services Analyst told her that her case was closed on May 1, 2022. CF at 41. Complainant averred that she asked how her case could be closed if she and her representative had not been notified or received a copy of the ROI. CF at 41. Complainant stated that the EEO Services Analyst told her that she could request a hearing but should attach a letter stating that she found out her case was closed on May 18, 2022. CF at 41. It appears that these documents were provided to Complainant and her representative via first class mail. CF at 85. On June 2, 2022, the Agency issued a final decision. The Agency stated that it was issuing the decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b) because Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. On June 10, 2022, the EEOC’s New York District Office received Complainant’s hearing request, which was docketed as Hearing No. 520- 2022-00326X. On June 15, 2022, Complainant filed the instant appeal. On July 6, 2022, the Agency provided Complainant and her representative with documents that were submitted after the completion of the investigative file, asking that they be added to Complainant’s copy of the recently submitted file. CF at 1-10. The document is an updated June 7, 2022, affidavit from the Acting Supervisor. CF at 2-10. The Acting Supervisor stated that, during the timeframe of the complaint, his organizational relationship with Complainant was Acting Supervisor. CF at 2. The Acting Supervisor stated that he was not present when the coworker verbally abused Complainant on July 19, 2021, and that he did not know if Complainant or anyone acting on her behalf reported any harassment. CF at 4-9. On November 29, 2022, an EEOC AJ issued an order dismissing Complainant’s hearing request, noting that the Agency had already issued a final decision, which Complainant had appealed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Carrier Technician at the Agency’s Garland-South Station in Garland, Texas. On April 17, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the basis of disability (physical- neck and shoulder) when: 1. Beginning on or about November 7, 2020 and ongoing, she was continually harassed (questioned) about her work restrictions and not provided work assistance; 2. Beginning on or about November 9, 2020, and continuing, she was required to do the walking portion of her route; 3. On December 23, 2020, she was yelled at and embarrassed in front of her coworkers; 4. On December 23, 2020, she was required to submit a new CA-17 and not paid for the time she missed from work to get the CA-17 completed; 5. On December 23, 2020, she was moved off Route 74 and required to case and carry Route 23; 6. On February 1, 2021, she was called to the supervisor’s desk to discuss her medical documents; 7. On March 23, 2021, she was harassed and referred to the District Reasonable Accommodation Committee (DRAC); 8. On April 2, 2021, her request for leave was not granted and she was charged Absent Without Leave (AWOL); and 9. On or about April 15, 2021, management gave her a modified assignment which changed her start time to 10:00 am and did not provide her with a mail cart. 2 The Agency dismissed a claim alleging that Complainant was attacked by a dog while on the job and not properly compensated for the time missed pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(1) as a collateral attack on the Office of Workers’ Compensation (OWCP), which has jurisdiction over issues of compensation for work-related injuries. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 71-75. We affirm the dismissal as the Commission has repeatedly stated that a complainant cannot use the EEO process to challenge actions which occurred during the OWCP adjudicatory process. See Janiece H. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC [number removed] (Jan. 8, 2016). The gravamen of Complainant’s claims amount to an allegation of a violation of the Rehabilitation Act because the Manager of Customer Service (Manager) subjected her to harassment based on her disability and forced her to work outside of her medical restrictions. Specifically, Complainant argues that the Manager marked her AWOL even though she had submitted a leave request which had been previously approved by the Supervisor of Customer Service (Supervisor), and that the Agency denied her a mail cart to help her with her duties. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing, but the AJ denied the hearing request as a sanction for Complainant’s failure to submit the required Preliminary Case Information and her failure to respond to the AJ’s Order to Show Cause. The AJ remanded the complaint to the Agency, and the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant, 59 (YOB 1962) worked as a Human Resources (HR) Generalist at the Agency’s Bellingham Customer Care Center in Troy, Michigan. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 70 and 92. According to Complainant, she had been detailed into her position for ten months prior to her selection, which became effective July 17, 2021. She stated that when she was offered a five percent (5%) salary increase, she told the HR Business Partner (Business Partner [age 58]) that she was eligible for an 8% increase. ROI at 71. Complainant initiated EEO contact on August 31, 2021. On November 17, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of age (59) and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 when on or about July 17, 2021, Complainant was awarded a 5% salary increase when selected for an HR Generalist position, while a peer selected for the same position was awarded an 8% salary increase. The basis of Complainant’s reprisal allegation is the instant complaint. ROI at 72. The Agency conducted an investigation into the complaint. The investigation revealed that Complainant’s coworker (Coworker [YOB: 1975]) was 46 at the time of her promotion effective on July 17, 2021. ROI at 98. Both Complainant and Coworker were selected and promoted to the position of HR Generalist HQ position, occupation code 0201-0140, on the Customer Care Team. ROI at 35, 92, and 98. An email was shared with Complainant that included the Form 50s of Coworker and Complainant evidencing their promotions to the position of HR Generalist. See ROI at 33-8. The email revealed that Coworker received an 8% raise, while Complainant only received a 5% raise. On June 13, 2015, the Postal Service issued a policy that governs promotional pay increases. That policy provides, “promotional pay increases will be determined based on 2 factors: distance from positions maximum salary, and the number of grades being promoted.” ROI at 86. The Postal Service’s policy does not provide for any other justification for promotional pay increases. The policy also contains an explanatory attachment that sets forth what promotional pay raise a candidate can receive under postal policy as follows: Promotional pay increase policy determined based on the following two (2) factors: a. Distance from maximum salary level of new grade (Employees will receive a minimum promotional salary increase of 3%, unless the increase takes their salary above the maximum of the new grade): • >20% = 3% up to 10% increase (inc) • 10%-20% = 3% up to 8% inc • < 10% = 3% up to 5% inc b. And, total number of grade levels being promoted (if applicable): • If 3 grades = 3% inc • If 4 or 5 grades = 5% inc • If 6+ grades = 8% inc. ROI at 87. Complainant’s Form 50 provides in the remark section “salary increase process under pay promotion policy effective 6/13/15. Level 19 promoted to level 21. Present increase 5% applied to current salary of $90,868.” Complainant’s Appeal Brief at 21. Coworker’s Form 50 contains the following statement in the remark section “salary increase process and promotional policy effective 6/13/15. Level 19 promoted to level 21. Percentage increase of 8% applied to current salary of $86,337.” Complainant’s Appeal Brief at 20. As both Complainant and Coworker’s pre-promotion salaries were between 10% to 20% of the top of the pay grade for EAS-21, and they fell within the 3% to 8% range for raise upon being promoted from their EAS-19 positions to the EAS-21 position of HR Generalist. ROI at 86-7 and Complainant’s Appeal Brief at 18. Complainant’s and Coworker’s respective ages were readily known to the Responsible Management Officials as it was reflected on their Form 50s. When Complainant was notified that she received the promotion, she was told that she would receive a 5% raise. According to Complainant, Business Partner told Complainant that she did not have a budget for an 8% raise and that she would have to get approval from a named individual. Business Partner also allegedly stated that Complainant did not have enough experience. ROI at 71. However, Complainant stated that she had been doing the job fully and successfully, she possessed a bachelor’s degree in business administration and had three years’ experience at the Troy Customer Care Center. Thus, she had higher education, more human resource experience, and more experience in the Customer Care Center than Coworker. ROI at 71; also compare ROI at 93-7 (Complainant’s resume) to ROI at 100-04 (Coworker’s resume). According to Complainant, Coworker’s education was limited to a high school certificate in cosmetology and licensing in cosmetology. ROI at 103. Complainant asserted that she worked in Human Resources for 32 months as a labor relations specialist from July 3, 2004 – March 30, 2007 as part of a detail assignment. ROI at 95. Complainant also asserted that the amount of training the respective candidates received while in detail reflected their readiness to assume the position. According to her, Coworker received more training than Complainant when she was detailed into the position of HR Generalist. Coworker allegedly received 1 hour on and 1 hour off the clock 1 on 1 training by an HR Generalist for 30 days when she was detailed into the position for a total of 60 hours of training. Complainant’s 1 on 1 training added up to less than 2 hours. ROI at 72. According to Business Partner, although she initially requested a 5% salary increase for Coworker, her manager (Manager), approved an 8% increase based on Coworker’s HR knowledge and experience. ROI at 77, 79, 92, and 100. Business Partner stated that she also offered a 5% salary increase to the last person she selected for the position of HR Generalist (YOB: 1976) in 2019, some two years prior. ROI at 78-9 and 83. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision (FAD) pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Supervisor Installation Management Officer, Quality Assurance Lead in Springfield, Virginia. Informal efforts to resolve his concerns were unsuccessful On November 9, 2021, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him based on race (African-American) and color (Brown). On December 6, 2021, the Agency issued a partial acceptance letter regarding the formal complaint. Therein, the Agency determined that the formal complaint was comprised of the following claims: 1. On April 17, 2021, Complainant alleged, that his named first-level supervisor, (S1) 2 informed co-workers and management Complainant was being removed from his role as a supervisor due to performance management issues; 3. On December 11, 2020, he alleged that while serving as a panel hiring manager, S1 repeatedly asked for the list of candidates, their resumes and the order they were ranked; 2 S1 identified his race as “primarily Northern European and American Indian” and his color as “medium sometimes burns, always tans.” ROI at 457. 5. After an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). 3 The claims are re-numbered herein for ease of reference. 4 Complainant does not contest that he informed the Agency that this claim was no longer valid. Thus, we decline to address this matter further herein. The Agency also dismissed claims (2), (4), (5), and (6) for failure to state a claim when viewing these matters as discrete acts. According to the Agency’s final decision, Complainant requested a final decision. 6 FAD at 3. The Agency found no discrimination. During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Special Agent at the U.S. Embassy in Lima, Peru. On April 17, 2019, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him based on age and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (prior EEO case and his wife’s prior EEO case). By letter dated May 31, 2019, the Agency accepted the formal complaint for investigation and framed his claims in the following fashion: Whether Complainant was discriminated against based on age (51) parental status, and reprisal when: 1. Since October 2018, Complainant has been subjected to a hostile work environment, including but not limited to the following matters: when on or about October 15, 2018, he was notified that he was not allowed to keep a rental car his wife had access to during a medivac; his Assistant Regional Director asked him more questions about his cases than he did of other agents; his general supervisor referred to his relationship with the Assistant Regional Director as “unhealthy;” comments adverse to Complainant were made to members of upper management including, but not limited to, the Acting Chief of Operations; 2. On or about November 28, 2018, his travel vouchers were not paid due to alleged erroneous payments made for 2017 and 2018; 3. On or about November 2018, Complainant was notified that he owed the Agency money for the 2017 and 2018 medivac evacuations; 4. On November 29, 2018, Complainant’s first-level supervisor, (S1) issued him an annual performance appraisal which, on various job elements, was lower than his 2017 appraisal; and 5. On April 9, 2019 his second-line supervisor refused to approve his request to alter the date he was scheduled to report to the Denver Field Division even though the Denver Field Division had approved his request. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 50. The Agency further set forth that the basis of parental status was not within the jurisdiction of the EEOC. ROI at 51. Finally, the Agency dismissed another claim on the grounds of untimely EEO Counselor contact. ROI at 52. 2 After an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. While this matter was before an EEOC AJ, Complainant withdrew the basis of age as well as claims (2) and (3). We therefore decline to address these matters further herein. Agency’s Response Brief Exhibit A. On October 19, 2021, Complainant withdrew his hearing request and requested an Agency final decision. On that same day, the AJ issued an Order of Dismissal remanding the matter to the Agency for a final decision. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency’s final decision found no discrimination. The final decision found that the alleged incidents were not sufficiently severe or pervasive to rise to the level of unlawful harassment. Final Agency Decision (FAD) at 11. The Agency further found that management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for Complainant not receiving an “Outstanding” rating on his 2018 performance evaluation (claim (4)). Specifically, the final decision set forth that Complainant had produced “just a few written work products during the rating period.” Id. The Agency further found that Complainant failed to establish that the Agency’s articulated reason for his rating was pretext for retaliation. FAD at 12. Finally, the Agency’s final decision found that management articulated a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for denying Complainant’s request to change his reporting date to the Denver Division. Specifically, the Agency’s final decision set forth that S2 had already approved Complainant’s request to end his tour in Peru on June 22, 2019, and that S2 believed that Complainant had to report to Denver when his tour in Peru ended. FAD at 12. The Agency’s final decision further found 2 Complainant does not expressly contest, on appeal, the Agency’s determination regarding the basis of parental status or the dismissal of one of his claims for untimely EEO Counselor contact. We therefore decline to address these matters further herein. that Complainant failed to establish that management’s articulated reason for this action was pretext for retaliation. FAD at 13. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Supervisory Border Patrol Agent (SBPA), GS-1896-13, assigned to the Brackettville Station, Del Rio Sector, in Brackettville, Texas. On September 16, 2020, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the basis of religion (non-Catholic) when, on August 11, 2020, Complainant was forced to attend a Catholic Church service while on-duty resulting in his shift change for the day. On August 11, 2020, the Chief Border Patrol Agent announced that on August 12, 2020, a funeral was scheduled for a Border Patrol Agent from the Del Rio Sector Brackettville Station, who had died in the line of duty. The service included three functions: the church service, the procession, and the formation (vehicle procession). Upon learning that all managers had to attend the funeral service, Complainant sent an email to the Patrol Agent in Charge (PAIC), stating, “Just to confirm what I was told verbally, all Supervisors have been ordered to attend the religious service and the gravesite service?” PAIC responded to the email stating, “Managers will attend the Line of Duty Ceremony and pay your respects as leaders.” However, due to COVID-19 restrictions, in person service was limited to family members only and the funeral service was livestreamed on the Del Rio Sector Facebook page. PAIC attended the in-person service and Complainant attended via livestream. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge. In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). In the decision, the Agency determined that Complainant failed to establish a prima facie case of denial of a religious accommodation. Although Complainant established that he held a bona fide religious belief, Complainant failed to demonstrate that his religious belief was in conflict with an employment duty. Complainant alleged that PAIC required that all SBPAs in the Station attend the Catholic Church services for the deceased BPA; however, PAIC indicated that he did not require that the SBPAs attend the church services. PAIC stated that there were three functions—the church service, the procession, and the formation (vehicle procession). PAIC stated that the only requirement was to attend the procession portion. PAIC maintained that the SBPAs were permitted to remain outside during the church services. PAIC noted he did not attend the mass because his religion also conflicted with Catholicism. Two SPBAs (SBPA-1 and SBPA-2) corroborated PAIC’s explanation that he did not mandate participation in the church services. SBPA-1 and SBPA-2 stated that PAIC required that the SBPAs attend the Line of Duty Ceremony and that attendance at the church services was voluntary. SBPA-2 explained that the Line of Duty Ceremony consisted of an honor guard, 21-gun salute, a riderless horse, and executive leadership speeches. Complainant stated that he did not have any objection to attending the procession or gravesite service. Furthermore, even assuming arguendo, that Complainant’s bona fide religious belief conflicted with PAIC’s requirement, the Agency found that Complainant failed to produce evidence that he notified the Agency of his belief and the conflict. In Complainant’s August 11, 2020 email requesting confirmation as to whether all SPBAs were required to attend the church service and gravesite service, Complainant did not notify PAIC of any conflict with his religion, and there is no other evidence in the record demonstrating that Complainant provided any such notification to management. As a result, the Agency concluded that Complainant was not denied religious accommodation or subjected to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-12 Senior Bankruptcy Specialist with the Agency’s Small Business/Self- Employed Division, Specialty Collection– Insolvency Office in Houston, Texas. On September 17, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her and subjected her to a hostile work environment on the bases of disability (Major Depression, Recurrence, Somatic Symptoms Disorder, Generalized Anxiety, TIA, Myofascial Pain, Acute Stress Disorder) and reprisal (prior protected EEO activity) when: 1. 1.Beginning February 2021 to the present, she has been denied paid leave under the Family Medical and Leave Act (FMLA); 2. On June 19, 2021, a manager reassigned all of a retired co-worker’s complex cases to her; 3. On August 3, 2021, she was denied eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave; 4. On August 24, 2021, her final appeal of a requested reasonable accommodation was denied; and 5. On October 26, 2021, her supervisor denied her official time request to work on her EEO complaint. Claims 1 & 3 – Leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) Complainant challenged leave issues, including her receipt of Absent Without Leave (AWOL) charges and placement in Leave Without Pay (LWOP) status in a prior EEO complaint before an EEOC Administrative Judge. On May 25, 2022, the Administrative Judge in that case found that the Agency had proven that it had placed Complainant in AWOL and LWOP status on various dates in February and March 2021, because Complainant had depleted her available paid leave balances and failed to report to work. In the instant complaint, Complainant again raised leave issues previously adjudicated, including her February and March 2021 receipt of AWOL charges and placement in LWOP status. Complainant also alleges that on August 3, 2021, her manager denied eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave. Complainant’s first-line supervisor (Supervisor1) explained that management’s calculations showed that Complainant had exhausted her paid, available sick leave by March 2021. Specifically, the Agency’s February 26, 2021, letter to Complainant regarding her request for FMLA provided that Complainant had only 32 hours of unpaid FMLA to use between March 1, 2021, and December 3, 2021. As such, on March 1, 2021, and on other dates, Supervisor notified Complainant that she had no paid leave available to use under FMLA. On various dates, including August 3, 2021, Supervisor granted Complainant FMLA-LWOP, rather than paid leave. Complainant did not request an audit of her leave until August 5, 2021. The audit of Complainant’s leave, conducted by a payroll representative, showed that Complainant had some paid leave available to use under FMLA. Accordingly, management retroactively granted Complainant paid leave, including for August 3, 2021. Complainant conceded that she ultimately received all paid leave that she requested and was entitled to receive. Complainant did not identify any similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding leave. Claim 2 – Reassignment of Casework In June 2021, one of Complainant’s GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialist co-workers retired. Complainant claimed that Supervisor emailed Complainant (a GS- 12) and two other GS-12 employees in the group to inform them that the now- retired employee’s cases would be reassigned among the three GS-12s. Complainant asserted that she should not have been reassigned this casework because she had previously submitted a request for reasonable accommodation and believed she should have been on indefinite weather and safety leave. 2 The Administrative Judge found that Complainant was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave, and that the Agency had met all its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act. The appeal is currently pending and docketed as EEOC [number removed]. Supervisor explained that she reassigned the cases because it was her job to assign inventory to employees in her group. Supervisor also explained that all reassigned work was appropriate for Complainant’s grade level. Supervisor further explained that the work was split among Complainant and the two other GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists in the group, based upon the alphabetical order of case names. The documentary record also contains a spreadsheet, provided by Supervisor1, showing the case assignments to Complainant and the two other Bankruptcy Specialists in the group. The record is devoid of similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding this claim. Claim 4 –Reasonable Accommodations On May 6, 2021, Complainant requested the following accommodations: (1) that her manager and/or secretary assistant print and mail her letters; and (2) a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her reasonable accommodation request to include reassignment. Complainant concedes that her medical impairment does not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. The Agency’s Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator met with Complainant on May 21, 2021, to hold an interactive meeting. Regarding her request for reduced workload and/or reassignment, the Agency issued a denial, noting that there was no medical explanation supporting Complainant’s need for such accommodations. The Agency’s denial also noted that lowering Complainant’s caseload would lower performance or production standards and would compromise the Agency’s ability to achieve its mission. Moreover, with an inventory of then only 25 cases, the undisputed record showed that Complainant already maintained a caseload well below other Bankruptcy Specialists and below the number of cases she typically held. 3 Regarding her request for reassignment, the Agency’s denial noted that Complainant was not eligible for reassignment because it is the accommodation of last resort (i.e., granted only when an employee is unable to meet the essential functions of her position). For example, to support a previous 2018 request for reduced inventory, Complainant’s psychologist had noted that Complainant desired a reduced inventory of approximately 38-40 cases. When Complainant requested reassignment as a reasonable accommodation in March 2020, the Agency explained that Complainant failed to submit medical documentation supporting that she was unable to meet the essential functions of her position. Rather, the evidence showed that Complainant wished to be reassigned because she had an unpleasant working relationship with her supervisors, and not because of any medical impairment’s effect on her ability to perform the essential functions of her job. To accommodate Complainant’s physical limitations, in response to Complainant’s May 6, 2021 reasonable accommodation request, the Agency approved Complainant to receive a small portable printer so that she could print and mail letters to taxpayers. While awaiting delivery of the smaller printer, Complainant’s management agreed to send Complainant’s correspondence for her. Before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket cancelling the printer because she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Complainant later averred that she would not be able to lift either the smaller printer or its paper. The Agency denied Complainant’s request for reconsideration of her reasonable accommodation denial. On July 12, 2021, Complainant appealed the Agency’s denial of her reconsideration request. On August 24, 2021, the Director of Collection Operations (Director) denied Complainant’s appeal. The denial noted that Complainant had summarily rejected the Agency’s offer to provide her with a smaller portable printer that she could lift. Further, the denial noted that Complainant had an already-reduced workload and was not eligible for reassignment because she was capable of performing the essential functions of her job. Claim 5 – Official Time On October 20, 2021, Complainant requested to use official time from approximately 10:30 a.m. on October 20 through 11:30 a.m. on October 21, 2021, to respond to an EEO Investigator’s request that Complainant complete an affidavit for the instant complaint. Complainant availed herself of six hours of official time on October 20, 2021, and four hours on October 21, 2021. Despite being provided these hours, Complainant did not complete her affidavit and requested additional time on October 25, 2021. On October 25, 2021, Supervisor approved Complainant’s request to use additional official time that day. On October 26, 2021, Complainant emailed the Department of Treasury, Office of Civil Rights and Diversity (OCRD) to request an extension of her deadline to complete her affidavit. In response, OCRD noted that Complainant could request an extension from the investigator if she needed more time to complete the affidavit. After receiving OCRD’s response, Complainant asked Supervisor for official time to complete the affidavit that day. When Supervisor asked Complainant if she had completed the affidavit, Complainant told Supervisor that she had two questions remaining. Because Complainant had already received approximately 18 hours of official time and because OCRD had instructed Complainant to contact the investigator if she needed an extension of her deadline, Supervisor denied Complainant’s request to continue working on her affidavit on official time on October 26, 2021. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC AJ. Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency. In the decision, the AJ determined that the alleged incidents were insufficiently severe or pervasive to establish a hostile work environment. Further, the AJ found that there was no evidence demonstrating that the conduct at issue was based on discriminatory or retaliatory animus. For example, Complainant failed to show that similarly situated employees outside of her protected classes were treated more favorably by being granted FMLA or other leave entitlements. Additionally, the record evidence showed that the reassigned cases from the retired, former coworker were split equally amongst Complainant and two of her Bankruptcy Specialists coworkers for unrebutted reasons relative to grade, skill level and appropriateness given Complainant’s low workload. With respect to her denial of reasonable accommodation claim, the AJ determined that in her May 6, 2021 request, Complainant requested that her manager and/or secretary assist her to print and mail her letters and also requested a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her request to include reassignment. During the investigation of the instant complaint, Complainant admitted that her impairment did not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. Moreover, she did not adduce any probative evidence that previously offered accommodations—a post of duty (with telework) away from her manager and communication primarily by email—did not enable the Complainant to perform the essential functions of her position. Further, the AJ found that the record supported the Agency’s denial of Complainant’s request for a reduced inventory. An agency is not required to change production standards, e.g., to lower an employee’s quota for cases. Complainant provided no evidence that she could not adequately perform her assignments given she had an unusually low inventory of only 25 cases. Finally, the AJ concluded that the undisputed record showed, after an interactive meeting, the Agency approved Complainant for a lightweight, portable printer. While awaiting delivery of the smaller printer, Complainant’s management agreed to send Complainant’s correspondence for her. However, before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket requesting cancellation of the printer delivery, stating that she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Management continued to print and mail her letters. As a result, the AJ found that the Agency did not deny Complainant reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. Finally, the AJ found that the Agency’s grant of 18 hours of official time was objectively reasonable for Complainant to complete her affidavit despite the investigators’ numerous questions. The record showed that Complainant’s time was spent including information and documentation she previously provided in previous complaints. The Agency was entitled to limit the Complainant’s use of official time to 18 hours to complete her affidavit for this complaint and to have her seek additional time from the investigator. Accordingly, the AJ concluded that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination, reprisal, or a hostile work environment as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Sexual Assault and Prevention Response Program Manager (GS-13) at the Agency’s Integrated Response Directorate (Violence Prevention) at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. On December 1, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African American) and age (49), and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity, when: 1. on October 18, 2021, Complainant learned that she was not selected for the position of an Interpersonal Violence Prevention Response Policy Analyst (GS- 14), announced under vacancy number 9L-AFPC-11219496-355928-FA. Complainant amended her complaint to allege reprisal when: 2. on March 3, 2022, Complainant learned that she was not selected for the position of an Integrated Resilience Division Chief (GS-14), announced under vacancy number 8Q-AFPC-484168-11360859-MER. On or about April 25, 2022, the Agency electronically issued a report of investigation (ROI) for claim 1 and Complainant’s notice of right to file a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge. Complainant “picked-up” the ROI on April 26, 2022. The Agency completed a supplemental ROI for claim 2, on June 9, 2022. Appeal Complaint File at 1266-1270, 347. The Agency issued a final decision on November 21, 2022, noting that it did not receive an election from Complainant of a hearing or a final decision within the time frame allowed. The Agency found that management officials provided legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for Complainant’s nonselections, and she did not show that the reasons were pretexts for discrimination or retaliation. The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that she was subjected to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Nurse Practitioner at the Agency’s facility in Hampton, Virginia. On July 6, 2021, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint on alleging that the Agency discriminated against her based on her race (African American), sex (female), and disability (Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), anxiety, and depression). By letter dated July 30, 2021, the Agency determined that the formal complaint was comprised of the following claims: (a) In January 2021, [named Physician - P1] took Complainant out of patient care to shadow him to re-learn his work processes. (b) On July 15, 2020, [P1] used profanity to Complainant when asking for support with managing a patient. (c) On May 20, 2021, Complainant was rated unsatisfactory on her FY 2021 nursing proficiency and placed on a Focused Professional Practice Evaluation (FPPE). (d) On July 12, 2021, [named Chief of Staff] issued Complainant a letter of admonishment. 2 Report of Investigation (ROI) at 28-29. The Agency accepted claims (a)-(d), defined as a hostile work environment claim, for investigation. The Agency also accepted claims (c) and (d) as timely raised discrete acts of disparate treatment. ROI at 28-30. After an investigation into the accepted claims, Complainant was provided a copy of the investigative file and requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). On August 25, 2022, the Agency filed a Motion for a Decision Without a Hearing (Agency’s Motion). The Agency’s Motion asserted that it had legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the actions at issue. The complaint also included three additional claims: (1) In September 2020, a named physician (P1) advised a Pharmacist to write her up after a disagreement about a medication dose; (2) in September 2020, a named Service Chief charged her with unprofessional behavior; and (3) Complainant was taken off of a compressed tour. The Agency dismissed claims (1)-(3) on the grounds that Complainant raised these matters in a prior EEO case. ROI at 28. On appeal, Complainant does not expressly contest the dismissal of claims (1)-(3). Therefore, we decline to address them further herein. However, these claims may serve as background evidence regarding the hostile work environment harassment claim currently before us. For example, the Agency asserted that P1 detected that Complainant had performance deficiencies. Agency’s Motion at 3-4. The Agency further asserted that the actions at issue were not sufficiently severe or pervasive to set forth an actionable harassment claim. Agency’s Motion at 7. In addition, the Agency, in its Motion, set forth that Complainant failed to present evidence that the alleged actions were based on her protected EEO classes. Id. On September 15, 2022, Complainant, through her attorney, filed a detailed response to the Agency’s Motion. Therein, Complainant asserted that a decision without a hearing is improper because material questions of fact exist and there is a need for credibility determinations that require a hearing. Response to Agency’s Motion at 9-10. Complainant asserted that P1 frequently referred to her disabilities and her need to take time off of work. Response to Agency’s Motion at 14. Complainant reasserted that the actions at issue rise to the level of discriminatory harassment. Complainant stated that P1 lied and misrepresented facts regarding her performance. Response to Agency’s Motion at 22-23. The AJ issued a decision by summary judgment finding no discrimination. The AJ’s decision adopted the Agency’s Motion with little additional analysis. The AJ set forth that the claims “appear to be typical disputes about performance….[and] the record does not reflect that management was motivated by discriminatory animus.” The Agency’s final action implemented the AJ’s decision. Complainant filed the instant appeal.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Letter Carrier at the Carrier Annex in Roswell, Georgia. On January 9, 2020, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the basis of disability (Major depression with possible schizophrenic episodes/perceived mental disability) when: 1. On August 26, 2019, Complainant was placed on emergency placement and not permitted to return to work; and 2. On March 20, 2020, Complainant did not receive her pay for pay period 06-20. Following an investigation, the Agency issued a final decision finding that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination. Complainant appealed and in Maxima R. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC [number removed] (May 3, 2022), the Commission reversed the Agency’s decision and found that Complainant was subjected to discrimination as to both claims. To remedy the discrimination, the Commission ordered the Agency, among other things, to conduct a supplemental investigation into Complainant’s entitlement to compensatory damages. The evidentiary record on compensatory damages in this case consists entirely of two affidavits submitted by Complainant. The first affidavit is part of the report of investigation (ROI) of the underlying complaint. The second is a document submitted as part of the supplemental investigation into Complainant’s entitlement to damages. Complainant averred that she felt embarrassed about losing her job and humiliated when she was forced to apply for lower-paying jobs. She further averred that the Agency’s actions made her feel worthless and depressed, and that they aggravated her pre- existing schizophrenia to the point where she began to hear voices more frequently than before. She stated that she began seeing a counselor through the Employee Assistance Program and that eventually she saw three psychiatrists, two of whom prescribed medications for her. In particular, she noted that she had been hospitalized for a week in March 2020, and that during her hospital stay, she was given Risperdal, an anti-depressant, and Lithium to control weight gain. ROI 84-86, 90-91, 148-52. In her supplemental affidavit, Complainant stated that due to her diminished income, she was forced to sell her home and move to a less desirable neighborhood, that her schizophrenia had gotten worse in that she continued to hear voices, that she had to liquidate her Thrift Savings Plan account, and that she stopped communicating with her family and had become a recluse. Supplemental Affidavit (July 18, 2022), pp. 2-4. She requests the statutory maximum amount of non-pecuniary compensatory damages, $300,000.00. In its final decision, the Agency noted that Complainant’s affidavits did not include a “single medical document” describing any health problem associated with the time period August 2019 through April 2020. The Agency noted that, pursuant to an arbitration agreement, it awarded Complainant back pay for the time she was off and placed her on administrative leave through pay period 6-20. The Agency further noted that Complainant was able to utilize sick leave and annual leave beginning in pay period 7-20. The Agency ultimately found that Complainant failed to establish the necessary causal connection between the actions found to have been discriminatory and the symptoms she described. Nevertheless, the Agency awarded Complainant $20,000. in non-pecuniary compensatory damages. Complainant also made a claim for pecuniary damages to cover reimbursement for medical services in the amount of $2,569.00. While the Agency found that she had not presented enough evidence to link those expenses to the conduct found to be discriminatory, the Agency did award pecuniary damages covering reimbursement for a credit card late fee in the amount of $39. and $15. for mailing costs associated with the processing of the instant complaint, for a total of $54.10. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Real Estate Specialist (Acquisition) at the Agency’s Greensboro Facilities Field Office in Greensboro, North Carolina. On June 5, 2024, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency subjected him to discrimination and harassment on the basis of physical disability (foot injury) and mental disability (Anxiety, Depression, chronic Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder) when Complainant was forced to retire on January 26, 2024, and when: 1. In August 2023, Manager, Real Estate Acquisitions (Manager) began to harass Complainant about his absence from work; 2. On an unspecified date, Complainant was notified that Manager mentioned Complainant’s medical condition during a meeting; 3. In late September or early October 2023, Complainant’s Manager accused Complainant of not performing his duties in relation to the Philadelphia Roxborough Station and New Baltimore, Pennsylvania; 4. On January 26, 2024, Complainant’s Manager sent an email to his attention in which she harassed Complainant for his alleged poor performance related to reestablishing a USPS presence in Haskins, OH; and, 5. On an unspecified date, Manager attempted to controvert Complainant’s claim with the Office of Workers Compensation Programs (OWCP). In the Agency’s Partial Acceptance/Partial Dismissal of Formal EEO Complaint, the Agency accepted Claims 1-4 and dismissed Claim 5 for failure to state a claim because it was a collateral attack on another forum’s proceeding. The Agency dismissed Claim 5 finding the proper forum to raise a challenge to decisions made in the OWCP process is through that forum itself. The Agency instructed EEO Investigator (Investigator) to investigate the complaint of discrimination on July 8, 2024. Investigator sent Complainant a request for an affidavit to Complainant's email address of record and Complainant’s attorney’s address of record on July 15, 2024. The request was sent again on July 16, 2024. The affidavit request included notice that if Complainant did not submit a completed affidavit within 15 days of receipt of the request, Complainant's complaint may be dismissed for failure to cooperate. Investigator received completed affidavits from Manager and two witness affidavits, as well as additional relevant materials including but not limited to, Complainant’s position description; PS Forms 3871 Request for or Notification of Absence which Complainant submitted between August 2023 and January 2024; email communications between Complainant and Manager regarding the project in Haskins, OH; and retirement documents. Investigator did not receive a response from Complainant prior to the Investigator’s submission of the investigative file to the Agency on October 27, 2023. The Agency dismissed the complaint for failure to cooperate pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(7). The instant appeal followed.

test.background: The record reveals that, during the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Nutritionist, GS-0630- 13, at the Agency’s facility in Alexandria, Virginia. On August 18, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated and harassed her on the bases of sex (female), color (black), disability (femoroacetabular impingement with labral tearing), age (43), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity with respect to six (6) issues. She alleged that: 1. On December 8, 2017, management issued her a Letter of Counseling and accused her of lying about her disability to avoid work; 2. On October 30, 2017, management issued her 2017 performance appraisal, which contained exaggerated and/or false statements, and thereafter on December 1, 2017, denied her appeal of said performance appraisal; 3. On May 5, 2017, management denied her request for ad hoc telework; 4. On April 4, 2017, management issued her a Letter of Record accusing her of using dates of unscheduled leave; 5. On an unspecified date, management forced her to share her medical condition to the entire staff via email; 6. On several unspecified dates, she was subjected to various incidents of harassment, including but not limited to: a. On an unspecified date, management made false statements about her work performance and work product; b. On an unspecified date, management purposely misrepresented the Alternative Dispute Resolution process to her; and c. On an unspecified date, bulky pieces of furniture were purposely set in place to block her cubical, which impeded her walkway. According to the Agency, at the end of the investigation, Complainant, in March 2018, was provided a copy of the investigative file and was informed of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge, or alternatively to receive a final decision by the Agency. When Complainant, according to the Agency, did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. This appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a City Carrier at the Agency’s Post Office in Glenview, Illinois. Report of Investigation (ROI), at 6. On August 2, 2017, Complainant was issued a Last Chance Agreement (LCA) dated July 28, 2017, to resolve a Notice of Removal issued to Complainant on July 5, 2017. ROI, at 117-119. The LCA noted that Complainant agreed that he would have no more than three unscheduled absences in a six-month period, and he would be subject to removal if he violated the agreement. Id. On February 5, 2018, Complainant was issued with a second Notice of Removal for an apparent violation of the LCA. Id. at 114-116. In the removal, Complainant was cited with six instances of unscheduled leave from August 25, 2017, through December 1, 2017, and one hour of tardiness on January 24, 2018. Id. On June 30, 2018, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (African-American), sex (male), color (black), and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when on or around March 9, 2018, he was issued a Notice of Removal. 2 Following the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision on November 13, 2018, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The Agency specifically found that it articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions, and Complainant did not establish that its reasons were pretextual based on his protected classes. Complainant thereafter apparently requested a hearing on December 20, 2018, after the Agency issued its final decision on November 13, 2018. The assigned AJ dismissed Complainant’s hearing request on April 11, 2019, for being untimely pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f). On appeal, Complainant maintains that management violated his rights under the Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA), and that the Agency deleted documentation from its files in attempt to conceal its conduct. Complainant further maintains that his hearing request was timely, as he submitted his request on September 8, 2018. In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision finding no discrimination. The Agency also asserts that the AJ properly dismissed Complainant’s hearing request, which was untimely in accordance with 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f). 3

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Special Agent at the Agency’s Miami Division in Miami, Florida. 1. On February 9, 2017, Agency management denied Complainant’s request for a Law Enforcement Officer Identification Card (LEO ID Card); and 2. On March 28, 2017, Agency management denied Complainant’s appeal of the decision not to grant her a LEO ID Card. Complainant worked as a special agent (SA) at the time of her retirement. She stated that she decided to retire on August 3, 2016, and sent her retirement package to the Agency on that day, for overnight delivery. On August 5, 2016, while Complainant was on medical leave, three Agency employees came to her home to retrieve her service weapon, complete paperwork, and give her a security briefing. Complainant stated that, the week following the Agency employees visiting her home, one of those Agency employees (CW1) returned Complainant’s personally owned weapon (POW). Complainant stated that the documentation of her firearms training should have been included with her POW, but that paperwork was not returned when her POW was. Complainant stated that she was later informed by CW1 that a first-level supervisor (S1) stated that Complainant was not entitled to the firearm training documentation, her retired credentials, a retirement plaque, or a LEO ID. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 11. Complainant stated that during the six-months after her retirement, she was in contact with the Agency’s Human Resources Division (HRD) requesting her LEO ID. Complainant stated that her request for her LEO ID was denied on February 9, 2017, based on information from the Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR). Complainant appealed the denial of her LED ID to the HRD Assistant Director, who denied the appeal on March 28, 2017. The Agency stated that Complainant was proposed for removal, prior to her retirement, due to an investigation conducted by OPR. ROI at 89. Complainant’s proposed removal was related to an investigation initiated by Agency’s management. OPR proposed Complainant’s removal from Federal service on charges of False/Misleading Financial Information and Insubordination pertaining to repeated acts of falsified time and attendance documentation and failure to obey her supervisor’s instructions on six occasions. Complainant contacted an EEO counselor on March 22, 2017, and she was issued a Notice of Right to File on May 19, 2017. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision (FAD) pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. Report of Investigation file dated November 21, 2017. Report of Investigation file dated February 13, 2019.

During the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Medical Support Assistant (MSA), GS-5, at the Agency’s Bay Pines Medical Center in Bay Pines, Florida. In 2013, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that her supervisor was sexually harassing her. The supervisor was subsequently terminated in July 2014. However, in December 2014, the supervisor returned to the facility on numerous occasions. Due to the ex-supervisor’s presence, Complainant requested a reassignment to another MSA position, one where her ex-supervisor would not have access. Before being transferred, Complainant was informed that she was eligible for an upcoming non-competitive promotion to GS-6 MSA. In meeting with management regarding the move, she confirmed her eligibility for the promotion to GS-6. Complainant’s transfer was approved and effective December 29, 2014. In late February 2015, management issued a memorandum identifying the individuals who had been referred to Human Resources for the promotion. When Complainant asked why she was not included, the Agency explained that her current work in an inpatient area did not qualify. Believing that the Agency’s failure to promote her was reprisal for her prior EEO activity, Complainant filed an EEO complaint on April 27, 2017. Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ), but later withdrew her request. The case was remanded to the Agency, which issued a decision finding no discrimination. Complainant appealed the decision to the Commission. In Complainant v. Dep’t of Veterans Affairs, EEOC [number removed] (May 25, 2018), the Commission found the record contained evidence of pretext. The Agency explained that Complainant was not promoted to GS-6 simply because her requested transfer was granted and she was placed in a position that was not eligible for the promotion. However the record established that when Complainant requested the move, she also inquired about maintaining her eligibility for the upcoming promotion. See id. In response, the management official told Complainant that she would be moved to a position that allowed for the promotion to GS-6, because she was already in such a position. See id. Following this initial meeting with Complainant and her union representative, the management official purportedly met with two other managers. See id. The Commission observed that the record did not contain any information regarding the content of the subsequent meeting/s or information on what positions were available. See id. Moreover, management did not inform Complainant that her new position was ineligible for the promotion and Complainant’s SF-50 was never updated to reflect the move. See id. The Commission concluded that “due to the Agency’s actions, Complainant received a significantly less desirable reassignment after a report of harassment which the Agency does not dispute occurred.” See id. The Agency was ordered to offer Complainant the promotion, provide back pay, consider compensatory damages, and train the responsible managers on their EEO obligations. Additionally, Complainant was entitled to attorney’s fees and costs. Complainant filed a request for reconsideration of the decision, limited to the matter of leave restoration. See Complainant v. Dep’t of Veterans Affairs, EEOC [number removed] (September 27, 2018). The request was denied. The Commission explained that the previous order instructed the Agency to calculate Complainant’s entitlement to “back pay and benefits,” which encompassed leave. Nevertheless, the Commission issued a new order, modifying the order in EEOC [number removed], for clarity. Complainant was expressly provided the opportunity to offer evidence regarding lost leave. See id. On August 13, 2018, Complainant’s attorney requested the Agency pay $35,862. for 101. hours of work at a rate of $350 per hour, as well as $407. in costs. The request was comprised of three petitions: the “Initial Petition”, for 60 hours completed between December 8, 2015 and June 4, 2018; “Second Petition”, for 19 hours expended from June 6 through June 29, 2018, on the matter of compensatory damages; and “Third Petition” for 22. hours worked between June 24, 2018 and August 2, 2018, on the request for reconsideration and compensatory damages. In a decision dated November 16, 2018 2, the Agency concluded that Complainant was only entitled to 47. hours ($16,730.00) and $302. in costs. The record reflects that, on November 30, 2018, the Agency issued a check payable to Complainant’s attorney in the amount of $17,032.83. As an initial matter, the Agency accepted Complainant’s attorney’s hourly rate ($350) and agreed that Complainant was a “prevailing party,” with respect to the finding of discrimination. The Agency, however, disagreed with the number of hours claimed by Complainant. The Agency excluded hours in three categories it labeled: “Non-productive Efforts”; “Not Prevailing Party”; and “Compensatory Damages”. The Agency determined that 37. hours expended on a hearing, that was later withdrawn by Complainant, were not productive or reimbursable. This included time spent on client conferences, discovery responses, and calls with opposing counsel. Because Complainant’s request for reconsideration (EEOC [number removed]) was denied, the Agency found that Complainant was not a “prevailing party” and not eligible for the 13. hours spent on the request. Finally, with respect to compensatory damages 3, the Agency observed that Complainant’s attorney sought 2. hours purportedly conducting research for compensatory damages, on July 18, 2018, when the petition was submitted on June 25, 2018. Complainant filed the instant appeal.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Safety and Occupational Health Specialist, GS-11, at the Agency’s Manufacturing Department in San Francisco, California. On August 29, 2018, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint claiming that the Agency subjected him to discriminatory harassment based on race (African-American) and color (black) when, in front of Complainant and a member of management, a white auditor visiting the office (“CW1”) made the comment “it must be my black humor.” When confronted by the Division Head that the proper phrase is “dark humor,” CW1 said, “I know what I said and what I meant.” Then CW1 turned to Complainant and said, “I could have said Black Face humor. After the investigation of the claim, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of the right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) or a final decision within thirty days of receipt of the correspondence. Complainant requested a final decision. On February 21, 2019, the Agency issued the instant final decision, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Visual Information Specialist at the Agency’s Office of the Associate Director of Communication, Division of Communications Services in Atlanta, Georgia. Complainant was reassigned from an enclosed office to a cubicle. Complainant objected, stating that her medical condition required that she be in a warm environment. The Agency provided a heater for her cubicle. Complainant argued that this accommodation was not effective and requested an enclosed office. Thereafter, she filed a grievance with the union. On August 12, 2015, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), color (Brown), disability (osteoarthritis, degenerative disk disease, three knee operations, migraines, sensitivity to light, and walks with a cane), age (58), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when: 1. on March 18, 2015, Complainant's request for reasonable accommodation (RA) was denied; 2. on March 18, 2015, the Labor Relations Specialist (LRS), shared Complainant's personal and confidential information without her permission with other Agency personnel; 3. on March 23, 2015, the LRS did not provide Complainant an official CDC 0. 1284 form concerning her requests for RA; and 4. on March 24, 2015, the LRS accused Complainant of misconduct and encouraged management to take disciplinary action against her. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. On September 21, 2018, over Complainant's objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s January 27, 2017, motion to dismiss the complaint. When the Agency failed to issue a final order within forty days of receipt of the AJ’s decision, the AJ’s decision became the Agency’s final action pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i). Specifically, the AJ found that, with respect to claim 1, Complainant had previously elected the negotiated grievance process as the forum in which to pursue the alleged removal of her accommodations and was precluded from pursuing the same claim in the EEO process. The AJ also determined that this claim was untimely and failed to state a claim. With respect to claim number 2, the AJ found that the communication in question did not disclose any medical information and did not constitute a breach of confidentiality. With respect to claim number 3, the AJ found that this claim was barred on the same preclusion grounds as claim 1. Finally, with respect to claim number 4, the AJ found that the statements alleged were not actionable and did not constitute “EEO retaliation.”

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Rural Carrier Associate at the Agency’s Zephyrhills, Florida Post Office. On April 30, 2018, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of religion (Christian), disability (FMLA/doctor appointments/entire body), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 when: 1. On January 4, 2018, he was given an Investigative Interview and subsequently on January 5, 2018, he was issued a Letter of Warning for Unsatisfactory Attendance; 2. Beginning on or about February 23, 2018, and continuing, he was required to work on Sundays; and 3. On March 4, 2018, he was required to perform clerk duties and sort Amazon parcels. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency sent Complainant a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge via certified-mail, signature required. On October 30, 2018, the report of investigation and notice of the right to a hearing were returned to the Agency. On November 16, 2018, asserting that Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. On December 19, 2018, Complainant simultaneously requested a hearing and filed the instant appeal. 2

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Staff Officer, Pay Band V, at the Agency’s St. Louis Human Development Directorate facility in St. Louis, MO. Complainant applied for a senior executive level position. Several other employees applied for the same position. An Agency panel reviewed the applications and background performance information. The Program and Office Administration Career Service Board did not forward Complainant’s application to the Executive Career Service Board for selection consideration. Complainant was not selected to proceed further in the process. On July 17, 2016, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of her race (African-American), sex (female), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, when she was not selected for promotion to the senior executive level. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew her request. The Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Full-Time Maintenance Mechanic, PS-07/O, at the Agency’s Chicago Metro Surface Hub in Elk Grove Village, Illinois. 1. On March 24, 2018 to April 14, 2018, Complainant was denied overtime opportunities; 2. On or around February 13, 2018, Complainant was denied a detail opportunity and career advancement; 3. On March 9, 2018, management reposted a previously eliminated position; 4. On dates not specified, management did not correctly post EAS position vacancies; 5. On June 12, 2018, management reverted vacant maintenance positions; and 6. On July 17, 2018, Complainant was sent home, told not to return to work until she had medical documentation for her recent absence, and charged absence without leave (AWOL) while she was off work at management’s instruction. The Agency dismissed Claims (3) and (5) for failure to state a claim because these claims constituted a collateral attack on a negotiated grievance settlement reached between the union and Agency management under the collective bargaining agreement. The Agency also dismissed Claim (4) for failure to state a claim because Complainant did not show that she was aggrieved by this allegation. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency asserted that it provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation (ROI) and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that management subjected her to discrimination or reprisal as alleged.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Lead Mail Processing Clerk, GS 7 at the Agency’s Atlanta Processing and Distribution Center in Atlanta, Georgia. On May 3, 2017, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint claiming that the Agency subjected her to discriminatory harassment based on her sex (female) when: 1. Complainant’s address to entry door #2 was revoked; 2. Complainant has not been granted access to all offices and locker rooms; 3. 4. Complainant has not been selected as the acting supervisor; 5. since November 2016, Complainant has not been paid higher level pay; and 6. on January 5, 2017, and other dates, Complainant has not been permitted to perform her Lead Clerk duties. After the investigation of the accepted claims, 2 the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of the right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) or a final decision within thirty days of receipt of the correspondence. Complainant timely requested a hearing. However, Complainant subsequently withdrew her hearing request. On April 17, 2019, the Agency issued the instant final decision, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination. The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant does not submit any statements or briefs.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Postal Inspector, GS-12, at the Agency’s Chicago Division in Chicago, Illinois. Complainant indicated that he had been employed by the Agency since January 2013. In December 2014, the Agency’s Office of Inspector General (OIG) interviewed him and informed him that he had an outstanding civil lawsuit from 1999. Complainant noted that the lawsuit was related to a rent dispute between him and his college roommates. Complainant indicated that in January 2015, while conducting his official postal inspection service responsibilities, he took time to take care of this debt by briefly attending a court case, meeting with the individual that he was indebted to and repaid the debt and returning to the court to submit proof of payment. Complainant stated that he was subsequently issued a notice of proposed removal and letter of decision for his misuse of official government vehicle, misuse of official information, and providing false information. On April 8, 2016, Complainant filed his complaint alleging discrimination based on race (Black) and sex (male) when on October 16, 2015, he was issued a notice of proposed removal which was subsequently upheld via a letter of decision dated February 12, 2016. Upon completion of the investigation of the complaint, Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). On June 30, 2017, the Agency filed a Motion for Judgment Without a Hearing and Complainant filed his response on July 12, 2017. Thereafter, the Agency filed a reply to Complainant’s response. On March 27, 2017, the AJ issued a decision without holding a hearing, finding no discrimination. Therein, the AJ adopted the Agency’s motion including the material facts therein. The Agency’s final order implemented the AJ’s decision. Complainant appeals the Agency’s final order.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Mail Handler at the Agency’s Dallas Network Distribution Center in Dallas, Texas. On June 16, 2017, the Agency issued Notices of Abolishment of Position to Complainant and other Mail Handlers. They were informed that they would be “unassigned regular” full-time employees, effective June 24, 2017, and were encouraged to bid on posted duty-assignments. On June 28, 2017, the Agency rescinded all the notices of abolishment and the employees were instructed to report for their regular schedules on July 8, 2017. On June 28, 2017, Complainant initiated pre-complaint counseling alleging age discrimination in a class action complaint. On July 10, 2017, the Agency sent Complainant information on the processing of class complaints. The Agency informed Complainant that class complaints were processed differently than individual complaints of discrimination; for example, that a class complaint is not investigated by the Agency but is forwarded to the nearest EEOC office where an Administrative Judge (AJ) is appointed to make an initial determination to accept or dismiss the complaint. On September 22, 2017, the Agency issued Complainant his notice of right to file a formal complaint. On September 25, 2017, Complainant filed a formal class complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against the class members on the basis of age when on June 16, 2017, Senior Mail Handlers received letters abolishing their bid assignments. On October 16, 2017, the Agency forwarded the class complaint to the EEOC’s Dallas District Office. On May 10, 2019, the AJ issued an Order to Show Cause to determine if a live claim remained following the resolution during the grievance process, which resulted in the Agency rescinding the letters. Complainant timely responded to the AJ’s order and stated that the Agency did not completely restore his abolished position. Specifically, Complainant stated that his off days were changed to Fridays and Saturdays, and that the Agency refused to change them to Saturdays and Sundays. On June 7, 2019, the AJ issued an Order Entering Dismissal pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(5), finding that the complaint was moot. The AJ found that the record showed that the Agency rescinded the letters of job abolishment, which placed the affected Mail Handlers back into their jobs with appropriate backpay.
