The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s dismissal, and it also concluded that Complainant’s individual complaint of discrimination was subject to dismissal as moot for the same reasons that support the dismissal of the class complaint. 2 Complainant filed the instant appeal and submitted a statement in support of his appeal. The Agency opposed Complainant’s appeal. We note that the Commission has the discretion to review only those issues specifically raised in an appeal. See Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614, at Chap. 9, § IV.A. (Aug. 5, 2015). On appeal, Complainant did not contest the Agency’s dismissal of his individual claim of discrimination; as such, we will not address that claim in the instant decision.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Transportation Security Officer at the Agency’s Los Angeles International Airport in Sacramento, California. On October 13, 2014, Complainant received her fiscal year 2014 performance rating score of 3.47, with an overall rating of “Exceeds Expectations.” Report of Investigation (ROI) at 93. On May 13, 2015, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), sex (female), and color (brown) when on October 13, 2014, she received an “Exceeded Expectations” performance rating. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge. Complainant requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency did not include a prima facie analysis of Complainant’s claim because management officials articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for Complainant’s performance rating. Complainant’s then first-line supervisor (S1) stated that he relied upon Complainant’s prior first- line supervisor (S2) because S1 did not supervise Complainant for the majority of the year. S1 noted that he did not observe Complainant performing at a level to obtain a score of 5 in the areas of critical thinking and teamwork. S1 also stated that he did not have any documentation to support higher scores. The Agency found that Complainant did not show that the reasons were pretext for discrimination. The Agency determined that Complainant did not provide any documentation to support a higher performance rating, or that S1 lowered her rating due to her color, race, or sex. The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Carrier Technician at the Bronx Soundview Station in Bronx, New York. Report of Investigation (ROI), at 10. On December 17, 2007, Complainant suffered an on-the-job injury, which resulted in two arthroscopy knee surgeries and was placed on limited duty. Id. at 81. Complainant stopped reporting for duty shortly after he suffered a second on-the-job injury on June 13, 2016, when he reportedly turned his ankle and twisted both his knees. Complainant thereafter filed a claim with the Office of Workers’ Compensation Programs (OWCP) concerning his June 13, 2016, injury, and received a decision from the OWCP dated March 15, 2017. The OWCP’s decision concluded that the “mechanism of injury is unclear. The evidence does not establish that [Complainant] stepped into a hole in the ground as claimed.” Supplemental Report of Investigation (Supp. ROI), at 194. Thereafter, beginning on May 16, 2017, Complainant was marked by management has having accumulated 472 hours of Absence Without Leave (AWOL). ROI, at 357. However, according to Complainant, after he was injured for a second time in June 2016, management failed to turn over his paperwork to the OWCP. Complainant believed that if his OWCP claim had been properly processed he would have received payment and medical treatment for his injury. Complainant believed that his OWCP documentation was suppressed by management in an attempt to force him to work full-time. Complainant however received a letter from the Department of Labor (DOL) dated July 12, 2016, noting that the OWCP was in receipt of his claim for a traumatic injury filed on June 15, 2016. Supp. ROI at 279. The Manager of Customer Service also attested that Complainant’s OWCP claim was submitted to the DOL in 2016 but was denied by DOL for not submitting the appropriate medical documentation. Id. at 168-169. Management subsequently presented Complainant with a Notice of Removal dated August 10, 2017. ROI, at 357. The Notice of Removal noted that Complainant failed to report for duty from May 16, 2017, through August 3, 2017, accumulating 472 hours of AWOL. Id. The Notice of Removal specifically stated that Complainant failed to call-in as required during his absences and failed to provide administratively acceptable documentation to support his absences. Id. According to the Manager of Customer Service, Complainant did not submit proper documentation to justify his absences, so she was directed by Human Resources to charge him with AWOL and issue him the Notice of Removal. Supp. ROI at 168-169. The Manager of Customer Service also attested that Complainant did not respond to communications timely and would submit documentation two to three months late. Id. The Manager of Customer service further explained that Complainant stopping calling and failed to report to work and she made it clear to him that if he did not call or report to work he would be marked as AWOL. Id. On October 12, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the basis of disability (physical) when: 1. The on-the-job injury he sustained on June 13, 2016, was not approved by the OWCP of the DOL; and 2. On August 10, 2017, he was issued a Notice of Removal for being AWOL. On November 9. 2017, the Agency issued a partial/acceptance dismissal of Complainant’s complaint. Therein, the Agency accepted claim 2 for investigation, but dismissed claim 1 for the failure to state a claim, finding that it constituted a collateral attack on the OWCP process. Following the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant initially requested a hearing. Thereafter, the AJ determined that Claim 1 was improperly framed by the Agency and found that claim 1 should have been framed as follows: Whether Complainant was subjected to disability-based disparate treatment in terms, conditions, and privileges of the Agency’s processing of Complainant’s documentation related to his Workers’ Compensation claim. The AJ also noted that Complainant withdrew his hearing request, and therefore remanded Complainant’s complaint to the Agency for a supplemental investigation. The Agency thereafter completed the supplemental investigation and issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), concluding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The Agency initially determined that Complainant failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination with respect to claims 1 and 2, finding that Complainant did not identify any employees outside his protected class who were treated more favorably. The Agency nevertheless assumed, without finding, that Complainant established a prima facie case of discrimination, but found that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. In so finding, the Agency noted that Complainant never submitted evidence to support his absences, did not respond to communications from management, and submitted documentation three months late, causing confusion. The Agency observed that Complainant was informed that his continued failure to report to work or call-in his absences would lead to discipline. The Agency noted that Complainant responded to management that injury compensation was “playing games” and that his lawyer would address the issue. The Agency found no evidence that management delayed the processing of Complainant’s OWCP claim or took any action that swayed the decisions made by the OWCP.

During the period at issue, Complainant was an applicant for the position of Assistant United States Attorney. On March 1, 2018, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her based on race (Caucasian), color (white), disability, and age (45). By letter dated March 26, 2018, the Agency accepted the formal complaint for investigation. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. On June 28, 2019, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s Motion for a Decision Without a Hearing. The AJ framed Complainant claims in the following fashion: Whether Complainant was discriminated against based on race, color, age, or disability when: 1. She was not selected under a vacancy announcement for an Assistant United States Attorney position; and 2. She was not appointed as an Assistant United States Attorney under the Schedule A hiring authority for disabled persons. The AJ found that the Agency articulated, legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. Specifically, the AJ stated “[a]ll applications meeting the minimum requirements were sent to the First Assistant United States Attorney [F1], the Agency official with primary oversight of the selection process. [F1] conducted a general review of all the resumes and identified the top competitive resumes. His first pass review reduced the pool by about half. Complainant did not make the cut. [F1] rated Complainant “in the bottom 50% of applicants.” AJ Decision at 2. Regarding Schedule A hiring, the AJ found that Complainant had not established that she was subjected to discrimination. The AJ found that Complainant failed to submit medical documentation that she wanted to be considered for Schedule A hiring in a timely manner. AJ Decision at 7. The AJ further found that Complainant failed to establish that the Agency’s articulated reasons for its actions were pretext for discrimination. The Agency subsequently issued a final order on August 6, 2019 adopting the AJ’s finding of no discrimination. 2 The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant submitted a statement that was not responsive to the AJ’s decision or the Agency’s final action. In response, the Agency’s requests that we affirm its final action. We presume, for purposes of analysis only and without so finding, that Complainant is an individual with a disability.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as an Information Technology (IT) Specialist, 2210, GS 11 at the Agency’s Red River Army Depot in Texarkana, Texas. The record supports that Complainant had previously filed formal complaints in 2005, 2006, and 2009 against the Agency in her non-selection for three other GS 12 positions. selected for the position of Information Technology Specialist, GS-2210-12, from Announcement Number SWDX13481071851147. After its investigation of the instant complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC or Commission) Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The Agency issued a motion for summary judgment and Complainant filed a response. On May 1, 2019, the AJ issued a decision by summary judgment in favor of the Agency. On June 25, 2019, the Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding of no discrimination. The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant argues that in addition to being discriminated against based on her race, age, and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity, she was also subjected to a hostile work environment based on her race, national origin, color and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity. Complainant further argues that because of participation in prior protected EEO activity, she has not been selected for five GS-2210-12 promotions from 2005 through 2015. Finally, Complainant contends that the EEO investigator failed to develop an impartial and appropriate factual record and the Agency should be subjected to sanctions.

During the relevant time, Complainant worked as a General Expediter at the Agency’s St. Louis Metro Annex in Hazelwood, Missouri. On January 29, 2019, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint, claiming that the Agency discriminated against her based on race (African-American), national origin (American), sex (female), religion (Baptist), and color (brown) when: 1. On or around August 14, 2018, she was issued a Letter of Warning (LOW); and 2. On or around August 26, 2018, she was issued a LOW. After an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision on July 15, 2019, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination. Complainant filed the instant appeal. On appeal, Complainant contends she never received a copy of the report of investigation. Further, she asserts that, due to the death of her son in December 2018 and an injury at work in February 2019, she has “been incapable of mentally or physically handling my pertinent business.”

During the period at issue, Complainant was employed by the Agency as a Customer Service Supervisor, Customer Service at the Agency’s Murrells Inlet, South Carolina Post Office. On December 29, 2017, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her based on sex (female) when, after reporting that she was being subjected to ongoing threatening behavior from a subordinate employee, management failed to properly address the matter. On January 19, 2018, the Agency issued a final decision dismissing the instant formal complaint for failure to state a claim. On appeal, the Commission reversed the Agency’s dismissal and After its investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC or Commission) Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Thereafter, the AJ issued an Order to Show Cause why summary judgment should not be granted. Specifically, the AJ ordered Complainant to produce any documents in her possession that are not contained in the report of investigation which would support her claim. Subsequently, the AJ issued a decision by summary judgment in favor of the Agency finding no discrimination. The Agency issued its final action adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Complainant, on appeal, argues that she was prejudiced by the AJ’s failure to consider her September 18, 2019 Response to the Show Cause Order. In response, the Agency asserts that Complainant’s initial submission was unresponsive to the AJ’s Order to Show Cause.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-0592-7 Tax Examining Technician at the Agency’s Small Business/Self-Employed Service Center in Kansas City, Missouri. On October 1, 2017, a Supervisory Tax Examiner became Complainant’s first-line supervisor (S1). At all times relevant to her complaint, a Department Manager was Complainant’s second- line supervisor (S2), and a Program Manager was her third-line supervisor (S3). Complainant is African-American, and her color is light brown. Complainant identified her disability as a speech impediment, stuttering. Complainant averred that she is limited in her ability to speak in front of a crowd, express herself clearly in her meeting, or speak clearly and concisely over the telephone. Complainant alleged that, as a result of her stutter, management believes that she has a learning disability. According to Complainant, she engaged in prior protected activity by filing an EEO complaint in 2015 that named S2 as the responsible management official. Complainant stated that, although S1 was not her supervisor in 2015, S1 was a witness for her EEO complaint. Complainant attended Collection Statute Expiration Date (CSED) program training in October 2016. Complainant stated that, after she attended the training, she told her former supervisor (FS1) that she was still having a hard time understanding the CSED program. According to Complainant, she met with FS1 to discuss CSED on February 3, 2017. Complainant averred that she became anxious during the discussion, which raised her blood pressure, culminating in Complainant being taken to the hospital to be treated for high blood pressure. According to Complainant, on September 21, 2017, S1 emailed her and stated that she would not receive any more “read time” to learn CSED. Complainant averred that, although S1 was not her supervisor at that time, she had explained to S1 that she was having trouble understanding CSED and that it caused her anxiety. Complainant alleged that S1 told her that she had to get certified on the CSED program because she had been fully trained. According to Complainant, she was not the only employee who had trouble understanding the complexity of the CSED program. Complainant alleged that, as of January 2018, at least eight of her coworkers who attended CSED training were not CSED certified and had not been required to work CSED cases in more than four months. S1 stated that all employees had been trained on CSED and would be required to work the CSED program once they became certified. Complainant stated that she was scheduled to take a vacation day on September 29, 2017. Complainant averred that she told FS1 that she might come in to the office that day and that she would call if she did not come in. According to Complainant, she called FS1 to tell him that she was not coming in and to request leave for the already scheduled vacation day. On September 29, 2017, S1 issued Complainant a memorandum stating that Complainant had not completed her time and attendance for the week because she did not input her leave for September 29, 2017. The memo stated that it was a “courtesy” reminder to Complainant to timely and accurately complete her time and attendance. According to S1, when she became the new supervisor of Complainant’s team, she told the team members that she liked to document conversations in emails and memoranda to have a record of what was discussed. On October 4, 2017, S1 forwarded the team an email with a reminder about the housekeeping guidelines for the office. On October 10, 2017, S1 issued Complainant a memorandum for her failure to follow the housekeeping guidelines. In the memorandum, S1 stated that Complainant used an electric blanket during a training on October 3-4, 2017, and that Complainant did not unplug the blanket when asked by the instructor. S1 averred that electric blankets violated the housekeeping guidelines and asked Complainant to remove her electric blanket from the workplace. According to S1, the reason for the memorandum was that Complainant had ignored the instructor’s request to unplug the blanket, on top of the fact that the electric blanket violated the housekeeping guidelines. According to Complainant, a Caucasian coworker (C1) who had Halloween decorations in her cubicle that violated the guidelines was not issued a memorandum for failing to follow the housekeeping guidelines. Complainant averred that C1 had two 36-inch skeletons on the outside of her cubicle wall that S1 asked her to take down because the decorations violated the fire code. Complainant stated that, when she asked C1 whether she had received anything in writing, C1 told her that she had only received a verbal warning. Complainant stated that, on October 24, 2017, S1 gave her a memorandum documenting an Embedded Quality Review System (EQRS) review, which stated that Complainant’s performance had dropped and that her performance appraisal could be affected. Complainant averred that she asked why the review was in a memorandum and that S1 told her that it was her practice to document such matters in memoranda and that S2 was aware of the matter. Complainant stated that she reached out to the union. According to Complainant, S1 later asked for the memorandum back and tore it up. S1 stated that she asked Complainant for the document back in order to be consistent with other supervisors who did not issue memoranda for performance matters after discussing the issue with S2. According to Complainant, on October 31, 2017, S1 approached her to discuss the suspended cases in her inventory. Complainant stated that she tried to explain how previous supervisors had taught her to work these cases but that S1 interrupted her, talking over her and telling her that she should know better and had been in her position long enough to know how to process cases. Complainant alleged that S1 said, “I’m gonna kill you.” Report of Investigation (ROI) at 121. Complainant stated that she was utterly shocked and amazed by S1’s remark and that she did not feel safe and feared for her life. According to Complainant, S1 also said, “You gonna make me kill you” before she left Complainant’s desk. ROI at 122. Complainant stated that, later on October 31, 2017, S1 emailed her and told her to come to her office. Complainant alleged that, in S1’s office, S1 said, “I could kill you” and gave her negative feedback on her work process. ROI at 122. S1 stated that she was talking to Complainant about her inventory on October 31, 2017. According to S1, she told Complainant to ask the Lead Tax Examining Technician (C2) for help and joked that Complainant could say, “[S1] is going to kill me if I don’t close this case.” ROI at 272. S1 averred that she was joking and stated that both she and Complainant laughed. Complainant denied that S1 was joking when she said she would kill her. According to Complainant, she does not have a friendly relationship with S1, and they do not joke with each other. The record contains an October 31, 2017, email from one of Complainant’s coworkers (C3) to a union representative. In the email, C3 stated that she was at her desk and could hear S1 “going off” on Complainant. ROI at 189. According to C3, Complainant did not understand what S1 was talking about, and S1 was “talking to her like a dog…bullying her.” Id. Complainant averred that she reported S1’s threats to kill her to the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA). TIGTA investigated Complainant’s report that S1 threatened to kill her. S1 stated that she was interviewed by TIGTA on November 3, 2017. On November 20, 2017, TIGTA forwarded its report of investigation to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, which declined to prosecute S1 due to lack of federal interest. S1 stated that, as a result of Complainant’s report to TIGTA, she was given a coaching mentor to work on communicating with her subordinates and was required to take training on communication. According to S2, although she had not observed S1 harass Complainant, she knew that S1 struggled with effective communication. S3 stated that S1’s tone can come off as rude and added that S1 has been counseled for unprofessional behavior. Complainant averred that S1 attempted to provide side-by-side instruction on CSED with her on November 15, 2017. Complainant alleged that she was uncomfortable with the situation after S1 had threatened to kill her. Complainant stated that she was nervous and scared to have S1 sitting behind her. According to Complainant, S1 later issued her a memorandum about the instruction, noting that Complainant appeared uncomfortable and distracted and kept pulling her coat and scarf on and off. The record contains a November 15, 2017, memorandum from S1, which discussed the errors Complainant made, noted that Complainant did not ask for help, and added, “You appeared to be distracted, pulling your coat and scarf on and then taking the coat off and turning your desk fan on, while shuffling your notes on your desk.” ROI at 157. Complainant stated that S1 gave her a mid-year evaluation on January 5, 2018. According to Complainant, S1 told her that her performance had declined in several areas and warned, “One more bad review will kill you.” ROI at 136. S1 stated that she told Complainant, “another error is going to kill your accuracy.” ROI at 272. According to S2, the goal was for employees to reach 93 percent customer accuracy, but Complainant’s customer accuracy was 57. percent from October 1, 2017, through February 15, 2018. On December 14, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint, which she subsequently amended, alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), color (light brown), disability (speech impediment), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (prior EEO complaint) when she was subjected to harassment, including when: 1. Since October 1, 2017, management continually issued her memoranda for work performance issues, required her to work a difficult program not required of all employees, threatened to lower her performance evaluation, yelled at her, talked over her, made belittling remarks to her, and made three threatening remarks to the effect of, “I’m going to kill you”; and 2. On January 5, 2018, during her midyear review, S1 stated, “one more bad review will kill you,” and Complainant continued to receive negative memoranda. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Neither Complainant nor the Agency submitted a statement or brief regarding the appeal.

The record reflects the following chronology of events. During the relevant time period, Complainant was an Electrician Supervisor at the Agency’s Portsmouth, Virginia facility. Complainant filed an EEO complaint on August 30, 2018. In a Corrected Partial Dismissal letter dated March 15, 2019, the Agency determined that the formal complaint was comprised of the following claims: 1. Was [Complainant] discriminated against based on race (African American) and age by [a named management official] on April 17, 2018 when he received a negative performance evaluation. 2. Was [Complainant] discriminated against based on race, age, and reprisal and subjected to a hostile work environment when he was not promoted to Zone Manager, GS-2805-12. The Agency accepted claim (1) for investigation. However, the Agency dismissed claim (2) on procedural grounds. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 40-41. In a September 19, 2019 Order on Initial Conference, the EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) noted that Complainant does not contest the dismissed claim. In addition, Complainant does not expressly contest the dismissed claim on appeal. Thus, we decline to address the dismissed claim further herein. Upon completion of the investigation, Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC AJ. On October 23, 2019, the EEOC AJ issued a decision dismissing Complainant’s complaint on procedural grounds. To the extent that Complainant was alleging that he was subjected to discrimination based on the Agency’s April 17, 2018 mid-term progress review, the AJ dismissed this matter for failure to state a claim and for alleging a proposal to take a personnel action. The AJ further found that the crux of Complainant’s claim were the comments in his 2017 (rather than 2018) performance evaluation. To the extent Complainant was challenging his 2017 evaluation, the EEOC AJ dismissed this claim for untimely EEO Counselor contact. The AJ reasoned that Complainant’s 2017 performance evaluation was dated October 17, 2017, for its final rating but Complainant did not initiate EEO Counselor contact until May 4, 2018, outside of the applicable time period. On November 26, 2019, the Agency issued a final order implementing the AJ’s decision dismissing Complainant’s complaint on procedural grounds. Complainant does not submit a statement or brief on appeal.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as an Attorney Advisor in Norfolk, Virginia. On September 16, 2019, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency subjected her to discrimination based on race (African-American). In its final decision, dated January 8, 2020, the Agency determined that Complainant’s complaint was comprised of the following claim: On July 5, 2019, and again on August 14, 2019, Complainant became aware that the Legal Service Command management hired a white female, as a GS-14 Attorney Advisor in the General Law Division in 2017, to perform the same duties that Complainant was forced to perform as a GS-13 Attorney Advisor when she worked at the same field office. The Agency dismissed the formal complaint on the grounds that Complainant previously raised the same claim which is currently pending before the EEOC. The Agency reasoned that Complainant previously raised this matter in a prior EEO complaint, Agency Case No. HS-USCG- 00420-2018 and is pending before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Specifically, the Agency stated “[t]he record showed Complainant not only recited identical facts, but also implicated identical responsible management officials with very slight exceptions.” Final Agency Decision at 2. The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant asserts that the Agency’s framing of her claim does not fully capture all her issues. Specifically, Complainant states that “the elements of the current complaint are not identical …[to] the matter pending before the EEOC because the [prior] complaint does not allege that the Agency used a fraudulent position description…as a basis of discrimination…The use of the fraudulent position description as alleged in the signed statement of [C1] was not investigated as part of [the prior complaint]…” Complainant also asserts that she has named several individuals as responsible management officials that she did not name in the prior complaint. In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision dismissing Complainant’s complaint. The Agency further asserts that the fact that C1 was unhappy with her assigned duties is immaterial to either of her complaints.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant was a former Police Officer, GS- 7, at the Agency’s West Roxbury VA Medical Center (VAMC) facility in West Roxbury, Massachusetts. On March 15, 2019, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency subjected him to unlawful retaliation for prior protected EEO activity when, on February 7, 2019, he was placed on a cautionary list of employees who left the Agency under negative terms, including conduct unbecoming. The Agency accepted the complaint and conducted an investigation which revealed the following pertinent results. Complainant was employed at the Agency from January 19, 2010 to February 3, 2013. In March 2015, Complainant’s name was added to a “Cautionary List,” which was a list of former employees known only to the Human Resources Division of the VA Boston Healthcare System and prospective Agency employers. On or about November 1, 2018, Complainant received a report of investigation for an unrelated complaint indicating that he had been placed on the “Cautionary List” for former employees. On December 15, 2018, Complainant submitted a request under the Freedom of Information Act for a copy of the “Cautionary List that the VA Boston Healthcare Human Resources Employee/Labor Relations keeps on file [which] documents former employees who left the facility under negative terms including conduct unbecoming.” On February 7, 2019, the Agency responded to Complainant’s request and provided a document indicating Complainant’s name was on the Cautionary List. On February 11, 2019, Complainant contacted an EEO Counselor regarding the instant complaint. After its investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC or Commission) Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The Agency submitted a Motion to Dismiss. The AJ subsequently issued a Decision and Order dismissing the complaint pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(2), for untimely EEO Counselor contact. The Agency issued its final order adopting the AJ’s dismissal. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Staff Assistant, GS- 14, at the Agency’s VA Office of Construction and Facilities Management (CFM) in Washington, D.C. period of June 2017 to April 25, 2018, she was denied a reasonable accommodation and subjected to a hostile work environment. Specifically, Complainant alleged that: 1. Beginning in June of 2017 and continuing, Complainant’s Program Manager was “badmouthing [Complainant’s] work performance” to her co-workers. 2. During January of 2018, the Program Manager told Complainant that she did not know that Complainant was going on leave, when Complainant had requested leave in October of 2017. 3. On February 21, 2018, the Program Manager denied Complainant’s reasonable accommodation request. 4. During February of 2018, the Program Manager questioned Complainant about her use of the computer system but did not question other employees. 5. In March of 2018, after Complainant requested telework to accommodate her surgery, the Program Manager incorrectly sent Complainant to others, who told Complainant that the approval needed to come from the Program Manager. 6. Despite Complainant’s raising harassment concerns to management, the Associate Executive Director took no action for months to address the alleged harassment. 2 At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When, according to the Agency, Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. Upon receipt of the Agency’s final decision on the merits, Complainant filed the instant appeal. On appeal, Complainant contends that the Agency improperly issued a Final Agency Decision although Complainant had submitted a timely hearing request. Complainant provided a receipt showing the delivery of her hearing request. She asks that the FAD be reversed and that she be allowed to have a hearing. During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Federal Air Marshal in San Francisco, California. On July 12, 2017, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him based on disability (caregiver for his father). 2 By letter dated January 4, 2018, the Agency accepted the formal complaint for investigation and determined it was comprised of the following claim: Since October 2014, and ongoing, Complainant has been denied a hardship transfer and voluntary lateral transfer to care for his father with a disabling condition. After an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Over Complainant's objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s February 28, 2020, motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on April 2, 2020. The AJ found that Complainant is not entitled to a reasonable accommodation for having a disabled parent. Under a disparate treatment analysis, the AJ found that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions which Complainant failed to establish was pretext for discrimination. The AJ found that the Agency stated that Complainant’s request for a hardship transfer did not meet the Agency’s criteria set forth in its policy. Specifically, the AJ found that the Agency determined that Complainant’s father’s medical issues accompanied the aging process and did not rise to the level of a serious medical condition. Finally, the AJ found that the Agency stated that Complainant was not approved for a voluntary lateral transfer because he did not have enough seniority to be transferred. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding of no discrimination. The instant appeal followed. Complainant reiterates that the Agency should have allowed him to transfer to care of his father with various medical conditions. In response, the Agency requests we affirm its final order implementing the AJ’s decision without a hearing finding no discrimination.

Complainant claimed that the Agency discriminated against him based on national origin (Hispanic), sex (male), and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (participating in the EEO process by assisting co-worker with her EEO complaint). Whether Complainant was subjected to hostile work environment based on his national origin (Hispanic), sex (male) and/or reprisal for his prior EEO activity when: 1. From July 10, 2017, through August 15, 2017, [S2] failed to give him preferable work tasks; 10. At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-0592-7 Tax Examining Technician at the Agency’s Small Business/Self-Employed Service Center in Kansas City, Missouri. On October 1, 2017, a Supervisory Tax Examiner became Complainant’s first-line supervisor (S1). At all times relevant to her complaint, a Department Manager was Complainant’s second- line supervisor (S2), and a Program Manager was her third-line supervisor (S3). Complainant is African-American, and her color is light brown. Complainant identified her disability as a speech impediment, stuttering. Complainant averred that she is limited in her ability to speak in front of a crowd, express herself clearly in her meeting, or speak clearly and concisely over the telephone. Complainant alleged that, as a result of her stutter, management believes that she has a learning disability. According to Complainant, she engaged in prior protected activity by filing an EEO complaint in 2015 that named S2 as the responsible management official. Complainant stated that, although S1 was not her supervisor in 2015, S1 was a witness for her EEO complaint. Complainant attended Collection Statute Expiration Date (CSED) program training in October 2016. Complainant stated that, after she attended the training, she told her former supervisor (FS1) that she was still having a hard time understanding the CSED program. According to Complainant, she met with FS1 to discuss CSED on February 3, 2017. Complainant averred that she became anxious during the discussion, which raised her blood pressure, culminating in Complainant being taken to the hospital to be treated for high blood pressure. According to Complainant, on September 21, 2017, S1 emailed her and stated that she would not receive any more “read time” to learn CSED. Complainant averred that, although S1 was not her supervisor at that time, she had explained to S1 that she was having trouble understanding CSED and that it caused her anxiety. Complainant alleged that S1 told her that she had to get certified on the CSED program because she had been fully trained. According to Complainant, she was not the only employee who had trouble understanding the complexity of the CSED program. Complainant alleged that, as of January 2018, at least eight of her coworkers who attended CSED training were not CSED certified and had not been required to work CSED cases in more than four months. S1 stated that all employees had been trained on CSED and would be required to work the CSED program once they became certified. Complainant stated that she was scheduled to take a vacation day on September 29, 2017. Complainant averred that she told FS1 that she might come in to the office that day and that she would call if she did not come in. According to Complainant, she called FS1 to tell him that she was not coming in and to request leave for the already scheduled vacation day. On September 29, 2017, S1 issued Complainant a memorandum stating that Complainant had not completed her time and attendance for the week because she did not input her leave for September 29, 2017. The memo stated that it was a “courtesy” reminder to Complainant to timely and accurately complete her time and attendance. According to S1, when she became the new supervisor of Complainant’s team, she told the team members that she liked to document conversations in emails and memoranda to have a record of what was discussed. On October 4, 2017, S1 forwarded the team an email with a reminder about the housekeeping guidelines for the office. On October 10, 2017, S1 issued Complainant a memorandum for her failure to follow the housekeeping guidelines. In the memorandum, S1 stated that Complainant used an electric blanket during a training on October 3-4, 2017, and that Complainant did not unplug the blanket when asked by the instructor. S1 averred that electric blankets violated the housekeeping guidelines and asked Complainant to remove her electric blanket from the workplace. According to S1, the reason for the memorandum was that Complainant had ignored the instructor’s request to unplug the blanket, on top of the fact that the electric blanket violated the housekeeping guidelines. According to Complainant, a Caucasian coworker (C1) who had Halloween decorations in her cubicle that violated the guidelines was not issued a memorandum for failing to follow the housekeeping guidelines. Complainant averred that C1 had two 36-inch skeletons on the outside of her cubicle wall that S1 asked her to take down because the decorations violated the fire code. Complainant stated that, when she asked C1 whether she had received anything in writing, C1 told her that she had only received a verbal warning. Complainant stated that, on October 24, 2017, S1 gave her a memorandum documenting an Embedded Quality Review System (EQRS) review, which stated that Complainant’s performance had dropped and that her performance appraisal could be affected. Complainant averred that she asked why the review was in a memorandum and that S1 told her that it was her practice to document such matters in memoranda and that S2 was aware of the matter. Complainant stated that she reached out to the union. According to Complainant, S1 later asked for the memorandum back and tore it up. S1 stated that she asked Complainant for the document back in order to be consistent with other supervisors who did not issue memoranda for performance matters after discussing the issue with S2. According to Complainant, on October 31, 2017, S1 approached her to discuss the suspended cases in her inventory. Complainant stated that she tried to explain how previous supervisors had taught her to work these cases but that S1 interrupted her, talking over her and telling her that she should know better and had been in her position long enough to know how to process cases. Complainant alleged that S1 said, “I’m gonna kill you.” Report of Investigation (ROI) at 121. Complainant stated that she was utterly shocked and amazed by S1’s remark and that she did not feel safe and feared for her life. According to Complainant, S1 also said, “You gonna make me kill you” before she left Complainant’s desk. ROI at 122. Complainant stated that, later on October 31, 2017, S1 emailed her and told her to come to her office. Complainant alleged that, in S1’s office, S1 said, “I could kill you” and gave her negative feedback on her work process. ROI at 122. S1 stated that she was talking to Complainant about her inventory on October 31, 2017. According to S1, she told Complainant to ask the Lead Tax Examining Technician (C2) for help and joked that Complainant could say, “[S1] is going to kill me if I don’t close this case.” ROI at 272. S1 averred that she was joking and stated that both she and Complainant laughed. Complainant denied that S1 was joking when she said she would kill her. According to Complainant, she does not have a friendly relationship with S1, and they do not joke with each other. The record contains an October 31, 2017, email from one of Complainant’s coworkers (C3) to a union representative. In the email, C3 stated that she was at her desk and could hear S1 “going off” on Complainant. ROI at 189. According to C3, Complainant did not understand what S1 was talking about, and S1 was “talking to her like a dog…bullying her.” Id. Complainant averred that she reported S1’s threats to kill her to the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA). TIGTA investigated Complainant’s report that S1 threatened to kill her. S1 stated that she was interviewed by TIGTA on November 3, 2017. On November 20, 2017, TIGTA forwarded its report of investigation to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, which declined to prosecute S1 due to lack of federal interest. S1 stated that, as a result of Complainant’s report to TIGTA, she was given a coaching mentor to work on communicating with her subordinates and was required to take training on communication. According to S2, although she had not observed S1 harass Complainant, she knew that S1 struggled with effective communication. S3 stated that S1’s tone can come off as rude and added that S1 has been counseled for unprofessional behavior. Complainant averred that S1 attempted to provide side-by-side instruction on CSED with her on November 15, 2017. Complainant alleged that she was uncomfortable with the situation after S1 had threatened to kill her. Complainant stated that she was nervous and scared to have S1 sitting behind her. According to Complainant, S1 later issued her a memorandum about the instruction, noting that Complainant appeared uncomfortable and distracted and kept pulling her coat and scarf on and off. The record contains a November 15, 2017, memorandum from S1, which discussed the errors Complainant made, noted that Complainant did not ask for help, and added, “You appeared to be distracted, pulling your coat and scarf on and then taking the coat off and turning your desk fan on, while shuffling your notes on your desk.” ROI at 157. Complainant stated that S1 gave her a mid-year evaluation on January 5, 2018. According to Complainant, S1 told her that her performance had declined in several areas and warned, “One more bad review will kill you.” ROI at 136. S1 stated that she told Complainant, “another error is going to kill your accuracy.” ROI at 272. According to S2, the goal was for employees to reach 93 percent customer accuracy, but Complainant’s customer accuracy was 57. percent from October 1, 2017, through February 15, 2018. On December 14, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint, which she subsequently amended, alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), color (light brown), disability (speech impediment), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (prior EEO complaint) when she was subjected to harassment, including when: 1. Since October 1, 2017, management continually issued her memoranda for work performance issues, required her to work a difficult program not required of all employees, threatened to lower her performance evaluation, yelled at her, talked over her, made belittling remarks to her, and made three threatening remarks to the effect of, “I’m going to kill you”; and 2. On January 5, 2018, during her midyear review, S1 stated, “one more bad review will kill you,” and Complainant continued to receive negative memoranda. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Neither Complainant nor the Agency submitted a statement or brief regarding the appeal.

The record reflects the following chronology of events. During the relevant time period, Complainant was an Electrician Supervisor at the Agency’s Portsmouth, Virginia facility. Complainant filed an EEO complaint on August 30, 2018. In a Corrected Partial Dismissal letter dated March 15, 2019, the Agency determined that the formal complaint was comprised of the following claims: 1. Was [Complainant] discriminated against based on race (African American) and age by [a named management official] on April 17, 2018 when he received a negative performance evaluation. 2. Was [Complainant] discriminated against based on race, age, and reprisal and subjected to a hostile work environment when he was not promoted to Zone Manager, GS-2805-12. The Agency accepted claim (1) for investigation. However, the Agency dismissed claim (2) on procedural grounds. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 40-41. In a September 19, 2019 Order on Initial Conference, the EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) noted that Complainant does not contest the dismissed claim. In addition, Complainant does not expressly contest the dismissed claim on appeal. Thus, we decline to address the dismissed claim further herein. Upon completion of the investigation, Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC AJ. On October 23, 2019, the EEOC AJ issued a decision dismissing Complainant’s complaint on procedural grounds. To the extent that Complainant was alleging that he was subjected to discrimination based on the Agency’s April 17, 2018 mid-term progress review, the AJ dismissed this matter for failure to state a claim and for alleging a proposal to take a personnel action. On November 26, 2019, the Agency issued a final order implementing the AJ’s decision dismissing Complainant’s complaint on procedural grounds. Complainant does not submit a statement or brief on appeal.

After an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Over Complainant's objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s February 28, 2020, motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on April 2, 2020. The AJ found that Complainant is not entitled to a reasonable accommodation for having a disabled parent. Under a disparate treatment analysis, the AJ found that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions which Complainant failed to establish was pretext for discrimination. The AJ found that the Agency stated that Complainant’s request for a hardship transfer did not meet the Agency’s criteria set forth in its policy. Specifically, the AJ found that the Agency determined that Complainant’s father’s medical issues accompanied the aging process and did not rise to the level of a serious medical condition. Finally, the AJ found that the Agency stated that Complainant was not approved for a voluntary lateral transfer because he did not have enough seniority to be transferred. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding of no discrimination. The instant appeal followed. Complainant reiterates that the Agency should have allowed him to transfer to care of his father with various medical conditions. In response, the Agency requests we affirm its final order implementing the AJ’s decision without a hearing finding no discrimination.

During the period at issue, Complainant was employed by the Agency as a Customer Service Supervisor, Customer Service at the Agency’s Murrells Inlet, South Carolina Post Office. On December 29, 2017, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her based on sex (female) when, after reporting that she was being subjected to ongoing threatening behavior from a subordinate employee, management failed to properly address the matter. On January 19, 2018, the Agency issued a final decision dismissing the instant formal complaint for failure to state a claim. On appeal, the Commission reversed the Agency’s dismissal and After its investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC or Commission) Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Thereafter, the AJ issued an Order to Show Cause why summary judgment should not be granted. Specifically, the AJ ordered Complainant to produce any documents in her possession that are not contained in the report of investigation which would support her claim. Subsequently, the AJ issued a decision by summary judgment in favor of the Agency finding no discrimination. The Agency issued its final action adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Complainant, on appeal, argues that she was prejudiced by the AJ’s failure to consider her September 18, 2019 Response to the Show Cause Order. In response, the Agency asserts that Complainant’s initial submission was unresponsive to the AJ’s Order to Show Cause.

The record reflects the following chronology of events. During the relevant time period, Complainant was an Electrician Supervisor at the Agency’s Portsmouth, Virginia facility. Complainant filed an EEO complaint on August 30, 2018. In a Corrected Partial Dismissal letter dated March 15, 2019, the Agency determined that the formal complaint was comprised of the following claims: 1. Was [Complainant] discriminated against based on race (African American) and age by [a named management official] on April 17, 2018 when he received a negative performance evaluation. 2. Was [Complainant] discriminated against based on race, age, and reprisal and subjected to a hostile work environment when he was not promoted to Zone Manager, GS-2805-12. The Agency accepted claim (1) for investigation. However, the Agency dismissed claim (2) on procedural grounds. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 40-41. In a September 19, 2019 Order on Initial Conference, the EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) noted that Complainant does not contest the dismissed claim. In addition, Complainant does not expressly contest the dismissed claim on appeal. Thus, we decline to address the dismissed claim further herein. Upon completion of the investigation, Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC AJ. On October 23, 2019, the EEOC AJ issued a decision dismissing Complainant’s complaint on procedural grounds. To the extent that Complainant was alleging that he was subjected to discrimination based on the Agency’s April 17, 2018 mid-term progress review, the AJ dismissed this matter for failure to state a claim and for alleging a proposal to take a personnel action. The AJ further found that the crux of Complainant’s claim were the comments in his 2017 (rather than 2018) performance evaluation. To the extent Complainant was challenging his 2017 evaluation, the EEOC AJ dismissed this claim for untimely EEO Counselor contact. The AJ reasoned that Complainant’s 2017 performance evaluation was dated October 17, 2017, for its final rating but Complainant did not initiate EEO Counselor contact until May 4, 2018, outside of the applicable time period. On November 26, 2019, the Agency issued a final order implementing the AJ’s decision dismissing Complainant’s complaint on procedural grounds. Complainant does not submit a statement or brief on appeal.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as an Attorney Advisor in Norfolk, Virginia. On September 16, 2019, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency subjected her to discrimination based on race (African-American). In its final decision, dated January 8, 2020, the Agency determined that Complainant’s complaint was comprised of the following claim: On July 5, 2019, and again on August 14, 2019, Complainant became aware that the Legal Service Command management hired a white female, as a GS-14 Attorney Advisor in the General Law Division in 2017, to perform the same duties that Complainant was forced to perform as a GS-13 Attorney Advisor when she worked at the same field office. The Agency dismissed the formal complaint on the grounds that Complainant previously raised the same claim which is currently pending before the EEOC. The Agency reasoned that Complainant previously raised this matter in a prior EEO complaint, Agency Case No. HS-USCG- 00420-2018 and is pending before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Specifically, the Agency stated “[t]he record showed Complainant not only recited identical facts, but also implicated identical responsible management officials with very slight exceptions.” Final Agency Decision at 2. The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant asserts that the Agency’s framing of her claim does not fully capture all her issues. Specifically, Complainant states that “the elements of the current complaint are not identical …[to] the matter pending before the EEOC because the [prior] complaint does not allege that the Agency used a fraudulent position description…as a basis of discrimination…The use of the fraudulent position description as alleged in the signed statement of [C1] was not investigated as part of [the prior complaint]…” Complainant also asserts that she has named several individuals as responsible management officials that she did not name in the prior complaint. In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision dismissing Complainant’s complaint. The Agency further asserts that the fact that C1 was unhappy with her assigned duties is immaterial to either of her complaints.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant previously worked for the Agency as a Computer Analyst/Programmer for 12 years at the Agency’s Information Technology Solution Center (ITSC) in Eagan, Minnesota. Supplemental Report of Investigation (Supp. ROI), at 102-103. Complainant was eventually promoted to the DCS-21 grade-level. Supp. ROI, at 106. Complainant worked for the Agency until June 2013 when she resigned from her position to care for her dying mother who resided in the country of Vietnam. Id. at 103. Complainant subsequently sought to become re-employed with the Agency after caring for her mother, who had passed away, and she applied for two positions within the Agency’s ITSC in Eagan, Minnesota. Supp. ROI, at 104. From February 4 through February 12, 2016, the Agency advertised a job vacancy for a Computer Analyst/Programmer at the DCS-19 level (Position 1), at the ITSC. The Agency advertised Position 1 for external candidates. Complainant, being an external applicant, applied for Position 1 even though the position was graded lower than the position she previously held. On February 23, 2016, a Union Steward filed a grievance on behalf of employees, contending that the Agency had violated the Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) by not advertising the position for internal candidates first. Supp. ROI, at 413. The grievance was denied, however, after the Computer Operations Manager and the Labor Relations Specialist determined that the job vacancy had been correctly advertised for external candidates. As a result, the selection process for external candidates moved forward and Complainant was interviewed by a three-person selection panel on March 15, 2016. Supp. ROI, at 104. The panel believed that Complainant was the best qualified, and she therefore was the only candidate who was asked to come back for another interview. On March 29, 2016, Complainant sat down for a second interview with the Computer Operations Manager alone in his office. Id. The interview, however, was very informal with the Computer Operations Manager having no prepared written questions, and he also took no notes during the interview. Hearing Transcript (Hr’g Trans.), at 199-200. Following the March 29, 2016, interview, the Computer Operations Manager reportedly told panel members that Complainant had a “communication problem,” and he therefore decided to not recommend Complainant for the position. Hr’g Trans., at 62-63. On or about April 14, 2016, the Labor Relations Specialist reportedly discussed with a Human Resources (HR) Generalist a belief that the vacancy had in fact been incorrectly advertised for external candidates, which amounted to a violation of the CBA. Hr’g Trans., at 268-270. The Labor Relations Specialist thereafter entered into a settlement agreement with the Union, which required canceling the job vacancy for the Position 1. Id. According to the Labor Relations Specialist, he was not aware that Complainant was the leading candidate for the position at the time the settlement agreement was reached with the Union. Id. at 296. Meanwhile, on April 15, 2016, the HR Generalist emailed Complainant in response to her request for update on the selection process. Therein, the HR Generalist wrote to Complainant that the position was “withdrawn and we have closed the processing of all applicants. This was based on a decision by Human Resources and does not reflect on you or your application for employment. . . .” Supp. ROI, at 112-113. Months later in October 2016, the Agency advertised another job vacancy for a Computer Analyst/Programmer at the DCS-19 level (Position 2), and Complainant applied. Hr’g Trans, at 48. A three-person selection panel was again convened. Id. at 306-307. Two of the three members on the panel were not part of the panel for Position 1. Therefore, one panel member served on both panels for Position 1 and Position 2. The panel, however, after reviewing Complainant’s application, did not rank Complainant as a top candidate, and therefore they chose not to interview her and consider her for the postion. Id. at 409-410. As a result, the Computer Operations Manager, who again served as the selecting the official, did not evaluate Complainant. Procedural History On September 7, 2016, Complainant filed an EEO complaint, as amended, alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (Asian), sex (female), and age when: 1. In April 2016, she was notified that she was not selected for the position of Computer Analyst / Programmer Associate in Eagan, Minnesota because the job posting had been cancelled after her interviews (Position 1). 2. She was subjected to reprisal for her prior protected EEO activity (instant EEO complaint) when in October 2016 she was not selected for the position of Computer Analyst / Programmer Associate in Eagan, Minnesota (Position 2). 2 3. The Agency Representative stated to Complainant’s Representative that: “I can tell you that she [Complainant] is never going to be hired back.” Following the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). 3 Complainant timely requested a hearing. On February 21, 2017, the AJ issued an order for the Agency to supplement the investigation regarding Position 1. Therein, the AJ specifically ordered the Agency to produce all notes and scoring documentation relating to the ranking of the candidates for Position 1. Complainant only alleged that she was subjected to discrimination based on reprisal with regard to claim 2, and therefore did not allege that she was subjected to race, gender, or age discrimination regarding Position 2. The record contains a Report of Investigation as well as a Supplemental Report of Investigation. Complainant’s request to amend to include claims 2 and 3 was accepted by the AJ. The AJ thereafter held a hearing on April 17, and April 18, 2019, on claims 1 and 2. 5 Meanwhile, during the April 18, 2019, hearing, Complainant orally made a motion before the AJ, requesting judgment as a matter of law in her favor and sanctions against the Agency because it failed to produce/preserve individual panel members’ scoring documentation relative to the AJ’s February 21, 2017, order. Complainant maintained that this scoring documentation was necessary to address whether she had been subjected to retaliation with respect to Position 2. AJ’s Decision The AJ however denied Complainant’s motion for judgment and sanctions, noting that Complainant produced no evidence showing that the employees serving on the selection panel for Position 2 were aware of her protected EEO activity. The AJ therefore found that Complainant did not establish a prima facie case of reprisal with regard to Position 2, and consequently determined that the requested scoring documentation concerning Position 1 did not have any evidentiary value. The AJ found, however, that Complainant did establish that she was subjected to discrimination when she was not selected for Position 1. The AJ determined that Complainant’s race was a motivating factor in the Agency’s decision not to select her for Position 1. The AJ specifically found that the Computer Operations Manager’s testimony, that he was prepared to hire Complainant, was not credible and not supported by the evidence in the record. The AJ noted that the Computer Operations Manager expressed that Complainant had a communication problem, but the Agency presented no evidence that Complainant’s accent interfered with her job performance when she previously worked for Agency in same position. 6 Notwithstanding, using a mixed-motive analysis, the AJ found evidence that the advertising of Position 1 for external candidates did violate the CBA. The AJ observed that the Labor Relations Specialist credibly testified that he independently reached the conclusion that the posting of Position 1 violated the CBA, and therefore he determined that the Union’s grievance must be settled, resulting in the cancelation of the selection process for Position 1. The AJ found no evidence that the Labor Relations Specialist was motivated by discriminatory or retaliatory animus. The AJ therefore determined that the hiring for Position 1 would have been canceled even absent the Computer Operations Manager’s discrimination. In addressing Position 2, the AJ noted that the panel, based on their evaluations of the applications, recommend three candidates for interviews. The AJ noted that as Complainant was not ranked as a top candidate by the panel, she did not receive an interview for Position 2. The AJ granted the Agency’s motion for Summary Judgment on December 6, 2018, regarding claim 3, but denied the Agency’s motion as to claims 1 and 2. As Complainant did not specifically raise claim 3 on appeal, we exercise our discretion to not address this matter in our decision. The Agency has not contested the AJ’s finding of discrimination. In finding no evidence of reprisal, the AJ observed that all three panel members credibility testified that they were not aware of Complainant’s protected EEO activity. The AJ found that the panel members credibly testified that no individual influenced their ranking of Complainant’s application. The AJ therefore determined that Complainant did not establish a prima facie case of reprisal with respect to Position 2. Due to the AJ’s mixed-motive finding with regard to Position 1, the AJ ordered the Agency to train and consider taking disciplinary action against the Computer Operations Manager; post notice of the finding of discrimination; and award Complainant a reasonable amount in attorney’s fees. The AJ however did not award Complainant compensatory damages or back pay in light of the mixed-motive finding of discrimination. 7 The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s decision in its entirety.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as an Emergency Operations Specialist, NQ-02, at the Agency’s National Nuclear Security Administration in Washington, D.C. On December 12, 2016, Complainant submitted two leave requests for the dates of May 3-6, 2017, and May 11-13, 2017. On or about February 15, 2017, a supervisor (S1) notified Complainant that his leave request was denied. On May 23, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (African-American) and color (Black) when his leave request was denied. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. On July 1, 2019, the AJ assigned to the case issued a notice of intent to issue summary judgment. Over Complainant’s opposition, the AJ issued a summary judgment decision on July 22, 2019, finding that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully adopting the AJ’s decision. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Supervisor, Distributor Operations, EAS-17, at the Agency’s Processing & Distribution Center in Dallas, Texas. On March 16, 2019, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of sex (female), disability (coronary artery disease), and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when, on January 25, 2019, she was not provided work accommodation when her work hours were changed from 5:00 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. (day shift) to 8:30 p.m. to 5:00 a.m. (night shift). The Agency stated that at the conclusion of its investigation, it provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation (ROI) and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination or reprisal as alleged.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Ratings Veteran Service Representative at the Agency’s facility in Washington, D.C. On March 16, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of disability (Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) 2 and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity. For purposes of analysis only, we assume, without finding, that Complainant is an individual with a disability. 1. On or about January 11, 2017, Complainant was not selected for the position of Management Program Analyst, GS-13, advertised under vacancy announcement No. 397-17-112GD-RUI1866699. 2. On or about January 11, 2017, Complainant was not selected for a work detail. 3. On May 25, 2017, Complainant was denied a reasonable accommodation. 4. ON June 23, 2017, Complainant was not selected to participate in the Virtual Aspiring Leaders Program. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). On September 11, 2019, the Agency issued a final decision concluding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The Agency found that management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions regarding claims (1), (2), and (4). Regarding claim (1), the non-selection, the Agency found that the best qualified candidates were selected based on their interview responses. Regarding claim (2), not being selected for a detail, the final decision set forth that management denied that the selectees for the position at issue in claim (1) were detailed to these positions prior to their selection. Regarding being assigned to a detail in general, the final decision set forth that management asserted that generally Appeals Management Center (AMC) employees are not detailed to external departments except to participate in leadership programs; however, management noted that the Agency did solicit employees to assist in details for the planned realignment of the AMC and that there was no record of Complainant volunteering for this detail assignment. Finally, regarding claim (4), Complainant not being recommended for the Aspiring Leaders Program, the Agency, in its final decision, set forth that management did not select Complainant for participation in this program because she was not satisfactorily performing her duties at the time in question. The Agency further found that Complainant failed to establish that the Agency’s articulated reasons were pretext for discrimination and/or retaliation. Regarding claim (3), denial of a reasonable accommodation, the Agency found that Complainant asserted that she was able to perform the essential functions of her position but not under her supervisory chain at the time. Thus, the Agency found it was not obligated to reassign her to a different supervisor. The Agency further found that even assuming arguendo that Complainant was not medically able to perform her essential job duties that it did subsequently reassign Complainant to a different position. The instant appeal followed. Complainant does not submit a statement or brief on appeal.

At the time of events giving rise to Complainants’ complaints, Complainant 1 worked as a Program Specialist, GS-09, at the Agency's Food and Nutrition Service (FNS), Western Regional Office (WRO), Food Distribution Programs (FDP), Community Nutrition Branch (CNB), Special Nutrition Programs Branch (SNPB), located in San Francisco, California. Complainant 2 worked as Management Services Specialist, GS-09 at the Agency's FNS, WRO, Grants Management and Administrative Services (GMAS) Division, Administrative Services Unit (ASU), in San Francisco, California. Complainant 3 and Complainant 4 both worked as Program Specialists, GS-09, FNS, WRO, SNPB, in San Francisco, California. In June of 2015, FNS Agency representatives attended the West Coast Regional Returning Peace Corps Volunteers (RPCV) Conference and Recruitment Fair. Report of Investigation (ROI), at 523. Therein, the Agency collected applications from Complainants as well as from other applicants for positions with the Agency. Id. Complainants applied for positions by submitting application materials, including a cover letter and resume, transcript, and a description of their Peace Corps service. A separate sub-Agency, the Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), was assigned to determine applicants’ non-competitive eligibility for Program Specialist positions and to perform the GS-level classification determination on behalf of the Agency. First Supplemental Report of Investigation (First Supp. ROI), at 24. The FSIS’s Human Resources (HR) received about 22 applications to review from the Agency, and two female FSIS HR Specialists (HRS 1 and HRS 2) were assigned to review the applications to determine eligibility and grade classification for the prospective candidates. Second Supplemental Report of Investigation (Second Supp. ROI), at 30-32. HRS 1 reviewed 14 applications (encompassing 12 female and two male applicants), including the applications of Complainant 2 and Complainant 4. First Supp. ROI, at 124. HRS 1 classified six applicants eligible at the GS-07 grade-level, including Complainant 2 and Complainant 4 because they only possessed bachelor’s degrees. Id. HRS 1 classified both male applicants eligible at the GS-07 grade-level as well. Id. HRS 1 also classified six females to be eligible for the GS-09 grade-level or above because they had obtained master’s degrees. Id. One female candidate’s application was still pending, and another female applicant was found not to be eligible by HRS 1. Id. 3 [number removed], et al. HRS 2 was assigned to review the applications of eight applicants (encompassing six female and two male candidates) including Complainant 1 and Complainant 3 who both did not possess master’s degrees. HRS 2 classified Complainant 1, Complainant 3, three other female candidates, and one of the male candidates to be eligible for the GS-07 grade-level. HRS 2 found three female applicants and one male applicant to be eligible for the GS-09 grade-level. 3 As such, from August 2015 through October 2015, Complainants and other applicants who only possessed bachelor’s degrees began working for the Agency at the GS-07 grade-level in Program Specialist positions. Applicants who possessed master’s degrees began working at the GS-9 grade-level. 4 Notwithstanding, all four Complainants were promoted to the GS-09 grade-level within a year or so of their hiring on or before October 1, 2016. Second Supp. ROI, at 65, 114, 135, and 176. On September 6, 2016, the Agency again requested that FSIS perform grade classifications for hiring. The FSIS’s Branch Chief reviewed applications from two male applicants (Comparator 1 and Comparator 2) and solely found them to be eligible for hire at the GS-09 grade-level based on their education and experience.
