At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-2210-14 Information Technology (IT) Branch Chief at the Agency’s Region IV office in Atlanta, Georgia. 1. In early 2015, Complainant’s supervisor (S1) transferred one of Complainant’s IT staff members without first providing notice; 2. On June 14, 2015, management detailed Complainant’s IT Operations Team Lead for 60 days without discussing the action with him, which had a negative impact on Complainant’s daily activities with staff and day-to- day operations; 3. On September 30, 2015, he was falsely accused of providing unsatisfactory or untimely information regarding Critical Vulnerability Progress Update reports; 4. On December 9, 2015, he was falsely accused of missing a deadline on an IT Life Cycle assignment; 5. On December 15, 2015, he was purposely locked out of FedHR Navigator and could neither review his third and fourth quarter evaluations nor provide a response to the adverse comments made on his performance appraisal; 6. On January 29, 2016, he was informed that: a. He would receive an Unsatisfactory Performance rating for the 2015 reporting period; b. He would be placed on a 60-day Performance Improvement Plan (PIP); c. His Within Grade Increase was being withheld; and d. If he did not successfully complete the one-year probation period after the PIP, he could be demoted, transferred, or terminated; 7. On February 4, 2016, he was placed on a PIP; and 8. On February 22, 2016, the Region Security Office Chief informed Complainant that his Top-Secret Clearance was being downgraded to Public Trust. On October 3, 2016, 182 days after he filed his complaint, Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). 2 The EEOC’s Atlanta District Office received Complainant’s hearing request on October 13, 2016. The Agency did not notify Complainant until February 14, 2017, that, because the Agency had not completed the investigation within 180 days of Complainant filing his complaint, he had the right to request a hearing before an EEOC AJ or to file a civil action. On December 3, 2016, a Supervisory AJ (AJ-1) issued an “Order Directing Agency to Produce Electronic Complaint File”, which required the Agency to produce the complaint file within the earlier of 15 days of receipt of the order or from receipt of Complainant’s hearing request. The order also notified the Agency that sanctions could be imposed if the Agency could not show good cause for not providing the complete investigative file within 15 days or if the Agency failed to adequately investigate the complaint in accordance with Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO MD-110) (Aug. 5, 2015). On February 28, 2017, Complainant filed a “Motion for Default Judgment” asserting that, more than 300 days after he filed his complaint, the Agency had still not begun the investigation. Complainant argued that the Agency’s failure to complete the investigation within 180 days pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(e) compromised the integrity of the federal sector EEO process and that a default judgment in Complainant’s favor was appropriate. On April 12, 2017, the Agency responded to AJ-1’s December 3, 2016, order to produce the investigative file. The Agency explained that, since November 2015, it had experienced an interruption in conducting investigations because it did not have available contract investigators who met the Agency’s security requirements. The Agency indicated that, despite utilizing a competitive process to hire qualified investigators, it was still experiencing significant delays in investigating EEO complaints. According to the Agency, it had assigned Complainant’s materials to an investigator and estimated that the report of investigation would be completed by May 22, 2017. Agency Response at 3. On June 12, 2017, AJ-1 issued an “Order to Show Cause”. AJ-1 observed that the Agency had failed to provide the investigative record within 15 days of receipt of the December 8, 2016, order, and directed the Agency to show cause why sanctions should not be imposed within 10 days from the date of the order. The Agency did not file a response. On June 20, 2017, the Agency provided a copy of the investigative file to the EEOC and transmitted a copy of the investigative file to Complainant on June 28, 2017. On September 25, 2017, the Agency filed its opposition to Complainant’s motion for default judgment. The Agency argued that a default judgment was inappropriate because Complainant could not establish a prima facie case of discrimination based on age, disability, or reprisal. The Agency further argued that sanctions were not warranted because it had good cause for the delay in completing the investigation: namely, the unavailability of investigators. In the Agency’s view, its situation was distinguishable from other cases because the delay was attributable to “an unanticipated security clearance issue that arose in 2015 in regard to FEMA’s contract investigators”, rather than inadequate or untimely performance by Agency employees or contract investigators. Agency’s Response at 27. According to the Agency, the delay did not prejudice Complainant nor undermine the integrity of the system. The 223-day delay in completing the investigation, asserted the Agency, was not as significant as the delay in cases where sanctions were imposed. On November 14, 2017, Complainant replied to the Agency’s response to the motion for default judgment, noting that the Agency’s response was untimely and should not be considered. Complainant argued that default judgment was appropriate because the Agency disregarded its obligation to investigate his complaint and had failed to timely respond to AJ-1’s orders. According to Complainant, the Agency’s excuse did not absolve the Agency from its responsibility to timely investigate complaints. Complainant also contended that the investigation was woefully inadequate, noting that the investigative file did not include his affidavit, which he timely submitted to the EEO Investigator. On March 5, 2019, the EEOC reassigned the case to another AJ (AJ-2). On June 28, 2019, AJ-2 issued an “Order on Complainant’s Motion for Default Judgment” (Sanction Order), an “Order Denying Agency Motion for Partial Dismissal”, and an “Order to Produce Revised Report of Investigation”. 3 In the Sanction Order, AJ-2 found that, although the Agency was required to complete its investigation and provide the report of investigation to Complainant no later than October 3, 2016, the Agency did not provide the investigative file to Complainant until June 28, 2017, 268 days after the deadline. AJ-2 also concluded that the report of investigation was “deficient” because it included “hardly any documentary evidence” and because the affidavit from S1 was “unsigned and therefore, unsworn.” Sanction Order at 2. AJ-2 stated that the unavailability of investigators did not amount to good cause and was an affront to the EEO process that the Agency did not ensure it had the resources needed to timely complete investigations. AJ-2 found that, although the Agency’s actions warranted the imposition of sanctions, default judgment was not appropriate in this case. AJ-2 stated that default judgment was not warranted after considering the following factors: (1) the extent and nature of the noncompliance and the justification presented by the non-complying party; (2) the prejudicial effect of the noncompliance on the opposing party; (3) the consequences resulting from the delay in justice; and (4) the effect on the integrity of the EEO process. However, AJ-2 did not explain why, after consideration of these factors, default judgment was not warranted. Id. Instead, AJ-2 ordered 12 hours of training, regarding the proper processing of EEO complaints, for those Agency officials responsible for the inadequate number of investigators available to investigate EEO complaints. In addition to identifying the responsible officials, the Agency was required to file a statement explaining why it did not have enough EEO investigators to timely complete investigations and what actions it has taken to address the problem. AJ-2 also found that Complainant was prejudiced by the inadequacy of the investigation and ordered the Agency to bear a portion of Complainant’s discovery costs. Specifically, AJ-2 ordered the Agency to pay reasonable attorney’s fees for up to five hours preparing requests for production of documents and reviewing the Agency’s responses to his requests for production. In the Order to Produce Revised Report of Investigation, AJ-2 ordered the Agency to submit a revised version of the report of investigation that had sequentially numbered pages. AJ-2 also ordered the Agency to pay for the costs of taking the deposition of S1, including the court reporter fee, the fee for one copy of the deposition transcript, and reasonable attorney’s fees for up to 15 hours preparing for and taking the deposition. On July 29, 2019, the Agency submitted statements from Office of Equal Rights (OER) Director and the Civil Rights Program Manager in response to AJ-2’s “Order on Complainant’s Motion for Default Judgment”. The Agency indicated that the three employees (two former OER Directors and the former Formal Complaints Unit Branch Chief), who were responsible for the Agency’s inadequate number of investigators, no longer worked for the Agency. The Agency provided documentation showing that all three employees had retired or resigned, in 2017 or earlier. On October 15, 2019, the Agency filed a motion for summary judgment. Complainant responded to the Agency’s motion for summary judgment on October 30, 2019. In turn, the Agency submitted a reply on November 6, 2019. The Agency’s motion and its reply relied on the transcript of Complainant’s deposition, excerpts from the transcript of S1’s deposition, and other documents that the Agency produced, for the first time, during discovery. On May 8, 2020, AJ-2 issued a decision granting the Agency’s motion for summary judgment, finding that there was no genuine issue of material fact regarding whether the Agency subjected Complainant to discrimination based on age, disability, and/or reprisal. Regarding claims (1) through (3), AJ-2 found that Complainant could not establish a prima facie case of reprisal because S1 did not learn of Complainant’s EEO activity until November 27, 2015, after the incidents at issue. AJ-2 further found that the Agency provided legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. AJ-2 determined that, because he asserted nothing more than unsupported allegations and speculation that the actions were based on his age and/or disability, Complainant was unable to establish pretext for age and/or disability discrimination. For claims (4) through (8), AJ-2 noted that Complainant relied on the temporal proximity between when S1 learned he was named as a witness and the adverse actions, which AJ-2 reasoned was insufficient to establish pretext for reprisal. On May 8, 2020, AJ-2 also issued an “Order Regarding Filings to Address Appropriate Award of Attorney’s Fees and Costs”. Since the Agency officials responsible for the lack of investigators were no longer Agency employees, AJ-2 declined to order the Agency to provide additional EEO training. Complainant was ordered to submit a statement of attorney’s fees and costs, limited to the discovery costs identified in the Sanction Order. Further, AJ-2 directed the parties to contact each other by May 18, 2020, to discuss stipulating to the amount of attorney’s fees and costs. On May 19, 2020, the parties filed a “Joint Stipulation on Award of Attorney’s Fees and Costs”. The next day, AJ-2 issued an “Order Awarding Attorney’s Fees and Costs as a Sanction Against the Agency”, awarding Complainant the stipulated amount of $5,580. ($4,999. in attorney’s fees; $580. in costs). Additionally, AJ-2 issued an “Order Entering Judgment”, entering judgment consistent with the May 8, 2020, decision and the May 20, 2020, order awarding attorney’s fees and costs. On June 22, 2020, the Agency issued a final action implementing AJ-2’s decision.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Mentoring Program Manager, GS 14 at the Agency’s ICE Headquarters in Washington, D.C. subjected to numerous incidents of harassment, including but not limited to: his second-line supervisor, the Chief of Staff (CoS) for the Office of Training and Development, offered him no feedback on his Individual Development Plan; he was removed from his temporary duty reassignment to a supervisory position and returned to his nonsupervisory position; his November 2013 and February 2014 performance appraisals contained negative narratives and led to him being excluded from receiving performance evaluation bones; his supervisors, the CoS and the Unit Chief (UC), revoked his telework agreement; the UC assigned him a 2015 annual performance rating of “Achieved Expectations” and a total numerical score that left him ineligible to receive merit pay; and the UC repeatedly scolded him in a harsh and demeaning manner in front of other employees. 2 At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew his request. Prior to the issuance of the final decision, the Agency determined that a supplemental investigation was necessary. The supplemental investigation was completed on May 29, 2020 and thereafter, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision found that, with respect to the discrete claim of Complainant’s 2015 performance appraisal, the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its action and Complainant did not submit any evidence to support his assertions of pretext. The decision also found that Complainant had not established that he was subjected to a hostile work environment because the incidents taken together were neither severe nor pervasive enough to constitute a hostile work environment. The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged.

At the time this matter arose, Complainant was an applicant for employment with the Agency. Announcement No. BOP-N-0007-001-2013. The record reflects that the position was at the United States Penitentiary in Hazelton, West Virginia. By letter dated July 28, 2014, the Agency forwarded the formal complaint to a contract investigation firm. On September 10, 2014, the contract investigation firm submitted the report of investigation to the Agency. On October 23, 2014, Complainant filed a hearing request and a Motion for Default Judgment. On October 27, 2014, the Agency transmitted the Report of Investigation (ROI) to Complainant and the EEOC Hearings Unit. On October 23, 2015, the assigned AJ held an Initial Conference. At this conference, the AJ granted the Agency permission to file a response to Complainant’s Motion for Default Judgment. On October 29, 2015, the Agency filed its opposition to Complainant’s motion. In its Opposition, the Agency acknowledged the 37-day delay and asserted that the Agency had a high number of EEO investigations being worked on during this time period. In addition, the Agency argued the delay was brief, and Complainant was not prejudiced by the delay. On December 3, 2018, the AJ issued an Order granting Complainant’s Motion for Default Judgment. The AJ found that the ROI was transmitted 37 days after the 180-day time period set forth in the Commission’s regulations. The AJ found that the Agency also failed to issue Complainant a notice, as required by 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(g), that it was unable to timely complete the investigation. The regulation indicates the notice must provide an estimated date for the completion of the investigation and inform a complainant of their right to request a hearing or file a civil action, in the event a complainant does not want to wait until the completion of the investigation. In reaching her determination to issue default judgment against the Agency, the AJ reasoned as follows: [t]he Agency failed to notify Complainant in a timely manner that the investigation would not be completed in 180 days nor did it give an estimate of when it would complete the investigation as required by [Commission regulations] so Complainant could make an informed decision on what to do next…Despite the Agency’s arguments, I find that the Agency has failed to establish good cause for its failure to provide Complainant with a copy of the investigative file within 180 days from the filing of her complaint or issue a written notice to the Complainant informing that it was unable to complete its investigation within the time limits required [by the Commission’s regulations]. AJ Decision at 3-4. The AJ cited Royal v. Dep’t of Veterans Affairs, EEOC [number removed] (Sept. 25, 2009), in support of her decision to issue default judgment in favor of Complainant. The AJ ruled: In the present case, despite Agency’s contention that issuance of the ROI was delayed in an effort to thoroughly investigate Complainant’s charge, the record shows that the Agency did not assign an investigator to Complainant’s claim until July 28, 2014, yet the Agency did not issue the ROI to Complainant until October 27, 2014, which was four months (126 days) after Complainant filed her charge. Moreover, that record shows that the contractor issued the Agency the ROI on September 10, 2014, yet the Agency did not issue the ROI to Complainant until October 27, 2014. As articulated in Royal, I find that the Agency in this case failed to commence an EEO investigation that could reasonably be completed within the 180-day period following the filing of the formal complaint… AJ Decision at 5. Finally, the AJ found that Complainant established a prima facie case of sex discrimination and, as such, was entitled to personal relief, including damages. A hearing on damages was held on July 20, 2020. On September 30, 2020, the AJ issued a decision on damages and attorney’s fees. The AJ ordered training for all human resources professionals who participate in the hiring process at the facility at issue, the posting of a notice at the facility regarding the finding, an award of back pay,2 $30,000 in non-pecuniary compensatory damages, and $41,005. in attorney’s fees. The record reflects that the Agency filed two motions for the AJ to reconsider her decision issuing default judgment, which the AJ denied. On November 5, 2020, the Agency issued a final order rejecting the AJ’s default judgment sanction and filed an appeal with the Commission. The record reflects that Complainant was subsequently hired at the facility in the position of Correctional Officer in January 2018. AJ Damages Decision at 5. On October 30, 2020, subsequent to the AJ issuing her decision and prior to the Agency issuing its final order, Agency’s Counsel (who represented the Agency during the proceedings before the EEOC AJ) submitted a brief to the Agency’s Complaint Adjudication Office (CAO) (the Agency entity that would issue the final order in the instant matter) in Opposition to the AJ’s Default Judgment, Damages, Attorney’s Fees, and Costs. Therein, Agency Counsel, in a lengthy legal analysis, requested that CAO reject the AJ’s default judgment. In response, Complainant’s attorney sent an email to the Agency on October 30, 2020, that the AJ had already issued a decision in this matter and that the Agency should not consider new evidence in reaching its final In its final order, the Agency asserted that the AJ’s sanction of default judgment was too harsh a sanction for a 37-day delay in transmitting the ROI to Complainant. Specifically, the Agency stated, “the AJ imposed the harshest sanction available against [the Agency], without finding that [it] failed to comply with an AJ order or instruction, and without any explanation of how the sanction imposed was the least severe but still effective sanction, given the 37-day delay in transmitting the record to Complainant.” Final Order at 8. The Agency determined that the instant matter was more similar to Gray v. Dep’t of Def., EEOC [number removed] (March 1, 2007), in which the Commission found that an AJ abused her discretion when she imposed default judgment as a sanction for an agency’s delay in completing an investigation that was less than three months later than the 180-day deadline. Id. at 8-9. The Agency also contested the AJ’s determination that Complainant established a prima facie case of sex discrimination. Id. at 10. Complainant filed a statement in opposition to the Agency’s appeal. Complainant, through her attorney, requests that we affirm the AJ’s decision issuing a default judgment against the Agency. Complainant asserts that the Agency’s dismissive attitude toward the delay in transmitting the ROI is an “insult” to the integrity of the EEO process and that a default judgment is the proper sanction against the Agency. Complainant also asserts that the AJ properly found that she established a prima facie case of sex discrimination.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a City Carrier at the Harlingen Post Office in Harlingen, Texas. 1. On August 5, 2013, she was told that if she got off the Overtime Desired list, she would be sorry; 2. In approximately the end of April or first of May 2013, she was stopped and provoked during route inspection; 3. In September 2013, she was forced to take her vacation on Leave Without Pay (LWOP); 4. In approximately the end of April or first of May 2013, she was denied a route adjustment; 5. On unspecified dates, she was denied assistance in fixing problems with her route, and management did not take appropriate action to prevent customers on her route from abusing her; 6. While she was out due to her injury on October 21, 2013, she was forced to come in for an investigative interview; 7. On November 7, 2013, she was issued a 7-Day Suspension; 8. On January 6, 2014, she was denied access to her local personnel folder; 9. On January 7, 2014, she was told that if she did not come in on January 10, 2014, for her job offer, she would be reported to the Office of Workers’ Compensation Programs (OWCP); and 10. On January 9, 2014, management threatened to deny her job offer. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing, but on September 30, 2020, the AJ remanded the complaint to the Agency for the issuance of a final decision because Complainant “[f]ailed to fully and sufficiently respond to the Agency’s Discovery Requests.” In compliance with the AJ’s order, the Agency issued its October 21, 2020, final decision finding no discrimination. In her Order dismissing the hearing request, the AJ noted that, on June 16, 2014, the parties were informed of their right to engage in discovery, and that they must cooperate with each other in honoring discovery requests. The parties were also told that they were expected to initiate and complete needed discovery with a minimum of intervention by the AJ. Finally, the AJ noted that the parties were further advised that responses to discovery requests were required to be made within 30 days from receipt of those requests. The Agency initiated discovery on June 26, 2014, by serving Complainant and her representative with “Interrogatories and a Request for Production of Documents” (Discovery Requests). Accordingly, Complainant’s responses were due no later than July 26, 2014. On July 25, 2014, Complainant’s representative requested a 30-day extension of time to respond to the Discovery Requests, and the Agency consented. Complainant’s deadline to respond therefore became August 25, 2014. On August 21, 2014, Complainant’s representative requested an additional two-week extension of time to respond to the Discovery Requests, but the Agency denied the request. On August 27, 2014, the Agency’s representative sent Complainant a copy of its Motion to Compel, advising that Complainant’s discovery responses were due, and requesting that she immediately provide full responses. The Agency’s representative added that if they were not received, the Agency would file the Motion to Compel. Complainant did not respond and on September 3, 2014, the Agency filed a Motion to Compel in which it asked that Complainant be compelled to provide complete responses to the Agency’s Discovery Requests and that, should she fail to do so, she be sanctioned by the dismissal of her complaint. On September 3, 2014, the AJ granted the Agency’s Motion to Compel. On November 18, 2014, the Agency filed a Motion to Dismiss, noting that almost five months had elapsed since it had served Complainant with its Discovery Requests, and almost three months since the AJ had granted Agency’s Motion to Compel. The Agency asked that Complainant be sanctioned by the dismissal of her complaint. On December 22, 2014, the Agency filed a Supplement to its Motion to Dismiss, indicating that on December 19, 2014, Complainant had provided the Agency with a document entitled “Complainant’s Response to Agency’s Discovery.” The document was six pages of typed notes, wherein the AJ noted that it appeared Complainant had gone through the Report of Investigation (ROI) and “commented, clarified, or supplemented what was written therein.” Complainant opposed the Agency’s Motion to Dismiss, claiming that she had sent the Agency’s representative over 200 pages of documents, which were divided by “bright yellow paper,” marked to identify that section’s contents. On January 8, 2015, the Agency filed a Second Supplement to its Motion to Dismiss alleging that Complainant’s response to its Discovery Requests was deficient. On January 23, 2015, Complainant opposed the Agency’s motion, arguing that responses to some interrogatories could be found in the Report of Investigation, and that she had properly identified comparators by alleging that “all of the male employees were treated more favorably than Complainant in every aspect of their day-to-day work.” On March 26, 2016, the AJ issued an Order denying the Agency’s Motion to Dismiss, in which she noted that when she had previously granted the Agency’s Motion to Compel, Complainant was represented by a non-attorney. When Complainant opposed the Agency’s Second Supplement to the Motion to Dismiss, she was represented by an attorney who, in her opposition to the Agency’s motion, described a litany of personal problems that Complainant had been having which had prevented her from being more involved in her case. The AJ stated that she agreed that Complainant’s responses to the Agency’s Discovery Requests were deficient, and she ordered Complainant to fully respond to the Agency’s Discovery Requests within 30 days of her receipt of the order, and advised that the failure to comply with the Order could result in sanctions pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.109(f)(3). On May 5, 2016, the Agency filed a Third Supplement to its Motion to Dismiss indicating that Complainant had not provided it with any additional responses to its Discovery Requests since the AJ issued her March 26, 2016, Order. On May 24, 2016, Complainant responded to the Agency’s Third Supplement to the Motion to Dismiss. The AJ found that: Complainant’s continued insistence on responding to the Agency’s Discovery Requests by referring to [her] Informal Complaint (42 pages), Formal Complaint (seven pages), and her Report of Investigation [ROI] affidavit (34 pages) is deficient. Not all the information contained in those documents is responsive to the Agency’s Discovery Requests, and the Agency is not required to go through scores of pages and tease out what might be responsive to its requests. Nor was it sufficient for Complainant to continue to identify all similarly situated co-workers whom she alleged were treated more favorably than she, as “all of the male employees,” which, as the Agency pointed out, numbered in the hundreds. As noted above, the AJ found that Complainant failed to fully and sufficiently respond to the Agency’s Discovery Requests, and that a sanction was appropriate; therefore, she denied Complainant’s request for a hearing on the merits of her case, and remanded her complaint to the Agency for issuance of a final decision. On appeal, Complainant argues that “[m]ost of the [A]gency discovery requests had already been answered in full by [Complainant] and contained in the ROI.” Complainant also maintains that she “[a]nswered each interrogatory fully, stating exactly where in the record it existed. The responding party is not required to give a narrative answer to an interrogatory, but may instead produce records/documents, whereby the burden of deriving or ascertaining the answer is substantially the same for the requesting party as it is for the producing party.” Complainant further notes the four-year delay between the AJ’s March 26, 2016, Order, and her September 30, 2020, dismissal of the hearing request. According to Complainant, “If the judge had wanted to demand more from [Complainant] than what the law requires, then the Judge should have clearly stated so in her order and allowed [Complainant] an opportunity to cure.” The Agency argued on appeal that, “[i]t is clear from the record that Complainant failed to fully respond to the Agency’s discovery, thereby depriving the Agency of information relevant to the case and to which the Agency is entitled in order to fully defend itself in the case.” Furthermore, the Agency noted that even though Complainant was notified by the AJ that the failure to comply with her March 26, 2016 Order could result in sanctions pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.109(f)(3), Complainant “continued in her failure to fully respond and her failure caused the Agency to expend significant attorney time and resources in preparing and submitting pleadings addressing that failure.”

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as an Airway Transportation Systems Specialist at the Agency’s Atlanta Terminal Radar Approach Control Service Operations Center, Systems Support Center in Peachtree City, Georgia. On February 3, 2020, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (African-American), age (68), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 when, on December 19, 2019, he learned he was not selected for a position (No. ASO-ATO-19-B292-63954) that was announced in his office. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant, through counsel, requests that the Commission sanction the Agency with a default judgment for failure to timely investigate the instant complaint. Complainant also continues to argue that his non-selection was due to his applicant score being purposefully lowered.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Benefits Authorizer at the Agency’s Mid- Atlantic Payment Service Center (MAPSC) in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. On May 12, 2020, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging: 1. On January 13 and February 14, 2020, the Agency subjected Complainant to Weingarten meetings 2 in unlawful retaliation against him for engaging in prior protected EEO activity. A “Weingarten meeting” is a pre-disciplinary investigative meeting between management officials and a bargaining unit employee, who is entitled to union representation. 2. From February 2018 until June 2020, Complainant was subjected to ongoing harassment based on his race (African American), sex (male), and in reprisal for prior EEO activity (EEOC [number removed]) when he was subjected to a 5-day suspension in February 2018, a 14-day suspension in March/April 2019, and Weingarten meetings in 2018 where he was accused of selling marijuana on Agency property and another in early 2019 where he was accused of hanging up on SSA customers. 3 After an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination or unlawful retaliation. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Rural Carrier, P-02, at the Agency’s Post Office in Harrisburg, North Carolina. On November 26, 2019, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency subjected her to discrimination and a hostile work environment in reprisal her for prior protected EEO activity when: (1) since August 26, 2019, Complainant was followed and written up on her route; and (2) on September 7, 2019, Complainant was issued a Notice of Removal for Failure to be Regular in Attendance. Complainant’s immediate supervisor was the Supervisor of Customer Services (S1). Report of Investigation (ROI) at 65. Complainant had filed a prior EEO complaint against S1 and the Postmaster (S2) in March 2018. As additional background, the record reflects that the Agency had issued Complainant a prior removal action in December 2017, which was settled on April 1, 2019. ROI at 88, 90. Claim 1 – Heightened Scrutiny Complainant claimed that after she returned from being on leave for an on-the- job injury, in June 2018, S1 subjected her to heightened scrutiny. She claimed that she was the only one that S1 followed all the time. S1 acknowledged that he followed her on the identified 10 dates as Complainant alleged, but S1 testified that the street observations did not result in any written report or adverse personnel action. S1 stated he monitored Complainant as part of his supervisory responsibilities. S1 also said that Complainant did not complain to him regarding harassment. Claim 2 – Notice of Removal The record includes the Notice of Removal dated September 3, 2019. ROI at 101- 102. The Notice states that Complainant was charged with absences from July 9, 2019 through July 26, 2019. In addition, the notice referenced dates in June 2019. It is undisputed that she was charged with six unscheduled absences and failing to be regular in attendance. On September 3, 2019, Complainant told S1 that she was not feeling well and asked to be taken off the schedule. S1acknowledged that she requested to be off. ROI at 79. S1 issued her the removal notice on September 7, 2019. Although Complainant disputed one of the dates at issue, Complainant acknowledged, during the investigative interview, that she failed to be regular in attendance. S1 acknowledged that he supervised others, who had unscheduled absences and were not removed, but he averred that no other employee had missed as many days as Complainant had missed. ROI at 80. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ assigned to the matter issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully adopting the AJ’s decision. This appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Facility Engineer, GS-0801-13, in the Agency’s Office of Information Technology in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. On September 9, 2020, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (African-American), disability (physical), and age (62) when, on June 12, 2020, he received notice that he was not selected for the position of Supervisory Facilities Engineer, GS-14, located in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, under Vacancy Announcement No., CARX-20-10810406-ASm-DH. The selecting official for the position was the Director, Data Center Facilities, Connectivity and Physical Security, National Data Center Operational and Logistics. (Caucasian, Year of Birth 1979, no stated disabilities) (SO). The SO was Complainant’s second line supervisor. He acknowledged that he was aware of Complainant’s race, but not his age or disability. Complainant applied for the position of Supervisory Facilities Engineer, GS-14, under vacancy announcement CARX-20-10810406-ASm-DH. 2 Nine candidates, including Complainant, met the minimum qualifications for the position and were referred by Human Resources for consideration. The record shows that the SO utilized the Direct Hire Authority for the selection at issue. Report of Investigation (ROI), at 59. The Direct Hire Authority does not require a screening panel. Nevertheless, a panel was selected which consisted of three Panel Members (PMs), who reviewed and evaluated the resumes and scored the candidates. The candidates with the highest scores were invited to be interviewed. The highest scoring candidate (Caucasian, unknown disability or age) received a score of 33. out of 43.25. Complainant was ranked seventh, with a score of 25. out of 43.25. Complainant averred that the Vacancy Announcement was intentionally reposted under the Direct Hire Authority “to subjectively minimize [his] qualifications” and eliminate Veterans preference. Complainant believed that he was intentionally ranked low to render him ineligible for an interview, which was a prerequisite for selection. The SO averred that, although he was not required to do so under the Direct Hire Authority, he chose to “use the internal control measures of a panel to select the best candidate overall.” The record shows that the selectee was a younger Caucasian male. The SO averred he was unaware of the selectee’s age or any disability. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). In the decision, the Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that Agency management subjected him to discrimination as alleged. This appeal followed. The record shows that there had been two announcements for the position at issue. The second announcement had a clarification that stated that “Veterans who are preference eligible may apply under the Veterans Employment Opportunity Act (VEOA)” and referenced the announcement number as CARX-20-10742781-KMc, Control Number [number removed]. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 81. This announcement was open from May 7, 2020 to May 13, 2020. Significantly, the Job Announcement CARX-20-10810406-ASm-DH, Control Number [number removed], included a Clarification, which referenced “Veterans Preference.” The announcement stated “Since the Direct Hire Recruitment Authority is being used, traditional Veterans Preference rules do not apply. Qualified Veterans will, however, be given full consideration for this position.” ROI at 66; Tab 7-2, 7-15.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as an EEO Specialist, GS-0260-12, at the Defense Commissary Agency in Fort Lee, Virginia. Specialist position at Defense Logistics Agency, Aviation (Richmond, VA) advertised in job announcement DLAAvn-20-10737786-MP. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. When Complainant did not respond, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision by summary judgment in favor of the Agency. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. 2 The AJ found that, taking the facts as presented in the report of investigation and viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to Complainant, he failed to create a genuine issue of material fact to establish discrimination based on race, sex, age, or reprisal. Assuming for the sake of argument that Complainant could establish a prima facie case of discrimination and retaliation, the AJ found that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. Specifically, the AJ determined that “Complainant has not demonstrated that he [is] plainly superior to” the selectee. For example, the AJ noted that both Complainant and the selectee “occupied positions that were similar to [the position] that was advertised.” Also, in comparing Complainant’s resume to the selectee’s resume, the AJ concluded that “Complainant’s qualifications are not plainly superior to those of the selectee,” as selectee’s resume showed she had experience in recommending and writing acceptances and dismissals of complaints, while Complainant’s resume mentions only that he completed a two-day course on the subject, and that his writing experience dealt mostly with writing counseling summaries but not with other types of written reports. The AJ also considered the selecting official’s (SO), EEO Manager, GS-0260-14, interview notes from her interviews with both Complainant and the selectee. For Complainant, SO noted that he was pleasant and articulate, that he mentioned writing acceptance and dismissal letters about 30 years ago when he worked for a state agency, and that he indicated his coworkers and supervisors would say that his weakness is that his work is sometimes late. SO also wrote Complainant had a “good interview, however he does not have much experience with formal processing.” On appeal, Complainant submitted a brief in which he appears to discuss a claim from a past complaint, [number removed]. That complaint involved Complainant’s nonselection for another EEO Specialist position with the Agency in which he was not chosen for an interview. The prior complaint proceeded before a different AJ, who granted the Agency’s motion for a decision without a hearing in that case. Complainant did not appeal the result of the prior complaint at the time the final decision was issued; on appeal here, he references only the present complaint’s Agency number and EEOC hearing number in his submissions. Therefore, we will address only the claim in the complaint at issue, [number removed]. Complainant’s comment during the interview that his work is sometimes late or untimely raised concerns for SO, as mentioned in her interview notes, because EEO work is often time sensitive. In comparison, SO’s notes during the selectee’s interview included “Excellent interview,” that selectee writes accurate reports, as well as letters of acceptance and dismissals that seldom require a rewrite, that she displayed an in-depth understanding of the federal complaint process, and that she relayed her manager often said she wished she had more employees like the selectee. The AJ concluded that, despite Complainant’s own contention that his qualifications for the position were stronger than the selectee’s, Complainant failed to show that SO’s reasons for choosing the selectee for the position were pretextual.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Claims Specialist, GS-11, at the Agency’s Brick Field Office in Brick, New Jersey. 043. Complainant did not challenge the framing of the complaint when he received the Agency’s Notice of Acceptance and we therefore find it is properly framed. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. Over Complainant’s objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision by summary judgment in favor of the Agency. The AJ found that, taking the facts as presented in the report of investigation and viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to Complainant, he failed to create a genuine issue of material fact to establish discrimination. The selecting official (SO), District Manager of the Neptune District Office, was Complainant’s second-level supervisor at the time of selection. The Acting Area Director (AAD) served as the concurring official for the selection and was Complainant’s third-level supervisor. A Human Resources Specialist (HRS) processed the vacancy announcement and assessed whether applicants were eligible to apply for the position. Applicants applied online and completed a self-assessment portion of the application. HRS stated that based on applicant responses, an automated process then sorted the applicants into two groups: competitive merit promotion applications and lateral reassignment applications. Because the vacancy at issue was for a GS-12 position, an applicant, like Complainant, who was below the GS-12 level was sorted into the competitive merit promotion group. Applicants who met the qualifications of a permanent GS-12 were sorted into the lateral reassignment group. The AJ found that the record showed SO had discretion to select a candidate from either of the two best-qualified lists and was not required to look at both the competitive merit promotion and the lateral assignment lists before making a selection. SO averred that in situations such as this, she generally reviews the lateral reassignment list first because it includes people already performing successfully at the necessary grade level. Based on her review of the three lateral reassignment applicants’ applications and reference checks from their current supervisors, SO selected the selectee from the lateral reassignment best-qualified list. According to SO, she chose the selectee because she could provide strong technical support to the smaller field office in addition to good leadership skills. SO did not review any competitive merit promotion candidates. AAD discussed SO’s selection of the selectee with SO and concluded SO had demonstrated that the selectee was the best candidate on the lateral assignment list. The AJ concluded that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for not selecting Complainant for the temporary promotion and that Complainant could not connect his nonselection to his national origin, sex, or age. The AJ found that Complainant could not establish pretext, as there was no evidence to demonstrate that management was motivated by discrimination in the hiring process. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a City Letter Carrier at the Agency’s Saint Andrews Post Office in Charleston, South Carolina. 1. On February 27, 2020, he was temporarily removed from his permanently- assigned duty station. 2 Complainant later amended his complaint, alleging that the Agency discriminated against him based on reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when: 2. On July 8, 2020, he was given a Pre-Disciplinary Interview, and subsequently, on July 28, 2020, was issued discipline. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. Over Complainant’s objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision by summary judgment in favor of the Agency. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. The AJ concluded that, taking the facts as presented in the report of investigation and viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to Complainant, that Complainant failed to create a genuine issue of material fact to establish discrimination based on sex or reprisal. The AJ found that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions that Complainant failed to rebut as pretextual. The AJ found that both of Complainant’s claims stemmed from two separate allegations of sexual harassment made against him. First, Complainant, in his role as president of his union, was assigned to represent an Agency employee (E1) in a grievance she filed about a proposed removal. E1 accused Complainant of seeking sexual favors in exchange for his representation in the grievance. The Agency investigated the allegation and, based on Agency policy, temporarily reassigned Complainant to a different duty station in order to separate him and E1. As part of the investigation, E1 provided the Agency with several tape recordings of someone she claimed was Complainant discussing his union representation of her and making inappropriate comments. Complainant claims that the tapes are inauthentic and that he is not the one speaking on the recordings. The second sexual harassment allegation occurred after a supervisor observed Complainant hugging another Agency employee (E2) on the workroom floor and moving his hands towards her buttocks while he did so. As a result of its investigations into the two accusations regarding E1 and E2, the Agency issued Complainant a 14-day suspension on July 28, 2020, which the union grieved. The complaint originally included the following additional claim: “In August 2019, a coworker filed a Civil action against the union accusing you of sexual harassment while acting in your official capacity as a Union Steward.” The Agency dismissed this claim pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(2) for untimely EEO counselor contact and, in the alternative, for failure to state a claim, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(1), as a collateral attack on another forum’s proceeding. On appeal, Complainant does not dispute the dismissal of this claim, and we therefore do not address it further herein. As part of the grievance process, an arbitrator found that the Agency had not met its burden of proof regarding E1’s allegation, but the arbitrator sustained the charges in connection with the touching of E2 and reduced Complainant’s punishment to a Letter of Warning. The AJ determined that the behavior Complainant was accused of justified his temporary reassignment and the 14-day suspension. Regarding the allegations by E1, the AJ found the Agency largely based its decision to discipline Complainant on the tapes E1 provided and that Complainant could not show the Agency’s belief in the tapes’ authenticity was pretextual. The AJ also noted that Complainant did not directly address the accusations regarding E2, but instead attached to his affidavit the answers he gave during an investigative interview where he responded to the question of whether he denied or confirmed touching E2’s buttocks with, “I do neither.” The AJ found that Complainant’s equivocal responses failed to show that the Agency’s credence of the allegations regarding E2 was pretext for discrimination.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Carrier Technician at an Agency facility in Washington, D.C. On January 18, 2020, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of sex (female) and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity. By letter dated February 14, 2020, the Agency accepted Complainant’s complaint for investigation and determined that it was comprised of the following claim: On September 16, 2019, Complainant was disqualified from her new bid assignment. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. On August 11, 2021, the Agency filed a Motion for a Decision Without a Hearing (Agency’s Motion). Complainant did not file a response. On June 9, 2022, the AJ issued a decision by summary judgment finding no discrimination or unlawful retaliation was established. The AJ found that the Agency articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for its action and that Complainant failed to establish that the articulated reason was pretext for discrimination and/or retaliation. AJ Decision at 4. The AJ set forth that the Agency determined that Complainant was ineligible for the bid position in question because she did not have a Commercial Driver’s License. Id. On June 22, 2022, the Agency issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

During the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Supervisor, Distribution Operations, at the Agency’s Brooklyn Processing and Distribution Operations in Brooklyn, New York. 1. The last week of April through the first week of May 2020, her name was left off the supervisors’ schedule and she had to report to the office to be assigned an operation; 2. On May 13, 2020 and ongoing, her name was removed from the schedule and she was told that she was not needed to work on her 6th day; and 3. On unspecified dates, she was not allowed to report early or stay after her tour in order to work “T-time” unlike other supervisors. After its investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC or Commission) Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Following the review of the Report of Investigation and the parties’ NOI responses, the AJ determined that the record was sufficiently developed to support a decision by summary judgment in favor of the Agency, concluding no lawful retaliation was established. At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Customer Service Representative, GS-0962-08, at the Agency’s Columbus West E65 Office in Columbus, Ohio. On July 12, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the basis of disability (blindness) when: 1. 2. from December 22, 2016, through July 24, 2018, Agency management subjected Complainant to a hostile work environment; 3. between July 6, 2017, and July 11, 2017, management disclosed Complainant’s medical information in a public folder; and 4. on June 19, 2017, management did not provide Complainant with the necessary training to use Job Access With Speech (JAWS) software he was provided as a reasonable accommodation. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation (ROI) and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. After conducting discovery, which included several depositions and a request to consolidate the instant complaint with another complaint consisting of seven claims, Complainant withdrew his hearing request. The AJ denied Complainant’s request to consolidate and remanded the matter to the Agency for a final decision. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision (FAD) pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). In the decision, the Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove Agency management subjected him to discrimination as alleged as to Claims (1), (2), and (4). However, the Agency concluded that Agency management violated the Rehabilitation Act as alleged in Claim (3) and awarded Complainant $500. in compensatory damages. The Agency invited Complainant to submit a petition for attorney’s fees. Complainant sought $35,687. in attorney’s fees and $1,647. in costs. Complainant argues the fees were reasonable because Complainant’s counsel “engaged in discovery, including defending Complainant’s deposition.” To justify the hourly rates charged, the petition included affidavits from four of five attorneys who worked on Complainant’s case and noted that the fifth left the firm prior to the conclusion of the case. In its decision on attorney’s fees, the Agency accepted the hourly fees for the four attorneys who submitted affidavits. According to the Agency, “we can only calculate rates for the employees whose affidavits have been included.” The Agency noted that Complainant prevailed on only one of four claims, and that the claims were fractionable. In this case, succeeding on the per se violation only required Complainant to demonstrate that his medical records were exposed, even if inadvertently. The Agency found that Complainant’s fee petition contained multiple entries that did not pertain to Claim (3). Further, the Agency discounted the time and effort Complainant’s attorneys needed to devote to Claim (3): [T]here is very little indication that Counsel’s litigation strategy, hours billed, consultation, or legal efforts contributed significantly to the FAD finding because the Agency’s FAD finding the per se Rehabilitation Act violation was based solely upon the affidavits and evidence in the ROI, which the Agency produced before Complainant engaged Counsel. The Agency further discounted work performed by other individuals identified in the fee petition because Complainant did not explain their positions and roles. As to the costs Complainant requested, the Agency noted that Complainant provided supporting receipts, but did not explain whether the costs were related to Complainant’s successful claim or to his unsuccessful claims. Thus, the Agency determined that these costs were not reimbursable. The Agency concluded that, out of the $35,687 in attorney’s fees, $21,750 was properly supported by verified affidavits. Further, the Agency concluded that Complainant’s reimbursable attorney’s fees should be divided by 11, to account for all 11 claims Complainant raised in both the instant EEO complaint and the EEO complaint he sought to consolidate at the hearing stage. Since Complainant was successful on only one claim, the Agency awarded Complainant $1,973. in attorney’s fees and no costs.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a General Engineer, NH-0801-04, at the Agency’s Space and Missile Defense Command (SMDC), Army Forces Strategic Command, Future Warfare Center (FWC), Decision Support Directorate, located at the Redstone Arsenal in Alabama. opportunity to compete, for the position of Supervisory Operations Research Analyst, NH-1515- 04. On December 7, 2018, a canvass for a permanent reassignment to a Supervisory Operations Research Analyst, NH-1515-04, position was sent to all SMDC personnel. The announcement defined the area of consideration as current Department of Army and Department of Defense employees at the NH-04, or equivalent, level. In other words, the canvass invited those who were NH-04 or equivalent (GS-14 to GS-15) to respond. Both Complainant and the selectee were NH-04s. The Selecting Official (SO) had served for over a year as the Acting Division Chief and during that time, he encountered managerial challenges. When he decided to find a person to fill the position permanently, he decided to require supervisory experience. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 211-215. The canvass included a requirement that the applicant be either a current supervisor or have had a year or more of supervisory experience. ROI at 124-125. Complainant was aware of the announcement. Two people applied. Complainant did not apply, and her name did not appear on the referral list. A three-person review panel scored the applicants’ resumes. The panel then interviewed the candidates and aggregated resume and interview scores. The highest rated candidate per the aggregated score was recommended for selection. SO was the selecting official and the Approving Official (AO) approved the selection of the selectee. ROI at 219-20. SO averred that Complainant was not considered, because her name was not included on the referral list. ROI at 216. He also stated that he followed the panel’s recommendation, which recommended the selectee. ROI at 211. Complainant averred that, because fewer than three people applied and in the absence of a qualified person to fill the position, the position had to be openly competed, in which case she could have competed and been selected. ROI at 205, 262. She claimed that since the male selectee was not qualified, because he did not meet the stated qualifications as his National Guard non-competitive service did not qualify him for a competitive service requirement. The Lead Human Resources Specialist of the Civilian Human Resources Agency, Northeast Region, confirmed that her office reviewed the candidates’ qualifications. ROI at 230-232. Both candidates were evaluated using a competitive process before HR extended the job offer to the selectee. She declared that the selectee possessed the requisite supervisory experience and qualifications, as expressed in the canvass. ROI at 230-232. Complainant avers that she was prevented from applying for the position through a fair and open competition, because the position was not announced on USA Jobs, or via another means, other than a canvass. S1 declared that he did nothing to prevent Complainant from applying for the position and did not write the canvass in a way that excluded her from applying. ROI at 212-213. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before a EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ assigned to the matter issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency finding that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination or reprisal as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully adopting the AJ’s decision. This appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Nurse Case Manager, VN 2, at the Agency’s Greater Los Angeles Medical Center in Los Angeles, CA. On November 14, 2019, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the basis of race (African-American) when on September 26, 2019, she learned her request for a non-competitive promotion was denied. The pertinent record shows that Complainant, who is a Level II Registered Nurse (RN) sought promotion to Level III during the 2015-2016 rating period. Complainant’s Caucasian coworker applied for promotion at the same time. The record shows that one other RN was promoted during the subject timeframe. On September 26, 2019, she learned that the Caucasian colleague had been promoted in 2017 or 2018. Complainant is the only African American in the Inpatient Care section. Complainant is one of 39 Inpatient and Outpatient Nurses reporting to the Deputy Nurse Executive (bi-racial) (S1), who became her supervisor in 2019. After each rating period, individual nurses are reviewed by a local board for promotion eligibility. An unfavorable decision by the local board can be reviewed through an appellate process. The nurse can first request reconsideration from the local board itself. If that reconsideration is unsuccessful, the nurse can request review from the central office (VACO). Complainant’s 2015-2016 performance was rated as “high satisfactory,” but she was not recommended for promotion to Nurse III, because she did not meet the “Dimensions Requirement.” Report of Investigation (ROI), Exhibit 7-15. Her 2016-2017 performance evaluation was signed by the Board on June 6, 2018. She was rated as “satisfactory”, but she was not recommended for promotion, because she did not meet the Dimensions Requirement. ROI, Exhibit 7-15. Following the February 2017 unfavorable initial decision from the local board, Complainant requested reconsideration in May 2017. ROI at 250-52. In June 2017, the local board denied the request. ROI at 271-72. In July 2018, Complainant requested review from VACO. ROI at 275. VACO received Complainant’s request, but there is no indication in the record that VACO ever issued an official decision on the request. Complainant filed a grievance regarding the matter. In September 2019, Complainant met the new Deputy Chief Nurse Executive (S1). Complainant asked S1 to look into mistakes she believed occurred in the review of her promotion candidacy. S1 was not her supervisor at the time of the initial submission of her paperwork. S1 said he would look into the issue. On September 26, 2019, S1 informed Complainant that her paperwork had been properly submitted to VACO and that he believed that the matter was closed. S1 offered to coach and assist Complainant to be prepared for the next promotion cycle, but Complainant declined his offer. On October 2, 2019, she made EEO contact, alleging that her newly appointed supervisor (the new Deputy Chief Nurse Executive) discriminated against her when he declined to investigate, to her satisfaction, her concerns with the process pertaining to her prior request for a non- competitive promotion. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before a Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). The AJ assigned to the matter issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency. In the decision, the AJ determined that Agency management had articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. Specifically, S1 had only just started his new position and met Complainant for the first time on September 10, 2019. In the initial meeting, Complainant raised concerns over her old promotion candidacy from 2016 to 2017. S1 looked into the matter, and offered that from his vantage point, nothing seemed amiss. He further offered that since he was not involved in the earlier decisions, he saw nothing further for himself to do other than consider the matter closed and move forward. The AJ noted that the fact that S1 declined to resurrect such a stale issue made sense under the circumstances as there was no evidence that S1 even had any authority to change the outcome. Instead, S1 explained that he offered to help Complainant focus on gaining her promotion in the next review cycle. The AJ found that Complainant failed to provide any evidence demonstrating that S1 acted with discriminatory animus or that his reasons for his actions were pretext for unlawful discrimination. As a result, the AJ found that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully adopting the AJ’s decision. This appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Senior Advisor at the Agency’s Combined Security Transition Command-Afghanistan Resource Management facility in Bagram, Afghanistan. On August 15, 2018, the Senior Procurement Advisor (Senior PA) and PA removed Complainant from his post awards duties and assigned him to do administrative duties, such as mail movement tracker, telephone calls and other office functions; and threatened to send him home if he did not do the office work. 3. In August 2018, the Senior PA denied Complainant’s request for a one-year deployment extension. 4. On October 30, 2018, the PA placed comments regarding Complainant’s performance standards and feedback on an unprotected shared drive. 5. On November 12, 2018, the Senior Resource Management Advisor (Senior RMA) reassigned Complainant from Camp RS Headquarters to New Kabul Compound. 3 At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ initially assigned to the case granted the Department of Defense’s motion to join the Department of the Army as a party to this complaint. 4 The AJ now assigned to the case granted the Agency’s March 1, 2021 motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision by summary judgment in favor of the Agency on July 30, 2021. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 279. Complainant alleged reprisal was a basis only for claim 5 as it was the only one which occurred after his initiating EEO contact with a counselor which is his only EEO activity. At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Mail Processing Clerk, PS-06/O, at the Agency’s Processing and Distribution Center in Fort Wayne, Indiana. He joined the Agency in 1978. On March 2, 2021, Complainant received a Letter of Warning (LOW) for allegedly walking away from his assigned sorting machine while it was still in operation. As Complainant had previously walked away from his sorting machine on two prior occasions, the Agency determined that a LOW was warranted. 1. On December 5-11, 2020, and March 9-31, 2021, Complainant was harassed; 2 and 2. On or around March 2, 2021, Complainant was issued a LOW. On May 4, 2021, the Agency notified Complainant that it would only accept claim 2 for investigation because claim 1 failed to state a claim under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(1). In dismissing claim 1, the Agency reasoned that Complainant’s bare bones allegations did not sufficiently establish that he had been aggrieved by the Agency’s actions, as Complainant “did not expound on this issue by specifying how [he] was allegedly harassed and to what frequency.” Furthermore, the Agency noted that “[o]ther than being issued a LOW, [Complainant] listed no specific dates or incidents or descriptions of how [he] was harassed.” Relying, in part, on Bejar v. Department of Veterans Affairs, EEOC [number removed] (February 12, 2008) and Owens v. Social Security Administration, EEOC [number removed] (August 24, 2006), the Agency concluded that dismissal of the claim was warranted. At the conclusion of the investigation into claim 2, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the Report of Investigation (ROI) and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination, as the Agency had legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for issuing Complainant a LOW, which Complainant failed to rebut. This appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant disputes the Agency’s final decision and maintains, in relevant part, that the Agency committed crimes and violations against humanity by committing “systemic verbal and written fabrications, behavioral threats and denials with signature” and “systemic verbal assults [sic].” In support to his contention, Complainant resubmits his formal complaint and the memoranda that he submitted in prior EEO and non-EEO complaints. He requests the maximum compensatory damage award times 37. The Agency, however, did not file any contentions in opposition to Complainant’s appeal. Complainant alleged, in part, that management “support[ed] insurrections and systemic[ally] breached anti-discriminatory practices that promote[d] inept cupuliable [sic] negeliences [sic],” made unspecified “innate systemic verbal and written threats,” and committed “known crimes against humanity and the acknowledged USPS-NRP mirrored dilemmas.” See Formal Complaint, Report of Investigation (ROI) at 00006-8. He further alleged that management “daily exercised anoesis and known acrimony without dignity and respect,” “direct[ed] personal manipulations that alter[ed] mail processing personnel efficiency and mail processing productive equipment,” and “direct[ed] personal improprieties that [violated] the known all employee USPS-Zero Tolerance Policy.” Id.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Rural Carrier at the Agency’s Acton Station in Granbury, Texas. The complaint originally alleged genetic information under GINA as a basis for discrimination, but Complainant withdrew this basis during the investigation. 1. On March 8, 2019, Complainant received her paycheck for February 16, 2019, through March 1, 2019, and she became aware that management failed to properly enter her leave into the payroll system; 2. From on or about February 2, 2019, to March 2, 2019, she was not been permitted to make changes to the route adjustment on her route which has affected her pay; and 3. On or about February 27, 2019, she was not permitted in the building. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. The AJ assigned to the case determined sua sponte that the complaint did not warrant a hearing and, over Complainant’s objections, issued a decision by summary judgment in favor of the Agency. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. The AJ found that, taking the facts as presented in the report of investigation and viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to Complaint, she failed to create a genuine issue of material fact to establish retaliation. The AJ concluded that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions that Complainant failed to rebut as pretextual. Regarding claim 1, Complainant stated she had requested Leave Without Pay (LWOP) while she was out of work for a surgery but saw on the corresponding paycheck that management had not properly entered her leave. Instead, her supervisors entered the leave under Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) sick time. During this time period, management entered their employees’ payroll time into the system. Complainant’s supervisor, Acting Manager (AM), had been on leave when Complainant requested LWOP, and Complainant had been using FMLA sick leave prior to AM’s absence. Upon her return, AM incorrectly continued to enter Complainant’s time as FMLA sick leave. After Complainant notified her of the error, AM submitted a leave adjustment request form to correct the mistake. Regarding claims 2 and 3, the AJ found that these incidents occurred when Complainant was on leave due to the surgery. While Complainant was out, the Agency’s adjustment team conducted route adjustments at the Acton Station. Complainant stated that she was not permitted to access the building while she was on leave when she attempted to put up certain labels related to her route and complete other tasks related to her route adjustment. Complainant asserted that as a result of not being allowed to perform those tasks, she was unable to make certain edits to her route that subsequently impacted her pay. AM averred that she denied Complainant access to the workroom floor and did not allow her to work on the labels for her route. When Complainant tried to enter the building, AM informed her that a Rural Carrier Assistant would put up the necessary labels on Complainant’s route. AM explained to Complainant that because she was out on medical leave, allowing her to conduct work related to her route would constitute “working off the clock.” However, while she was on leave, Complainant was permitted to communicate with the adjustment team over the telephone concerning edits to her route. The AJ found that Complainant failed to show the Agency’s articulated reasons to be pretext for retaliation.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a System Engineering Technical Assistance contractor at the Agency’s Program Executive Office Command Control Communications (PEO-C3T) facility in Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland. On March 20, 2020, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (African-American), color (Black), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 when: 1. On or around August 2019, the Readiness Management Division (RMD) Acting Chief (Acting Chief) removed most of Complainant’s responsibilities and assigned them to the new Logistics Management Specialist; 2. On or around October 2019, the Acting Chief charged him 10 hours of leave for reporting to work on travel days for a Temporary Duty (TDY) that was approved by management; 3. On January 9, 2020, the Acting Chief assigned him a task of great magnitude with a suspense date of January 10, 2020; 4. On January 9, 2020, the Acting Chief excluded him from meetings and emails for which he was the task lead; 5. On February 13, 2020, the Acting Chief told him, “I’m getting pissed. All I get is resentment from you. I do not like your ace. When I look at you, all I see is attitude on your face. If you can’t do what I order you to do, I will find someone else to do it. I don’t have time to help you. If you can’t do it, I will replace you.” 6. On February 18, 2020, he was placed on administrative leave without pay from his company, Amentum, after notifying the Command of an allegation of hostile work environment notice that was forthcoming from the EEO office; 7. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Over Complainant’s objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s July 29, 2021, motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on April 4, 2022. At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Contract Officer at the Agency’s VA Regional Procurement Office (West) facility in Vancouver, Washington. 1.
