At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Nuclear Materials Courier at the Agency’s Office of Mission Operations, Agent Operations Eastern Command, Office of Secure Transportation (OST) in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. 1. On March 15, 2016, he was subjected to physical fitness testing standards, which he alleges contain no age-graduated scoring considerations, which are harmful to his existing physical disability, and which changed the conditions of his employment; 2. On March 15, 2016, while performing physical fitness testing (using the new physical fitness testing standards), he sustained physical injury (i.e. Rhabdomyolysis); 3. On March 15, 2016, the Training Specialist, the Fitness Coordinator, and the Deputy Director of Operations (Deputy Director) failed to provide adequate safety measures, emergency responses, and properly trained staff; these alleged failures resulted in his injury and hospitalization on March 15, 2016; 4. On the basis of disability only, he was denied participation in six mission trips and one Operational Readiness Training exercise/event during the months of March, April, and May 2016. Complainant stated that he was in a motor vehicle accident in 2001 and as a result, had a compressed disc in his lower back, pain in his back and hip, and limited range of motion of his right leg. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 120. He stated that he needed assistance to walk for 4-6 weeks after the accident and thereafter, was assigned a 10% disability rating of his lower extremities. See ROI at 120. He did not request a reasonable accommodation and stated he was always able to perform his duties. See ROI at 122-23. While performing the physical fitness test on March 15, 2016, he suffered exertional Rhabdomyolysis, which resulted in kidney failure, and a torn rotator cuff. See ROI at 119-20. He stated that he was out of work for three months as a result of the injury. See ROI at 120. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew his request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision found that Complainant did not establish that he is an individual with a disability due to a motor vehicle accident he suffered in 2001 because the evidence in the record indicated that Complainant’s impairment was limited in time and none of the management officials were aware that Complainant had a disability. The decision further found that while Complainant did establish that is an individual with a disability due to the injury he suffered on March 15, 2016, he did not establish that any of the incidents were based on his disability because they occurred prior to the injury. The decision finally found that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions in requiring Complainant to undergo physical fitness testing under the revised standards and Complainant did not establish that any of the reasons were a pretext for discrimination. The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged.

See ROI at 256-57. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision dismissed claim 5 pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(2) for untimely counselor contact, finding Complainant did not contact an EEO counselor until four years after the discriminatory incident. 3 Complainant’s formal complaint indicated race and sex/gender identity as the bases. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 20. We find upon a review of the record that Complainant intended to raise race (Asian) and sex (male) as the bases. We note that the Agency’s decision inadvertently stated that it was dismissing claim 4 for untimely counselor contact but the decision makes it clear that it was claim 5 that was dismissed. The decision went on to find that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for all of the non-selections and for omitting the SOQ from the posting in claim 4, and that Complainant did not establish that the Agency’s reasons were a pretext for discrimination. The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed the Agency’s decision. In response, the Agency filed a brief urging affirmance of its decision.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Supervisory Emergency Management Specialist, GS-0089-15, Information Technology Service Division, Office of Resource Management at the Agency’s Office of the Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response (OASPR or ASPR) in Washington D.C. 1. On September 19, 2018, he requested the OASPR Human Resources leadership investigate harassment (non-sexual) claims that were reported by anonymous employees. Whether he was subjected to discrimination and harassment (non-sexual) on the bases of sex (male), age (over 40), and in reprisal for opposing an unlawful discriminatory practice when: 2. On December 7, 2018, the Agency assigned him to the Cybersecurity Advisor, GS-15, position effective December 10, 2018. 3. On December 10, 2018, he learned that management had impeded his ability to compete for the Director, Office of Security, Intelligence, and Information Management (SIIM), GS-15, position. 4. On January 7, 2019, he learned that the Agency selected another employee outside of the Agency as the Director, SIIM, GS-15, position. 5. a. In November 2018, and ongoing, management impeded his ability to compete for a SES (Senior Executive Service) position. b. On December 4, 2018, OASPR management subjected him to coercive and threatening behavior. c. On December 10, 2018, and ongoing, OASPR management removed him from participating on the ASPR Senior Leadership Team. d. On January 7, 2019, the Agency informed him that he would be moving from his window office on the fifth floor to the building’s basement. Complainant has not challenged the Agency’s framing of the complaint. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before EEOC Administrative Judge or a final Agency decision. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f). Complainant requested a final Agency decision without a hearing. The Agency issued a final decision finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The Agency dismissed claim 1 for failure to state a claim since it involved unidentified employees and not Complainant. Regarding claims 2 and 5b, the record reveals that in 2018, OASPR went through a realignment of staff. As a result, OASPR employees were reassigned based on the organization’s needs. The record indicates that during the realignment period, Complainant was detailed to the Acting SIIM Director position. Complainant does not claim this detail was discriminatory. Complainant’s second-level supervisor (S2), Assistant Secretary for OASPR, a political appointee, stated that in July - fall 2018, an Associate Deputy proposed Complainant’s detail to a Cybersecurity Advisor position. On December 3, 2018, S2 met with Complainant and offered Complainant the Cybersecurity Advisor position that was proposed by the Associate Deputy. S2 indicated that based on Complainant’s resume, Complainant had very deep cybersecurity experience. Complainant told S2 that he would think about the offer. S2 stated that on December 4, 2018, S2 stopped by Complainant’s office but Complainant was angry and hostile and told S2 that he was not interested in the Cybersecurity Advisor position because he was not an expert in the field and expressed his interest in applying for a SIIM Director, SES, position instead. S2 told Complainant that the SIIM Director position was not a SES position rather it was a GS-15 position. The record indicates that on December 7, 2018, Complainant’s first-level supervisor (S1), an SES, Deputy Assistant Secretary, issued Complainant a notice of his reassignment to the Cybersecurity Advisor, GS-15, position due to the organization consolidation and prioritization of cybersecurity. S1 indicated that Complainant was being reassigned in order to meet the needs of the organization as well as taking into consideration Complainant’s background and qualifications. The notice indicated that there would be no change to Complainant’s position description. The record indicates that Complainant’s position title remained as a Supervisory Emergency Management Specialist, GS-15. Complainant’s coworker (C1), female, a GS-15 employee, position title unknown, at the Incident Management Team Program, indicated that in 2018, OASPR went through a realignment of positions. As a result of the realignment, C1 stated, employees were reassigned to different positions, some employees were allowed to choose and some employees, including C1, were assigned to positions they were not qualified for, placing them outside the scope of their pre- alignment position description. C1 indicated that as a result of the realignment, she was reassigned to the Intel Division which did not align with her abilities. The Chief of Staff, SES, OASPR, indicated that Complainant was serving as the Acting SIIM Director prior to his reassignment to the Cybersecurity Advisor position and management lost confidence in his ability to serve in that Acting position. The Chief of Staff stated that since Complainant had cybersecurity talents and expertise, he was best used to improve OASPR’s cyber capabilities which were lacking. Regarding claims 3, 4, and 5a, S1 and S2 indicated that no one impeded Complainant’s ability to compete for the SIIM Director position or an SES position. The HR Director indicated that she was a selecting official for the SIIM Director, GS-15 position at issue. The HR Director stated that there was no vacancy announcement created for the position; rather, under the Agency’s merit promotion plan, she utilized a shared certificate, which was a list of candidates eligible for the position posted in another Agency. The HR Director noted that the shared certificate process was very popular because HR had a lot of turn over, and they were taking a long time to get vacancy announcements posted. Complainant had not applied for a particular position at another agency and thus was not on the shared certificate. Therefore, Complainant was never considered for the position. The HR Director indicated that she selected a female (Selectee), from outside the Agency, for the SIIM Director position. Regarding claim 5c, S2 indicated that since Complainant was reassigned to the Senior Cybersecurity Advisor position, he did not need to participate on the OASPR Senior Leadership Team meetings. Regarding claim 5d, S2 stated that due to Complainant’s reassignment to the Senior Cybersecurity Advisor position, his office was also changed to the floor where everyone within his new office was located. Based on the foregoing, the Agency issued its decision finding that Complainant failed to establish discrimination as alleged. On appeal, Complainant requests that the Commission sanction the Agency by issuing a default judgment due to the Agency’s failure to issue a final decision in a timely manner. Complainant indicates that although he requested a final decision on September 17, 2019, he did not receive a final Agency decision until September 21, 2021. Complainant states that the Agency’s delay caused him harm to his career and emotional distress. In response to Complainant’s appeal, the Agency acknowledges that it took more than 60 days to issue a final decision as required by 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). However, the Agency states that it has not acted in a manner that would warrant a default judgment and Complainant has not demonstrated that he has been prejudiced by the delay.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as an Intelligence Specialist at the Agency’s 706th Military Intelligence Group facility in Fort Gordon, Georgia. On May 23, 2018, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (African-American), sex (male), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 when: 1. he was not selected for the Intelligence Specialist (Staff Officer) position advertised under Announcement No. 706-0132-FTGORD-005. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Over Complainant’s objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s November 19, 2019, motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on September 28, 2021. The AJ found that even assuming arguendo that Complainant established a prima facie case, the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the non- selection and Complainant did not submit any evidence to support his assertions of discriminatory animus. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed the Agency’s final order, arguing that the AJ erred in granting the Agency’s motion for summary judgment and that he has established that he was subjected to discrimination. In response, the Agency urged affirmance of the AJ’s decision.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Motor Vehicle Operator at the Agency’s Anniston Building in Anniston, Alabama. 1. On March 10 and 12, 2020, Complainant was dispatched twice to pick up a load and take it to shipping at 2:50 pm, despite management knowing his shift ended at 3:30 pm. On both occasions, he was not allowed to leave until after 4:00 pm, resulting in him planning for someone to pick up his daughter from school; 2. On March 2, 2020, during a telephone conversation, his Supervisor told him, “this is ridiculous,” commenting on his request for two hours of official time to meet with his EEO representative to work on his EEO complaint; 3. On February 4, 2020, Complainant’s Division Chief never met with him to discuss changing his overall work schedule and to remain on the 0630-1530 work shift; 4. In December 2019, Complainant’s verbal request for three hours of leave for repair of his home’s heating unit during the winter was denied; 5. On November 19, 2019, Complainant received a poor performance appraisal; 6. In November 2019, during a truck driver’s meeting, the Deputy Commander told Complainant, “Yeah, and if you do it again, I will fire you,” and “Yes, I can do that, do you want to challenge me?,” and told the Supervisor to “be hard on all truck drivers.” 2 At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. When the Complainant did not respond, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s September 17, 2021, motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on October 18, 2021. The AJ found that there were no genuine issues of material fact and that Complainant did not establish that he was subjected to discrimination. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed the Agency’s final order, arguing that the Agency did not fully investigate Complainant’s claims and that the AJ did not adequately review the evidence. In response, the Agency contends that Complainant has not identified any reversible error in the AJ’s decision and that the AJ’s decision should be affirmed. We note that Complainant’s complaint also includes race, color, and sex as additional bases but a review of the pre-complaint documents and Complainant’s affidavit indicates that Complainant only argued disability and reprisal as the bases of his claim. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 8-9; 100-109. The Agency’s notice accepting Complainant’s complaint appears to have inadvertently listed reprisal as the only basis but we further note that the investigation correctly included disability as one of the bases. See ROI at 73-75; 85.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Medical Records Technician, GS 7 at the Agency’s Dwight David Eisenhower Army Medical Center, Patient Administration Division (PAD) in Fort Gordon, Georgia. a) On or around August 2017, Complainant’s reasonable accommodations were not received; b) The Supervisor Medical Records Technician (Supervisor) did not respond to her request for Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA) submitted in August 2017; c) The Supervisor informed her that she wrote a statement she was three minutes late around December 2017, and continued to check her arrivals and departures for breaks and lunch; d) Between March 2 and 13, 2018, Complainant did not have a work computer; e) The Supervisor did not inform her that her position was grandfathered into the new two-year probationary period; f) The Supervisor provided copies of Bible verses, read, and explained the scriptures to her and her office mates; g) She was not counseled or notified there was a problem with her job performance; h) On March 23, 2018, she learned she was terminated from her position during her two-year probationary period. 2 The record indicates that Complainant never submitted a request for a reasonable accommodation and her request for FMLA leave was granted in part and Complainant did not respond to the request for additional medical information. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 213; 546-47. The memorandum notifying Complainant of her termination stated that Complainant was being terminated for her failure to meet the production standards identified in her performance objectives and for being observed sleeping at her desk on two separate occasions. See ROI at 246-47. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Over Complainant’s objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s February 5, 2020, motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on September 27, 2021. The AJ found that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions and that there was no evidence to indicate that any of the Agency’s actions were due to any protected basis. The AJ therefore concluded that Complainant had not established that she was subjected to either discrimination or a hostile work environment. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed, arguing first that the AJ erred by granting summary judgment because the AJ simply accepted the Agency’s explanations without question. On the merits, Complainant argues that the AJ erred in finding that Complainant did not establish that the Agency discriminated against her when it terminated her after failing to accommodate her disabilities. The Agency accepted claim (h) as a discrete incident of discrimination and the other incidents as part of Complainant’s hostile work environment claim. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 138-41. In response, the Agency contends that the AJ correctly found that there were no genuine issues of material fact and that there was no evidence indicating discriminatory animus.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Hearings Customer Service Representative GS-8, at the Agency’s Hearing Office in Kansas City, Missouri. On May 17, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of age, disability, and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when: 1. From February 16, 2021, and continuing, the Supervisor subjected Complainant to harassment by giving her an overwhelming number of daily work assignments, and daily reviews of her performance. 2. On March 12, 2021, the Supervisor placed Complainant on an Opportunity to Perform Successfully (OPS). 3. On February 16, 2021, Complainant was required to resume performance of the Verbatim Hearing Reporter (VHR) duties from which she had been exempted. Furthermore, on the face of her formal complaint, Complainant alleged that she had received “threats of termination,” and that management had done “any and everything within their power to force [her] into retirement.” In an attachment to her complaint, she reiterated “management staff has left me with no other recourse, other than to concede to being forced out of my position and into retirement!” On June 22, 2021, the Supervisor issued a Proposal to Terminate to Complainant, notifying her that her employment would be terminated within 30 days of receipt of the Proposal. The Proposal to Terminate described that Complainant’s performance was unacceptable and that the Supervisor tried to assist Complainant improve her performance by giving her a “fair share” of daily work assignments (claim 1) and placing her on an OPS plan (claim 2). Believing that was being forced to retire, Complainant submitted retirement paperwork on July 27, 2021. On August 2, 2021, the Agency began its EEO investigation into the formal complaint. Complainant informed the investigator that she had received a Proposal to Terminate, and that she believed the Supervisor had “set her up” for “forced” retirement by giving her an “overwhelming [number of] daily tasks” (claim 1) and placing her on an OPS plan (claim 2). By memorandum dated August 6, 2021, the Supervisor notified Complainant that he had made the decision to terminate her employment with the Agency effective August 6, 2021. However, the Supervisor sent Complainant an email afterward to inform her that he rescinded his decision because she filed retirement paperwork in July. Complainant’s representative forwarded the memorandum and email to the investigator and reiterated that the Agency’s actions had “forced” Complainant into “involuntary retirement.” The investigation was concluded on October 1, 2021. There is no indication in the record that the Agency accepted Complainant’s constructive discharge claim as part of her original complaint or as an amendment to it. Therefore, it does not appear as part of the report of investigation. The Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request an EEOC hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), with appeal rights to this Commission. The decision concluded that no discrimination was established as alleged. The Agency’s final decision did not address Complainant’s constructive discharge claim. Complainant appealed the Agency’s decision to the Commission. She did not submit a brief or statement with her appeal.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Mail Handler at the Agency’s Merrifield Post Office in Merrifield, Virginia. 1. On dates to be specified since October 18, 2020, Complainant was denied acting supervisor advancement opportunities; and 2. On November 3, 2020, Complainant was issued a Letter of Warning. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ assigned to the case determined sua sponte that the complaint did not warrant a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on January 19, 2022. The AJ found that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions and Complainant did not submit any evidence to support his assertions of discriminatory animus. The AJ therefore concluded that Complainant failed to establish that he was subjected to discrimination as alleged. When the Agency failed to issue a final order within forty days of receipt of the AJ’s decision, the AJ’s decision became the Agency’s final action pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i). Complainant appealed. On appeal, Complainant largely reiterates his assertions that he has been treated unfairly in not being made an acting supervisor and in being issued a Letter of Warning. 2 The Agency did not file a response.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Work Leader, WL- 4102-09, at the Agency’s Pearl Harbor Navy Shipyard & Immediate Maintenance Facility in Hawaii. 1. on March 29, 2019, and April 26, 2019, Complainant learned that he was not selected for the Painter Supervisor I position (Announcement No. ST-10407873); and 2. The Shop 64 Process Manager issued Complainant a Letter of Caution for a minor accident when other employees without prior EEO activity caused more damage and were not disciplined. 2 Regarding Claim (1), the record reveals that Complainant and three other employees applied for the position. The Shipyard Production Superintendent was the selecting official. The Superintendent testified that the announcement sought to fill three vacancies. Therefore, he assembled a resume review panel and ranked the applicants’ resumes. At the end of the review process, Complainant received the lowest scores among the four applicants and was not selected. Complainant argued he should have been selected because his resume and work experience were plainly superior to the younger selectees. Complainant also argued that he was the only candidate with supervisory and project management training. The Superintendent determined that no interviews were necessary because “there was enough of a point difference in resume review that interviews were not deemed needed.” Further, Complainant scored lower than the three selectees because of: [t]he details of the job experiences in Complainant’s resume in relation to the criteria used to score resumes. The selected candidates describe in detail their experiences as a painter or painter work leader, which makes them the most qualified for the position of painter supervisor. When you look at Complainant’s resume, there is very little relevant job experience detailing his duties as a painter and/or painter leader. Majority of his resume details his duties and accomplishments while working for the military or military assistance role. The Superintendent added that, while Complainant may have had more years of service or felt that he had more experience, “his resume did not clearly document and expand on all the experience he has relevant to the position.” One of the resume review panelists, a Shop Resource General Foreman, said that he “rated Complainant the way [he] did because Complainant mentioned working on projects that were not in execution and his knowledge of the corporate applications were questionable.” The record contains a matrix of scores. Therein, Complainant received a total of 47 points out of a possible 80 points. Two candidates tied for second place with 52 points, and the best candidate had 64 points. Complainant withdrew an additional allegation regarding management threatening to cut third shift during the investigation. In Claim (2), Complainant did not discuss his own accident, but focused on an incident involving another Agency employee. In that incident, the employee drove a government vehicle into a fire hydrant. Complainant asserted that the employee was not disciplined. The Shop 64 Process Manager testified that he investigated the accident and determined that Complainant was driving a forklift without a valid forklift driver’s license and “knowingly did not conduct an Operators Daily Checklist (ODCL) as is required prior to any forklift operation.” The Shop Resource Foreman added that the identified comparator employee had a driver’s license and stayed on the scene of the accident, whereas Complainant did not have the necessary driver’s license, and left the scene of the accident. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. On September 8, 2020, the AJ dismissed Complainant’s hearing request without prejudice. The AJ noted that Complainant had two additional EEO complaints pending. One complaint (Complaint 1) was in the investigative stage while the other was in federal court (Complaint 2). Complaint 2 was being held in abeyance pending the resolution of the instant complaint and Complaint 1. The parties agreed that the instant complaint and Complaint 1 overlapped on factual and legal grounds. Thus, the AJ dismissed the instant complaint with instructions to Complainant that he may reactivate his request for a hearing within 30 days of the date he received the Agency’s report of investigation for Complaint 1. On November 23, 2021, the AJ denied Complainant’s August 19, 2021 motion to reactivate his hearing request in the instant complaint. The AJ explained that Complainant admitted that the 30- day reactivation period began on February 18, 2021, and that his failure to reactivate his hearing request within the prescribed time was a mistake. However, the AJ noted that Complainant did not explain when he learned of his mistake or what efforts he made to cure the error. The AJ further did not accept Complainant’s explanation that the parties were engaging in settlement efforts. Thus, the AJ denied the hearing request and remanded the complaint to the Agency, and the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). In the decision, the Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that he was subjected to discrimination as alleged. The Agency found that the Superintendent’s reasons for not selecting Complainant and the Manager’s reason for issuing Complainant a letter of caution were legitimate and nondiscriminatory. The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to show these reasons were pretext for discriminatory or retaliatory animus. As a result, the Agency found that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination, reprisal, or a hostile work environment as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a General Business Industrial Specialist at the Agency’s Joint Program Office facility in Arlington, Virginia. On June 23, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of sex (male), color (White), and age (67) when: 1. On December 15, 2020, he was subjected to disparate treatment when he was not selected for Program Manager, NH-0340-04 position advertised under Vacancy Announcement No. 2. On January 12, 2021, he was subjected to disparate treatment when a member of the Agency’s Senior Executive Service made remarks that she believed Complainant’s age and retirement eligibility were motivating factors for his nonselection; and 3. On or around February 11, 2021, during a town hall meeting, comments were made that made it clear to him his age was a motivating factor in his not being selected for a position he had applied for in October 2020; The Agency dismissed claims 1 and 2 pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(2) and accepted claim 3 for investigation. 2 As to claim 3, Complainant asserted that he was subjected to disparate treatment when the comment was made. Complainant attended a Program Executive Officer Town Hall on February 11, 2021, that included approximately 1,200 attendees. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 407. During the Town Hall, Lieutenant (Lt.) General, a member of the Agency’s Senior Management, stated that the majority of senior leadership was “pale, stale, and male.” ROI at 408, 416. Complainant explained that this remark made it “crystal clear” that he was “being forced out of my job because of my age” and was evidence of “the trifecta of discrimination for age, race, and sex.” ROI at 144, 408. Lt. General indicated that he made the “stale, pale, and male” comment because he wanted to encourage greater diversity, because senior management was working hard on diversity and inclusion and their Diversity and Inclusion Action Group was starting up. ROI at 416, 418. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency’s final decision restated the dismissal of the claims 1 and 2. As to claim 3, the Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to disparate treatment as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

During the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Supervisory Social Worker at the Agency’s Community Engagement and Reintegration Services, Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System in Los Angeles, California. 1. On October 26, 2020, Complainant was not selected for the Social Work Supervisor, Assistant Domiciliary Chief position; and 2. On April 21, 2021, Complainant was not selected for the Social Work Supervisor, Assistant Domiciliary Chief position. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Over Complainant's objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s January 24, 2022, motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on March 16, 2022. The AJ found that the Agency provided legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for both claims. As for the position in claim 1, Chief and Acting Domiciliary Chief (ADC) reviewed and scored the resumes. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 66, 72. The record indicated that Complainant received a resume score of 20 and the selectee (Selectee 1) received a score of 28. ADC and Chief indicated that Selectee 1 was chosen because she had the highest resume score and because of her extensive business experience, experience in system redesign, project management, crisis management, and performing exceptionally well in the Acting Chief position for a “good part” of the prior year. ROI at 66-67, 73. As to claim 2, Chief, ADC, and the Acting Medical Director (Acting MD) served as members of the selection panel. They reviewed and scored the resumes. The eight candidates with the highest resume scores were then interviewed by the panel and given interview scores by each panel member. The selection panel chose the selectee (Selectee 2) who had the highest overall score of 129 based on the panel’s resume and interview scores. Complainant had a score of 89. Chief specified that Selectee 2 demonstrated an understanding of internal and external customers and the expectations of the position, including policy development. ROI at 70. ADC and Acting MD noted that Selectee 2 also had the ability to bring people together and experience in improving systems management. ROI at 76, 80. Finding that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the selections in claims 1 and 2, the AJ turned to Complainant to establish that the Agency’s reasons were pretext. The AJ considered Complainant’s arguments that the selection processes did not comply with Agency policy and that she had more years of experience. However, the AJ found that Complainant’s arguments alone were not sufficient to establish that the Agency’s articulated reasons were pretext for discrimination. Therefore, the AJ concluded that Complainant failed to establish discrimination based on her race, sex, and age as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed without comment or brief.

During the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Level GS-7 Medical Instrument Technician (MIT) at the Agency’s Cardiology Department in its Medical Center in Saint Louis, Missouri. On July 29, 2019, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (African-American), sex (male), and age (67) when, on December 4, 2020, he was not selected for the Level GS-8 MIT position under Vacancy Announcement No. CBSS-10948311-21-GLP. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ assigned to the case determined sua sponte that the complaint did not warrant a hearing and, on March 16, 2022, issued a Notice of Proposed Summary Judgment (Notice). In the Notice, the AJ found that the Agency provided a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for Complainant’s nonselection for the position. Non-Invasive Cardiology MIT Supervisor (Supervisor) was the selecting official for the position. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 87. Supervisor explained that Complainant was not on the list of qualified candidates provided from the Human Resources (HR) department. Supervisor received a list of internal candidates only. HR Specialist, who referred applicants, stated that Complainant applied to the external announcement and the selection was made from the internal certificate. The AJ found that Complainant failed to provide any evidence that the Agency’s articulated reason was pretextual. The AJ afforded both parties the opportunity to respond to the Notice. Over Complainant's objections, the AJ issued a decision without a hearing on March 31, 2022, incorporating the facts and legal arguments from the Notice. When the Agency failed to issue a final order within 40 days of receipt of the AJ’s decision, the AJ’s decision finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged became the Agency’s final action pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i). The instant appeal followed. Neither party submitted a brief on appeal.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Clerk at the Agency’s Florissant Post Office in Jefferson City, Missouri. Supervisor Customer Service (Supervisor) was his first-level supervisor. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 92. 1. On February 2, 2021, he was issued a letter of warning; and 2. On February 27, 2021, his work hours were changed. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ assigned to the case issued a Notice of Proposed Judgment (Notice) indicating his intent to issue a decision without a hearing. Subsequently, the AJ determined that the complaint did not warrant a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on February 18, 2022, incorporating the reasons provided in the Notice. The AJ found that the Agency provided legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for each of the claims. As to claim 1, Supervisor issued Complainant a Letter of Warning for failing to maintain a regular work schedule, based upon Complainant’s failure to report to work on a day that he was scheduled to work. As to claim 2, Supervisor asserted that Complainant’s duty hours were changed for operational reasons. Specifically, Supervisor said that Complainant was best qualified to process certain mail parcels that did not arrive at the facility until later than his prior start time. Turning to Complainant to establish that the Agency’s reasons were pretext for discrimination, the AJ found that Complainant did not do so. Concerning claim 1, the AJ noted that Complainant claimed that the Letter of Warning was issued because of “personal” reasons and the only reason provided to him was “rules and regulations.” The AJ noted that Complainant asserted that his medical condition was the reason for the Agency’s action because Supervisor “mentioned,” however, Complainant did not explicitly state what Supervisor said or explain how his medical condition was referenced. As such, the AJ determined that this alone was insufficient to demonstrate that the Agency’s reason was pretext for discrimination based on his disability. As to claim 2, the AJ noted that Complainant asserted that Supervisor changed his work hours because he did not follow her instructions. The AJ found that, even if that was correct, that is insufficient to prove pretext. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Complainant did not provide arguments in support of his appeal. The Agency contends that the AJ’s decision was proper and their decision implementing it should stand.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Mail Processing Clerk in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. On July 22, 2020, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of her race (African American), national origin (African American), color (Black), sex (female), and disability (depression and anxiety). The Agency dismissed Complainant’s complaint on procedural grounds and Complainant filed an appeal. In EEOC [number removed] (Feb. 11, 2021), we reversed the dismissal and remanded the matter to the Agency for an investigation. Upon completion of the investigation, Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). The AJ issued an Order for Supplemental EEO Investigation on March 25, 2022. Therein, the AJ reframed the issues as follows: Complainant was discriminated against and subjected to a hostile work environment…when: 1. She was not granted a reasonable accommodation after requesting an accommodation from [a named management official] on or about March 15, 2019; and 2. On April 5, 2019, Complainant was issued a Notice of Removal for Failure to Maintain Regular Attendance, Absent Without Official Leave (AWOL), and Failure to Comply with Agency Directives. The AJ ordered a supplemental investigation on the denial of a reasonable accommodation claim. Upon completion of the supplemental investigation, the Agency filed a Motion for Summary Judgment on June 7, 2022. On June 20, 2022, Complainant filed a response to the Agency’s Motion. On July 19, 2022, the AJ granted the Agency’s Motion and issued a finding of no discrimination without a hearing. Regarding Complainant’s removal under a disparate treatment analysis, the AJ found that assuming arguendo that Complainant established a prima facie case of discrimination, the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. The AJ stated that “the removal notice noted that since her fourteen-day suspension on February 8, 2019, Complainant had eighteen unscheduled absences.” AJ Decision at 4. The AJ further found that Complainant failed to establish that the Agency’s articulated reason for its action was pretext for discrimination. The AJ further found that Complainant failed to establish that the Agency denied her a reasonable accommodation. The AJ reasoned: Complainant’s attempts to request an accommodation do not save her claim. Complainant alleged she discussed a possible disability with [named Agency officials] on December 17, 2018, when she was issued a seven-day suspension and on February 8, 2019, when she was issued a fourteen-day suspension, and at her March 1, 2019 investigative interview and each time she was referred to the EAP. It is undisputed Complainant did not contact EAP until February 25, 2019. Her individual opinion that she might have a disability that was affecting her attendance was not sufficient to establish a disability or to require the Agency to provide a reasonable accommodation. …On March 1, 2019, Complainant stated in her investigative interview that she could not provide an answer why she was late through February 2019 but that she had an appointment with EAP, which may be able to explain her issues. Again, this statement, by itself was not sufficient to establish a disability or request a reasonable accommodation. At best, the earliest Complainant put the Agency on notice of an alleged disability and requested an accommodation was by her March 15, 2019 letter addressed to [a named management official. The letter mentioned side effects from medication, which Complainant had just begun taking that day, and depression and anxiety and requested an accommodation to provide necessary time to recover. Regardless, an agency is not required to excuse past misconduct even if that misconduct resulted from Complainant’s disability. This is because a reasonable accommodation request is forward-looking, meaning the Complainant is entitled to an accommodation only from the date the disability is disclosed…Thus, the March 15, 2019 letter, to the extent it constituted a valid accommodation request, did not excuse Complainant’s prior absences. AJ Decision at 8-9. The Agency issued a final action dated July 27, 2022 implementing the AJ’s decision without a hearing finding no discrimination. Complainant filed the instant appeal. On appeal, Complainant asserts, as she did in her response to the Agency’s Motion, that the Agency’s supplemental investigation was inadequate. Specifically, Complainant states that the supplemental report of investigation did not contain witness statements she submitted regarding her request for reasonable accommodation. Complainant asserts, that according to her physician, she had been dealing with depression and anxiety months prior to receiving treatment from the EAP. Moreover, Complainant asserts that the Agency improperly terminated her when she was still under treatment from the EAP. In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final action implementing the AJ’s decision. The Agency asserts that Complainant did not contact EAP until February 25, 2019, and that Complainant’s personal opinion that she might have a disability that was affecting her attendance was not sufficient to establish a disability or require the Agency to provide a reasonable accommodation.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Nuclear Medicine Physician, GS-15, with the Imaging Service for the Veterans Affairs Medical Center in Martinsburg, West Virginia. On March 30, 2017, Complainant contacted an EEO Counselor regarding unlawful discrimination and a hostile work environment. On May 4, 2017, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency subjected her to discrimination and a hostile work environment based on religion (Muslim) and sex (female). On June 21, 2017, the Agency issued a Notice of Partial Acceptance on Complainant’s complaint noting she alleged that she was subjected to a hostile work environment based on religion (Muslim) and sex (female) consisting of 15 separate events. The Agency found four of the events listed were timely raised discrete acts and accepted them for investigation as independently actionable claims of disparate treatment (events 1, 13, 14, and 15). Complainant filed an objection to the Notice of Partial Acceptance. On July 27, 2017, the Agency issued a Response to Disagreement with Notice of Partial Acceptance noting Complainant disagreed with the framing of four of the events listed, and requested to add the basis of retaliation to her complaint. The Agency stated it would make the changes necessary as stated in Complainant’s disagreement letter and issue a new notice of partial acceptance. A Revised Notice of Partial Acceptance was issued on July 27, 2017, framing Complainant’s complaint as alleging she was subjected to a hostile work environment based on religion (Muslim), disability, sex (female), and in reprisal for protected EEO activity as evidenced by fifteen events. The Agency accepted five events for investigation as independently actionable claims of disparate treatment (events 1, 12, 13, 14, and 15) and stated that all the events would be considered as part of Complainant’s overall harassment claim. Complainant filed an amendment to her complaint dated July 26, 2017. Complainant requested the following two events be added to her complaint: on June 30, 2017, the Agency summarily suspended Complainant’s clinical privileges and notified her that it is considering permanently revoking her clinical privileges; and on July 10, 2017, the Agency initiated a summary review of Complainant’s employment as a probationary employee. Complainant stated these two events were a direct continuation of the pattern and practice of harassment previously raised. Further, she noted the harassment had escalated, “with the termination of [her] employment and revocation of her clinical privileges now the apparent goal.” Complainant argued the new claims were like or related to those raising during counseling and should be added to the claims already accepted for investigation. On July 27, 2017, the Agency issued a Notice of Amendment of the EEO Complaint, acknowledging receipt of Complainant’s amendment. The Notice stated that the current accepted claim, as indicated in the Revised Notice of Partial Acceptance letter dated July 27, 2017, is one of hostile work environment consisting of 15 events and five disparate treatment claims. The Notice acknowledged that on July 26, 2017, Complainant requested her complaint be amended to include two additional events based on religion and sex. The Agency found the new claims like or related to those raised in the original complaint. The Agency defined the amended complaint as containing the following claims: Complainant was subjected to a hostile work environment based on religion (Muslim), disability, and sex (female) as evidenced by the following events: 1. In November 2015 and ongoing, Supervisor of Nuclear Medicine (Supervisor), and Chief of Imaging Service (Chief), became uncooperative and aggressive towards the Complainant after learning she was a Muslim and proceeded to change her position by removing her supervisory, leadership, and other duties; and cancelled her supervisor training, which undermined and denigrated her amongst her peers as a physician that's supervised by a technologist. 2. On February 23, 2016, Supervisor failed to respond to the Complainant’s emails regarding patient care. 3. On February 25, 2016, Complainant felt threatened when she asked Supervisor to leave her office after they had a meeting regarding a position disagreement. 4. From June 2016 to December 2016, Chief was amused when Complainant informed her that someone was placing candy wrappers in her inbox and commented “infantile.” 5. In October 2016, Complainant’s performance was underrated by Chief when she used the incorrect scoring system. 6. From December 2015 to December 2016, Supervisor ignored Complainant’s warning of multiple patient care and performance behavior issues. At one point Complainant was forced to apologize for reporting a patient care issue. 7. In December 2016, Complainant was denied pay for performance and her request for a pay panel review was also denied. 8. In January 2017, Chief denied Complainant’s request for reasonable accommodation. 9. On March 28, 2017, Chief embarrassed the Complainant during a meeting when she dismissed her concerns about patient care. 10. On March 30 and 31, 2017, Supervisor communicated in an angry tone “you only want to win. I'm done with you” after Complainant voiced her concerns about appropriate patients released processes. 11. In April 2017, Chief accused Complainant of over-usage of Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA) and taking unauthorized time off. 12. In April 2017, during a Human Resource meeting with Chief, Complainant’s personal medical information was disclosed to the group. 13. On April 24, 2017, Complainant’s credential file was not presented during a meeting which caused a delay in her renewal privileges. 14. On May 22, 2017, Chief initiated a review of Complainant’s work product, manipulated the review, and refused to submit her application for renewal of clinical privileges and credentials to the Executive Committee of Medical Staff. 15. On June 1, 2017, the Acting Chief of Staff handed the Complainant a letter of investigation for her work performance. 16. On June 30, 2017, Senior Management summarily suspended the Complainant’s clinical privileges and notified her of a proposal to permanently revoke her clinical privileges. 17. On July 10, 2017, Senior Management initiated a summary review of Complainant’s employment as a probationary employee. The Agency accepted events 1, 12, 13, 14, and 16 for investigation as timely independently actionable claims of disparate treatment. The Agency noted these events were sufficiently related to the overall pattern of harassment that they would be included for consideration in the analysis of the overall harassment claim (events 1 - 17). Complainant’s complaint was assigned for investigation on August 23, 2017. Investigator 1 conducted an investigation from August 31, 2017, to October 6, 2017. The investigative report was submitted to the Regional EEO Officer on October 9, 2017. On February 15, 2019, the Office of Employment Discrimination Complaint Adjudication (OEDCA) sent the matter for a supplemental investigation to the Office of Resolution Management (ORM). It was noted the supplemental investigation was needed due to the first investigator not using a revised version of event 14; failing to investigate the bases of race, disability, and reprisal; and failure to investigate the additional accepted events in claims (16) and (17). The matter was assigned for investigation on March 4, 2019. Investigator 2 conducted an investigation from March through April 2019. The report was submitted to the Regional EEO Officer on April 19, 2019. On July 10, 2019, Complainant requested a hearing on her complaint. The case was assigned to an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). On September 11, 2019, the AJ dismissed Complainant’s hearing request and remanded the matter to the Agency for issuance of a final decision. On June 10, 2021, the Agency issued a final decision on Complainant’s complaint. In its decision, the Agency stated that at the conclusion of the investigation, Complainant was notified of the right to request a hearing by an EEOC AJ or an immediate final decision without a hearing. Specifically, the Agency stated that “Complainant acknowledged receipt of that notice on October 27, 2017.” The Agency stated that when Complainant failed to respond to the notice, the file was forwarded to OEDCA for an immediate final decision. 2 Further, the Agency stated the record indicated that Complainant was subsequently terminated from her position effective August 4, 2017. The Agency noted that documentation from ORM shows that Complainant did not follow the “proper channels” she was instructed to follow in order to amend her complaint while it was pending hearing or to initiate a new complaint by calling the EEO counseling line. Thus, it noted ORM did not accept Complainant’s termination claim via amendment or investigate the removal as part of Complainant’s discrimination and harassment claim in this case. The Agency analyzed events 8, 12, 13, 14, and 16 as independently actionable claims and events 1 - 17 as an overall harassment claim. The Agency found Complainant failed to establish that she was subjected to discrimination or harassment as alleged. Thereafter, Complainant filed the instant appeal.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Rating Veterans Service Representative at the Agency’s Regional Office facility in North Little Rock, Arkansas. 1. On May 16, 2020, he became aware of his non-selection/failure to promote to the Supervisory Veterans Service Representative, GS-13 position under Vacancy announcement 350-20-DLM-10787513-NBU. 2 Complainant asserted that he was subject to discrimination based on race, age, sex, and reprisal when he was not selected for an interview for a position for which he was well-qualified and the selected candidates, who were younger, white women, were less qualified than he was. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 67-69. He stated that his prior protected activity consists of being interviewed by the Administrative Review Board in a complaint of discriminatory and unfair labor practices and filing a complaint with the Office of Special Counsel. See ROI at 63. The Assistant Veterans Service Center Manager (Assistant Manager), who determined the best qualified candidates from the applicant list and served on the interview panel, stated that the criteria to be deemed best qualified was whether the applicant was meeting or exceeding all elements of their performance standard from October 1, 2019 to March 31, 2020. See ROI at 81. If an applicant was not meeting or exceeding all elements of their performance standards, they were deemed to be not best qualified. See ROI at 81. She stated that she found Complainant not to be best qualified because he was not meeting all elements of his performance standards during the relevant time. See ROI at 83. Complainant’s recent performance appraisal rated Complainant as not meeting the goal of Fully Successful on the Quality element of his evaluation. See ROI at 204-207. The Assistant Manager explained that the best qualified candidates were then scored and ranked based on their resume, previous supervisory experience, interview questions, and a written exercise. See ROI at 83. She further stated that of the two selectees, one had extensive supervisory experience within the Agency and while the other did not have previous supervisory experience, both selectees demonstrated through the interview and the written exercise a high likelihood of success in the position. See ROI at 84. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). the decision found that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for not selecting Complainant for the position and that Complainant did not submit evidence to support his assertions of discriminatory animus. The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed, arguing that the Agency’s explanations of its actions was untrue and should not have been accepted. In response, the Agency urges affirmance of its final decision. The Agency dismissed Complainant’s allegation that the Agency subjected him to a hostile work environment between March 8, 2019 and October 2019 for untimely counselor contact. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 35-37.

Sent long-winded and threatening emails regarding cases and assignments; c. Ignored Complainant in discussing case matters; and d. Addressed him with black vernacular phrases, such as “shuckin’ and jiving” and “hemming and hawing.” 2. The AJ noted that Complainant’s response brief was twice the length the AJ had specifically stated in the Post Conference Order and struck pages 16-30 of Complainant’s response.
