The Agency investigated the accepted claims from July 22 to September 1, 2021. The Agency indicated that on September 15, 2021, it provided, via certified mail, Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f). The Agency stated that Complainant reported she did not receive the mail and thus, on October 14, 2021, it reissued a copy of the report of investigation along with her right to hearing, via Agency’s Secure Access File Exchange filesharing electronic system, to Complainant. Complaint #2: [number removed] On July 9, 2021, Complainant filed Complaint #2 alleging discrimination based on race (African American), disability, sex (female), and in reprisal for prior EEO activity when: 14. On June 7, 2021, she was denied Family and Medical Leave Act leave for her May 2021 surgery. 15. On an unknown date, she was denied her reasonable accommodation request for telework and a handicap parking space. On July 30, 2021, the Agency dismissed claim 15 for raising a matter that had not been brought to the attention of an EEO Counselor, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(2). The Agency investigated claim 14 from August 30 through September 28, 2021. The Agency indicated that on October 14, 2021, the Agency, via its Secure Access File Exchange filesharing electronic system, provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation, including a notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC AJ. The Agency stated that it reissued the report of investigation on October 27, 2021, and again on November 10, 2021, because Complainant did not retrieve the original notices. On January 26, 2022, the Agency, consolidated the complaints and issued a final Agency decision finding no discrimination as alleged. The Agency stated that Complainant failed to make an election to request a hearing by the deadline, i.e., by November 13, 2021 (30-days after October 14, 2021) for Complaint #1, and by December 10, 2021 (30-days after November 10, 2021) for Complaint #2. On March 18, 2022, Complainant appealed the Agency’s decision indicating that the Agency’s final decision was “wrong,” and there was an error in the Agency’s processing of her claims. In response to Complainant’s appeal, the Agency indicated that Complainant’s appeal should be denied as untimely. Specifically, the Agency stated that Complainant received the final Agency decision on January 26, 2022, but she did not file an appeal until March 18, 2022, which was beyond the 30-day time limit. In the alternative, stated the Agency, the Commission should affirm its final decision finding no discrimination. The record reveals that on October 6, 2021, Complainant, via EEOC Public Portal, requested a hearing before an EEOC AJ for both complaints and uploaded a copy of a Request for a Hearing Form, dated September 30, 2021, for Complaint #1, which was docketed under Hearing No. 570- 2022-00017X; and a copy of a Request for a Hearing Form, dated October 1, 2021, for Complaint #2, which was docketed under Hearing No. 570-2022-00018X. The record indicates that on January 24, 2022, the AJ issued a Notice of Intent to Sanction for each complaint because the Agency failed to submit the complaint file and/or the report of investigation. On March 24, 2022, the Agency filed a separate response to each Notice of Intent to Sanction, indicating that sanctions against the Agency were not warranted because it was not served with a notice that Complainant filed a hearing request, and it was not on notice of any order or other requirement until March 10, 2022. Specifically, the Agency stated that Complainant did not use Request for a Hearing Form that was provided to her when the report of investigation was transmitted to her. In that form, Complainant was informed to choose the Agency, in EEOC Public Portal, as “DoD Office of Secretary/Washington Headquarters Services.” Instead, Complainant used an outdated version of Request for a Hearing Form which did not indicate an option to request a hearing in the EEOC Public Portal and thus no instruction choosing the Agency therein. The Agency stated that Complainant’s hearings were docketed, via EEOC Public Portal, with the Agency as “DoD Armed Forces Retirement Home” on October 6, 2021. At that time, the Agency EEO Program Director (“EEOP Director”) or the Agency’s EEO office did not have access to “DoD Armed Forces Retirement Home” via FedSEP and thus, the Agency never received the October 6, 2021, filings. The Agency indicated that on March 10, 2022, the EEOP Director requested and received access to the “DoD Armed Forces Retirement Home” FedSEP box as a stopgap measure while discussing with individuals at the EEOC (Office of Federal Operations and Washington Field Office) other ways to ensure more effective usage of FedSEP, given the large population, consisting of multiple agencies, serviced by “DoD Office of Secretary/Washington Headquarters Services.” On March 10, 2022, the EEOP Director promptly uploaded a copy of the final Agency decision in FedSEP, and on March 11, 2022, the Agency counsel requested an extension to respond to the AJ’s Notice of Intent to Sanction. The Agency argued that the AJ should dismiss Complainant’s hearing requests because they were not properly filed. The Agency indicated that Complainant did not send a copy of the hearing requests to the Agency’s EEO office as instructed and as such it properly issued a final Agency decision for both complaints. The Agency stated that Complainant appealed the Agency’s decision and the AJ proceeding with a hearing would be inappropriate. Further, the Agency stated that the AJ lacked jurisdiction to hear Complainant’s complaints because Complainant filed her hearing requests prematurely before her receipt of the investigative report and before 180 days had elapsed under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(h). The Agency indicated that regarding Complaint #1, filed on April 5, 2021, Complainant’s hearing request form was dated September 30, 2021, i.e., before she received the reissued investigative report on October 14, 2021, and before 180 days had elapsed from the filing of the complaint. Regarding Complaint #2, filed on July 9, 2021, the Agency stated that Complainant’s hearing request form was dated October 1, 2021, i.e., before she received the investigative report on November 10, 2021, and only 84 days after the filing of a formal complaint. Based on the foregoing, the Agency asked the AJ to withdraw the Notice of Intent to Sanction the Agency and dismiss Complainant’s hearing requests as they were not properly filed and because the AJ lacked jurisdiction. On May 6, 2022, Complainant submitted to the AJ a motion, in part, to consolidate cases, motion for sanctions, and request for a hearing. Complainant indicated that she timely filed hearing requests for her complaints and the Agency was on actual notice of the filings. Complainant argued that the Agency failed to respond and therefore sanctions against the Agency were warranted. Specifically, Complainant stated that she provided a copy of her October 1, 2021, hearing request of Complaint #2 to the EEOP Director on October 6, 2021, via email, as an attachment. Complainant included a copy of her October 6, 2021, email showing it was sent to the EEOP Director, and a Senior EEO Specialist, stating, “Good Afternoon, Here’s your copy of the request for hearing attached above. The formal complaint investigation was completed. I wanted to timely request a hearing.” The email message reflects Complainant attached a copy of the request for hearing on Complaint #2. On June 30, 2022, the AJ issued an Order of Dismissal of Complainant’s hearing requests for her complaints. Specifically, the AJ stated that since Complainant filed an appeal of the consolidated final Agency decision, the AJ no longer had jurisdiction over the complaints.

During the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Vocational Rehabilitation Specialist at the Agency’s Behavioral Service Line, Gulf Coast Health Care facility in Biloxi, Mississippi. Compensated Work Therapy Program Manager (Manager) was her first-level supervisor. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 85, 119. 1. On October 15, 2019, Manager, issued Complainant a sick leave certification letter; 2. On November 13, 2019, Manager issued Complainant a Letter of Admonishment; and 3. On November 20, 2019, Manager rated Complainant lower than deserved on her annual performance evaluation. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ assigned to the case determined sua sponte that the complaint did not warrant a hearing and over Complainant's objections, issued a decision without a hearing on March 4, 2022. The AJ found that the Agency provided legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions for each claim. In claim 1, the AJ noted that Manager issued Complainant a sick leave certification at the recommendation of Labor and Employee Relations. Complainant used 107 hours of sick leave between April 15 and October 10, 2019. ROI at 126. The sick leave had two concerning patterns. When Manager assigned Complainant a patient, Complainant would enter sick leave into the leave system, send Manager an email, and then go home. The second pattern was one in which Complainant would take sick leave on days immediately surrounding days when she was scheduled to be off work. ROI at 127. As to claim 2, Manager issued Complainant a proposed admonishment on October 22, 2019, for conduct and behavior issues. ROI at 30. There were six specifications enumerated on the proposed admonishment. Two of these specifications involved telling Manager not to come to scheduled meetings and four were concerning Complainant’s unwillingness to respond to Manager’s instructions. Id. After the proper procedure was followed, Manager upheld the admonishment on November 13, 2019. ROI at 276. Regarding claim 3, Manager asserted that he took the concerns outlined in the proposed admonishment into account with Complainant’s performance review. He found that Complainant did her job but did not perform beyond that which was expected. As such, he rated Complainant “fully successful” for her performance review. ROI at 143-149. The AJ found that Complainant was unable to provide sufficient evidence to demonstrate pretext. As such, Complainant failed to prove discrimination as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Complainant raised generalized concerns regarding the lack of discovery due to the issuance of summary judgment.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Budget Analyst at the Agency’s Efficiency and Renewable Energy (EERE) Office in Washington, D.C. In the Agency’s July 22, 2021, acceptance of Complainant’s May 14, 2021, amendment request, the Agency noted that reprisal only applied to claim 2 as Complainant alleged that her protected EEO activity was the instant complaint. 1. on or around February 1, 2021, Complainant was informed by email that the Department’s tentative job offer to Complainant for the position of Budget Director, EERE, had been rescinded; and 2. on May 14, 2021, Complainant was not selected for the position of Budget Director. Complainant worked in the Department’s Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy (EERE) as a Budget Analyst, in Washington, D.C., from September 10, 2018, until March 10, 2021. Report of Investigation, Part 1 (ROI1) at 279. From approximately October 2019 until March 10, 2021, Complainant also served as the Acting Budget Director. ROI1 at 312. On December 30, 2020, Complainant received a tentative job offer for the position of Budget Director, EERE Office. ROI1 at 153. On January 20, 2021, the Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary (Principal), began her position as the new Principal and Acting Assistant Secretary for EERE. Once in position, the Principal stated that she studied position descriptions for various key positions to ensure that the organization was structured appropriately. ROI1 at 391. She found that many position descriptions did not accurately reflect what was needed. For the Budget Director position in particular, the Principal noted that the position was “watered down” and did not require specialized budget expertise. The Principal asked the Human Capital (HC) Office to correct the position description, noting the expectation that the Budget Director would have to engage in very in-depth and critical budget formulation and execution-related functions. The Principal was not involved in rewriting the position and noted that she was unsure who in the HC Office handled the revisions. The Principal also noted that the position was misclassified as under Program Management job series when it should have been posted under a Budget Analyst job series. Supplemental Report of Investigation (SROI) at 60. The Principal’s request led HC to recall the Budget Director vacancy for which Complainant had applied. ROI1 at 391. The Principal noted that her review also led the Advanced Manufacturing Office (AMO) Director position to be recalled and a tentative offer for that position was also rescinded. SROI at 59. Additionally, her review also led to the Federal Energy Management Program Director position being reclassified. SROI at 60. On February 1, 2021, Complainant was informed by email that the Agency’s tentative job offer to Complainant for the position of Budget Director had been rescinded. ROI1 at 185. The letter informed Complainant, in part, the following: Based on expansive platform changes which will heavily impact EERE programs, the Budget Director role in EERE must be updated to reflect the changed priorities of the Administration and the Department, as well as the specialized budget formulation and execution expertise and broader responsibilities of the position to address the anticipated increases in appropriations for EERE programs. Due to the increased technical qualifications required, we must pursue re- classification and re-advertisement of this Senior Executive Service (SES) position. The vacancy announcement will be closed, and the Department will not proceed any further in the hiring process. Your Qualifications Review Board submission will not be considered by the U.S. Office of Personnel Management for certification. However, you remain eligible to apply to competitive SES announcements and you are encouraged to apply for the reformulated budget position when it is re-advertised in the near future. ROI1 at 186. The Budget Director position was later reposted under the Budget Analyst job series with a revised description. On April 23, 2021, Complainant interviewed for the newly re-posted Budget Director position with an interview panel 3 comprising of the Budget Officer and Director for Budget and Planning (Director). The Budget Officer stated that she gave Complainant acceptable ratings for the interview, noting that she found Complainant’s responses, using “industry experience” versus “government experience”, to be lacking. SROI at 31. The Budget Officer did not recommend her for a second-round interview. Id. The Director stated that based on responses to the standard six questions asked of each candidate, Complainant’s score was lower than the three candidates selected as Best Qualified. SROI at 71. On May 13, 2021, the panel submitted the three Best Qualified candidates to the Deputy Assistant Secretary of Operations (Deputy Assistant), who was the selecting official. SROI at 38. The panel unanimously chose three candidates to submit based on the quality of their responses during their respective interviews. SROI at 72. The Deputy Assistant stated that she made her decision based on the recommendation of the interview panel. SROI at 143-147. The Deputy Assistant spoke with all three Best Qualified candidates and made her final decision based on the panel’s recommendation and her conversations with the candidates. SROI at 146. The Deputy Assistant stated that the Selectee: had a tremendous breadth of experience with Federal budgeting and program reviews. In speaking with [the Selectee] it became evident that he had significant experience in leading a diverse skill set of federal employees, providing strong leadership, developing staff and creating a cohesive team which aligned with the needs for this position. The interview panel was comprised of three individuals, but the third individual had a scheduling conflict and was not present during the interview. SROI at 146. On May 14, 2021, Complainant was informed that she was not selected for the position of Director, Budget Office. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Both parties provided appellate briefs.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Fraud Detection National Service Immigration Officer at the Agency’s Texas Service Center in Dallas, Texas. 1. on October 18, 2018, management unfairly referred Complainant for a sexual misconduct investigation; 2. on October 22, 2018, Complainant was given a lower rating on his fiscal year 2018 Performance Plan and Appraisal than he believed was warranted by his performance; 3. on October 23, 2018, Complainant was demoted from his position as an Immigration Officer, GS-13 to an Immigration Services Officer, GS-12; and 4. on April 9, 2019, Complainant’s request to volunteer for the border surge capacity force was denied. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. At the Initial Conference held on February 15, 2022, the parties agreed that accepted claim 3 was properly appealed to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) and therefore not at issue in this case. The Agency submitted a Motion for Summary Judgment (Motion). Complainant responded to the Motion. On March 4, 2022, the AJ issued a decision without a hearing. After making all reasonable inferences in favor of Complainant, the AJ determined that there were no material facts in dispute. The AJ dismissed claims 1 and 4 for failure to state a claim, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(1). Alternatively, the AJ also determined the merits of claims 1, 2, and 4. The AJ that the Agency had articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. Regarding claim 1, the Agency conducted a standard investigation as required by procedures when a complaint is made with the Office of the Inspector General. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 156. Following the internal investigation, the Agency determined that the claims against Complainant were unsubstantiated, and the matter was closed with no disciplinary action taken against Complainant. ROI at 119; 156. Regarding claim 2, the AJ determined that the Agency gave Complainant a mid-cycle review indicating that he was not performing at an acceptable level. ROI at 120; 231. The review noted that Complainant was not completing at least ten Statement of Findings (SOF) per month and that his totals were well below the required amount each month. Complainant’s mid-cycle clearly noted that he was not performing at or above expectations. This, amongst other metrics, impacted Complainant’s year end evaluation. Id; see also at 200. Finally, regarding claim 4, the AJ determined that the record demonstrated that Complainant had been demoted the year prior and was thus ineligible to apply as a volunteer. ROI at 122; 129. Additionally, the Agency indicated that Complainant’s work was not at the expected level to be able to serve on the voluntary force. ROI at 136. Finding that Complainant failed to demonstrate that the articulated reasons were pretext for discrimination, the AJ granted the Agency’s motion for summary judgment. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s decision. The instant appeal followed.

After an investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). On August 24, 2021, Complainant requested a hearing. The Agency submitted a motion to dismiss the hearing request, for failure to abide by the time limits, which Complainant opposed. The AJ denied the hearing request on the grounds that pursuant to 29 CFR §1614.107 Complainant failed to submit a timely request for hearing. The AJ found Complainant’s request was over eight months late. The AJ remanded the formal complaint to the Agency for issuance of a final decision. Prior to the issuance of an Agency final decision, Complainant filed the instant appeal, attaching a copy of the AJ’s dismissal of the hearing to his Notice of Appeal, without additional elaboration. Complainant did not submit a brief on appeal. In opposition to the appeal, the Agency contends Complainant failed to establish his discrimination claims and the AJ did not err in dismissing Complainant’s request for hearing as untimely. After Complainant filed the instant appeal, however, the Agency issued the instant final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Transportation Assistant at the Agency’s Joint Personal Property Shipping Office facility in Fort Belvior, Virginia. On August 30, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the basis of race (Caucasian) when: 1. On March 18, 2021, he was not selected for a Quality Control Supervisor position (Announcement Number: NCAS210018282844, Control number [number removed]) and a person of non-Caucasian descent was selected for the position. Complainant stated that he applied for the position and was interviewed on April 28, 2021. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 194. He believes he should have been hired for the position because he is more qualified than the Selectee, has more years of experience, and is a disabled veteran. See ROI at 194-95. Complainant asserted that he believes the Selectee was scored higher in the ratings because he was pre-selected. See ROI at 195. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision found that assuming arguendo that Complainant established a prima facie case, the Agency articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for the non-selection, because the Selectee received the highest score from the resume review and the interview and the Selectee demonstrated more management experience in his interview. The decision further found that there was no evidence in the record to support Complainant’s assertions of discriminatory animus and concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed, reiterating his argument that he is more highly qualified than the Selectee and contending that the Agency’s officials’ stated reasons were false. In response, the Agency argues that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its action and there is no evidence in the record to support Complainant’s assertions.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as an Assistant Director at the Agency’s Office of Financial Institutions and Business Liaison (OFIBL) at its Headquarters in Washington, D.C. 1. Complainant was subjected to a hostile work environment, including but not limited to, the following incidents: a. On February 18, 2020, her first day of employment, the Deputy Assistant Director (Deputy) stared intensely at Complainant during a meeting with a mean look that persisted throughout the entirety of the meeting; and on the same day, during a one-on-one meeting between Complainant and the Deputy, the Deputy never said hello, made Complainant feel unwelcomed and uncomfortable, said Complainant had come to work in the worst workplace in the entire city; and made derogatory comments about the staff members. b. On February 21, 2020, the Deputy refused to answer any of Complainant’s questions during their meeting and yelled and screamed at Complainant. The Deputy also refused to share and transfer information with Complainant, such as a shareholder contact list, spreadsheets and other standard operating procedures necessary to manage office operations. c. On or about February 27, 2020, the Outreach Policy Analyst (Outreach Analyst) stated that he preferred to report to the Deputy (who lacked supervisory authority) rather than to Complainant. d. On multiple occasions between February and July 2020, the Outreach Analyst refused to share information with Complainant and frequently uttered explicit vulgarities when she inquired about his late arrival to the office, the status of his work assignments, and his absence from mandatory meetings. e. In March 2020, the Deputy sent Complainant a harassing email stating Complainant did not notice or acknowledge the Deputy at management meetings, even though Complainant did not facilitate or lead the meetings. f. In March 2020, during a meeting in the office of the Deputy Associate Director, External Affairs (External Affairs Deputy), Complainant asked the External Affairs Deputy if the hostility and harassment demonstrated against her by the Deputy and the Outreach Analyst and, at the time, another OFIBL staff member was related to her race. The External Affairs Deputy told Complainant she was not sure and to give them more time to come around and get on board because of prior tension on the team prior to Complainant’s onboarding. g. On May 11, 2020, the Deputy made an implicit racial remark about a minority trade association, stating that it was not very organized. h. On May 19, 2020, during a telephone conversation between the External Affairs Deputy and Complainant to discuss a series of hostile emails sent by the Outreach Analyst, and in preparation for mid-year performance reviews, Complainant asked the External Affairs Deputy again if she thought race had anything to do with how the Deputy and the Outreach Analyst were treating her. The External Affairs Deputy replied that she would find it hard to believe anyone in OFIBL challenged Complainant’s predecessor (a white male) like they were challenging Complainant. i. On or about May 20, 2020, after Complainant requested the names of stakeholders and their contact information, the Outreach Analyst once again refused to share the information and said her request made him uncomfortable. He also defied her directive to share stakeholder emails with her so she could keep leadership informed with timely status updates. j. On or about June 25, 2020, the Outreach Analyst sent a Director Briefing Memo to the Policy Associate Director (Policy Director) without first getting Complainant’s review or approval. The Outreach Analyst later referred to Complainant as a shark, stating he had “jumped the shark” to get the assignment to the Policy Director. k. On or about August 14, 2020, after Complainant asked the Deputy in a one-to- one email to make a simple edit to a Briefing Memo, the Deputy added 10 staff members to her reply. In the reply, the Deputy challenged Complainant by asking where she wanted the edit to be made, despite Complainant’s clear instructions in that regard and demanding Complainant provide an example of another staff member complying with her directive. The Deputy refused to edit the document as instructed. l. At an August 11, 2020 staff meeting, the Deputy refused to speak to or acknowledge Complainant when Complainant said, “Hi, [Deputy], how are you?” After Complainant greeted the Deputy four more times, the Deputy responded in a stern, angry, agitated, elevated voice, saying, “Look, I’m fine! I’m fine!” m. On or about September 9, 2020, the Deputy and the Outreach Analyst sent a hostile and harassing email to all OFIBL staff, challenging Complainant’s management authority to assign work. The Deputy falsely asserted assignments were unfair and prepared charts and calculations to discredit, disparage and embarrass Complainant and sent them to staff and Complainant’s Supervisor, the Assistant Director, Office of Stakeholder Management (Supervisor), via email. The Outreach Analyst joined the Deputy and sent emails to Complainant, other staff, and the Supervisor, further asserting there were flaws in Complainant’s reasoning and questioned her ability to assign work. n. Complainant followed up with the Supervisor and was told on or about September 10th, that in light of her complaint, he and the Policy Director had spoken to the Deputy and the Outreach Analyst about their treatment of her, but the Supervisor told her the Deputy and the Outreach Analyst might not change their hostilities towards Complainant right away and it might take them time to come around. o. On September 28 and 30, 2020, Complainant was not invited to participate in Director-level stakeholder calls while the Deputy was, even though previously there had been no known instances where staff from Complainant’s office had been invited to a director-level stakeholder call, where she was not also invited to participate. p. On or about September 29, 2020, Complainant asked the Deputy to inquire about why a call with Bureau officials had been recorded. On September 30, 2020, instead of making the inquiry as directed, the Deputy instead caused further reputational risk to Complainant via email, by telling the stakeholder that “at the last-minute, [Complainant] jumped on the call,” implying she was not an invited participant. q. On October 7, 2020, during a meeting between CFPB’s Division of Research Markets and Regulations (RMR) and the Office of Financial Institutions and Business Liaison, the Deputy asserted and falsely accused Complainant of being the sole decision-making authority for whether or not other Bureau managers and staff are allowed to join director-level calls. r. On April 6, 2020, the Outreach Analyst sent Complainant a “rude and disrespectful” response to the entire team implying she could not comprehend information by stating “Did we make your head spin? Kudos to us.” s. On March 10, 2021, the Supervisor told Complainant that he expected her to meet approximately once a week virtually and 1:1 with her direct reports. t. On March 11, 2021, the Supervisor declined Complainant’s request for a third party to be present for 1:1 meetings with the Deputy. 2. Whether the Supervisor subjected Complainant to disparate treatment when on April 1, 2021, he issued her a Letter of Reprimand. 2 The Agency investigated the complaint. In brief, the evidence developed during the investigation showed Complainant asserted that from her first day at the Agency, the Deputy and another of her subordinates, the Outreach Analyst, have engaged in insubordination and hostile behavior that impeded her ability to carry out her job. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 137-140. She stated that she is convinced the behavior must be racially motivated because she has asked and been told several times that the Deputy and the Outreach Analyst behaved differently under the leadership of Complainant’s predecessor, a white male. See ROI at 137-40. While the Deputy and the Outreach Analyst both denied that they have ever behaved inappropriately, accusing Complainant of being unfairly accusatory, two of Complainant’s other subordinates and the Senior Advisor to the Supervision, Enforcement, and Fair Lending Associate Director (Senior Advisor), who was previously a management official on Complainant’s team, as well as the External Affairs Director, corroborated Complainant’s description of the Deputy’s and the Outreach Analyst’s conduct, stating that the Deputy and the Outreach Analyst consistently tried to undermine Complainant’s authority and make Complainant look bad. See, e.g., ROI at 1914-1923; 2127-33; 2162-71; 3910-12. For example, while the Outreach Analyst claimed that he did not provide Complainant with the contact information of external shareholders because of a concern with sharing personal information, Although Complainant included reprisal as a basis in her formal complaint, Complainant appeared to withdraw her retaliation claim in her affidavit. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 3-4; 135. Complainant’s predecessor stated that it was “laughable” to think that external shareholder information was personal information of the sort to raise such privacy concerns. See ROI at 1520-21; 2277. However, Complainant’s subordinates further stated that even prior to Complainant’s arrival, they had experienced issues with the Deputy’s behavior when she assumed a temporary detail position as the acting Assistant Director of OFIBL after Complainant’s predecessor left and prior to Complainant beginning her position. One of Complainant’s subordinates stated that the Deputy had generally tried to create a hostile work environment for OFIBL but that her conduct became worse after Complainant was hired because the Deputy felt she should have been made the permanent Assistant Director and was upset when Complainant was hired for the position rather than her. See ROI at 2129-2134. Another of Complainant’s subordinates confirmed that he believed the Deputy felt entitled to the position of Assistant Director and was upset when Complainant was hired and stated that he believed part of the Deputy’s conduct was motivated by political differences because the Deputy knew that Complainant had previously worked for the Obama White House. See ROI at 2165-67; 2184. The Letter of Reprimand was issued to Complainant for unprofessional behavior, including refusing to follow the Supervisor’s repeated instruction to engage in one-on-one communication with staff and not informing the Supervisor that Employee and Labor Relations had advised Complainant against proceeding with a personnel action. See ROI at 3713. The Letter found that Complainant’s actions demonstrated an unwillingness to work cooperatively with Employee and Labor Relations in addressing the conduct and performance issues on her team. See ROI at 3714. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing, but the AJ denied the hearing request on the grounds that the hearing request was untimely. The AJ noted that Complainant did not deny that she received a copy of the report of investigation on October 25, 2021, which clearly informed Complainant of the 30-day time limit to request a hearing, but that Complainant did not request a hearing until November 29, 2021. The AJ therefore dismissed the hearing request and remanded the complaint to the Agency. Thereafter, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision thoroughly recounted the relevant facts and found that management witnesses articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for issuing the Letter of Reprimand and Complainant’s disagreement with the Supervisor’s decision to discipline her was not sufficient to establish pretext. The decision further went on to acknowledge that the record clearly demonstrated that the Deputy and the Outreach Analyst had behaved in “inappropriate, disrespectful, unprofessional, and potentially insubordinate behavior” but found that, ultimately, the preponderance of the record did not establish that either the Deputy’s or the Outreach Analyst’s behavior was motivated by any of Complainant’s protected classes rather than disgruntlement over the Deputy not being hired to perform Complainant’s job. The decision therefore concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination or unlawful retaliation as alleged. The instant appeal from Complainant followed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Postal Police Officer at the Agency’s Career Development Unit facility in Potomac, MD. 1. On or about March 3, 2021 to March 23, 2021, he was denied mental health treatment through the Agency’s Self-Referred Counseling Program (SRCP); 2. On or about March 23, 2021, management failed to respond to his additional request to receive treatment through the Self-Referred Counseling Program; 3. On or about April 26, 2021, he sought treatment through another Agency program, Employee Assistance Program (EAP) and was denied treatment. 2 At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew his request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision found that the evidence indicated that Complainant was denied treatment through the SRCP because as a Postal Officer, he was not eligible for the program, and he was denied treatment through the EAP because it did not have the personnel to provide the necessary treatment. The decision found that Complainant offered no evidence to support his assertions of discriminatory animus and therefore concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed, arguing that the Agency’s explanations are not worthy of credence. 3 In response, the Agency contends that Complainant cannot establish that the Agency’s reasons are a pretext and that its decision should be affirmed.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as an Industrial Specialist, GS 13 at the Agency’s Mid-Atlantic Regional Maintenance Center in Norfolk, Virginia. On June 25, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), sex (female), and color (Black) when: 1. (Manager) dismissed her report of harassment onboard the USS Cole by the ship Commander, with examples of the harassment including: a. On April 22, 2021, the Commander compared her to the last Project Manager (PM) who was a white male, when he said, “Where have you been? I never went a single day without seeing the PM prior to your arrival.” b. On April 22, 2021, she received derogatory comments from the Commander in a “Reply All” email such as “I hope it is not your intention to allow the contractor to not complete this work. That is unacceptable.” c. When on or about April 26, 2021, she received an email reply from the Commander which told her he never had to have a conversation with someone of her rank or responsibility and asks if it alarms her since it was concerning to him; d. When on July 6, 2021, the Manager issued her a Letter of Expectations based on email feedback from the Commander. 2 Complainant was assigned to work as the Project Manager (PM) for the Maintenance Team of the USS Cole in December 2020, a position which entailed being responsible for expediting product completion deadlines and serving the customer, i.e., the USS Cole and its Commander, and ship forces. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 176; 613-21. The Commander stated that it was the usual practice for the PM to hold production meetings on the ship each day with the USS Cole’s leadership and respective contractors, which allowed for leaders to proactively socialize maintenance problems and solutions. See ROI at 458. He stated that the Commanding Officer and the PM were expected to work together to unite the maintenance team and ship’s force to complete the maintenance package on time. See ROI at 458. He stated that when Complainant started as the PM, he was upfront about the daily meeting requirement and was frank about the challenges that he and the previous PM had faced. See ROI at 459. He explained that the emails he sent her were to provide feedback about the status of the work being untimely and done with poor workmanship. See ROI at 460. He further explained that in his opinion, Complainant’s referring to any communication issues that led to the job being late or incomplete was due to Complainant’s own refusal to hold daily meetings. See ROI at 460. He stated that people at their level and pay grade were expected to execute at the highest levels and not allow excuses to get in the way of what is right for the ship, which always takes precedence. See ROI at 462. Complainant responded to that email by referring to her protected classes, stating “Please understand that I am a mid-level GS-13 Civil Service Employee with protected status under four categories: black, female, over 40 and disabled.” See ROI at 463. The Manager stated that he issued the Letter of Expectations after this email because he found it to be unprofessional and inappropriate for Complainant to bring up her protected classes because it was not germane to the conversation. See ROI at 435. He further explained that the Letter of Expectations was not disciplinary or a negative action. See ROI at 436. The Agency dismissed a claim that between June 2020 and November 2020, the commander of the USS Ramage yelled at her, stood in the way of timely project completion, and sent her command derogatory comments regarding her performance pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(2) for untimely counselor contact. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 137-39. Complainant stated that she felt the Commander’s emails to be demeaning because he was correcting her about something when he is a peer and not a supervisor. See ROI at 180. She asserted that she believed the Commander’s treatment of her and her supervisor’s lack of response to her allegation of harassment had to do with her protected classes because “[t]hey do not do this to people who are not a marginalized group in [her] experience.” See ROI at 182. Complainant acknowledged, however, that the only way in which she tried to make her supervisors aware of the alleged harassment was by adding her first-line supervisor (Supervisor) to the email chain with the Commander. See ROI at 181. Both the Coordinator and the Manager stated that to their knowledge, Complainant never actually mentioned that she believed she was being subjected to harassment to anyone in management. See ROI at 421; 434. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Over Complainant’s objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s April 1, 2022, motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on April 27, 2022. The AJ found that Complainant could not establish a prima facie case with respect to the Letter of Expectations and even if she could, there was no evidence to indicate it was due to discriminatory animus. The AJ further found that all of the alleged incidents of harassment taken together were not sufficiently severe or pervasive to constitute an unlawful hostile work environment. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed but did not make any specific arguments on appeal. In response, the Agency contends that the AJ correctly found that there was no evidence beyond Complainant’s bare assertions to indicate any discriminatory animus.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant was an applicant for the position of Program Specialist, Vacancy Announcement Number: CBSU-11140287-21-MJP, with the Agency’s Salt Lake City Medical Center in Salt Lake City, Utah. On September 17, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (African-American), sex (male), and age (51) when on August 5, 2021, Complainant learned he was not selected for the position of Program Specialist, Vacancy Announcement Number: CBSY-11140287-21-MJP. Complainant believed that his qualifications and history, including two masters’ degrees, military veteran status, previous employment with the Agency, and volunteer experience with a Community-Based Outpatient Clinic made him the superior candidate and that did not have his application appropriately considered. ROI at 38. The Human Resource (HR) Specialist stated that Complainant was qualified based on his veteran status and his information was forwarded to the Chief of Health Administration Service (Chief) on the Veterans Certificate list. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 49. The Chief was the selecting official for the position. The Chief made the selection for the position from an internal facility certification list. ROI at 43. The Chief verified with the HR Department that it was acceptable that she conducted interviews off the internal facility list first before moving onto additional certification lists. ROI at 42. The Chief stated that the Selectee was on the internal list and was chosen based on her extensive history of Community Care experience as an entry level Medical Support Assistant (MSA), a lead MSA, and a MSA Supervisor in Community Care. ROI at 43. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Complainant did not provide an appellate brief.

During the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Building Maintenance Custodian at the Oil City Post Office in Oil City, Pennsylvania. On August 30, 2022, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency unlawfully retaliated against him for engaging in prior protected activity when: 1. On or around April 29, 2022, he was issued a 14-Day Suspension. 2. On May 10, 2022, when Complainant was on approved annual leave, he became aware that management had asked the police to come to his home to perform a “welfare check. 3. On June 22, 2022, he was given an Investigative Interview. 4. On or around August 25, 2022, a form was created concerning cleaning duties that only he was required to fill out 5. On August 31, 2022, he was issued a Notice of Removal. 6. On or about October 3, 2022, the Postmaster told a prospective employer that he was banned from any USPS property, which kept him from getting the job. After its investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of the investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). The Agency determined that Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f). Therefore, the Agency issued a final decision, pursuant to 29 § 1614.110(b), finding no unlawful retaliation was established. The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant states that he received the Agency’s final decision on February 10, 2023. Complainant states that he noticed that the final decision indicated that on December 5, 2022, he had been sent a copy of the report of investigation and that the Agency determined that Complainant neither requested a hearing nor an Agency final decision. Complainant argues, however, that he had never received this document. Complainant therefore requests that he be allowed to proceed with the case by having an EEOC Administrative Judge adjudicate the matter.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Parcel Post Distribution Machine Operator at the Grand Rapids Processing and Distribution Center in Grand Rapids, Michigan. She was directly supervised by Supervisor of Distribution Operations (SDO). On November 3, 2022, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her in reprisal for protected EEO activity under Title VII when on June 19, 2022, she was removed from the building. The investigative record revealed that Complainant volunteered to work on June 19, 2022. She clocked in at 6:30 p.m. for the start of her shift. At 7:00 p.m., SDO conducted a sweep of the parking lot and saw Complainant in her car chatting on the phone with her shoes off. SDO questioned Complainant why she was not working in the building and told her that: 1) he would not approve the first half hour of her pay if she had not been working; and 2) she should go home if she did not intend to return to the building. SDO recalled that Complainant responded by swearing at him. Later, when Supervisor attempted to locate Complainant, he could not find Complainant anywhere in the building or the parking lot. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 60. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation (ROI) and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), which concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination or harassment as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

During the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Program Liaison Specialist at the Agency’s External Affairs Office in Washington, D.C. Complainant was a reservist employee with temporary/intermittent status. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 290. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 260, 262. After Complainant grew concerned about the manner in which the Agency provided assistive communication services to the public, she raised her concerns with management. During the relevant time, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Mail Processing Clerk in Birmingham, Alabama. 1. On or around September 19, 2022, management refused to schedule orientation around her physical therapy appointments. 2. Since her return to work on or around September 19, 2022 and continuing, Complainant has not been accommodated with a 5-pound lifting restriction and day shift work. 3.
