At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Claims Technical Expert (CTE), GS-0105-12, at the Agency’s Great Lakes Program Service Center in Chicago, Illinois. Complainant received a reprimand on July 20, 2021, for conduct unbecoming a federal employee. The reprimand cited two specifications: on June 16, 2021, Complainant refused to provide a status update on assigned cases, raised her voice, and continued to refuse during a subsequent meeting; and on June 23, 2021, she refused assistance with a mainframe password issue, leading to a two-hour work delay. Complainant’s first-line supervisor, Module Manager (S1), asserted that requesting status updates and assisting with password issues were common management practices. Complainant also claimed workplace harassment, alleging that S1 assigned duties preventing her from completing primary CTE tasks and treated her differently from other CTEs. She complained of accusatory, condescending, and rude communication. Complainant alleged that the reprimand itself constituted harassment, tarnishing her character, and that the issuance of a 3. Performance Assessment Communications Systems (PACS) rating for Fiscal Year 2021, lower than a prior 4. PAC rating in Fiscal Year 2019, was harassment. Complainant reported these concerns to the union and management. S1 denied the allegations explaining that work assignments aligned with the week's plan and that management routinely assisted employees with password issues. S1 denied claims of harassment in assigning duties and asserted that the reprimand and rating were issued in line with standard practices. On November 11, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her and subjected her to a hostile work environment on the bases of race (African-American), sex (female), color (Black), age (63), and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when: 1. On July 20, 2021, she received a reprimand; and 2. Beginning June 23, 2021 and present, with regard to work assignments, assignment of duties, condescending comments, spoken to in a loud voice, lowered PACS, reprimand, and questioning time to work on inquiries. 2 At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). In the decision, the Agency determined that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination or reprisal as alleged. The Agency dismissed an additional allegation as untimely raised with an EEO Counselor. Complainant raised no challenges regarding this matter on appeal and the Commission can find no basis to disturb the Agency’s dismissal decision. The Commission will, however, consider the claim as background evidence in support of Complainant’s hostile work environment claim.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a non-career City Carrier Assistant, Q-01, at the Uptown Station in New Orleans, Louisiana. The record reveals that on August 9, 2022, Complainant filed her complaint alleging discrimination based on race (Black/African American) and sex (female) when on May 18, 2022, she was terminated during her probationary period. The record indicates that on April 9, 2022, Complainant started her position subject to a 90-day probationary period. On May 13, 2022, Complainant was issued a Letter of Separation during her probationary period, in part, due to her unsafe work performance/accident on May 10, 2022. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at Exhibit 11. Complainant’s supervisor (S1), Supervisory Customer Services, EAS-17, indicated that Complainant was terminated during her probationary period because on May 10, 2022, she had an at fault Postal vehicle accident. Complainant’s manager (M1), Manager Customer Services, EAS-21, stated that on May 10, 2022, Complainant was assigned to three hours delivery on route 1547, but before she could complete her delivery, she side swiped a FedEx truck and totaled a Postal vehicle. Complainant claimed that she was treated differently than two other employees (E1 - African American, male, and E2 – White, female) who also had a car accident during their probationary period but were not terminated. M1 indicated that E1 tapped the side mirror of her vehicle, it had to be mounted back on, and there was no damage to a Postal vehicle. See ROI at Affidavit C, Page 5. M1 also indicated that there was no accident record of E2 at the Uptown Station. S1 indicated that she was not aware of E2’s accident. See ROI at Affidavit B, Page 65. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge or a final Agency decision. When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination. Further, the Agency articulated a nondiscriminatory reason for its action of which Complainant failed to show was pretext for discrimination. Complainant appeals from the Agency’s final decision.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a General Expeditor at the Agency’s Processing and Distribution Center in Duncansville, Pennsylvania. On January 13, 2022, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint, claiming that the Agency discriminated against her based on sex (female), age (48 years old at the time of the alleged incidents), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (grievances alleging a hostile work environment and the instant complaint). By letter dated February 3, 2022, the Agency accepted Complainant’s complaint for investigation and determined that it was comprised of the following claims: 1. On September 30, 2021, [Complainant was] placed on Emergency Placement; and 2. On or around October 14, 2021, [she was] issued a Seven-Day Suspension. After an investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of the right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. On January 31, 2023, the EEOC AJ issued an Order of Dismissal. Therein, the AJ dismissed the hearing based on Complainant’s request and remanded the matter to the Agency for a final decision. The Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination or unlawful retaliation. The Agency found that assuming arguendo that Complainant established a prima facie case of discrimination and/or retaliation, the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. Regarding Complainant being placed on Emergency Placement, the Agency found that management asserted that Complainant became argumentative and yelled after being given a work instruction. Final Agency Decision (FAD) at 18. Regarding Complainant being issued a suspension, the Agency found that management asserted that Complainant initially refused to leave the building after being placed on Emergency Placement and the police were called. FAD at 19, The Agency further found that Complainant failed to establish that the Agency’s articulated reasons for its actions were pretext for discrimination and/or retaliation. FAD at 22-23. The instant appeal from Complainant followed. In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision.

Complainant previously worked as a GS-6 Advanced Medical Support Assistant at the Agency’s Medical Center facility in Durham, North Carolina, from 2009 to 2017. Complainant retired from the Agency in July 2017. In 2018, Complainant began submitting applications for reemployment. Complainant stated that she applied on July 3, 2020, for a full-time Medical Support Assistant position in Emporia, Virginia. 2 20023000401 Complainant stated that on September 28, 2020, she was informed by the Supervisory Human Resources Specialist (SHRS), that she was not selected for the position of Medical Support Assistant under Vacancy Announcement Number 10855529-20FLM. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 216-218. Twenty-four applicants were deemed eligible for the position of Medical Support Assistant under Vacancy Announcement Number 10855529-20FLM. ROI at 250-251. Complainant’s name was not on the list of eligible applicants for the position. Seven applicants were interviewed. Three applicants declined the interview or did not answer the calls for the interview. ROI at 297-298. Five applicants were selected for the position of Medical Support Assistant under Vacancy Announcement Number 10855529-20FLM. ROI at 220. There were multiple locations in the vacancy announcement, but Complainant only applied for the Emporia location. The Agency determined that no candidates would be forwarded to the Emporia facility. ROI at 269-270 On March 30, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when, on September 28, 2020, Complainant was not selected for the position of Medical Support Assistant under Vacancy Announcement Number 10855529-20FLM. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a final decision from the Agency. 2

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant was an applicant for employment at the Agency. The record indicates that on March 3, 2023, Complainant contacted an EEO Counselor alleging discrimination when he was not offered a job under vacancy announcement number FAA-ATO- 21-ALLSRCE-73599. Unable to resolve the matter informally, Complainant filed the instant complaint on April 22, 2023. In his complaint, Complainant alleged discrimination based on race (White), color (white), and sex (male) when: On or around February 6, 2023, he became aware that management did not select him for an Air Traffic Controller (ATC) position advertised under vacancy announcement number FAA-ATO-21-ALLSRCE-73599. The Agency investigated the complaint and at the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant a copy of the report of investigation and a notice of his right to request a hearing before an AJ. 29 C.F.R. §1614.108(f). Complainant requested a hearing. The Agency filed a motion to dismiss the complaint stating that Complainant failed to timely contact an EEO Counselor pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(2). The Agency indicated that on July 30, 2021, Complainant submitted his application for the ATC position at issue, FG-3, a temporary not-to- exceed 13-month appointment, via Agency’s “AVIATOR” online application system. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 349. The Agency also indicated that Complainant received AVIATOR Application Status Message of his nonselection for the position on February 9, 2022. ROI at 358. The Agency stated that Complainant contacted an EEO Counselor regarding the nonselection on March 3, 2023, which was beyond the 45-day time limit set by the regulations. On February 4, 2024, the AJ issued an Order of Dismissal dismissing the complaint due to untimely EEO Counselor contact. The AJ stated that Complainant argued that he applied for other ATC positions but was not selected in 2015 and 2016. The AJ also stated that Complainant indicated that in January 2023, he learned that he was selected for an Alaska Flight Service position in Alaska for which he applied but it was an undesirable position and this selection and his prior nonselections triggered his suspicion of discrimination about the nonselection for the ATC position at issue, including prior nonselections. The AJ stated that Complainant knew or reasonably should have suspected discrimination concerning the nonselections at the time he learned of those nonselections, including the February 9, 2022 nonselection, and not when he was offered an Alaska Flight Service position that he found undesirable. The AJ granted the Agency’s motion to dismiss and found Complainant failed to timely contact an EEO Counselor regarding the complaint and Complainant failed to provide sufficient justification to extend or toll the time limit. The Agency issued a final order implementing the AJ’s decision. Complainant appeals from the Agency’s final order.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Senior Officer Specialist, Grade GS-8, at the Agency’s Metropolitan Detention Center in Los Angeles, California. According to his answers to EEO interrogatories, on November 17, 2022, Complainant was on duty at his post in the Control Room. His co-worker, CO1, though assigned to the Front Lobby, was in the Control Room to eat dinner. Another co-worker, CO2, who was assigned to the Control Room was also present. When the relief supervisor arrived in the Front Lobby, the relief supervisor found that CO1 was not at his post. CO1 assailed Complainant for failing to warn him about the relief supervisor’s presence. According to Complainant, CO1 said words to the effect that “I should have known not to trust a queer to watch my back.” (Complainant said that CO1 had previously made anti- LGBTQ+ comments to him in the past, but Complainant had ignored these.) CO1 then went to the Front Lobby to assist the relief supervisor with checking- in to the facility. Thereafter, Complainant stated that CO1 came back to the Control Room and CO1 called Complainant “fucking faggot, fucking homo, and gay motherfucker.” According to Complainant, CO2 laughed and repeated CO1’s insults. Complainant stated that he asked CO1 to leave the Control Room, but CO1 refused. Complainant said he called their supervisor, LT1, and reported CO1’s unauthorized presence in the Control Room. LT1 instructed Complainant to send CO1 to his office. Complainant relayed LT1’s message to CO1. Complainant stated that, at this point, CO1 called Complainant a snitch and said: "Meet me on the 7th floor of the parking structure, I'm going to handle you." Complainant claims that, before CO1 left the Control Room, CO1 delivered a karate-chop blow to Complainant’s neck. Complainant described the strike as painful and causing him to step back in order to maintain his balance. Complainant called the supervisor’s office and reported that CO1 had struck him. LT1 then went to the Front Lobby to talk to CO1 while a second supervisor, LT2, came to the Control Room where LT2 observed some redness on Complainant’s neck and took pictures thereof. Complainant said that the supervisors who interviewed him after CO1 had struck him advised Complainant to avoid leaving the facility at the same time as CO1. LT1 reported the matter to his supervisor (CAPT). On the following day, a Threat Assessment Committee was convened to address the matter. Following the Threat Assessment Committee, Complainant claimed that the Agency took no corrective action and noted that CO1 remained in the same position and shift. Complainant stated that he feared CO1 if he returned to work. Complainant accused management of sharing CO1’s anti-LGBTQ+ attitude and of retaliating against him for “rocking the boat” by complaining about discrimination in the workplace. On November 23, 2022, Complainant went to the Los Angeles police to pursue a restraining order against CO1. A Los Angeles police officer contacted CAPT who would not discuss the assault because it was under investigation. Thereafter, the Los Angeles police declined to investigate the Complainant’s report of assault further because it was deemed a matter of federal jurisdiction. Complainant ceased returning to work after November 23, 2022. Complainant filed a workers compensation claim for injuries from the assault that occurred on November 17, 2022. As a part of his request for sick leave, Complainant provided notes from his medical providers excusing his absence from work between November 30, 2022, and January 10, 2023. On December 29, 2022, Complainant initiated contact with the Agency’s EEO Counselor. In an email exchange dated January 2, 2023, Complainant and CAPT discussed covering Complainant’s absence with Continuation of Pay (COP) benefits. Complainant stated his understanding that until his worker's compensation claim had officially been approved, he would not be covered by COP benefits. Complainant stated he would use his sick leave balance and then his vacation or annual leave to cover his absence. On January 9, 2023, the Office of Workers Compensation Programs (OWCP) rendered an initial denial of Complainant’s workers’ compensation claim. Following OWCP’s denial, Complainant was paid COP benefits and he uses annual or sick leave to cover his initial absences. On February 9, 2023, CAPT requested Complainant update his status and provide updated medical documentation. CAPT further advised Complainant that he had just 39. hours of leave left and, after he exhausted that leave, the Agency would code him as being AWOL. In the evening of March 2, 2023, CAPT emailed Complainant that he had not been in contact with the Agency since January 2, 2023. CAPT stated the Agency had failed to reach Complainant for an update on his status. CAPT informed Complainant that he was being coded as AWOL because he had exhausted his leave. CAPT said that he would request local police conduct a welfare check unless Complainant responded by the next day. In the morning of March 3, 2023, local police from Complainant’s home of residence conducted the welfare check. Complainant complained that he had not seen the CAPT’s message because it was emailed the night before. Complainant further alleged that the local police officers told him that CAPT had stated that Complainant was “psychologically unstable.” On March 27, 2023, April 13, 2023, and May 15, 2023, the Human Resources Manager (HRM) sent letters to Complainant and his medical provider which indicated that Complainant had a medical condition that might affect his ability to safely perform his job. HRM requested clarifying medical information to assess Complainant’s ability to perform his essential duties. HRM asked Complainant to have his medical provider complete a requested medical assessment within fourteen days. On August 3, 2023, OWCP granted Complainant’s appeal of its denial of his workers compensation claim, and OWCP accepted his workers compensation claim for the traumatic injury that he sustained at work on November 17, 2022. As a result, Complainant’s AWOL was recoded to leave without pay (LWOP). On April 10, 2023, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him. The Agency framed Complainant’s claims as follows: 1. The Agency is liable for subjecting Complainant to a hostile work environment based on sexual orientation (bisexual) when, as he alleged, on November 17, 2022, CO1 shouted at him, threatened him, struck him in the throat, and used homophobic slurs, and another co-worker repeated the homophobic slurs and laughed; and In Bostock v. Clayton Cty., the Supreme Court held that discrimination based on sexual orientation or transgender status is prohibited under Title VII. 590 U.S. 644, 140 S. Ct. 1731 (2020); see also Macy v. Dep’t of Justice, EEOC [number removed] (Apr. 20, 2012) (an allegation of discrimination based on gender identity, change of sex, and/or transgender status states a claim of sex discrimination under Title VII because discrimination on this basis is inherently sex-based). 2. Whether, between November 17, 2022, and April 10, 2023, the Agency subjected Complainant to disparate treatment based on reprisal when, as he alleged, management denied him continuation of pay (COP) benefits, coded him as being absent without leave (AWOL), conducted a welfare check, and requested additional medical documentation. At the conclusion of the initial investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). The Agency’s initial report of investigation included Complainant’s sworn statement, as discussed above, and those of CAPT and HRM. CAPT stated that following the incident, he reassigned CO2 from the control room because he had allowed CO1’s presence when only CO2 and Complainant were authorized to be there. CAPT further said that CO1 and CO2 were issued letters reminding them to be professional to fellow staff. CAPT surmised that Complainant was not issued a similar letter because he absented himself from work. CAPT testified that the Threat Assessment Committee generated a report which concluded that Complainant’s assault allegation could not be substantiated. CAPT stated that he did remember homophobic slurs being mentioned in the Threat Assessment Committee’s report. He further indicated that the Threat Assessment Committee’s report consisted of memos submitted by the witnesses and notes taken by the officials regarding the witnesses’ live testimony. CAPT stated that the Threat Assessment Committee interviewed Complainant, CO1, CO2, LT1 and LT2. He could not recall whether there were pictures taken after the incident. He said there were no cameras in the Control Center, so there was no video available of the incident. CAPT referred the investigator to Human Resources for documentation from the Threat Assessment Committee. CAPT further explained that health and welfare checks were conducted whenever staff did not come to work and had not called in sick. HRM stated that his subordinate employee who served as Acting HRM convened the Threat Assessment Committee. HRM stated that he had no involvement with the Threat Assessment Committee and that Acting HRM possessed the documentation from the Threat Assessment Committee. HRM denied knowing of Complainant’s EEO activity until September 2023, after the incidents he alleged to be retaliatory had occurred. HRM stated that Complainant was denied COP pay because OWCP initially denied his workers compensation claim. HRM stated that Office of Personnel Management (OPM) rules compelled the Agency to code Complainant as AWOL because he remained absent and had no available leave to cover his absence. Furthermore, HRM stated that although Complainant was coded AWOL, his absence was ultimately recoded to LWOP such that Complainant was never actually charged for being AWOL. HRM stated that the welfare check was standard procedure and that Complainant, rather than being harassed by the local police welfare check, thanked the Agency for checking on him. HRM explained that he had requested medical information from Complainant and his provider because of Complainant’s continued absence and non-responsiveness to communications with the Agency. In a supplemental report of investigation, the Agency included statements from CO1, CO2, LT1 and LT2. CO1 admitted that he was in Control Room on November 17, 2022, and not at his assigned post in the Front Lobby but stated he was there to legitimately discuss appropriate matters with CO2. CO1 stated that he was merely joking with Complainant about "throwing him under the bus" by letting the relief lieutenant into the Front Lobby without giving him warning. CO1 denied knowledge of Complainant’s sexual orientation. CO1 denied saying "queer, fucking faggot, fucking homo, or gay motherfucker" to Complainant. CO1 claimed that he did not make threatening statements against Complainant. When LT1 interviewed him about what transpired on November 17, 2022, he counter-accused Complainant of being the aggressor by barking orders to leave the Control Room and pointing in CO1’s face and chest area. CO1 memorialized his account of the incident in a contemporaneous memorandum to LT1. CO2 claimed that he was unaware of Complainant’s sexual orientation. CO2 said he had been in the restroom and heard Complainant and CO1 yelling on November 17, 2022. He said that by the time he returned to the Control Room, the yelling between CO1 and Complainant had stopped. CO2 denied hearing that CO1 used anti-LGBTQ+ slurs or that he witnessed CO1 hit Complainant in the neck. CO2 disputed that he told Complainant that he did not want to get involved or indicated that he planned to write a false statement saying that he did not see anything. LT1 denied knowledge of Complainant’s sexual orientation. LT1 stated that he had instructed CO1 to report to his office after Complainant had reported that CO1 was refusing to leave the Control Room. LT1 stated Complainant called back and accused CO1 of striking him. LT1 then questioned CO1 in the Front Lobby. LT1 stated that Complainant did not report to him that CO1 had made anti-LGBTQ+ comments. LT1 directed CO1 to document his version of events in a memo. LT2 said that Complainant had called LT1 to report CO1 for not leaving the Control Room. LT2 said he answered the call when Complainant called back to report that he had been struck in the throat by CO1. LT2 said he found CO1 away from his post and instructed him to return to the Front Lobby. LT2 stated that he went to the Control Room where Complainant again told him about CO1 hitting him in the throat. LT2 stated that he observed some redness on Complainant’s neck area and that LT2 took pictures as a result. LT2 denied that Complainant had said anything about being called anti- LGBTQ+ terms. According to LT2, Complainant had only said that he and CO1 had a verbal confrontation that became physical over Complainant asking CO1 to leave the Control Room. LT2 denied knowing Complainant’s sexual orientation. In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final Agency decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). Regarding Claim 1, the Agency held that because Complainant did not initially report the anti-LGBTQ+ comments prior to his EEO Counselor contact, evidence was insufficient to establish that the harassment was based on Complainant’s sexual orientation. Regarding Claim 2, the Agency determined that Complainant failed to establish retaliatory animus. The final Agency decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Lieutenant at the Agency’s Federal Detention Center in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (FDC Philadelphia). At the relevant time, a Captain (Caucasian/White) was Complainant’s direct supervisor 2 and his second-level manager who was the Associate Warden (Caucasian/White) of FDC Philadelphia. On June 13, 2016, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race/color (African American/Black), and in reprisal for EEO-protected activity when: 1. On March 15, 2016, Complainant was reassigned out of Special Investigative Services (SIS); 2. On March 19, 2016 and March 22, 2016, Complainant was placed on Absent Without Official Leave (AWOL) status; 3. On April 30, 2016, his supervisor failed to train Complainant with additional use of force hands-on training; 4. On May 4, 2016, Complainant became aware that his supervisor gave him an unfavorable reference check, causing Complainant not to be selected for the position of Deputy Captain at Metropolitan Detention Center (MDC) Brooklyn; 5. On May 6, 2016, Complainant’s supervisor failed to provide Complainant with a timely yearly performance evaluation; 6. On August 1, 2016, Complainant was issued a written reprimand; Later, the Captain was promoted to the position of Associate Warden at another facility. 7. On August 25th, 2016, Complainant’s supervisor assigned Complainant to three consecutive quarters of sick and annual work schedule; and 8. On December 19, 2016, and December 20, 2016, Complainant was placed on AWOL status; and 9. From December 21, 2015 through October 23, 2017, Complainant was denied the opportunity to serve in a temporary position of acting captain or deputy captain during his supervisor’s absences. After an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The Agency, in its brief submitted on appeal, concedes that its report of investigation should have been provided to Complainant “on or before May 1, 2017” at the latest, even with an extension that was granted by Complainant. However, the report of investigation was not completed and provided to Complainant until November 29, 2017, seven months later and 538 days after Complainant filed his complaint. Complainant filed a motion for sanctions with the AJ based on the delay in receiving the report of investigation, noting that the Agency did not even begin the investigation until January 20, 2017, 225 days after the complaint was initially filed. Complainant argued that the unreasonable delays had significantly prejudiced his ability to prove his case because, among other things, key witnesses had difficulty remembering important details about the case due to the long hiatus between the filing of his complaint and their interviews by the investigator. In response, the Agency conceded that it had failed to meet the regulatory time frame for completing the investigation in this matter. The Agency explained that “the delay was caused by a backlog of cases in its EEO Office, created in large part by financial and administrative processes outside the Agency’s control.” In a decision dated December 16, 2019, the AJ sanctioned the Agency with a default judgement in Complaint’s favor. The AJ found that the Agency, without good cause, failed to complete the investigation within the required timeframe and failed to provide Complainant with its report of investigation within the required timeframe. The AJ further found, however, that the record did not support a finding that Complainant was not selected for promotion at MDC Brooklyn because of the negative reference from Complainant’s supervisor (claim 4). Nevertheless, the AJ found that, over approximately two years, the supervisor had created a hostile work environment based on Complainant’s race (African American) and in reprisal for Complainant’s EEO-protected activity. Specifically, Complainant had complained to the Associate Warden about his supervisor mistreating him and about how his supervisor had assigned duties in a manner that disadvantaged African American lieutenants. On July 8 and 13, 2020, the AJ held hearings on damages. On September 9, 2020, the AJ rendered a decision on damages. The AJ ordered the Agency to: to pay Complainant $85,000 in compensatory damages; conduct anti- discrimination training of management officials at FDC Philadelphia and Complainant's former supervisor (who the Agency had promoted to Associate Warden at another institution); to post a notice at FDC Philadelphia regarding the finding of discrimination for a two-year period; to reimburse Complainant with 40 hours of annual leave and to offer Complainant SIS training. In a separate decision, the AJ also ordered the Agency pay $94,235 for Complainant’s attorney’s fees and costs. The Agency subsequently issued a final order rejecting the AJ’s discrimination finding.

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Rubber Worker, WG-4301-09, at the Agency’s Red River Army Depot in Texarkana, Texas. On October 3, 2019, the Chief, Product Assurance Division (Caucasian/white), did not select Complainant for a competitive temporary promotion as a Rubber Inspector, WG-4301-10, position in the Support Inspection Section under Announcement Number: SWDX199933130176. On October 10, 2019, Complainant initiated contact with an EEO Counselor. The parties were unable to resolve the matter through informal EEO counseling. On March 3, 2020, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him based on race (African-American) and color (Black) when: On October 3, 2019, the Chief, Product Assurance Division, non- selected Complainant for a competitive temporary promotion as a Rubber Inspector, WG-4301-10, position in Support Inspection Section under Announcement Number: SWDX199933130176. After an investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). The report of investigation contained email correspondence between the EEO investigator and Complainant’s work email address (address ended in “civ.mil”). Complainant requested a hearing. On January 28, 2021, the AJ issued an Acknowledgment Order requiring a preliminary case information (PCI) report from the parties within 15 days of receipt of the order. The Agency timely filed a PCI. Complainant did not respond. On February 24, 2021, the AJ issued an Order to Show Cause and Intent to Sanction Complainant for failure to comply with the Acknowledgement Order. Complainant did not respond. On April 1, 2022, the AJ issued a second Show Cause and Intent to Sanction stating that unless Complainant established good cause for his failure to submit a PCI, his request for hearing would be dismissed. Complainant did not respond. On April 20, 2022, the AJ issued a Sanction and Dismissal Order for Complainant’s failure, without good cause shown, to fully comply with the acknowledgement order and the two show cause orders. The AJ noted that the show cause order, as well as the Acknowledgement Order, had been served on Complainant’s work email account (ending in “civ.mil”). AJ presumed Complainant had received the three orders, because no messages had been returned from the email address for Complainant which had been provided to the AJ from the Agency’s report of investigation. The AJ remanded the complaint to the Agency for issuance of a final decision, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), based on the evidence developed during its investigation of the complaint. The final Agency decision found no discrimination had been established as alleged. Complainant appealed.2

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Purchasing Agent at the Agency’s VA Medical Center in Decatur, Georgia. On August 12, 2020, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the basis of disability (anxiety; depression) when: 1. On June 2 and 3, 2020, Complainant was questioned about the leave she had taken under the Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA) and 2. On June 2, 3, and 24, 2020, Complainant was charged Absent Without Leave (AWOL). 2 Complainant stated that she has major depression and anxiety. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 66. She asserted that on June 3, 2020, her Supervisor questioned her about her FMLA leave which she asserted was “targeting” her due to her disability by marking her AWOL even though she was on FMLA leave. See ROI at 68. She acknowledged that after she told them about her FMLA leave, the Chief told her that the AWOL would be removed. See ROI at 69. The Supervisory Purchasing Agent (Supervisor) stated that the Chief of Prosthetics had him reach out to Complainant to clarify the situation with Complainant’s leave because HR had only provided the FMLA paperwork for January to February 2020 when it was requested. See ROI at 144-45. He asserted that once Complainant had verified that she had approved FMLA leave, her AWOL was removed. See ROI at 147. The Assistant Chief of Prosthetics (Assistant Chief) confirmed that Complainant was never officially marked AWOL and once her FMLA was verified, he instructed the timekeeper to enter in Complainant’s time as FMLA as required. See ROI at 124-25. Complainant’s time sheet records confirm that Complainant was not actually marked AWOL on the dates at issue. See ROI at 157. The Agency’s acceptance letter erroneously listed only June 24, 2020 as the date on which Complainant alleged she was charged AWOL but the investigation was later clarified at Complainant’s request to include June 2 and 3, 2020. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 31-36. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. On May 16, 2022, the Agency filed a motion for a decision without a hearing to which Complainant did not respond. The AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s motion and issued a decision without a hearing on June 16, 2022. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.
